News.title: Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month.

He said "deeper cooperation" on some key issues - including youth mobility, food and drink, and energy - would help drive economic growth in the UK.

In a statement to MPs, Burnham also warned the EU's Made In Europe plans posed "a risk to UK manufacturing" and said he was in talks to get "an arrangement" that worked for the UK. The EU proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors but could impact British industry and supply chains.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.

Although he said he was keen to negotiate a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham made clear Labour's manifesto commitments not to return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement, would stay in place until the next election.

Burnham said the "immediate priority" was securing a successful outcome at the November summit, adding: "I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.

"At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting."

While the prime minister has committed to the current Labour manifesto's red lines about Brexit, in interviews after Labour conference, he did not rule out a new manifesto, which could include re-joining the EU.

It is increasingly clear that economic growth, and cooperation on illegal immigration, are going to be at the centre of No 10's arguments when it comes to selling a closer relationship both at - and beyond - next month's summit.

The Brexit withdrawal agreement in 2020 agreed the UK's "divorce bill" payments to the EU, and allowed the rules and regulations in the UK to start to diverge from those in the EU, which was necessary in order to negotiate trade deal with other countries.

But the divergence in food standards caused problems for UK food exports to its largest market, a problem that Sir Keir Starmer started to try to fix by renegotiating some common rules to reduce red tape.

In May 2025, this resulted in a post-Brexit deal agreeing continued access to UK waters for EU fishing boats until 2038, in return for a deal to reduce checks on food exports to the EU, which meant the UK was able to sell raw burgers and sausages back into the EU for the first time since Brexit.

The summit next month will see a series of deals with the EU on the table, Burnham told MPs, including food and drink, energy trading, and coordinating on immigration.

Burnham claimed these agreements could add the equivalent of Â£10bn per year to the economy by 2040, arguing that it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn away from the chance to cut bureaucracy.

"At present entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay," he said.

"Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around Â£100m in lost exports.

"British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU, seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned - this is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage."

The prime minister said a fresh agreement at the EU summit would also "ease the pressure on prices in the supermarket".

He said securing an energy deal, involving emissions trading, could "lower energy costs for households and businesses alike", adding this could cut wholesale energy costs by 20% in Northern Ireland.

Burnham said he also hoped to rebuild links with EU police and security agencies to boost information-sharing and help tackle smuggling gangs.

And he said being open about a new relationship with the EU was necessary to get a good deal on all these things: "If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.

"Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain."

News.title: Government expands police support to political figures who are not MPs
News.content:
Political figures who are not currently MPs will be given police support, the home secretary has announced.

Shabana Mahmood told MPs there was "insufficient protection" for those serving in public life and that the new announcement will cover peers, former MPs and party spokespeople.

She also announced an urgent, independent review of security arrangements for high-profile figures including politicians and royals.

It comes three months after Reform UK spokeswoman and former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon, having been hit on the head with a hammer 21 times as she ate lunch.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder, and he was also charged with preparing acts of terror against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Kerry is alleged to have carried out research on prominent targets over a period of two years, including trying to gain entry into Farage's London home.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Mahmood said that "robust debate and criticism are part of this job - threats, abuse and violence are not."

She did not elaborate on what the support would involve, but told MPs it would include access to a named police officer and help with wider security measures.

The safety of politicians has been a prominent issue in recent years, following the murders of Conservative MP Sir David Amess in 2021 and Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016.

"We owe it to them and to everyone who believes in a fair and open country to ensure that those who serve at all levels receive the protection they deserve," Mahmood added.

The "root and branch" independent review into security arrangements will be led by former national security advisor Stephen Lovegrove, and will look into "physical threats, online risks and the dangers posed within our more polarised society".

Mahmood confirmed that the review will report within six months, and build on the existing work of Sir Robert Buckland, who is leading a separate review into the murder of Sir David.

In response, shadow home secretary Chris Philp welcomed the extension of protective measures, saying threats to elected representatives are threats to democracy.

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf welcomed the review, but added: "It is disappointing that it took the murder of one of our colleagues, countless threats towards our party spokespeople and months of campaigning from Reform UK to make this government take action".

Reform has in recent months accused the government of a "dereliction of duty" over Farage's taxpayer-funded security, claiming it had previously been "downgraded" - a charge that the Home Office has said is "categorically untrue".

Decisions over the security of current MPs and members of the House of Lords are made by the House of Parliament's security team.

There is a separate, independent committee, the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (Ravec), to deal with high-profile political candidates, which is staffed by officials from the Home Office, the Cabinet Office, and the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

The Jo Cox Foundation welcomed the home secretary's announcement but said "strengthening physical security" alone was not enough.

"We must also tackle the root causes - including online harms and education - to prevent future attacks," its chief executive Olivia Field said in a statement on X.

According to data released to the BBC in April, the number of alleged offences against MPs have increased year-on-year, with 976 recorded in 2025, compared to 364 in 2019.

MPs reported 4,064 crimes to the Met's Parliamentary Liaison Team between 2019 and 2025. Most offences were related to malicious communications followed by harassment, and criminal damage to a building.

In 2025, there were 50 death threats reported - up from 31 the previous year.

News.title: Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire mean for Ukraine?
News.content:
US President Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that an energy ceasefire had been reached between Ukraine and Russia that was "effective immediately".

Ukraine's President Zelensky responded by saying his country is willing to back an energy ceasefire if Russia does the same, adding it could "become a major step toward ending the war".

However, Moscow hasn't confirmed its agreement and Zelensky said Russia hit a Ukrainian power plant in Kharkiv "immediately after" Trump's post over the weekend.

The BBC's Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians are facing another winter with electricity outages that leave people without heat, light or even water.

News.title: Abramovich's close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest
News.content:
One of Roman Abramovich's closest associates misled a UK court to help secure ownership of Siberian oil fields, leaked documents seen by the BBC suggest.

Eugene Tenenbaum, a former director of Chelsea Football Club, helped to manage the billionaire's wealth at the time of the case in 2008, which Abramovich won.

Tenenbaum was giving evidence during proceedings taken against Abramovich by a company owned by another Russian billionaire, who was claiming the oil fields had been stolen from him and other investors.

The leaked documents now suggest there was a premeditated attempt by Abramovich to reduce the value of the other investors' stake in the Siberian venture.

Roman Abramovich's lawyers say their "client denies all the allegations made against him".

Lawyers for Eugene Tenenbaum say he "denies in the strongest terms any suggestion that he committed perjury or contempt of court".

The 2008 court case centred on the ownership of Siberian oil fields being developed jointly between Abramovich's company, Sibneft, and the Russian subsidiary of the British company, Sibir Energy PLC, owned by Russian billionaire Chalva Tchigirinsky.

Sibneft contributed money, while the subsidiary Yugraneft provided the licences for the oil fields.

Their partnership - which became known as Sibneft-Yugra - ended acrimoniously.

Sibir's 50% interest in the joint venture had been diluted, or reduced, to less than 1%. It said this had been done without its knowledge.

Unsuccessful attempts to sue Sibneft in both Russia and the British Virgin Islands led to the court proceedings in London.

At court in 2008, Yugraneft claimed "to have been the victim of a massive fraud directed by Mr Abramovich", as a result of which it had suffered a loss of "not less that $2 billion", which in 2008 was worth about Â£1bn.

But Abramovich's team claimed that Yugraneft had been unable to repay loans of more than $30m, so lost its right over the shares.

News.title: On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
News.content:
It was a journey at high speed through the desert - in a pick-up truck with armed fighters in the back. We were travelling with Yemen's pro-government forces, catching glimpses of the Arabian Sea, and forbidding mountain peaks in the distance. Houthi rebels were dislodged from here just days ago, we were told.

When you are battling over expanses of empty desert, progress can be hard to see. But these soldiers, in Shaab-al-Jinn in Lahj governorate, showed us new sandbagged defences - new lines in the sand.

"There was heavy fighting," said Tawfiq Al Haboun, a bearded commander in camouflage uniform.

"They have snipers, artillery and ballistic missile launchers."

Here in the far corners of the Middle East, a war is being waged with global implications.

Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. It's part of wider conflict, stretching from Tehran to Riyadh, where missiles slammed into the international airport this weekend. Yemen's Houthi fighters â already a threat to global shipping â are an increasing threat to Saudi Arabia. And they provide leverage for their backers in Iran, Saudi's regional rival.

Tawfiq Al Haboun pointed to shards of fibre glass and bits of metal at his feet â part of a downed Houthi drone that he said was carrying C4 explosives.

Commander Al Haboun is from the Southern Forces, part of the loose â very loose â alliance of groups fighting for Yemen's government, which is internationally recognised, and backed by Saudi Arabia and its air strikes.

The Houthis swept into the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, ousting the government. A year later a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened, trying to dislodge the Houthis. Despite years of devastating air strikes, that hasn't worked.

News.title: US actress Selma Blair arrested after allegedly attacking attendants on flight
News.content:
US actress Selma Blair has been arrested and taken to hospital after authorities say she attacked two flight attendants on a flight.

Airport officials said they responded to a call on Sunday about "a physically abusive passenger" on a Delta Airlines flight travelling from Los Angeles to New York. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.

The 54-year-old actress, known most famously for her roles in Legally Blonde, Hellboy and Cruel Intentions, was taken into custody and transported to hospital. The FBI is investigating.

Blair's publicist told the BBC that she "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".

"Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition," her publicist said.

The incident occurred around 2300 local time aboard Delta Airlines Flight 938.

According to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the flight crew allegedly restrained Blair on the flight. Air traffic control audio obtained by CBS includes the pilot calling for medical personnel to come to the plane, citing a "bloody nose as well as some bite marks".

In a statement to the BBC, the FBI, which is responsible for investigating all assaults aboard aircraft, confirmed that it is investigating "a potential assault aboard the flight" but would not comment further.

It's unclear whether Blair will face charges relating to the incident. The BBC has contacted New York prosecutors.

A spokesperson for Delta Airlines said that law enforcement responded as the flight arrived at John F Kennedy International Airport in New York, and that there was no operational impact to the flight because of the incident.

"Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," Delta Airlines said in a statement to the BBC.

Blair largely retreated from film work amid her 2018 multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis. In 2021, she announced she was in remission for the disease.

In 2016, she had another incident on a flight after a drunken outburst caused two nurses to have to subdue her on board.

She issued a public apology after the incident. She said she accidentally mixed her medication with alcohol and "made a big mistake" that caused her to "black out" and "say and do things that I deeply regret".

"I am a flawed human being who makes mistakes and am filled with shame over this incident. I am truly very sorry," she said at the time.

US media reported at the time that the actress was screaming uncontrollably and that nurses had to prop her up with a pillow and give her oxygen to calm down.

She was taken off the plane on a stretcher when the flight landed in Los Angeles from Mexico, and was taken to hospital.

News.title: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador
News.content:
The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.

Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".

Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.

The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.

Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.

It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran.

The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.

Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.

So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.

Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers â about a dozen B-1s from the base â back to their home stations on American soil.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

News.title: Schoolboy knife attacker texted 'sorry' to mum
News.content:
The mother of a teenage boy who stabbed a girl in a masked attack at a school said she received a message from her son saying "sorry" shortly after the attack, a trial has heard.

Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March following reports a 15-year-old had been stabbed in the back.

The defendant, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, denies attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.

After learning about the unfolding events on social media, his mother told the jury at King's Lynn Crown Court she "was in complete shock" when she realised her son was involved.

The mother told the trial that her son was "very quiet, very funny, very smart" and had a "dry sense of humour".

The court has previously heard how the defendant had written notes saying he hated women while the schoolgirl victim described to police how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed".

During Monday's proceedings, the mother described the night before the attack as "completely normal", and said her son left for school at his usual time the following morning.

She said she first became aware something was happening when she was "doom-scrolling".

She messaged her son asking if he was OK, but said she did not "get an immediate response".

"When you realise there has been an incident at the school and you don't hear from children, it's worrying," she said.

News.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey faces having to find Â£35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds.

Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said.

The Treasury declined to comment.

The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.

The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October.

"A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller.

"Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course.

"Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.

Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home.

"But Britain and our alliesâ¯can face up to these challenges together."

He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".

Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years.

"[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed."

Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending.

Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like Â£35bn."

She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise.

Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums."

News.title: Health and safety inquiry after fatal tiger attack
News.content:
A health and safety investigation has been launched into the death of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was closed over the weekend following reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway on Saturday afternoon.

An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.

"I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," a City of Doncaster Council spokesperson said.

Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.

"We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident," he said.

"At this time, we won't be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time."

The wildlife park remains closed for third day as investigations continue.

A park spokesperson said: "Due to the events over the weekend, the park will remain closed today. Thank you for your understanding."

News.title: Reform pledges to suspend UK's asylum system for up to five years
News.content:
Reform UK has announced plans to effectively close down the UK's asylum system for a full parliamentary term if elected.

The party said all new asylum applications would be rejected and existing applications voided, with all claimants marked for deportation. It said no grants of humanitarian protection or refugee status would be made, while legal refugee routes and resettlement schemes would end.

Reform said it would also scrap the asylum tribunal system and deport 90,000 people currently with appeal cases, with home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf saying "Britain is full".

Labour called the proposals a "clear sign of desperation and weakness" and the Refugee Council branded them "unworkable".

Reform said its existing plans to make migrants who have entered the UK illegally, overstayed a visa or originated from a safe country ineligible for asylum would effectively prevent any current asylum claimant "from ever having their case heard".

The party said it would therefore "suspend the asylum system entirely for a full parliamentary term".

A parliamentary term usually lasts five years unless an early UK general election is called.

Under further proposals, Reform said it would pull the UK out of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention to prevent legal challenges to its plans.

The party said it would ban British visas for countries such as Pakistan, Somalia, Eritrea, Syria, Afghanistan and Sudan if they refuse to allow deportation flights to land in their country.

News.title: Normandy veteran Henry Rice dies aged 100
News.content:
World War Two veteran Henry Rice, who survived a near-miss when a torpedo was fired at the boat he was on, has died at the age of 100.

Rice, from Cranleigh in Surrey, was a signalman aboard HMS Eastway as part of the Normandy landings, arriving at Juno Beach five days after D-Day.

He received the Legion d'honneur from the French government and had called for schools to teach children more about the Normandy landings because the "world is dangerous at the moment".

A spokesperson from the Spirit of Normandy Trust, a charity for veterans, said: "Henry was a great character, with a cheeky smile that endeared him to everyone he met."

Rice previously told the BBC that revisiting Normandy for a remembrance service in June this year meant "everything" to him.

"I've had a super lifetime," he said.

When thinking about veterans who had died, he added: "I find it too easy to wipe a tear away, so I don't let myself think too deeply. But when I'm on my own, then I do."

News.title: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths
News.content:
A public inquiry will examine the deaths of two men killed during an attack at a synagogue in Manchester.

Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from multiple stab wounds and fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, tried to get in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October 2025.

Announcing the inquiry, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "What happened that day must be fully understood."

Syrian-born UK citizen Al-Shamie was shot dead by police while he carried out his attack.

Police had already seized Al-Shamie's mobile phone containing details of his extremist mindset but did not analyse the contents until after he had attacked the synagogue.

It took place on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for Jews.

Mahmood said: "In recent days, we marked the first anniversary of the terror attack at the Heaton Park synagogue.

"On that awful day in October of last year, as our Jewish community celebrated Yom Kippur, two brave men â Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby â lost their lives, and three others were seriously injured.

"What happened that day must be fully understood. So, as requested by the coroner, I can today announce a public inquiry into the deaths of Mr Cravitz and Mr Daulby.

"This will ensure that all evidence can be heard, including any sensitive national security material that could not otherwise be fully heard in the coroner's court."

News.title: PC thought murderer was making 'empty threats' before arson attack
News.content:
The court heard Quinn and PC Mike Grundy went to the scene in Walkden around 01:25 GMT after Michelle Pearson called 999 because Bolland and three others were outside her house.

Bolland had been heard shouting "I'm going to break Kyle's jaw" and threatened to "boot the door down".

Quinn, as the senior officer, told the court she knew Bolland, two weeks earlier, had threatened to set fire to Michelle Pearson's house and smashed windows with a hammer.

There were also markers on databases about his drug use, firearms and violence.

Yet she chose not to arrest Bolland as she believed it was an "empty threat".

"As a police officer, you get to see the worst side of a community and unfortunately, Salford and what I saw in 14 yearsâ¦.individuals make threats like that, quite often."

She left Jackson Street around 02:30.

Her shift was not due to end until 05:00, the inquest heard.

Bolland's last known address was close by, but Quinn chose to go back to the police station.

When asked whether she should have tried to arrest him immediately, Quinn said "In hindsight, yes".

She told the court: "It's not that we had stopped dealing with the job, we had write-ups to do.

The family's barrister, Anna Morris KC asked if that work was more important than questioning Bolland - to which Quinn replied: "No".

Quinn said: "As a police officer, you get to see the worst side of a community and unfortunately in Salford and what I saw in 14 years, individuals make threats like that quite often.

"We didn't believe we needed to make an arrest, there and then, that night."

In his statement, Grundy had told Michelle he expected Bolland to be arrested.

It was suggested in the inquest that this was likely to have made Michelle feel she was not in any danger.

The inquest also heard that despite asking Michelle if she felt safe in the house, she sought not to try and move the family immediately to a secure location.

Quinn said she did not see the point in calling Michelle's housing provider, City West, because it was out of hours.

The inquest continues.

News.title: Russell Brand appears in court for start of rape trial
News.content:
There are six female complainants in the case.

During the selection process, potential jurors were asked a number of questions by the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan.

"Many of you will have heard of him", the judge said, adding that Brand had been on television "a great deal a couple of years ago.

The judge said: "About three years ago there was a television programme and a long article in the Times newspaper in which some allegations were made against him of sexual misconduct. They were allegations he firmly denied."

He asked potential jurors to tell him if they remembered watching the Channel 4 documentary or reading the article. Six put their hands up.

The judge also told them that the trial is expected to take about six weeks, but jurors might need to be available until 11 December.

The potential jurors were whittled down to 20.

Those jurors were told a smaller group of them would be chosen on Tuesday and sworn in for the trial before being sent home.

Before leaving court Bennathan warned them they must not carry out any research about Brand.

The actor and broadcaster rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

Brand went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

News.title: King, Queen and Prince William to visit Aberfan on 60th anniversary of disaster
News.content:
The King, Queen and Prince of Wales are set to visit Aberfan later this month to mark the 60th anniversary of the disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults.

Pantglas Junior School and surrounding houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and Prince William will join survivors, bereaved parents and members of the community on the anniversary to pay tribute to those who died.

The royals will visit the Aberfan Memorial Garden which stands on the site of the primary school, and go to the Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre.

Late Queen Elizabeth II's reaction to the disaster in Aberfan was said to be one of the biggest regrets of her 70-year reign.

News.title: Selma Blair arrested after she bit a flight attendant in alleged plane meltdown: report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Legally Blonde star Selma Blair has reportedly been arrested following an in-flight incident.

Blair — who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018 — was traveling Sunday on a Delta Airlines flight from Los Angeles to New York when she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another, TMZ reported. She also allegedly attempted to open the plane’s door mid-flight.

Dispatch audio obtained by the outlet revealed that the injuries included a bloody nose and bite marks. One of the flight attendants was reportedly taken to the hospital. Other audio revealed Blair screaming “No!” repeatedly as alarms went off in the background.

Sources told the New York Post that Blair was eventually subdued and taken in an ambulance to a nearby hospital once the plane landed safely. She allegedly kicked a cop and attacked a nurse, resulting in charges against her, the outlet reported.

The Cruel Intentions star, 54, “experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct,” her representative told the Post, but is “in stable condition.”

open image in gallery Selma Blair has reportedly been hospitalized after an in-flight incident ( Reuters )

The Independent has contacted Delta Airlines and a representative for Blair for comment.

A statement obtained by The Independent from the Port Authority Police Department, which oversees JFK Airport, said: “At approximately 11 p.m. at JFK Airport, PAPD responded to a call about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Airlines flight 938 which was parked at the gate after arrival from LAX.

“Suspect was identified as Selma Blair, a 54 year-old woman. She was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation. Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation,” the statement continued, confirming that the FBI is investigating the incident.

As it turns out, Blair has a history of biting others.

In her 2022 memoir, Mean Baby: A Memoir of Growing Up, she admitted to having bitten Kate Moss, Sienna Miller and Seth MacFarlane.

Blair has also suffered a previous flight meltdown, resulting in her being hauled off on a stretcher in 2016, TMZ reported.

The actor, who shared earlier this year that she was “relapse free” amid her MS diagnosis, was most recently seen in public at an October 1 event in New York City.

News.title: RAF Fairford incident ‘almost certainly’ directed by Iran’s security force, Burnham says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A suspected attack against RAF Fairford was “highly likely” to have been directed by Iran’s security force, the IRGC, prime minister Andy Burnham has said.

In an update to MPs in the Commons on Monday, Mr Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard.”

Five men were arrested close to the Gloucestershire airbase, which is used by the US, on Sunday 27 September. The suspects, who were British citizens from London in their 20s, were held over explosives and terrorism offences, but have since been released on bail.

open image in gallery US bombers depart RAF Fairford for home ( Getty )

Mr Burnham added: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to bring us harm”.

The US state department issued a statement endorsed by more than 20 countries on Monday condemning Iran for actions including “lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks” around the world.

Mr Burnham later told Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch: “We will continue to work with our US counterparts on RAF Fairford”.

Iran’s ambassador to the UK has also summoned to make clear that “Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil”, foreign secretary Ed Miliband also said.

Mr Miliband announced the designation of two Iranian nationals, named as head of counterespionage for the IRGC and a facilitator of plots against Iranian dissidents, for their “role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas”.

The foreign secretary further discussed “holding Iran to account for its actions” in a call with US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Monday.

Reporting on the talks, US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said: “They reiterated their shared commitment to safeguarding transit in the Strait of Hormuz and the importance of holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom.

“Secretary Rubio reaffirmed the value of our close partnership to stabilise global energy markets while also bringing the Russia-Ukraine conflict to an end through a negotiated settlement.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham gives an update on RAF Fairford to MPs on Monday ( Parliament TV )

A joint statement issued on behalf of the US, UK, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden on Monday condemned Iran’s actions across Europe.

They said the RAF Fairford incident “demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors”.

“This comes soon after the recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and US interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI),” the statement added.

Last week, the US air force pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford and redeployed them back to their home bases in the US.

According to reports in the US media, the decision to remove the bombers was in response to renewed security concerns about the safety of the base in Gloucestershire.

Seven suspects have now been arrested by police investigating the suspected terror plot against RAF Fairford, and subsequently released under strict bail conditions.

open image in gallery Five men were arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act in Fairford ( Reuters )

Three suspicious vans were stopped near the airbase on Sunday 27 September. No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized, police said.

In July, ⁠Britain used new powers designed to stop the use of state-sponsored proxies to ban support ‌for the IRGC ​and a linked group accused of being ‌behind attacks at locations linked ​to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media.

The nations said “any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable”.

Roger Macmillan, security expert and former Head of Security at Iran International, said: “The prime minister says it is almost certain that Iran’s IRGC directed an attack on British soil. Today's sanctioning of two men who live in Tehran is welcome, but it will not stop these attacks in the future. If the government believes what it is saying, it must bring forward the law to ban the IRGC and take stronger steps to resource the police and security services further to protect British subjects. Warning words are not enough."

Lord Walney, chair of the APPG for Defending Democracy said: "The news that the RAF Fairford attack was directed by the terror-exporting IRGC shows why the must consider Iran a hostile regime that is implacably imposed to British interests.”

He added that it was a “grave mistake” for foreign secretary Ed Miliband to have shaken hands with the Iranian foreign minister in a meeting last month, saying it gave “the stamp of legitimacy to this terror exporting Islamist regime”.

News.title: Dozens of Tennessee Walmart employees sick, hospitalized for ‘possible food-related illness’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nineteen workers at a Walmart Distribution Center in Lebanon, Tennessee, were reportedly transported to area hospitals following a suspected foodborne illness outbreak late last week.

Health and emergency authorities are investigating what caused the sudden outbreak of illnesses at the facility, located roughly 30 miles east of Nashville.

Emergency crews were first dispatched to the distribution center late Thursday night after receiving a report of “a female experiencing symptoms of a possible food-related illness,” as reported by ABC affiliate WKRN, citing the Wilson County Emergency Management Agency.

“Upon arrival, additional units were requested to assist,” the agency said in a statement shared Sunday. “Approximately 25 to 30 patients were triaged on scene, with 19 patients transported.”

Assistive support was provided by Mount Juliet EMS and Rutherford County EMS to manage the patients on site. Early accounts had indicated that up to 120 people felt sick and 30 were taken to hospitals, though official agency tallies later clarified the lower transport figures. Affected employees reported sudden nausea and vomiting stretching into Friday morning.

A suspected foodborne illness outbreak at a Walmart distribution center in Lebanon, Tennessee, sent 19 employees to local hospitals late last week ( AFP via Getty Images )

“The health and safety of our associates is a top priority,” Walmart said in a statement to WKRN on Sunday. “We’re working with local emergency management and health officials as they investigate.”

Public health officials have not yet confirmed the source responsible for the outbreak. It remains unclear whether those affected consumed food from an on-site cafeteria, a catered event or personal meals brought into the plant. Neither the Wilson County Health Department nor the Tennessee Department of Health had issued formal public statements as of Sunday evening.

The Food Poison Journal, published by the food safety law firm Marler Clark, reported that the sudden overnight onset of heavy vomiting is characteristic of toxins produced by bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus, or pathogens like norovirus.

The firm noted that confirming a source would require stool testing, dietary history interviews and laboratory testing of food samples, and advised any affected workers to seek medical care and notify local health officials.

News.title: Why was Shane Gillis given a platform on SNL — again?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In 2019, comedian Shane Gillis was announced as part of the new generation of cast members joining Saturday Night Live, alongside Bowen Yang and Chloe Fineman. But before he could make his debut, Gillis — then a fresh-faced 31-year-old stand-up and podcaster from Pennsylvania — was fired over resurfaced clips of him using anti-Asian slurs and making homophobic jokes. Gillis apologized at the time, stating he was “a comedian who pushes boundaries” but one who “sometimes misses.”

Yet that fallout didn’t stop SNL from inviting him back — three separate times. His latest appearance this past Saturday night ignited opprobrium when, during a bro-y stand-up opening monologue, he joked that women at the gym “now dress like wh***s.” “Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts?” he asked the audience, though it felt like he was only talking to the men in the room. He said women in the gym wear neon shorts with wrinkles that go “around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look…because they’re filming!”

The joke felt so overtly misogynistic I had to double-check the date: was this 2006 or 2026? Commentators noted that the material was especially tone-deaf given the national conversation surrounding the Cornell 7 case — the 2024 gang rape allegations involving seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell University — which SNL had addressed sensitively during Weekend Update just the week prior. Schitt’s Creek creator Dan Levy was among those criticizing Gillis’s monologue, posting on Monday: “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them wh***s; it makes the men calling them wh***s misogynists…I’m speechless that something like that can exist on live national television, and to be honest more men need to be standing up in opposition to it.”

If Gillis provokes such controversy, why on earth does SNL keep inviting him back?

For one, Gillis is close with SNL creator Lorne Michaels, who expressed frustration when NBC made the decision to fire the comedian in 2019. “He said something stupid, but it got blown up into the end of the world,” Michaels told The Wall Street Journal at the time. “I was angry. I thought, ‘You haven’t seen what we’re going to do, and what I’m going to try to bring out in him, because I thought he was the real thing.’” Michaels made clear that the decision came from network executives rather than himself.

open image in gallery Comedian Shane Gillis, who was fired from ‘SNL’ in 2019 before he even made his debut, faced backlash when he called women ‘w****s’ during his third time hosting the program ( Getty Images for Bob Woodruff Fo )

Gillis was also invited back because his commercial success is pretty undeniable. He’s one of the most popular touring stand-up comedians in the U.S. right now. His career has grown fast, perhaps thanks in part to his high-profile SNL firing. He’s had a 2023 Netflix special, Beautiful Dogs (his debut special, released on YouTube in 2021, has 58 million views on the platform). He has 3 million Instagram followers. He co-hosts the top comedy podcast with Matt McCusker, Matt and Shane’s Secret Podcast. He also co-wrote and stars in Netflix’s workplace comedy Tires, set at a fictional family-run auto shop, which earned a multi-season renewal alongside a broader production and stand-up deal with the streamer. His comedy style makes him extremely likable; he speaks to the crowd as if he’s messing around with his friends. Gillis is clever and dumb at the same time, in a way that makes him somewhat endearing. He doesn’t aim to come across as a polished entertainer, either.

The comedy in Saturday night’s monologue was very much Gillis’s brand. He combines brash anti-wokeness with heavy doses of self-deprecating jokes and a type of self-awareness that props up his everyman persona. In the opening monologue alone, he joked about growing up being bullied by his “two big fat b**** sisters” and his receding hairline that he claimed makes him look either “gay” or like Hitler. He also recounted being told he looked like a “gas station egg” during a sauna hangout session with his mates Theo Von and Joe Rogan — an anecdote hardly tailored to SNL’s progressive demographic.

open image in gallery Shane Gillis was invited back to ‘SNL’ because his commercial success is pretty undeniable ( NBC/SNL )

Host monologues should theoretically be smooth sailing for stand-up comedians, who dedicate their careers to getting laughs out of live audiences. But professional comedians are also judged more harshly, compared to, say, pop star Harry Styles when he’s on hosting duties. Gillis has been accused of bombing before — the comedian term for failing to make the audience laugh — when he hosted for the first time in 2024, and again in 2025. During both appearances, he received significant social media backlash from viewers who weren't happy that he joked about Down syndrome, compared liberals to Star Wars villains and so forth (you get the gist). On Saturday, he accidentally dropped an F-bomb during a sketch based on Dr. Seuss, and painstakingly read from a teleprompter afterwards. He apologized to the audience for swearing later on in the show, and TMZ reports today that the blunder won’t prevent him from being invited back again (The Independent has contacted NBC for comment).

Yet the accidental F-bomb wasn’t the most controversial part.

The joke about gym attire struck such a chord because acts of violence against women and girls are often blamed on what the victim is wearing or doing, rather than the acts of the perpetrator themselves. And it’s worth pointing out that the gym is an extremely difficult place for women to be comfortable. Personally, I take months to get comfortable when I join a new gym, mainly because I’m sussing out whether I need to keep a wide berth from any of the male members who may reveal themselves to be professional mansplainers or creeps. And I’d say that for every pair of neon shorts I’ve seen in the gym, I’ve probably seen a dozen more male nipples. If I were to be really granular about it, I’d say that Gillis’s observation in itself shows just how much women are being watched and monitored in gyms. It is cheap humor. And while the monologue may have landed a decade ago, it feels distinctly out of place today.

At a time when headlines are dominated by serious discussions around consent and violence against women, it remains baffling how a joke built around calling women “w****s” for wearing activewear made it onto primetime national television. But if you’ve got the backing of comedy’s holy duo Lorne Michaels and Joe Rogan, the invitation will be extended again and again.

News.title: Authorities name the attacker and most of the 8 victims in last week's Erie mass shooting
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A coroner on Monday released the names of the gunman and six of the eight people he shot and killed at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, including seven of his relatives.

The shooter in Friday's attack was Matthew Stone Sr., 45, according to Erie County coroner Lyell Cook. Stone took his own life at the home, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said.

According to Cook, the adult victims were Michelle Stone, 44; Angelina Stone, 24, who was due to give birth Monday; Jonathan Stone, 19; Matthew Stone, 21, and two women who lived at other addresses: Lora Roberts, 37, and Twila Tanner, 51. He said a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl also died, but that state law prevented him from releasing their names.

At a memorial to the victims, Julius Windham said his daughter Amarianna was the toddler who was killed. The girl's mother was Angelina Stone, who was also the mother of the boy who died, he said, noting that attacker was a grandfather and the family patriarch.

Family friend Nicole Eller said Roberts frequently went to the house to help during the pregnancy of her niece and neighbor, Angelina Stone.

Roberts, identified by friends as a mother of five who was engaged to be married, was a volunteer and former board member for a community group that helped homeless people. She wrote a July 15 Facebook post decrying recent shootings in Erie.

“Erie we need to do better!!" she wrote. "Life is precious and its heartbreaking to see so much pain and violence. Check on the people you love, and always choose kindness.”

Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.

Roberts and Tanner, who was the only non-relative, were killed outside the home, Lorah said.

The police chief hasn't said what the gunman's possible motives were, but he suggested that his mental health could have been a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.

Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh.

News.title: Home sales under contract plummet to 12-year low in US
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Home sales under contract have plummeted to a new low in 2026, an analysis has found.

Last month, the number of homes that entered a pending sale - when a seller accepts an offer from a buyer - fell 4 percent month-on-month, the biggest drop in more than three years, housing data platform Redfin announced Monday.

“This is a real-time indicator of what's happening in the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in September largely because mortgage rates rose steadily, surpassing 7% by the end of the month,” the company said.

Pending sales dropped in all 50 states for the first time in three years, too.

Last week mortgage rates climbed to 7.4 percent, reaching their highest level since November 2023, according to federal data.

A slowdown in the housing market isn’t always good news for sellers, but it can work to the advantage of buyers ( Getty Images )

The number of homes in pending status was lower in April 2020, at the beginning of the Covid pandemic, but Redfin excluded those figures from its analysis because it was an outlier.

Homes are also spending 51 days on the market - the amount of time a home is listed before the seller accepts an offer from a buyer.

Looking ahead, mortgage rates may not come down anytime soon. The Federal Reserve raised its interest rate by 0.25 percentage points in September, a move that fuels factors that often lead to higher mortgage rates.

Since that decision, home loan rates rose from 6.95 percent, on September 17, to 7.4 percent last week.

A continued slowdown in pending sales is bad news for sellers but good news for buyers, LendFriend Mortgage President Eric Bernstein told the National Association of Realtors in a September analysis of home-loan rates.

“Higher rates can cool buyer demand and create more negotiating leverage, depending on the local market,” Bernstein said.

“Buyers may have more room to negotiate the purchase price...In markets with limited inventory and strong demand, that leverage may be smaller, but in softer markets it can offset some of the added borrowing costs.”

Consumers looking to improve their chances of getting a lower mortgage rate should get loan quotes from multiple lenders, the National Association of Realtors recommended.

“Studies show that shopping around for a mortgage by gathering quotes from several lenders can make a difference,” the association wrote. “Rates can vary widely among lenders, making it worthwhile to compare multiple loan offers rather than accepting the first one.”

News.title: Emmerdale viewers hit with bombshell as Baby Tate's fate is revealed
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Emmerdale fans finally learned the whereabouts of Baby Tate in Monday’s episode as it emerged that the infant is safe and well.

The baby appeared in the arms of Graham Foster (Andrew Scarborough) at a secluded cottage, with Kim Tate (Claire King) arriving at the hideout with supplies, confirming her involvement in the plot.

The episode ended with the narration of a letter from Vinny (Bradley Johnson) to Nicola (Nicola Wheeler), in which he apologised for the tragic accident that claimed the life of her husband Jimmy King (Nick Miles), as Kim arrived at the cottage to visit the pair.

With the baby’s location still hidden from his father Joe (Ned Porteous), questions remain regarding how he will react upon learning that Graham defied his orders to put the child up for adoption.

Jimmy King (Nick Miles) was killed off in August ( ITV )

The baby, a Tate heir, provides Kim with an opportunity to redeem herself.

When Thea (Chelsea Edge) eventually learns the truth, Kim may finally be able to prove that she has attempted to make amends for the family’s past.

Emmerdale producer Sophie Roper said: “Kim was devastated at the prospect of Joe giving the baby up for adoption.

“While it initially appeared that Graham and Kim had resigned themselves to the plan, they have secretly intervened to ensure the baby remains safe and hidden away.

“Desperate for Joe not to come to regret his decision, Kim’s determined to find a way to reunite father and son but with Joe still consumed by grief over losing Dawn and Thea set on vengeance against Kim, can Kim and Graham continue to protect their secret?”

Emmerdale airs at 8pm on weeknights on ITV1 and STV or from 7am on ITVX and STV Player and YouTube.

News.title: WHO probes ‘unanswered questions’ over Russian plague worker
News.content:
The World Health Organization has said it still does not have enough information to rule out a lab accident after the death of a worker in a Russian plague lab.

Last week reports emerged that Darya Shipilova, a lab worker in Irkutsk, Siberia, had died of pneumonic plague after dropping a test tube containing samples of the pathogen Yersinia pestis, which causes the disease.

Some 200 people were quarantined and there were reports of a further case. Shipilova was working at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk.

Russian authorities have insisted that there was no lab accident and Shipilova’s mother, Svetlana, has also disputed that her daughter dropped a test tube.

“It’s impossible to break a test tube like that,” she said. “Even if you fling it at the wall. Only an amateur could say something like that,” she said.

News.title: El Nino, hunger and fuel threaten ‘perfect storm’, says UN
News.content:
A triple shock of rising energy prices, spiralling borrowing costs and a turbocharged El Niño could push “tens if not hundreds of millions of people” into poverty, the UN has warned.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) said the three “compounding crises” are hitting developing economies especially hard, with governments running out of resources to shield people from the fallout, in a new report.

“We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty,” said Alexander De Croo, the UNDP administrator, warning that surging oil and food prices mean families across the world have “no safety margin”.

“Governments of developing countries are left with impossible choices: cut support to their poorest citizens or risk their entire development agenda,” he added.

The report was published ahead of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, which kicked off in Bangkok on Monday. Debt pressures, energy prices and geopolitical tensions are high on the agenda.

But UNDP stressed that the meetings were taking place as three shocks converge, and the crisis morphs from a regional to a global one that’s affecting roughly 100 countries.

Seven months ago, when the war in Iran broke out, the UN agency warned that the conflict had triggered the “most severe oil supply shock in history”. That continues today – after a brief respite, oil prices have been pushed back beyond $100 a barrel, as hostilities have resumed in the Middle East.

But two more threats now “challenge the capacity of developing countries to manage the energy shock”, meaning developing economies “will have trouble funding their policy responses in the months ahead”.

News.title: Three tasks to get your home ready for autumn, according to a professional cleaner
News.content:
When I was sweating away this summer, I never thought the weather would turn, but it’s almost time to crank up our radiators and crack out the big duvet.

They’re the tasks no one likes doing, but luckily for you, I’ve worked as a cleaner for more than a decade. I’ve discovered some shortcuts to make the hated jobs that bit easier.

Tip one: Keep your summer duvet fresh in storage

If, like me, you want to get your winter duvet out, your summer one needs to be cleaned and packed away to keep it fresh come spring.

Start by spot cleaning any stains. You can just use a standard household fabric stain remover for this. If you want to wash your duvet, most domestic washing machines aren’t big enough to fit a double, let alone a king or a super king. Your best bet is to take them down to the laundrette and follow the care instructions on the label.

Sports.title: Boring Carrick’s Man Utd reign is unravelling exactly as it did at Middlesbrough from defensive fragility to no plan B

MIDDLESBROUGH fans tuning into Manchester United this season cannot help but be overwhelmed by a sense of deja vu.

The impressive job Michael Carrick performed by leading them back into Champions League after replacing Ruben Amorim last season is fast getting forgotten.



Those left at the end jeered, having already booed United midway through the first half and again at half-time, after the latest feeble showing against Tottenham.

Following a bright honeymoon, Carrick’s tenure is quickly regressing Riverside style.



A cycle of tactical stubbornness, poor and hesitant game management and defensive fragility led to his downfall in the North East after just under three years in 2025.

The Red Devils are now witnessing it firsthand.



United do have an identity, but it is as boring and uninspiring as a Carrick press conference. He probably has 4-2-3-1 in his lottery numbers too.

The words from opposition managers were particularly damning in those final months on Teesside. Praise for Carrick for “sticking to his principles” may as well have been translated to “Boro are easy to predict”.

While passing and ball retention stats remained high, the metrics that actually keep managers employed dropped alarmingly. Expected goals (xG), chance conversion and big-chance creation fell off a cliff. Despite loads of sterile possession, his side lacked urgency.

Sound familiar? United fans certainly feel so. They voiced that exact frustration against Spurs on Saturday, booing midway through the first half as the Red Devils drifted through another low-energy display.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Granted, during that dismal final fall in the 2024/25 campaign at Boro he was hampered by the loss of pacey winger Ben Gannon-Doak to injury and the January sale of Emmanuel Latte Lath. What is the excuse now?

Poor game management remains his most damaging flaw. Boro squandered 25 points from winning positions in his final season, and that inability to protect leads has resurfaced at United. When momentum turns, Carrick looks out-thought in the dugout.

At Boro, changes routinely occurred only after the team went behind, and even then, his interventions were largely like-for-like swaps.

Crucially, without the outlet of speedster Gannon-Doak, Carrick appeared unable to find a solution by changing shape. Instead, he continued to bang his head against a brick wall… no doubt slowly like his side’s play.



When the slump deepened, his reluctance to make decisive in-game changes caused uproar in the stands and, ultimately, internally too at Boro.

His stubborn insistence on slowly playing out from the back was laid bare during Boro’s 6-1 Carabao Cup semi-final second-leg thrashing at Chelsea in 2024. As Chelsea pressed ruthlessly to score four before half-time, a flexible coach would have instructed his team to go long to relieve the pressure on the overwhelmed defence and two midfield sitters. Carrick stood and watched things implode.

Changes routinely occurred only after going behind at Boro, usually limited to like-for-like swaps. When questioned by local reporters, he claimed the clock was “irrelevant” when judging changes. Yet his first substitution still consistently comes around the 65th minute.



Is it just his total confidence in his pre-game plans or is he unable to conjure up something in the heat of battle? Unfortunately, at present, it seems to be the latter.

Middlesbrough witnessed the complete arc of Carrick’s management. Shining bright first before the regression sets in and then the lack of adaptability and tactical nous to stop the rot proving to be his undoing.

We will soon find out whether he has learned from those past mistakes.

Sports.title: How Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage defied odds to go from working in restaurant and driving team bus to Premier League
Sports.content:
Next

THERE is a new sheriff in town at Selhurst Park and his name is Pierre Sage.

The Crystal Palace boss is no stranger to being underestimated, overlooked or simply not taken seriously.



But the Frenchman has made a career out of defying expectations and proving his doubters wrong.

Unlike his predecessor Oliver Glasner, who arrived in South London with a respectable playing career behind him and a Europa League triumph with Eintracht Frankfurt on his CV, Sage has always been something of an outsider.



And the 47-year-old is determined to prove his miracle season at Lens was no flash in the pan.

His start to life in South London has offered plenty of encouragement, even if results have not always gone his way.



But away from the touchline, it is his human touch that is beginning to make an impression.

Sources at Palace say Sage has shown a remarkable understanding of his players’ individual circumstances, knowing when to be a manager, a father figure or simply a big brother offering a reassuring arm around the shoulder.

Take star man Ismaila Sarr, for example.

The Senegal international was left devastated after his dream move to Liverpool collapsed during the summer transfer window.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Rather than simply demanding that he put the disappointment behind him, Sage has given the winger time and space to recover, both physically and mentally, as he works his way back into regular first-team football.

Sources close to Sarr have expressed surprise at the level of compassion shown by the Palace boss, particularly after it became clear the player would be staying at Selhurst Park.

And he has extended that same understanding to other members of the squad, reassuring those who needed convincing that there was still plenty to play for if everyone pulled in the same direction.

On Sunday, there was perhaps the clearest sign yet that his message is beginning to get through.

Palace’s 3-1 victory over Nottingham Forest, now managed by Glasner, handed Sage his first home Premier League win and gave the Selhurst Park faithful a glimpse of what might lie ahead.



In many ways, the Frenchman is attempting to recreate the magic he worked at Lens last season.

Few expected the unfancied club to challenge the established powers of French football when he took charge in the summer of 2025.

Yet Sage guided them to second place in Ligue 1, finishing just six points behind the mighty Paris Saint-Germain and securing a return to the Champions League.



Even more remarkably, he led Lens to their first-ever French Cup triumph, ending a 120-year wait for the famous trophy.

It was a season that transformed his reputation and left a lasting impression on those who worked under him.

Former Chelsea defender Malang Sarr, who played for Sage at Lens, believes Palace supporters will soon discover what makes their new boss special.

He told The Sun: “You will see, slowly the fans will begin to love him.

“He doesn’t like to show too much emotion but he sees everything. Last year he managed to create a brilliant atmosphere with a clear playing style that we all enjoyed.



“I think he will try and do that again in the Premier League. He has a good way of getting players to play for him and normally that is very important, so let’s see.”

Sage has also brought a philosophical approach to his new surroundings, shaped by a journey that could hardly be more different from that of the average Premier League manager.

And perhaps the clearest insight into his thinking came during the summer transfer window, when supporters were crying out for fresh faces and big-money reinforcements.



Rather than complain about the club’s spending power, Sage drew on lessons learned from watching his parents run a restaurant in Belley, a small town in eastern France.

He told The Guardian: “I’m not frustrated, we are not a bank.

“We do with what we have. My parents had a restaurant and I prefer every day there’s a lot of clients but it was not the case sometimes and we have to deal with that every day. In football it’s the same.”

It was a refreshingly grounded response from a man who knows what it means to work his way up from the bottom.

Unlike most Premier League bosses, Sage never played professional football.



He once dreamed of becoming a goalkeeper but never progressed beyond the amateur ranks.

Instead, he began coaching youngsters at just 16 and spent years learning his trade far away from the bright lights of Europe’s biggest stadiums.

He also helped with his parents’ restaurant business and, during his time coaching Annecy’s Under-19s, even drove the team minibus to and from matches.



There were no glamorous surroundings, enormous budgets or superstar players to manage.

Just a young coach with an appetite for learning and a stubborn determination to reach the top.

And as the saying goes, hang around a barbershop long enough and eventually you will get a haircut.

For Sage, the years spent studying the game, working behind the scenes and waiting patiently for an opportunity eventually paid off.

His coaching journey took him through Lyon‘s youth set-up and a spell working under former Newcastle defender Habib Beye at Red Star.



He later returned to Lyon as academy director before an unexpected opportunity changed his career.

When Fabio Grosso was sacked in November 2023, Sage was handed the first-team job on an interim basis.

Lyon were in desperate trouble, sitting bottom of Ligue 1 and staring at the prospect of a humiliating relegation battle.

But Sage inspired a remarkable turnaround, guiding them to sixth place and European qualification.

His reward was a permanent contract running until 2026, although the fairytale ended prematurely when he was dismissed in January 2025 following a disappointing run of results.



For some managers, such a setback might have proved difficult to recover from.

For Sage, it became the beginning of another extraordinary chapter.

Lens came calling after Englishman Will Still departed for Southampton, having guided the club to eighth place.

What followed was a season few associated with the French club will ever forget.



Malian midfielder Amadou Haidara, who played under Sage at Lens, told The Sun that his former manager’s ability to build trust within the dressing room was central to his success.

He said: “He’s a clever manager.

“I think he has a good relationship with the people he works with and the trust he builds reflects in the game.



“I think he will do well in the Premier League because he has all the ingredients.”

Of course, the jury is still out on whether Sage can reproduce those remarkable achievements in English football.

Since taking the reins at Selhurst Park, he has recorded four wins, one draw and three defeats across his opening eight competitive matches.

But Sunday’s victory over Forest, led by the very man he replaced at Palace, felt like more than just another three points.

It was a statement of intent, a reminder that Sage is capable of finding a way even when the odds appear stacked against him.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

And for a manager who has spent much of his career waiting for people to believe in him, that kind of victory can breed something even more valuable than confidence.

It could be the spark that turns a flickering flame into an inferno.

Sports.title: Renshaw stars as Australia close in on first Test victory in Durban
Sports.content:
Matt Renshaw continued to hog centre stage as Australia pushed closer to winning the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

Renshaw added a second-innings knock of 82 to his game-shaping 190 and was not finished there. After Australia declared with a lead of 420, the occasional off-spinner picked up his maiden Test wicket as the Proteas laboured to 102-4.

South Africa captain Temba Bavuma was his victim, caught off bat and pad by Nic Maddinson for just one. Josh Hazlewood had already got the ball rolling, dismissing Ryan Rickelton and David Bedingham, with Pat Cummins adding Tristan Stubbs before the close on day four.

Aiden Markram will resume on 45 not out alongside Wiaan Mulder but the odds are stacked against the hosts salvaging the game on day five. Australia were without Steve Smith's brilliance at slip after he was hit on the helmet by Anrich Nortje and was subsequently replaced in the field pending further assessments.

Renshaw's second innings bore almost no relation to his first. The 190 came at a strike-rate of 47. The 82 came at 82, with seven fours and two sixes in it.

Then it took a freak moment to end it. The ball went through Keshav Maharaj's hands more than once and off his own head before it stayed put, by which time the bowler was flat on the pitch.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Renshaw was caught and bowled by Keshav Maharaj in bizarre fashion after the decision was reviewed

Renshaw was on for twin centuries when it happened. Instead he finished with 272 runs for the match, which is close to the most any Australian has made against South Africa.

Three more runs would have put him level with Phillip Hughes, who made twin tons on this ground in 2009. Nine more and he would have passed David Warner's pair of centuries in Cape Town in 2014. Bradman's 299 not out was 28 away.

Nobody else in the Australian order got past 48. Maddinson stopped there, Marnus Labuschagne on 37, Smith on 27 and Alex Carey on 24.

Captain Cummins hurries things along for Australia

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Australia captain Pat Cummins smashed three sixes from four balls

Australia resumed on 33-0 and never looked like batting for time. They were 174-4 at lunch and 280 in front, with Maddinson's 48 from 38 balls setting the rate.

Labuschagne then produced the day's statistical curiosity. He made 37 from 58 balls, exactly what he managed in the first innings, which is only the 12th known instance of a batter matching his runs and his balls faced in both innings of a men's Test.

But Smith's 27 was the innings Nortje will remember. The bouncer that hit him on the helmet arrived on the fourth ball he faced and Smith answered by taking 14 off one Nortje over.

Cricket Australia said he was being assessed for concussion and he will be monitored for 24 hours.

Cummins made the rest a formality. His 32 not out took just a dozen balls, with Simon Harmer conceding three of his four sixes inside one over. The declaration came shortly before tea on 314-6.

Markram the last line of resistance for hosts

South Africa were left 421 to win, which no side in Test history has managed.

West Indies' 418 against Australia in Antigua in 2003 is still the mark and the best at this ground is 336, chased by Australia in 1950.

Batting out the day is the realistic hope and the record there is thin. Just two sides in the last 13 years have lasted 140 overs to save a Test.

Rickelton pulled at a short one in the fourth over and Carey took the catch, two runs made with Hazlewood again the bowler who had him.

Markram and Bedingham put on 66 in 19.4 overs before Hazlewood pinned Bedingham in front for 46. He was 49 first time round, so twice in the match he got into the forties and no further.

Image: South Africa's Aiden Markram was 45no at stumps

Three wickets went down for 13 runs from there and South Africa were 86-4, scoring across the innings at 2.48 an over.

Markram has needed 115 balls for his 45 not out and he was dropped on the way, on 15, when the chance hit Carey on the elbow and ran away past slip.

Among players still active, only Kusal Mendis of Sri Lanka averages more than Markram's 45.56 in a fourth innings. His 136 won the World Test Championship final against these same opponents at Lord's.

He has been in this position at this ground before, too. He made 143 here in 2018 chasing 417 against Australia, 340 minutes of work that still ended in defeat.

He will be hoping that something miraculous can happen on Tuesday with Australia needing six wickets to win and South Africa still requiring 319 runs.
