World.title: 2 Americans win Nobel Prize in economics for work on boom-bust cycles
World.content:
2 Americans win Nobel Prize in economics for work on boom-bust cycles

toggle caption i Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images



Two Americans have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on how to smooth boom-and-bust cycles to limit inflation and unemployment.

Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University were honored for their focus on how individual households and businesses make decisions on purchases and pricing — work that became the foundation of the "New Keynesian" approach to economics.

The importance of that work has been underscored in recent years by the pandemic, which pushed millions of people out of work, and the supply shocks that followed, driving up the cost of living.

Sponsor Message

"Regardless of the causes, an important goal for governments and central banks is to reduce the amplitude of these swings and limit the risk that the economy gets stuck in a situation with high unemployment or loses control over inflation," said John Hassler, the chairman of the economic prize committee. This award is not one of the original five, but a "memorial" prize that honors Alfred Nobel.



After the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes persuaded policymakers that government sometimes needed to stimulate demand during downturns to curb unemployment, or tamp down demand during boom times to limit inflation.

"This is the Keynesian recipe, and it worked well until it didn't," said Tim Boppart, a member of the prize committee. In the 1970s, the economy was hit by rising unemployment and inflation simultaneously.

"The Keynesian recipe was shattered," Boppart says. Hall and Woodford added some necessary ingredients, focusing on the individual households and businesses that help shape the larger economy.

Hall concentrated on demand and how households make purchasing decisions, guided not only by current purchasing power but what they expect their incomes will be in the future.

"If consumers see dark clouds on the horizon, they cut back on consumption already today," Boppart says.

Woodford focused on the supply side and how businesses set prices. Here again, expectations are key. Historically, it was costly to change prices, so businesses try to think ahead and set prices that would cover costs for an extended period.

Sponsor Message

Because both households and businesses are forward-looking, the Nobel laureates argued, policymakers should communicate their plans clearly to the public.

"One of the themes in my work is that government authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy, independent of what people in the economy understand," Woodford told reporters after the prize was announced.

Woodford says tools intended to smooth out boom-and-bust cycles work better when people know what the government is trying to accomplish, and he urged policymakers to talk directly to the public about "why the things that are being done are being done."

World.title: Carney’s Thanksgiving message directed at Alberta ahead of separation referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In a video released on social media on Thanksgiving Monday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said this year's holiday is different as Albertans prepare to vote next week in a referendum on the province's future in Canada. 'Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life. We have to be strong and we are stronger together,' he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the nation from a classroom in Alberta on Thanksgiving morning, addressing the non-binding question tied to Alberta’s potential separation from Canada in the upcoming referendum.

“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future,” Carney said as he sat at a desk in his alma mater, St. Francis Xavier High School, in west Edmonton.

“Now, I have some perspectives on this choice. I grew up in Alberta.”

Albertans are preparing to go to the polls on Oct. 19 for a 10-question referendum. The final question asks whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or hold a second, binding referendum on separating from the country.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What conversations are you having about the Alberta referendum with friends and family? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show.

“I'm back home a lot these days because we are building big things again in Alberta,” Carney said, referencing the federal government’s housing initiatives, a proposed high-speed rail route from Edmonton to Calgary and the newly proposed pipeline stretching from Alberta’s oilfield to the West Coast.

“We can't achieve any of this if we're divided. You can't build big things on fault lines.”

Carney continued, referencing recent threats to Canada’s economy and security.

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country,” he said. “It's yours, it's ours, and it's worth fighting for.”

CBC News requested comment from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the prime minister's address.

“We encourage Albertans to visit albertareferendum2026.ca where they can view the 10 ballot questions and access information on these important issues to inform their vote,” Sam Blackett, Smith's press secretary, wrote in an emailed statement.

World.title: ICE's surge in Minnesota could impact the U.S. midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For nearly two months this winter, Minneapolis was the explosive epicenter of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, leaving lasting fear and tension in the community. For The National, CBC’s Katie Nicholson goes there to find out how the scars of Operation Metro Surge could play out in the upcoming midterm elections.

Chairs scrape across the floor of a small St. Paul, Minn., community centre as neighbours start to file in for "democracy defender" training offered by one of several grassroots organizations in the state.

The attendees are preparing for potential scenarios of disruption at the polls for the Nov. 3 midterms.

They learn how to form groups in their neighbourhood, divide into zones and create communication networks so they can make sure they are in contact with everyone on their street.

At several points they break into groups to discuss: What if the administration starts pushing falsehoods about voting rules? What should they do if federal officers attempt to enter the polling places?

Community groups are holding 'democracy defender' training sessions like this one in St. Paul, Minn., to train citizens how to protect the polls if there is federal interference with voting on Nov. 3 and beyond. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)

Helen Kouba says she signed up because she felt she owed it to her seven-year-old after Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration’s sprawling immigration crackdown earlier this year.

“My trust in some of the systems that I was brought up to believe in and not question has faltered and it has been really disappointing and disheartening,” she said.

It’s been roughly nine months since 3,000 federal immigration officers flooded Minnesota, arresting some 4,000 people and clashing with residents trying to slow them down.

In January, two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed by federal officers just weeks apart, eventually leading to the ouster of two prominent Trump immigration officials: Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem and Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino.

The memorial to Renee Good, who was fatally shot by an ICE agent in Minneapolis in January, still draws visitors who come to pay their respects. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)

Many in Minneapolis, where the operation was centred, organized themselves into groups to respond to and observe ICE raids often by recording interactions with their phones, blowing whistles to alert others, blocking traffic to slow down Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, and by creating encrypted group chats to communicate.

Now many of those same people have signed up for training to protect the polls in a Senate race that could be pivotal.

Fears of federal overreach

The Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to assert control over aspects of voting even though elections are administered by the states.

It tried to put limits on mail-in voting, which was subsequently quashed by the Supreme Court. It has continued to sow seeds of doubt about election integrity and the statistically rare cases of non-citizens illegally casting votes. U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly refused to rule out sending federal officers to the polls, including the FBI and ICE.

In a Minneapolis neighbourhood where ICE made several raids over the winter, Shae Alcamo drops handwritten notes to her neighbours. She stops people on the street to make sure they are registered to vote and to see if they are interested in signing up to join the grassroots effort to protect the polls.

Shae Alcamo goes door to door in her Minneapolis neighbourhood to make sure everyone is registered to vote and to enlist help to keep the vote secure on election day. (Katie Nicholson/CBC)

“Ever since Metro Surge happened, I've really been focused on how we defend ourselves from the next threat,” she said.

“It's a really hard conversation about what is possible for us when we've already seen state violence take away two members of our community.”

Concerns about federal interference run well beyond the neighbourhoods of the Twin Cities, all the way to the office of Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon.

“I've had this job for a while, and never ever before have I had to seriously think about the prospect that our own federal government will be an instigator of something that could interfere with the freedom to vote,” said Simon, a Democrat.

“You have a very short runway, so to speak, if say the weekend before the election something happens, a new executive order or a new proclamation or declaration of some kind or deployment of federal law enforcement.”

Minnesota’s Secretary of State Steve Simon says he has never had to prepare for a scenario in which the federal government might interfere with the vote in his decade in the job. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)

Simon has been meeting with his counterparts in other states to plan for different scenarios as a precaution.

“Operation Metro Surge is still a fresh wound,” he said.

Simon said that one of the lessons Minnesota learned from Metro Surge was how effective non-violent pushback can be on what he called undue or unlawful interference in the community.

“We are ready now in a way that we might not have imagined we would have to be before Operation Metro Surge.”

WATCH | From Dec. 2025 — ICE met with organized opposition in Minnesota: Minnesota immigration crackdown met by organized opposition | Duration closed caption 5:36 An immigration crackdown in Minnesota is being met by organized opposition from people who are angry about U.S. Donald Trump’s anti-Somali tirades. For The National, CBC’s Katie Nicholson goes to Minneapolis and finds a community coming together to try and protect its neighbours.

Minnesota could be ‘decider’

In a midterm election where the balance of power in Congress is at stake, University of Minnesota political scientist Larry Jacobs said “Minnesota could be the decider.”

For Democrats to take control of the Senate, they’d need to win at least 17 of the 35 seats up for election this time — including several close races without incumbents , like Minnesota.

“It had been assumed that Minnesota would be safely Democratic in terms of a new senator being elected. But now we're seeing polls, and it's a toss-up,” said Jacobs.

“That's gonna be perhaps a deciding factor in whether the Democrats or Donald Trump maintain control of the U.S. Senate.”

Political scientist Larry Jacobs says Metro Surge could tip the race for Minnesota's open Senate seat toward the Democrats. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)

Former NFL sideline reporter and Republican candidate Michele Tafoya is neck-and-neck in the polls with the state’s Lieutenant Governor and Democrat Peggy Flanagan. The race has tightened, in part, Jacobs said, because of a number of damaging headlines about fraud and wasteful spending which have marred the state’s Democratic leadership.

Jacobs said many other issues have captured voters' attention in the months since Operation Metro Surge including affordability, the price of gas, and the Iran war.

But the very populations targeted by the immigration crackdown could determine the outcome of the Senate race.

“We may have a very, very close Senate race ... and the impact of Donald Trump's Metro Surge and the immigration policy in general could be just what's needed to tip the race away from the Republicans and towards the Democrats,” he said.

The Somali community in particular — targeted during Operation Metro Surge and frequently insulted by the U.S. president — typically turns out in high numbers to vote in a state which regularly has the highest voter turnout. Minnesota has the largest Somali community in the U.S.

On Thursday, Trump again resurfaced his attacks on Somali Minnesotans in a social media post saying they had taken over the state and there was “Violence Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State.” He also offered to send the federal government to the rescue.

Anti-immigrant rhetoric posted by Trump on Truth Social on Thursday. (realDonaldTrump/Truth Social)

“There's always been a number of Somalis, perhaps a third or a quarter, who had voted for the Republican Party,” Jacobs said. “But with the Metro Surge, there's been some erosion of that support for the Republicans within the Somali community and among other immigrants.”

Immigrant communities pivotal

In 2024 Salman Fiqy stood behind Trump at a rally in St. Cloud, Minn., and worked on his campaign. For nearly a decade he said he felt a natural affinity with the GOP ticket.

“Somalis are a very religious, very conservative community and that conservatism drew me to the Republican Party,” he said.

Salman Fiqy split from the Republican party when U.S. President Donald Trump called the Somali community 'garbage.' He says he is now politically homeless. (Mia Sheldon/CBC)

But all that changed in December 2025 when Operation Metro Surge began. Fiqy remembers the exact moment he broke with the party he had long supported.

“It was when Trump was sitting in his office and he called the Somali community ‘ garbage ’, that was the thing that broke the camel's back,” Fiqy said. “But also I'm still a conservative, but I'm disavowing my connection with the Republicans as it is right now.”

Fiqy said if the Republicans want to do better in Minnesota, a traditionally blue state, they need to make inroads with immigrant communities. He accuses the Republican party of being spineless in its reaction to Trump's comments about Somalis.

Metro Surge disrupted the work he and other conservatives had done, Fiqy said.

“It actually struck fear in our community to the point where it disrupts the daily activities of the Somali community, who are — the majority of them — are citizens,” he said.

Fiqy believes Somali Minnesotans are going to show up at the polls in full force for Flanagan in the Senate race.

"Because Somalis are typically very politically engaged and especially if they feel a threat, then they respond in the election," he said.

World.title: 'More men need to be standing up': Dan Levy calls out Shane Gillis SNL joke about women's clothing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Warning: This article contains offensive language.

Dan Levy isn't laughing at Shane Gillis's Saturday Night Live monologue — and he's not happy with men who find it funny, either.

In a Sunday Instagram video, Levy didn't mention Gillis by name, but called out the reference to women who wear short shorts to the gym as "whores," which Gillis made the night before in an introductory segment while hosting the long-running sketch comedy show.

"I haven't been to the gym in so long, I didn't know women just dress like whores now," Gillis said . "I'm sorry, there's no other way to describe [it]."

Gillis critiqued the neon short-shorts that he says he sees women wear at the gym, comparing the attire to the "artificial bait" of a fishing lure.

"And don't look; you're not allowed to look," Gillis said.

Shane Gillis, shown hosting the ESPY Awards in Los Angeles in 2025, drew criticism over the weekend for a joke included in his SNL monologue. (Mark J. Terrill/The Associated Press)

In response, Levy took to Instagram to voice his anger with the comments, saying he was "speechless" a joke of that nature would be broadcast on live television.

"Women wearing short shorts at the gym doesn't make them whores," Levy, star of Schitt's Creek who hosted SNL himself in 2021, said in an Instagram video. "It makes the men calling them whores misogynists."

"And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it's complacency that has created the environment [in] which women are sexually assaulted," Levy went on.

The Canadian-born comedian added that the objectification of women in the media by men will lead other men to "treat them like objects," and he said that everyone should be standing up for women in order to prevent their mistreatment.

The backlash to Gillis's comments comes amid a wave of outrage against the men who've become known as the Cornell 7, who are accused of a 2024 gang rape at an Ivy League frat house, and support for their accuser known only as Jane Doe.

The case has ignited scrutiny over the school's handling of the situation as well as conversations about consent and the culture that would have allowed the situation to happen in the first place.

Plenty of SNL fans also criticized the joke and those on the show who approved it, especially given the ongoing conversation around the alleged rape at Cornell.

"Who on earth approved the "wh*res" joke?! Read the room," one commenter said on the video of Gillis's monologue posted to the SNL Instagram account.

"Shane is very aware of the current moment with Jane Doe. And he chose that joke anyways," another wrote.

Others commented under Gillis's most recent, unrelated Instagram post, saying the monologue was misogynistic and enabled rape culture. Some fans came to his defence, saying the comedian should be able to make the jokes.

WATCH | Students march at UBC in support of Jane Doe: Students march at UBC in support of alleged Cornell University gang-rape victim | Duration closed caption 1:26 Dozens of students rallied at the University of British Columbia in solidarity with the alleged victim of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity. The victim, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil suit against the school and seven men, alleging the university protected the accused.

Gillis is no stranger to controversy, including on the SNL stage. In 2019, the comedian was hired and then quickly dropped as a cast member on the show after podcast clips of Gillis making homophobic jokes and using an Asian slur circulated.

He's since hosted the show on three occasions, however — in 2024, 2025 and again last Saturday. During his first SNL appearance, Gillis joked about a family member of his with Down syndrome, and he has been criticized for his use of homophobic language on podcasts.

LISTEN | In 'Tires', is Shane Gillis making fun of his character, or just being himself?: Commotion with Elamin Abdelmahmoud 15:33 What do we do with Tires?

The comments about women's appearances at the gym weren't the only ones to raise eyebrows this Saturday, either. He also said he'd "balded directly into an Adolf Hitler haircut" that he struggles to adjust without looking "gay."

"You're either gay or you're Hitler. Isn't that where we're at as a country," he quipped.

World.title: Canada, U.K. allies vow action after RAF Fairford terror plot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand joined her counterparts in 28 other countries in a statement condemning Iran's attacks against them and vowing to take action against anyone acting on behalf of Tehran. The statement comes after the U.K. cited Iran's involvement in a suspected plot targetin g the RAF Fairford airbase in Britain.

The alleged terror plot was foiled Sept. 27 when police arrested five London-based men on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offenses after a tip-off that three vans had been heading to the military airfield, which has been used to strike Iran.

The statement released Monday said the U.K. had concluded the incident demonstrates the Iranian regime's "continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors" and comes after a recent string of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, U.S. interests and Iranian journalists.

Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), a group tied to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), claimed responsibility for that string of attacks.

"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," the statement reads.

It is signed by the foreign ministers of Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States.

"Iran should be in no doubt that we are united and remain committed to safeguarding our sovereignty and strengthening our international coordination," the statement also said.

The RAF Fairford airbase in Fairford, England, is seen last week after police declared a major incident there and arrested several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. The men have since been released on bail. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)

U.K.'s Burnham says plot 'likely' co-ordinated by Iran

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford airbase in Britain was "highly likely" to have been co-ordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the IRGC.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been co-ordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told Parliament.

Tehran has rejected any suggestion it was involved in the Fairford incident, saying it amounted to "unfounded and malicious ​speculations." Iran's ambassador to the U.K., Seyed Ali Masouvi, denied any Iranian role in the suspected RAF Fairford plot, according to Iran's state news agency.

Details around the suspected plot remain thin. The five detained men were later released without charge on ‌police ⁠bail "under stringent conditions," and two other arrested men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been released.

Detectives have said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in vans seized along with the five men. However, both police and Burnham have pointed toward the involvement of a foreign state.

"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, seen at an event in Manchester, England, last week, told U.K. Parliament Monday the suspected plot against RAF Fairford was likely co-ordinated by Iran. (Christopher Furlong/Reuters)

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said he had summoned the Iranian ambassador while the ministry announced two Iranian nationals had been sanctioned.

The two men were Ruhollah Bazghandi, who Britain said was the IRGC's head of counterespionage operations, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, a facilitator for the already sanctioned Zindashti criminal network, which is accused of involvement in several plots against Iranian dissidents.

World.title: Democrats condemn 'deeply disturbing' raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's home ahead of U.S. midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. federal agents searched Ilhan Omar's home earlier on Monday as part of a criminal investigation, The Associated Press and other U.S. media outlets reported. Democratic leaders in the U.S. House of Representatives condemned the raid on Omar's home as 'deeply disturbing' and accused the Trump administration of a 'rogue abuse of power' just weeks ahead of November's midterm elections.

Democratic leaders in the U.S. House of Representatives have condemned a raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's home as "deeply disturbing" and accused the Trump administration of a "rogue abuse of power" just weeks ahead of November's midterm elections.

U.S. federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home earlier on Monday as part of a criminal investigation, The Associated Press and other U.S. media outlets reported, citing unnamed sources.

Citing two sources familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity, AP said Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents carried out the search of Omar's home. But the news agency said the nature and the scope of the investigation were unclear.

In a written statement later on Monday, Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said U.S. President Donald Trump had targeted Omar — a Minnesota congresswoman and the first Somali-American lawmaker in Congress — with "vile personal attacks" for years.

"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," reads the statement.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is shown at a news conference on Jan. 28 in Minneapolis. (Adam Gray/The Associated Press)

It was also signed by House minority whip Rep. Katherine Clark and Rep. Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

"The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," they said.

Federal criminal investigation

In a written statement to CBC News, the Justice Department said HSI agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" in the Washington, D.C., area, which had been secured by the department.

"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," it said.

U.S. Vice-President JD Vance has accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, without providing details, and has said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller were trying to figure out how to investigate the congresswoman.

Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies." Her office in March dismissed Vance's claims as fabricated and defamatory.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month that there was an "ongoing investigation" and "something's going to happen," AP reported.

Omar responded to Monday's raid on social media, saying it was "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced," she wrote on X.

Jacklyn Rogers, a spokesperson for Omar, also said in an email to CBC that "the Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."

Department of Homeland Security officers carry boxes from the Washington, D.C., residence of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

Target of Trump's attacks

Omar has been a frequent target of attacks by Trump and members of his Republican Party.

In February, Trump said Omar and fellow progressive Democrat, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, "should be institutionalized" and sent "back from where they came" after they shouted at him during his State of the Union address.

WATCH | Omar shouts at Trump during speech: ‘You killed Americans!’: Ilhan Omar shouts at Trump during speech | Duration 0:34 Trump’s comments about illegal aliens sparked shots from the chamber by Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar. After Trump asked attendees to stand if they agreed the government's duty is to protect citizens, not illegal aliens, he shamed those who remained seated. Omar repeatedly shouted, ‘You killed Americans!’

The Republican leader, who has carried out an immigration crackdown since he returned to the White House in early 2025, also has described Somali immigrants as "garbage" and said, "we don't want them in our country."

In a social media post last week, Trump said "the once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants."

Omar, a staunch critic of Trump's immigration policies, condemned the comments. "Trump's obsession with demonizing the Somali community is dangerous and reprehensible," she wrote on X.

Midterm elections loom

Monday's raid comes just weeks before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, with Republicans trying to retain slim control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Omar, who is running for re-election, represents a safe Democratic district where she won re-election in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points.

Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect the ‌outcome of any election or benefiting a candidate or political party.

The department has historically avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election.

Several Democrats spoke out in defence of Omar on Monday, with Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois calling the raid "an absolute abuse of power" and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, another fierce Trump critic, describing it as "straight out of the authoritarian playbook."

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz also said on social media: "Americans see this for what it is — President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."

World.title: How did Spain's housing crisis get so bad it forced the PM to call a snap election?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election on Oct. 5 amid unprecedented nationwide demonstrations over housing affordability.

The election, scheduled for Nov. 29, will bring Sánchez's parliamentary term to an end six months early, marking a bold political gamble by a prime minister known for taking risks.

The announcement followed the government's failure to secure parliamentary support for two proposed measures designed to address Spain's housing crisis. But a day after calling the election, the government approved the two decrees with some modifications. They include capping rents, a temporary ban on evictions and restricting companies from buying homes.

"It is only now, with protests and unrest spreading across Spain, that they have started paying attention to social housing and to the question of where people in this country can afford to live," said Sofía Olivares, 25, a student and spokesperson for housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo (Right to Housing).

While polls point to a right-wing victory, Sánchez is betting that the housing crisis will give him the political momentum needed to secure a parliamentary majority. Since becoming prime minister in 2018, he has had to rely on support from other parties to govern, as his socialist party has never held a majority in parliament.

By making housing affordability the centrepiece of his campaign, Sánchez hopes to unite progressive voters while deflecting attention from other pressing political vulnerabilities. Chief among these are corruption investigations targeting his inner circle and the ongoing crisis in Ceuta.

This past summer, an influx of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco reached the Spanish enclave. While most have since returned, thousands remain on the streets or in makeshift camps, overwhelming local infrastructure and fuelling calls from the right for stricter migration controls.

WATCH | Thousands of Moroccan migrants depart after pouring into Spanish enclave: Thousands of Moroccan migrants leave after storming Spanish enclave | Duration closed caption 1:56 Thousands of migrants from Morocco are voluntarily leaving Spain's Ceuta territory in North Africa, a day after pouring across the border. Ceuta's local government now believes as many 60,000 people came across as Spain considers tightening its border restrictions.

Protests follow eviction, death of senior

The housing demonstrations erupted following the forced eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, who became a national symbol of the crisis before her death on Oct. 7.

In Madrid, protesters camped outside in scenes reminiscent of the Indignados, or 15-M, movement in 2011, an uprising that reshaped Spanish politics by breaking up the two-party monopoly and giving rise to smaller political parties.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, 87, waits for police to arrive before being evicted from her home in Madrid on Sept. 23. She died on Oct. 7. (Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press/The Associated Press)

In Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, part of the Spanish archipelago off the west coast of Africa and one of Spain's most popular tourist destinations, residents have also taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest over housing.

Olivares, of Derecho al Techo, blames the regional government for placing tourism above housing. "It constantly holds back housing policies to prioritize tourism," she said, arguing that limited land and a lack of rent controls have further worsened the crisis.

Over the past year, families across the Canary Islands — one of Spain's poorest regions, where almost 30 per cent of people are at risk of poverty — have faced dozens of evictions. This week alone, the housing group has supported more than nine families facing eviction.

Sofía Olivares, right, of the housing advocacy group Derecho al Techo is shown at a protest to stop the eviction of eight families, in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain, on Oct. 7. (Sonia Håkansson Rivero)

"Property funds buy the buildings they live in, refuse to renew their contracts and throw them out onto the street,” Olivares said, adding that promises to rehouse tenants are often broken.

The lack of public housing is another major concern. "We've also been about 10 years without any type of social housing being built in the Canary Islands," she said, adding that more than 30,000 people in the islands alone are on waiting lists for public housing.

Social housing accounts for about 1.7 per cent of Spain's housing stock, well below the level in most European Union countries. The Bank of Spain estimates that the country currently lacks about 750,000 homes, a deficit expected to exceed one million by 2028.

Demonstrators calling for a change in the tourism model in the Canary Islands gather in front of beachfront tourist accommodations in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria on May 18, 2025. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)

Right-wing parties expected to win: polls

Right-wing parties have argued that Sánchez's relatively open approach to migration is placing pressure on Spain’s housing market.

Unlike many European leaders, Sánchez has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. Earlier this year, his government also launched a sweeping regularization program aimed at integrating hundreds of thousands of undocumented workers into the formal economy.

Polling points to a conservative coalition led by the People’s Party, alongside the anti-immigration party Vox, as the most likely outcome of next month's election. Such a result would bring the far right into Spain's national government for the first time since the country's transition to democracy in 1975, following Francisco Franco's dictatorship.

The People's Party warns that the rent caps proposed by Sánchez will backfire by driving homes off the market. The government's measures also largely failed to win the support of the real estate industry, which says they don't address the root cause of the problem: Spain’s structural housing shortage.

"We are trying to address a supply crisis without sufficiently increasing supply," said María Matos, head of research and a spokesperson at Fotocasa, one of Spain's leading real estate platforms.

"By focusing on regulating properties, rental contracts and landlords, we risk making it even harder to bring homes on to the market."

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is shown at the Moncloa Palace in Madrid on Oct. 6. He has argued that migration is necessary to sustain economic growth. (Bernat Armangue/The Associated Press)

Fotocasa's latest data suggests landlords may already be responding to new housing measures. "In just eight days, long-term rental supply fell by 4.2 per cent,” Matos said. She warns that "measures designed to protect tenants can end up creating barriers for those still trying to find a home."

She also called for greater investment in public housing. "Since 2013, the development of new social housing has practically come to a standstill, forcing more households to compete in the private market."

Matos said she wants more land to be made available for development, alongside faster planning approvals. "We need to unlock public and private land, and speed up building permits to prevent projects from being delayed for years."

A man sleeps on a street near a protest calling for political action to address Spain's housing crisis, in Barcelona on Oct. 6. (Nacho Doce/Reuters)

Garazi González, 36, who now lives with her partner and their baby in an apartment building belonging to his family, said she has experienced the affordability crisis first-hand and supports the protests "100 per cent."

Four years ago, after renting an apartment in central Madrid for eight years, she saw her monthly rent rise from 800 to 950 euros (about $1,275 to $1,500 Cdn). Her landlady then proposed raising it to 1,500 euros ($2,400 Cdn).

"She said prices in the area had gone up and she couldn't keep charging me so little. She gave me just one month to leave," González said.

"I know people whose rents were raised to push them out, or who live in fear of being evicted from homes they've lived in for years. Others live in gentrified areas where vulture funds buy entire buildings and kick everyone out."

Despite her disappointment with the current government, González said preventing the far right from returning to power is now her biggest priority.

"I'm not entirely happy with the left because they haven't done enough on housing or other issues,” she said. "But I want to prevent fascism from coming back. I care about protecting social rights.... As a woman and a mother to a daughter, I worry deeply about her future."

World.title: 'We can’t deal with it in Canada': Some women turn to Mexico for endometriosis care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Noelle Menu, 37, says the pain began to darken her reality at a pivotal moment in her life — once she and her husband decided to try for kids, when she was 26.

She stopped taking her birth control, which she had been on for a long period, and said she began experiencing pain she'd never had before.

The pain came to define and limit her life, she said, and it seemed nothing could relieve it. She suffered through delays in diagnosis, as well as emergency room visits, a hysterectomy and being placed on waitlists stretching years to see specialists and receive treatment.

At that point, it was "literally destroying my life," she said, "and to hear it’s about three to four years to see somebody here, I was just so emotional, so devastated."

Soon, she realized: "We can’t deal with it in Canada."

So Menu and her husband pulled from their savings and went into debt to seek private treatment at EndoGlobal in Tijuana, Mexico, which cost about $35,000 including airfare, a multi-day hotel stay and other costs.

It’s a journey some Canadian women suffering from endometriosis are taking because they feel their health-care system has failed them.

The condition affects one in 10 women, and Canada is doing a "poor" job at providing them care, according to a November 2025 report by the House of Commons health committee — and in addition to causing undue pain, the lost productivity due to the disorder costs the Canadian economy some $2.5 billion a year.

WATCH | Why Menu spent $35K on endometriosis surgery in Mexico: Calgary woman spends savings on endometriosis surgery in Mexico | Duration 1:06 Noelle Menu, a Calgary woman living with Stage 4 endometriosis, says doctors dismissed and misdiagnosed her for years, even after multiple surgeries and thousands of dollars spent on private health care. After being told she'd have to wait 30-40 months to see a specialist, Menu says she and her husband drained their funds to travel to Tijuana, Mexico, for surgery, at a cost of about $35,000.

Gender bias plays a role

Endometriosis is a chronic condition where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus begins to grow and spread to other parts of the body. This tissue thickens and breaks down according to a woman's menstrual cycle, and can cause severe inflammation, scarring and pain during periods.

It can take an average of five years to be diagnosed with endometriosis in Canada, the parliamentary committee found, while some people have waited for up to 20 years before doctors linked their pain to the disease.

Even after that, it can take, on average, between six to 18 months to see a specialist and up to 24 months for surgery, it said.

It can be difficult to diagnose because its symptoms can resemble other conditions, and the level of reported pain sometimes doesn't match detectable tissue growth.

WATCH | Similar issues in P.E.I.: Islanders with endometriosis say it's taking too long to get medical care | Duration closed caption 1:58 Some people on P.E.I. living with endometriosis say they've been waiting a long time to get the specialized treatment they need. For some, it’s been years. CBC's Gwyneth Egan has more.

The report found that gender bias plays a significant role in those issues — along with a taboo around discussing menstrual issues, it is often assumed that this kind of pain is "just part of being a woman."

Menu, a supply-chain systems adviser, said she was forced to reduce her workday in half because of the pain. Sometimes, she could barely make it through to the evening.

"This disease is just debilitating for some women, and I really wish there was more awareness around it and that doctors would take us women seriously."

Days before her flight, she told CBC News, "It’s hard to be so hopeful just because of the previous surgeries I’ve had, but I’m feeling a lot more hopeful this time."

Dr. Jorge Zavala is one of the founders of EndoGlobal, and he says endometriosis mimics cancer in the way that it spreads, without being as destructive.

Dr. Jorge Zavala, one of the founders of EndoGlobal, says there is a general lack of awareness around endometriosis among doctors who don’t necessarily know what to look for in a patient to get to an accurate diagnosis. (Alessandro Molatore/CBC)

Zavala said doctors generally lack awareness about the condition, which is why diagnoses can take so long.

"As a doctor, if you’re not trained in something, you’re not going to be able to diagnose it. It could be poking your eye, but if you are not trained to see it, you’re not going to see it," said Zavala.

2-year wait time for surgery

Vanessa Papiernik, 42, says it took about 30 years for her to arrive at her diagnosis — and it came with a cancer scare.

Papiernik, a veterinarian in Victoria, said she suffered through nine months of "significant" and "debilitating" pain until she landed an appointment for a colonoscopy.

"I was purely in survival mode," said Papiernik.

Vanessa Papiernik, 42, undergoes pre-surgery exams at the EndoGlobal treatment centre. She says it took about 30 years for her to arrive at her endometriosis diagnosis and it came with a cancer scare. (Alessandro Molatore/CBC)

She would take Advil, put on maternity clothes because of the bloating and strap a heating pad around her waist to go to work.

"I would push the pain aside, but as soon as I got home, I would realize, 'Wow, this is very dangerous, what I’m going through right now.'"

Her colonoscopy found a mass. For two weeks as she waited for the biopsy results, she feared it was cancer; her sister had died from colon cancer 10 years earlier. However, the results showed it was endometriosis that had infiltrated through the layers of her colon.

She was referred to a centre in Vancouver, but faced a one-year wait to see a specialist, plus another year for surgery, said Papiernik.

"Living like this for two years was just not an option for me," she said.

The post-surgery recovery floor at EndoGlobal in Tijuana. (Alessandro Molatore/CBC)

She eventually booked a trip to the same centre as Menu, landing the same week the Calgary woman was scheduled for her own procedure.

There were more than 30 Canadian women receiving treatment there within the same timeframe, said Papiernik.

"We need to really come face to face with the fact that this is, to some extent, it’s discrimination against women," said Dr. Nicholas Leyland, president of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.

"If this were happening with the same degree of pain in a male, it would have been fixed a long time ago."

'Complex surgical issues'

Leyland said that there are not enough specially trained gynecologists in Canada to deal with "the complex surgical issues," and that the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach to care, including psychologists and physiotherapists.

The House of Commons report’s top recommendation called on Ottawa to "develop a national action plan on endometriosis" to deal with the "gaps and barriers that hinder awareness, diagnosis and treatment."

The federal government responded saying that Statistics Canada would gather data on conditions like endometriosis; the agency has been collecting responses since Sept. 28 and will do so till Jan. 15, 2027.

The Canadian Institute of Health Research has also invested $4.9 million in endometriosis research between 2020 and 2025, Ottawa said.

Shortly before her procedure, Menu said doctors in Mexico found a large mass that threatened to block her bowels and send her into septic shock. She said she was two weeks away from emergency surgery.

"For me to hear that I could have been in emergency surgery and my specialist appointment [in Canada] was a 30- to 40-month wait…. It makes me so mad," said Menu, in a late-September interview with CBC News after her surgery.

With the help of her husband, Menu took a walk around the post-surgical floor, which has about 14 beds.

Most of her neighbours were Canadian women. They greeted each other as they passed.

"I was just so grateful that they were able to find everything," said Menu.

"I’m on the other side of it now. I’m really happy for that."

World.title: Michael Jordan jersey sets $14M US record for basketball memorabilia, auction house says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A game-worn, autographed Michael Jordan road jersey from the 1998 NBA Finals has been privately sold for $14 million US, an auction house announced Monday, calling it the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia.

Pennsylvania-based Hunt Auctions announced the private treaty sale and identified the buyer as Miami real estate investor Ron Firman. The red jersey is the one Jordan wore in Game 2 of that series on June 5, 1998; he and the Chicago Bulls beat the Utah Jazz that night to even the matchup at a game apiece.

Jordan and the Bulls would go on to win the series in six games, the sixth and final title of his Hall of Fame career. That 1997-98 season was the subject of the 10-episode "Last Dance" documentary series that was released in 2020.

"While Michael Jordan's importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art," said David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions. "We are very pleased to have been able to facilitate this historic sale which serves as another benchmark for our industry."

The $14 million price would be the second-biggest known cost for a game-worn jersey, behind the $24.12 million paid in 2024 for the jersey worn by Babe Ruth of the New York Yankees when he hit the "called shot" home run against the Chicago Cubs at Wrigley Field in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series.

This sale becomes at least the third time a Jordan jersey from that 1998 finals has fetched at least $10 million. A jersey from Game 1 was sold at auction for about $10.1 million in 2022 and a jersey from Game 3 was auctioned last month for about $12.3 million.

"Michael Jordan was an incredibly talented player who is admired around the world." Firman said in a news release distributed by the auction house. "I'm very excited about the purchase."

The jersey that Firman purchased was originally bought from the Bulls by a private collector in 2003, Hunt said, adding that it "has remained within a succinct chain of custody having only changed hands once from the original purchaser."

Just about anything related to the 1998 finals and Jordan's final season with the Bulls has been the subject of massive interest in the collector space. In 2023, a pair of Air Jordan sneakers that he wore in Game 2 against the Jazz was sold by Sotheby's for $2.2 million, touted at the time as "a new world record for the most valuable sneakers ever sold."
