World.title: From real-world Catrinas to AI cinema: An artist’s next Día de Muertos chapter
World.content:
When we started working around Día de Muertos in 2019, none of us imagined where it would lead.

At the beginning, we were simply a group of friends traveling through different parts of Mexico, creating Catrina makeup, putting together wardrobe and photographing the results against landscapes we loved. There was no elaborate business model behind it. We enjoyed creating characters, traveling and showing a little of Mexico through photography.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Alejandro Su | Creative Director (@alesuart)

Eventually, people began asking if they could take part in what they were seeing.

A photo session slowly became an experience. Visitors wanted makeup, but they also wanted to understand where the tradition came from. They wanted to visit the places we photographed, try the food, meet local people and experience Día de Muertos beyond the image they had seen online.

That changed our work considerably. Over the following years, we began incorporating photography, transportation, lodging, traditional food and tours with certified guides. The makeup was still important, but it became one part of something larger.

By 2024, the Catrina market had also changed. There were many more artists offering Día de Muertos makeup and photography, and for a while I wondered whether it was time for me to stop doing it altogether.

Instead, I decided that we needed to evolve. I became less interested in making another Catrina portrait and more interested in building complete worlds around the people we photographed.

Building El Viaje de las Ánimas

One of the projects that pushed that idea further was El Viaje de las Ánimas.

The project had been in my head for years. It actually came from a dream, and I kept the idea almost entirely to myself while I tried to save enough money to produce it properly.

For around four years, I thought about how to turn that image into something physical. When we finally made it, almost everything had to be real. The Catrinas were real models. The cempasúchil was natural. We needed costumes, makeup, transportation, lodging and a large amount of coordination.

The production took place in Xochimilco. We rented three trajineras for more than 11 hours and moved large quantities of cempasúchil into the location. More than 12 people were involved.

Seeing something that had existed in my imagination for years finally become real was incredibly satisfying. It was also expensive and logistically difficult.

That experience made me much more aware of the relationship between an idea and the resources needed to execute it. Sometimes the image you want to create only exists for a few hours, yet reaching that moment can require years of savings, weeks of preparation and a large team.

I began thinking about what else we could create if those physical limitations were different.

Learning AI instead of expecting instant results

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Alejandro Su | Creative Director (@alesuart)

I became seriously interested in artificial intelligence at the beginning of 2026. Like many people, I started by experimenting, and, honestly, my first results were not very good.

The images could be interesting, but they did not have the consistency, quality or level of control I expected. Characters changed between shots. Locations changed. Cameras behaved unpredictably. A scene that looked good on its own often did not work when placed next to another scene.

That was when I realized how different generating an image is from telling a story.

I decided to slow down some of our regular Catrina productions and travel projects and dedicate more time to studying these tools. There was a lot to learn. If a character walks into a room, where is the door? If the camera cuts to the opposite side, is the geography still correct? If the same person appears five minutes later, do they still look like the same person? If a dog follows someone through several scenes, does its behavior make sense?

These may sound like very basic filmmaking questions, but generative models do not necessarily solve them for you.

One idea I began exploring during this period was something I call “Sacred Nature.” The concept came from looking at things we see every day — flowers, landscapes, plants — and asking what would happen if we treated them as something monumental.

Instead of using nature as background decoration, I wanted it to dominate the frame: giant flowers, exaggerated natural environments and landscapes that made familiar elements feel extraordinary.

AI gave me a way to experiment with that scale without physically building everything.

Adding AI to the work we already had

We now use AI in several parts of our workflow, although we are still learning constantly. Sometimes it is very practical. We can recover an image that was slightly blurred, refine details, assist with video editing or reconstruct a shot that did not work as expected.

During high season, it can also help us deliver photography more quickly while maintaining the visual identity we have developed with our photographers over the years.

Other times, AI allows us to take an existing production somewhere completely new. A real portrait can inspire an environment that would have been impossible for us to build physically. An idea that would once have required a huge set can now be tested before we invest in making it real.

I do not see that as replacing our previous work. We still work with real makeup, real flowers, photography, travel, models and cultural experiences. Those things remain central to what we do. AI simply gave us another tool.

The most important result of that evolution so far has been “Cada Noviembre.”

The real stories behind ‘Cada Noviembre’

“Cada Noviembre” was inspired by three different experiences. The first happened in Oaxaca.

One of the things I love about traveling during Día de Muertos is how easily people begin talking to you. There is often a warmth and openness that leads to conversations you would never expect. During one of those trips, we met a man who told us he was the last living member of his family. Every year he visited the cemetery and went from grave to grave, remembering the relatives who were no longer there.

He had even purchased his own grave. He wanted to prepare it himself and know what it would look like before the day came when he would occupy it. I never forgot that conversation.

Years later, it became the foundation for Juan, the main character in “Cada Noviembre.”

The second part of the story came from my own life. Juan suffers from a progressive pulmonary illness. I chose that because of my own experiences with pulmonary hospitals and because of the people I have met there.

When you spend time in hospitals, you hear stories. You see other families. You begin to understand how differently illness changes everyday life. Film frequently uses cancer to represent serious illness. I wanted to talk about something I knew more personally.

The third element was the dog. I kept thinking about a simple question: What happens when a dog loses the person it considers its family?

In the film, Juan initially does not want the stray xoloitzcuintle following him. Over time, however, the animal becomes part of his routine. They walk together. The dog waits for him. Their relationship develops quietly until companionship becomes family.

I wanted that relationship to feel ordinary rather than magical. The xolo does not understand death like a person. It simply remembers routines.

For me, that made the ending much stronger.

Making the film

We made “Cada Noviembre” in approximately three weeks with a team of five people. Three people worked on sound, one person supported editing and post-production, and I handled the generative visual production. I wrote the screenplay, directed the project, developed the characters and created the AI-generated video sequences.

It was a very intense three weeks.

The biggest challenge was continuity. Juan could not suddenly become another person between scenes. The cemetery needed to remain geographically consistent. The xolo had to look and behave like the same animal. Juan’s house, his cane, the photographs, flowers and lighting all had to remain recognizable.

Even Juan’s walking pace mattered because his illness progresses throughout the film.

Sometimes we generated a shot where the performance worked perfectly but the camera angle was wrong. Other times the picture worked and the audio did not. We learned to reconstruct certain shots instead of throwing everything away and starting again.

The process became much closer to filmmaking than I initially expected. There were scripts, revisions, continuity problems, sound problems, editing decisions and many failed takes — except our “takes” were generations.

A Mexican story traveling internationally

Today, “Cada Noviembre” is participating in an international AI film festival. What makes me proud is not simply that it was made with artificial intelligence. What matters to me is that Día de Muertos is at the center of it.

This is the same culture we began working with when we were painting Catrinas with friends in 2019.

Then we traveled through Mexico. Then we created cultural experiences. Then came El Viaje de las Ánimas, which we built almost entirely in the physical world.

Now we are telling a complete cinematic story using another set of tools.

The film has received responses from people in Mexico, the United States and other countries. Some identify with Juan’s illness. Others have lost parents or grandparents. Others simply recognize the loyalty of a dog waiting for someone it loves.

That response has convinced me that technology is not the part people ultimately remember. They remember the story.

What AI changes, and what it does not

Artificial intelligence has made things possible for us that would have been financially unrealistic only a few years ago. A small independent team can now attempt visual ideas that once might have required a much larger production budget. That is exciting.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Alejandro Su | Creative Director (@alesuart)

But I also think people underestimate how much human work remains.

AI does not know why Juan matters. It does not know what Día de Muertos means to my family or to the people we have met throughout Mexico. It does not automatically understand when a cultural detail feels authentic and when it feels like a stereotype.

Those decisions still belong to us.

For our team, AI is not a replacement for the work we have done since 2019. It is part of its evolution. We still want to travel. We still want to work with flowers, makeup, photography and real people. We still want to create physical experiences.

Now we can also take the stories we discover along the way and imagine them at a scale that previously felt impossible.

We started with Catrina makeup. Today, we are making films.

The tools have changed considerably, but the reason we create has stayed surprisingly simple. We want to tell stories about Mexico and find new ways to share them with the world.

Alejandro Su is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: How a Baja road rally found an unexpected oasis in San Ignacio
World.content:
On Day 8 of the Baja XL Rally down the Baja California Peninsula, we passed through San Ignacio in Baja California Sur. Again.

It was beautiful and vibrant, as visitors and locals wandered around the old stone streets. Small family-owned restaurants with open patios filled the square, the smell of fresh food sizzling on a skillet. Misión San Ignacio, founded nearly 300 years ago, was still proudly presiding over the square, and this was our first time seeing it all in daylight.

Then a siren in the distance, and a voice booming over a PA system: “Wooo, the Fire Department San Ignacio is here! Welcome, Baja XL!” The vice mayor and his brother, the comandante, were arriving to greet us, and had decided to make an entrance the best way they could, with their prized fire truck and ambulance.

It was a welcome sight after the grueling week that had preceded, but a week we wouldn’t soon forget.

The BajaXL Rally

My teammate Derek and I were not only taking part in the Baja XL but also filming a documentary about it.

Like the famous Baja 1000, the XL takes on the same rugged wilderness, only it isn’t a race. It is a backcountry expedition, much longer than the 1000, lasting 10 full days.

When the original organizer stepped down, Dave Moore and Wilson Craig, the rally’s “co-jefes,” took up the torch to keep the Baja XL alive as a community event.

This was the first community-led Baja XL: no sponsors, no official organization, no emergency support. No winners. No losers. No competition.

Derek and I dove into the experience a touch overconfident. We are seasoned emergency-management professionals, and his daily driver, a mostly stock F-150, seemed like a solid rig.

However, we quickly realized we were in over our heads before we even started, but that is another story.

Giving back to Baja

The Baja XL selects a charity for each rally. For ours, Dave and Wilson had chosen the schools in the village of San Ignacio, so every team brought backpacks and hard-to-source school supplies for the kids — colored pencils, crayons, coloring books and workbooks.

Before the rally, Dave and Wilson had also organized a charity bingo in Benicia, California. Our first trip into San Ignacio had come a few days earlier, to deliver the donations and to find shelter after some rough days off-roading.

We’ve got cows

By Day 3 we had dug out one truck twice, watched two teams break and one turn back, and blown the bushings on a rear shock. We were getting our asses kicked, Baja checking the ego we had brought across the border. We did not clear the dirt until after dark, then drove the highway at night.

Just as we cleared town, a black cow stepped into our lane from the centerline, washed out by oncoming headlights. He was so big his head was above the driver’s side mirror. A sliver of luck and Derek’s last-second save threaded the needle.

Forget the plan. We got off the road and found food and sleep in the first town we came to. Anything to get out of the truck.

That is how we rolled into San Ignacio for the first time, catching a glimpse of the square illuminated only by the light spilling from the few stores and the one family-run taquería still open.

All I could do was laugh

We started Day 4 hoping to turn the trip around, but Day 4 had other plans in store for us.

We woke to a leaking water line and a lake developing in our room. To be fair to Ignacio Springs, they had done us a solid: with no rooms left, they gave us a roof and a bed in a partially built expansion across the road. They could have turned us away.

Derek went to let the staff know, and I went out to make a tailgate brew. I overindulge in caffeine, so I had brought grounds, a Jetboil and a camping French press. Nearly 20 years as a firefighter means I am used to coffee that could float a horseshoe.

Unfortunately, as I set up one of the few joys I had lugged into Baja, I set my thermos on fire because I had forgotten to remove the plastic guard on the bottom. Everything was derailing so fast, all I could do was laugh.

The owners made things right and refunded our payment. They were extremely kind, and for that alone I would go back and try one of their yurts. That kindness, in hindsight, was the front edge of our turning point, and a first introduction of what San Ignacio is like.

‘Good vibes from here on’

Eventually we cleared out and, well behind schedule, followed Dave and Wilson to the school to drop our donation. The school was not what you are picturing. No classrooms, no playground, no school buses. It was a grove of palm trees with a large clearing in the middle, beside the water. A woman directed us to a table to add our donations to the others.

By the time the last truck came through, the Baja XL teams had donated enough backpacks and school supplies for all 120 kids in the village’s three schools, plus toys, stickers and soccer balls.

The woman who received the donations had a relaxed, positive energy. “Good vibes from here on. No more breakdowns,” she said as we loaded up to head out. It was not a wish for our trip. It was more of a statement. I like to think it was someone in touch with the place, letting Baja know it was safe to allow us passage and show us why people fall in love with the land and people.

If that was the case, Baja heard the message. We rounded the southern end of the peninsula and started back north. We had cleared halfway. Day 8 brought us back to San Ignacio.

A heartfelt thanks

That morning, at a fuel shack in a speck of a town, Wilson received a video message from the mayor and other San Ignacio officials thanking the rally for the school supplies.

Wilson messaged back and learned the volunteer fire department could barely afford fuel for its trucks. A collection went around on a payment app, our version of passing the hat, enough to fill the fire truck, the ambulance and the service vehicles, and the route bent back to San Ignacio.

The approach to San Ignacio announces itself. The trail turns green, then the palms, then the square. In daylight we could finally see the Misión San Igancio that had stood sentry over the square in the dark.

Welcomed inside to film, we stood at the far end of the nave, in front of the ornate altar, and stared up at the domed ceiling and open beams.

‘You saved a life with this’

In the distance, a siren sounded, and from around the bend at the end of the road, a fire truck came into view with lights flashing. Juan, the vice mayor, was driving and on the PA, welcoming our rally into town. His brother Marco Antonio, the comandante, followed in the ambulance.

After all those years in the fire service, I can spot an old rig in a heartbeat; this one was about 40 years old and still said Riverside County on the side. These guys were stoked for what they had, and they deserved to be. Juan and Marco showed us “the most complete ambulance in all of Baja.” We arranged the donation, shared Baja XL challenge coins and a few gifts, and headed out to the trails.

We set up camp around a tiki just off the beach near Guerrero Negro, beside the largest saltworks in the world, and the sun set as we got the fire going. Around that fire, Wilson’s phone lit up with a thank-you video from Juan: the fire truck at a fuel pump, the ambulance pulling up on the other side.

“Thank you, Wilson, Baja XL and everyone in the U.S. We love you. You saved a life with this.”

The oasis we didn’t know existed

Baja withholds no challenges. That’s part of its appeal. But it also rewards deeply those willing to face the challenges. When we needed it most, San Ignacio showed us what an oasis is: a bed when there was nowhere else to sleep, kindness when the room flooded, a woman at a school promising no more breakdowns, and a reason to come back.

Between Day 4 and Day 8, between a leaking water line and a siren welcoming a convoy of strangers, San Ignacio was the same. We were not.

What’s next for Baja XL?

The 2027 Baja XL has chosen the San Ignacio Fire Department as its charity, with Bingo for Bomberos on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, at The Chill in Benicia. Details on supporting the charity and on joining the rally are on the Baja XL website and social media channels.

“Into Uncertainty,” the documentary shot from inside the rally, was completed in August 2026 and has been submitted to Sundance, SXSW, Big Sky and Slamdance.

Go see Baja, and go see San Ignacio. If you see Juan and the fire truck, tell him we said hello.

Ryan G. Christen is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Venezuela’s Rodríguez Launches Food Plan at FAO in Rome
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

VENEZUELA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven oil reserves.

— What happened Delcy Rodríguez launched the Venezuela Alimenta plan in Rome.

— When Monday, 12 October, at the FAO World Food Forum.

— The US angle Per El Nacional, she blamed US sanctions for a 16% output fall.

— The bill A local economy law goes to the National Assembly soon.

— Still open The plan’s budget, timeline and funding sources were not given.

Venezuela’s acting president used a United Nations stage to launch a zero-hunger plan. She also blamed Washington’s sanctions for years of lost food production.

Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president, launched the Venezuela Alimenta plan in Rome on Monday, 12 October, at a food forum. The host was the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the United Nations agency that leads global efforts against hunger.

She also blamed more than 1,000 US sanctions for a 16% fall in food output, according to El Nacional. The remarks matter in Washington, which backs talks between her government and the opposition that resume on Wednesday.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Venezuela ranks 13th of 14 with 27.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (81); weakest: economic relationships (0). Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Venezuela Alimenta Plan Promises

Venezuela’s Foreign Ministry said Rodríguez activated the plan from FAO headquarters with the goal of “Hambre Cero”, or zero hunger. The ministry said the plan aims to link every stage of national food production with social distribution networks.

Rodríguez said the plan would “engranar todos los procesos productivos de alimentos”, meaning it would mesh all food production processes together. She named three priorities: stronger models, national unity and a higher international profile.

The Foreign Ministry also said the government will push a law on the local economy. It is meant to connect community producers with large agro-industrial firms.

El Nacional, a Caracas daily, reported that the bill will go to the National Assembly in the coming days. Neither source gave a budget, a timeline or a list of measures for the Venezuela Alimenta plan.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Rodríguez Blames US Sanctions

According to El Nacional, Rodríguez blamed “más de 1.000 medidas coercitivas unilaterales” imposed by the United States, mostly from 2017 onwards. She said they cut the agri-food chain’s output by 16% by blocking credit and imports of seeds, machinery and parts.

She also credited national political dialogue and diplomatic talks with the United States for helping end the supply crisis. Food, she said, should never be used as a tool of pressure or political confrontation.

Rodríguez cited figures from the FAO’s SOFI 2026 hunger report, saying undernourishment fell from 5.3% in 2025 to 3% this year. On her figures, about one Venezuelan in 33 would still be undernourished.

These figures come from her speech and were not checked against the FAO report itself. El Nacional also reported that some Venezuelans living in Rome protested against her presence at the forum.

What It Means for US Readers

The speech shows the Caracas government blaming US sanctions in public while it negotiates under US sponsorship. That double message will shape how Congress and the State Department judge any further sanctions relief.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio backed the talks after meeting opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera in Washington on 9 October, El Nacional reported. A new round between the 2015 National Assembly bloc and the government starts on Wednesday, 14 October.

For US investors and food exporters, a push for local production could mean fewer import openings over time. For now, no tariff, quota or import rule has been announced alongside the plan.

What Is Not Known

The government has not published the text of the local economy bill or the cost of the Venezuela Alimenta plan. It is also unclear how the plan would be financed while some US measures remain in place.

The 16% figure and the count of more than 1,000 measures are the government’s own claims. No independent study cited in Rome confirms them.

What Comes Next

The next step is the bill’s arrival at the National Assembly, which the government says will happen within days. The talks with the opposition resume on Wednesday, 14 October.

In Rome, Rodríguez also met Angola’s president, João Lourenço, and Dominican president Luis Abinader, the Foreign Ministry said. The speech does not change any US sanction by itself.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is the Venezuela Alimenta Plan?

It is a government programme launched on 12 October to link food production with social distribution networks. Its stated goal is zero hunger.

Who Is Delcy Rodríguez?

She is Venezuela’s acting president and leads the government in Caracas. She is negotiating with the opposition in talks backed by the United States.

What Did She Say About US Sanctions?

She said more than 1,000 US measures cut farm and food output by 16%. She also credited talks with Washington for easing the supply crisis.

When Do the Venezuela Talks Resume?

A new round between the government and the 2015 National Assembly bloc starts on Wednesday, 14 October. Marco Rubio said on 9 October that the process has US support.

World.title: Paraguay Economic Activity Jumps 6.7%
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PARAGUAY · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened The central bank published August activity data on Monday, 12 October.

— The figure The monthly activity index rose 6.7% from August 2025.

— Previous value Growth was 5.5% in July and 5.7% for January to August.

— The driver Industry, electricity and construction grew 12.2% year on year.

— The weak spot Primary output fell 2.7% as maize, wheat and cotton harvests shrank.

— Credit rating Fitch rates Paraguay BB+, one notch below investment grade.

Paraguay’s economy accelerated in August, powered by electricity, factories and construction. Smaller harvests were the main drag.

Paraguay economic activity grew 6.7% in August from a year earlier, the Banco Central del Paraguay (BCP) said on Monday, 12 October. That was faster than July’s 5.5% and lifted growth for the first eight months to 5.7%.

The figures matter to US holders of Paraguay’s dollar bonds, since Fitch rates the country one notch below investment grade. Paraguay, a landlocked soy and beef exporter between Brazil and Argentina, is also Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in South America.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Electricity and Factories Drive the August Jump

The IMAEP, the central bank’s monthly indicator of economic activity, is an early guide to gross domestic product. Its secondary sector, covering manufacturing, electricity, water and construction, grew 12.2% year on year.

Electricity generation showed a large annual increase, the BCP said, without giving a figure. Paraguay co-owns two giant hydropower dams, Itaipu with Brazil and Yacyretá with Argentina.

Manufacturing grew 8.2% on the year, led by oils, dairy, milling and bakery, and pharmaceuticals. Meat processing, sugar, drinks and tobacco, and textiles declined.

Construction also grew, helped by faster work on public and private projects. From January to August, the secondary sector expanded 5.9% and manufacturing 4.2%.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Paraguay economy Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Farm Output Falls as Services Grow More Slowly

The primary sector, which includes crops and livestock, fell 2.7% from August 2025. The bank blamed smaller harvests of maize, wheat, cotton and yerba mate, the leaf used for a popular tea.

Livestock grew on higher pig and poultry slaughter and more milk and eggs. Cattle slaughter, however, kept falling as ranchers rebuild their herds.

For the full year, the BCP still expects a good farm result, mainly from a larger 2025/2026 soybean crop. Primary-sector growth for January to August stood at 8.5%.

Services grew 4.5% in August and 4.9% in the first eight months. Commerce, finance, real estate and information services rose, while transport, hotels and restaurants, and telecoms declined.

Core Growth Broadens Beyond Dams and Harvests

The BCP also publishes a measure that strips out agriculture and the two binational dams. That core measure rose 6.5% year on year in August, up from 4.3% in July.

So far this year, the core measure is up 5.1%, against 4.9% through July. The faster pace suggests growth is spreading beyond hydropower and harvests.

La Nación, an Asunción daily, reported the release on Monday as a sign of a robust economy. The central bank stressed that the August numbers are based on preliminary information.

What It Means for You

For US bond investors, faster growth supports Paraguay’s credit story. Fitch affirmed the country’s BB+ rating with a positive outlook, the central bank said on Wednesday, 30 September.

BB+ is the highest sub-investment-grade rating on the Fitch scale. A positive outlook signals that an upgrade is possible, though not guaranteed.

The guaraní traded at about 5,768 per US dollar early on Monday, on open.er-api.com data. ABC Color reported on Sunday that the falling dollar is challenging motorcycle makers, who want a more predictable exchange rate.

The data arrived on the day China sanctioned a Paraguayan minister over Taiwan. Paraguay’s government rejected the sanctions and reaffirmed its support for Taiwan, La Nación reported.

What Is Not Known

The August figures are preliminary and may be revised with the next report. The BCP gave no growth rate for electricity generation or construction.

No market consensus forecast for August was available for comparison. It is also unclear whether recent flooding along the Paraná River, reported by La Nación, will weigh on activity in later months.

What Comes Next

The BCP publishes the index with a lag of about 42 days. September data are therefore expected around mid-November.

Full-year growth depends heavily on soybeans and hydropower. One strong month does not guarantee that the 5.7% year-to-date pace will hold.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is the IMAEP?

It is the monthly activity indicator of the Banco Central del Paraguay, covering farming, industry and services. Economists use it as an early signal of gross domestic product.

How Fast Did Paraguay Economic Activity Grow in August?

It grew 6.7% from August 2025, according to preliminary central bank data. Growth for January to August reached 5.7%.

What Held Growth Back?

The primary sector fell 2.7% on smaller maize, wheat, cotton and yerba mate harvests. Cattle slaughter also declined as ranchers rebuild their herds.

Why Does It Matter to US Investors?

Paraguay issues dollar bonds, and Fitch rates it BB+ with a positive outlook. Strong growth can support the case for a future upgrade to investment grade.

When Is the Next Release?

September data are expected around mid-November, given a publication lag of about 42 days. The August figures may be revised then.

World.title: Peru Proposes School Expulsions in 3 Tiers
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PERU · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened President Keiko Fujimori presented school discipline guidelines on Monday.

— The core change Expulsion returns for students who commit very serious offences.

— The structure Offences are graded as minor, serious or very serious.

— The numbers School violence reports reached 4,759 in September, up 70.6%.

— The US parallel Washington ordered new school discipline guidance in April 2025.

— Still open The legal instrument and the date it takes effect are unknown.

Peru’s conservative government wants schools to expel the most disruptive students again. The plan echoes the push for stricter school discipline in the United States.

Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori presented school discipline guidelines on Monday, 12 October, that would revive expulsions for the gravest offences. The move mirrors a US debate that led to a White House order on school discipline in April 2025.

Andina, Peru’s state news agency, reported that Fujimori said order “must also return to the schools.” She added that the government would not accept bullying, school violence or sexual harassment.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the School Discipline Guidelines Say

The document is called the Guidelines for the Management of School Discipline, according to Andina. It sets duties for principals, teachers, parents and the regional and local education offices that run Peru’s public schools.

Offences are graded as minor, serious or very serious, with sanctions meant to be proportional to each level. Separation or expulsion of a student is among the possible measures for the most serious cases.

Teachers would regain authority to correct and guide students, and a conduct grade would return. Students are urged to report incidents to a teacher or the principal.

Those accused of abuse would be referred to the Public Ministry, Peru’s independent prosecution service. Victims should not be forced to leave their school, Andina reported.

The government also says no expelled student may be left without schooling. Andina lists reinsertion schools, hybrid classrooms, community centres and psychological support as options.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Peru politics Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Peru Is Acting Now

Fujimori leads Fuerza Popular, a conservative party that campaigned on law and order. During her campaign she proposed large prisons modelled on El Salvador’s.

Reports of school violence have climbed sharply this year. The education ministry’s SíseVe system logged 4,759 reports in September, up 70.6% from 2,789 a year earlier, RPP reported.

From January to September, the system logged 16,550 reports, up 24.9% on the same period of 2025. RPP noted that the system counts reports, not unique cases, so one incident can appear more than once.

The push followed an abuse case at the Liceo Naval Almirante Guise, a navy-run school in Lima, in September. Education Minister José Antonio Chang then announced a protocol to expel students for serious misconduct.

On Tuesday, 6 October, Chang said expulsion “definitely returns,” El Peruano, the official gazette, reported. He said the draft would be open for comments for five to ten days and then take effect.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the plan follows the same path as Washington’s own policy shift. On 23 April 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order titled “Reinstating Common Sense School Discipline Policies.”

That order told the US Department of Education to issue new guidance on discipline and civil rights. Peru now joins a regional turn towards stricter rules in schools and on the streets.

American families who live in Peru and use local schools should watch for tougher codes of conduct. It is not yet clear how the rules will apply to private and international schools.

What Is Not Known

The government has not named the legal instrument or published a final text in the official gazette. It is not known which offences will count as very serious or who will decide on an expulsion.

No figure has been given for how many students could be affected. It is also unclear how the reinsertion schools will be funded or staffed.

What Comes Next

The guidelines take effect only once they are formally approved, according to Andina. Schools will then get a deadline to adapt their internal rules.

Monday’s presentation does not mean that any student can be expelled yet. The government chose to present the text publicly and open a debate first, Andina reported.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Peru announce on Monday?

President Keiko Fujimori presented guidelines for managing school discipline on Monday, 12 October. They grade offences in three levels and allow expulsion for the most serious ones.

Are expulsions already allowed?

No, the guidelines take effect only after formal approval. Schools will then receive a deadline to update their internal rules.

Why is Peru doing this now?

Reports of school violence reached 4,759 in September, the highest monthly figure since at least 2024. An abuse case at a navy-run school in Lima also prompted the change.

How does this compare with the United States?

In April 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order on reinstating common-sense school discipline policies. Both governments argue that teachers need more authority in the classroom.

Sources: Andina, 12 October 2026; Andina, guidelines preview, 12 October 2026; El Peruano, 6 October 2026; The White House, 23 April 2025; RPP, 6 October 2026; RPP, 20 September 2026 (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.title: Ecuador Rains Affect 17,056 People Since 29 August
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

ECUADOR · WEATHER

Key Facts — What happened Ecuador’s risk agency counted 17,056 people affected by rains on Sunday.

— The alert A national El Niño red alert has run since 29 August.

— Hardest hit Esmeraldas province accounts for 12,484 of the people affected.

— The damage 4,862 homes affected, 16 destroyed and one person killed.

— Still open The weather service warns of heavy rain until Wednesday, 14 October.

Six weeks of El Niño rains have now affected more than 17,000 people across Ecuador. More storms are forecast for the coast and the Andes until Wednesday.

Ecuador rains have affected 17,056 people since 29 August, the national risk agency reported on Sunday, 11 October. Ecuador uses the US dollar and is the world’s largest banana exporter, so its weather matters to US importers and shoppers.

The agency, the Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos (SNGR), issued its 30th situation report at 5:46 p.m. local time. It counted 330 adverse events in 22 of Ecuador’s 24 provinces, with Esmeraldas on the Pacific coast hit hardest.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 with 38.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (14). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B); 51 homicides per 100,000. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Risk Agency Reported

Floods made up 181 of the 330 events, or 54.85%, according to the report. Landslides accounted for 68 events and windstorms for 24, across 100 cantons and 200 parishes.

The agency classed 1,354 people as damnificados, its term for people whose homes or livelihoods suffered severe losses. In all, 18,410 people were touched by the rains in some way, the report said.

One person has died since the alert began, swept away by the current of the Calichana river on 26 September. The report lists that death under El Oro province, on the southern border with Peru.

The rains damaged 4,862 homes and destroyed 16, the agency said. Eighteen schools had their classes disrupted, two health centres were hit and one bridge was destroyed.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Ecuador Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Esmeraldas Bears the Brunt

Esmeraldas, a coastal province bordering Colombia, accounts for 12,484 of the people affected and 3,714 of the damaged homes. The Esmeraldas river burst its banks on 29 September, flooding three river islands in the provincial capital.

A provincial state of emergency runs from 7 October to 7 December, according to the report. A school in the province has served as a temporary shelter since 3 October.

Guayas, the province around the port city of Guayaquil, follows with 2,168 people affected. Los Ríos has 1,532 and Manabí 231, the agency said.

On Sunday afternoon, residents reported heavy downpours in northern Guayaquil, including Alborada, Sauces and Kennedy, Primicias reported. By 5 p.m., the municipal agency Segura EP had logged rain incidents in eight sectors but no floods.

More Storms Forecast Until Wednesday

The national weather service, Inamhi, issued a warning valid from Sunday afternoon until 10 a.m. on Wednesday, 14 October, Expreso reported. The Guayaquil daily said Inamhi rated the threat medium to very high, with the heaviest rain expected through Tuesday.

Erfen, the national committee that studies El Niño, says the phenomenon remains active and is strengthening, El Universo reported. The newspaper said rain above normal levels is likely on the coast in October.

What It Means for You

For US importers, the report lists 1,304 hectares (about 3,200 acres) of crops affected and 332 hectares lost. It does not say which crops, and nothing in it points to a disruption of banana or shrimp shipments so far.

For US travellers, landslides have closed roads in the Andes and storms can delay transfers on the coast. Visitors should follow SNGR and US Embassy Quito alerts and allow extra time for road travel this week.

What Is Not Known

The report does not say how many people remain in shelters or how much the damage will cost. It also gives no figure for injured or missing people.

Figures are moving quickly, and Expreso cited a later agency tally of 336 events and 1,306 damnificados at 10 p.m. on Sunday. The agency itself says its numbers may change as field teams collect more data.

What Comes Next

The agency publishes new situation reports as the rains continue, and the Inamhi warning runs until Wednesday. The red alert has no end date, and the Esmeraldas emergency lasts until 7 December.

The red alert is a preparedness level, not a national state of emergency. On Sunday, 148 of Ecuador’s 223 cantonal emergency committees were active, the report said.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people have Ecuador’s rains affected?

The national risk agency counted 17,056 people affected between 29 August and Sunday, 11 October. It classed 1,354 of them as having suffered severe losses.

Which part of Ecuador is hit hardest?

Esmeraldas province on the northern Pacific coast is hit hardest, with 12,484 people affected. It has been under a provincial state of emergency since 7 October.

Will the rains affect bananas and shrimp sold in the US?

The report lists about 1,636 hectares of crops affected or lost, without naming the crops. It does not point to any disruption of exports so far.

Is it safe to travel to Ecuador this week?

There is no national travel restriction, but storms are forecast until Wednesday, 14 October. Travellers should follow local alerts and allow extra time on roads.

Sources: SNGR Situation Report No. 30; SNGR red alert rain reports; Expreso; El Universo; Primicias; Expreso (Cuenca road closure) (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.title: Uruguay Cabinet Backs Bill to Allow Retirement at 60
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

URUGUAY · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Uruguay’s cabinet approved a bill for optional retirement at 60 on Monday.

— Who qualifies Workers with at least 30 years of social security contributions.

— The incentive Each year worked beyond 60 raises the pension, up to age 65.

— Lowest earners The bottom 30% of pensions keep pre-2023 benefit levels or better.

— US comparison Americans can claim Social Security at 62; full age is 67.

— Still open No cost estimate or bill text was published on Monday.

Uruguay’s left-wing government wants to soften the 2023 pension reform that is raising the general retirement age in steps to 65. The bill now goes to Parliament for debate.

Uruguay’s cabinet approved on Monday, 12 October, a bill letting workers with 30 years of contributions take retirement at 60. President Yamandú Orsi’s government will now send the draft law to Parliament, the presidency said.

The plan would partly undo a 2023 reform that raises the general retirement age from 60 to 65 in steps. For US readers, it is a test of fiscal discipline in a country whose dollar bonds carry investment-grade ratings.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 with 45.9 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (88); weakest: future resources (23). Alignment group: Hedging. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Cabinet Approved

The decision came at a Council of Ministers that Orsi chaired on a national holiday. Alejandro Sánchez, the secretary of the presidency and Orsi’s top aide, announced it after the meeting.

The presidency’s release says the bill creates “a new optional retirement ground at 60 years of age.” It applies to people who have paid into the system for at least 30 years.

Orsi’s Frente Amplio, or Broad Front, a left-wing coalition, took office on 1 March 2025. The 2023 reform, Law 20,130, was passed under his conservative predecessor, Luis Lacalle Pou of the National Party.

Montevideo Portal, a leading Uruguayan news site, reported that the meeting took place at the Suárez y Reyes presidential residence. Sánchez said the bill fulfils a Frente Amplio campaign pledge and an agreement reached in a national social dialogue on pensions.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Uruguay politics Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Retirement at 60 Would Work

Workers aged 60 to 65 with 30 years of contributions could choose to retire early or keep working. Those who wait would receive a higher pension for each year they postpone, up to the general age of 65.

The release says the plan favours people with the lowest incomes. The bottom 30% of pensions could retire at 60 on terms equal to or better than those before Law 20,130.

The rule would cover the state social security agency, Banco de Previsión Social (BPS), and private pension funds (AFAPs). Separate funds, such as those for professionals, notaries and bank staff, could join if their boards decide.

Sánchez stressed that this is a general law, unlike the narrow exceptions in the 2023 reform for some construction workers. “Each one will decide at the moment of retiring,” he said, according to Montevideo Portal.

He argued the option matters most for people in physically demanding jobs and for those who lose work late in life. “People are left without work at 62 and have to wait until 65,” he said, even with 30 years of contributions.

Why the Government Says It Can Afford It

The presidency’s release quotes Sánchez as saying the design “does not compromise the financial sustainability” of the social security system. He added that the average retirement age in Uruguay is already 63.

The cabinet also reviewed official figures showing poverty fell from 17.7% to 14.8% in the first half of 2026. Sánchez said about 95,000 people left poverty, while poverty among children under six fell from 32.4% to 24.9%.

What It Means for You

Uruguay sells US dollar bonds abroad, and pension spending is one of the costs that rating agencies watch closely. Investors will want the cost estimate and the funding plan before judging the bill.

The design echoes US Social Security, where people can claim early at 62 with a smaller monthly check. Americans born in 1960 or later reach full retirement age at 67, two years later than Uruguay’s general age.

Foreigners who work formally in Uruguay pay into the BPS and an AFAP like local staff. Whether they gain anything depends on reaching the 30-year contribution threshold, which few short-term expats will meet.

What Is Not Known

The government released no cost estimate, no bill text and no formula for the yearly bonus for waiting. It also gave no date for the first debate in Parliament.

It is unclear how the opposition parties that passed the 2023 reform will vote. Sánchez only said he expected lawmakers to give the bill priority.

What Comes Next

Sánchez said the bill will go to Parliament this week, though it is not yet decided which chamber gets it first. The cabinet also heard a progress report on a national science plan, whose final roadmap is due in May 2027.

Monday’s decision does not change anyone’s pension yet. The 2023 schedule, which reaches 65 for people born in 1977 or later, stays in force unless Parliament passes the new law.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Uruguayans retire at 60 now?

Only people born in 1972 or earlier, who keep the old rules, can do so today. The 2023 reform raises the age in steps to 65, and the new option needs approval from Parliament.

Who could use the new option?

Workers with at least 30 years of contributions to the BPS and an AFAP could use it. Separate funds for groups such as professionals and bank staff may opt in.

Is retiring at 60 compulsory?

No, it is voluntary, and workers can keep working until 65. Each year they wait would raise their pension.

How does this compare with the United States?

US workers can claim Social Security from 62 with reduced benefits. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.

Sources: Presidency of Uruguay, Council of Ministers release, 12 October 2026; Montevideo Portal; IMPO, Law 20,130 (promulgated 2 May 2023); US Social Security Administration (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.title: Panama Probes 10 October US Jet Strike on Its Ship
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PANAMA · SHIPPING

Key Facts — The country Panama, a close US partner, registers ships from owners worldwide.

— What happened A US fighter jet disabled the Panama-flagged ship Ocean Molica.

— Where and when Gulf of Oman, Saturday, 10 October, according to US Central Command.

— Panama’s response The Maritime Authority opened flag-state inquiries on Sunday evening.

— The crew The US command says nobody aboard was harmed.

— Still open Crew size, nationalities, owner and cargo have not been disclosed.

Panama is checking the crew and hull of a ship under its flag after a US jet struck it near Iran.

Panama’s Maritime Authority has opened inquiries after a US fighter jet disabled the Panama-flagged ship Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman. US Central Command says the vessel was trying to run the American naval blockade of Iranian ports on Saturday, 10 October.

The case puts Panama, a close US partner whose flag flies on ships worldwide, inside Washington’s pressure campaign on Tehran. It matters to Americans because the blockade moves oil prices, shipping insurance and crew safety near the Strait of Hormuz.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Panama ranks 11th of 14 with 34.2 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (64); weakest: military means (11). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the US Says Happened

US Central Command (CENTCOM) runs American forces in the Middle East and enforces the blockade. It said one of its fighter jets hit the Ocean Molica’s stern with a precision munition, fully disabling its propulsion.

CENTCOM said the crew ignored repeated warnings after leaving an Iranian port and trying to transit regional waters. The command said nobody aboard was harmed, a claim Panama has not yet confirmed independently.

CENTCOM’s statement, posted on X on Saturday evening US time, said the ship is also known as Arika Sun. Neither CENTCOM nor Panama has published an IMO number, the unique identifier used to track ships.

CENTCOM said it has enforced its renewed blockade of all ships entering or leaving Iranian ports since 14 July. Over those three months, it reported disabling four commercial vessels, turning back 135 and destroying 10 tankers linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Panama Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Panama’s Response as Flag State

The Autoridad Marítima de Panamá (AMP) registers ships under Panama’s flag and supervises its merchant fleet. It said in a statement on Sunday evening that US Central Command forces had hit the vessel.

As flag state, meaning the country whose law governs the ship, Panama said it is querying the operator and other parties. Its Merchant Marine directorate is checking the health of every crew member and the ship’s structural condition.

The authority said the physical safety of seafarers is the absolute priority of the Panamanian state. It reminded the international fleet to follow two of its Merchant Marine Notices, MMN-04/2025 and MMN-05/2026.

The statement did not criticise Washington, name the owner or say what cargo the Panama-flagged ship carried. It also gave no crew numbers or nationalities and said its inquiries were ongoing.

Why the Case Matters for Panama’s Flag

Panama earns fees by letting foreign owners register ships under its flag, so its name appears on vessels worldwide. That business makes Panama a frequent party when navies stop or strike ships in conflict zones.

On Tuesday, 6 October, the AMP said Vietnamese shipowners reaffirmed confidence in its registry after meeting President José Raúl Mulino. The Ocean Molica case now tests how the registry balances that commercial appeal with its close security ties to Washington.

What It Means for You

For US investors, each blockade strike is a reminder that Gulf shipping risk can lift oil prices, freight rates and insurance premiums. Shipowners using Panama’s flag now face the same warning CENTCOM gave this crew: heed blockade instructions or risk a strike.

For US policy, the case shows Washington enforcing the blockade even against a ship flagged by a close partner in the Americas. Panama has so far responded with a technical flag-state review, not a diplomatic protest.

CENTCOM tells crews near Hormuz to monitor notice broadcasts and heed blockade warnings. It also asks them to call US naval forces on VHF channel 16 when operating in the Gulf of Oman.

What Is Not Known

Panama has not confirmed CENTCOM’s account that the crew ignored warnings or that nobody was hurt. The number of crew members, their nationalities, the owner, the cargo and the ship’s current position are not public.

It is also unclear whether the ship will be towed, repaired or detained. Panama has not said whether its inquiry could lead to action against the operator or the vessel’s removal from its registry.

What Comes Next

The AMP said its flag-state inquiries are ongoing, and La Estrella reported it will keep following the case. Further statements from the authority or CENTCOM would be the first official word on the crew and the ship’s fate.

The inquiry does not mean Panama is challenging the US blockade or the legality of the strike. The authority said it is following the protocols that apply to it as flag state of the Panama-flagged ship.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to the Ocean Molica?

A US fighter jet disabled the ship in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, 10 October, according to US Central Command. The command said the crew ignored repeated warnings while trying to run the blockade of Iranian ports.

Why is Panama involved?

The ship sails under Panama’s flag, which makes Panama the flag state responsible for its registration and safety oversight. Panama’s Maritime Authority said it is checking the crew’s health and the ship’s condition.

Was anyone hurt?

US Central Command said no crew member was harmed in the strike. Panama’s Maritime Authority has not yet confirmed that and says it is still checking.

How many ships has the US stopped under the blockade?

US Central Command said that since 14 July it has disabled four commercial vessels and turned back 135. It also said it destroyed 10 tankers linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.

Sources: Autoridad Marítima de Panamá, Comunicado 52; Autoridad Marítima de Panamá, Vietnamese shipowners; La Estrella de Panamá (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.title: Peru Under-19 Volleyball Wins Worlds Spot
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PERU · SPORTS

Key Facts — The country Peru has now won ten silver medals at this youth championship.

— What happened Argentina beat Peru 3-0 in Sunday’s South American under-19 final.

— The score Sets ended 25-12, 25-12 and 25-15 in Maracaibo, Venezuela.

— The prize Both finalists qualified for the 2027 Under-19 World Championship.

— Still open Official releases did not name the 2027 host or dates.

Peru’s under-19 women lost the South American volleyball final to Argentina in straight sets on Sunday night. Both teams still head to the 2027 world championship.

Peru volleyball fans watched their under-19 women’s team lose the South American final 3-0 to Argentina on Sunday, 11 October. The match in Maracaibo, Venezuela, still capped a historic week, because Peru had already booked a world championship place.

For US fans, the semifinals settled two of South America’s places at the 2027 Under-19 World Championship. American teams qualify separately through NORCECA, the confederation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Final Unfolded

Argentina won the final 25-12, 25-12 and 25-15, according to the Argentine Volleyball Federation (FeVA), the sport’s national governing body. The Instituto Peruano del Deporte (IPD), Peru’s state sports agency, confirmed the same scores in a release on Sunday night.

The match was played at the Pedro Elías Belisario Aponte gymnasium in Maracaibo, the host city in western Venezuela. Argentina’s federation said its team, nicknamed Las Panteritas, dominated the final from start to finish.

Sofía Baldo led Argentina with 19 points and was named the tournament’s most valuable player. Catalina Borrero Müller added 15 points, and she and Emma Oldani joined Baldo in the all-star team.

Argentina finished the event unbeaten, with three group wins, a 3-1 semifinal win over hosts Venezuela and Sunday’s title. One of those group wins came against Brazil, the team Peru later knocked out.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Peru Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Peru’s Road to the World Championship

Peru sealed its world championship ticket on Saturday, 10 October, with a 3-2 semifinal win over Brazil. Infobae Perú reported set scores of 25-15, 16-25, 25-21, 17-25 and 15-7.

Setter Marcela Manrique ended that match with an ace, according to the same report. Coach Martín Escudero and his staff then ran onto the court to celebrate with the players.

In the group stage, Peru beat Chile 3-1, Venezuela 3-1 and Uruguay 3-0, the IPD said. The silver is Peru’s tenth in the history of the South American championship for this age group.

The IPD listed a 14-player squad under Escudero. IPD president Óscar Fernández Cáceres congratulated the team for representing the country with distinction.

Why the Result Matters for Peru

The IPD described women’s volleyball as a sport that has given Peru many joys over the years. The agency said it provides subsidies to the Peruvian Volleyball Federation and training facilities at the Videna high-performance centre in Lima.

What It Means for US Readers

The United States does not compete in South American events, so no US team played in Maracaibo. American teams chase world championship places through NORCECA, the regional body for North America, Central America and the Caribbean.

Peru and Argentina could therefore meet US players at the 2027 world championship, if the United States also qualifies. Neither official release mentions US college or club links for players in either squad.

FeVA listed a 9 p.m. Buenos Aires start for the final, which was 8 p.m. Eastern Time on Sunday. It said Voleysur, the South American confederation, would carry the match online.

What Is Not Known

Neither the IPD nor FeVA named the host country or the dates of the 2027 Under-19 World Championship. The Peruvian Volleyball Federation had not posted its own report on the final by midday Monday in Lima.

The official releases also do not name the third-placed team or say whether South America gets a third berth. Player ages and club affiliations were not published either.

What Comes Next

The next stage is the 2027 Under-19 World Championship, organised by FIVB, volleyball’s world governing body. The draw and venue were not part of Sunday’s announcements from either country.

The result does not affect Peru’s senior women’s team, which plays in separate events and rankings. For this generation, the focus now shifts to preparing for the world stage next year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Won the South American Under-19 Women’s Volleyball Final?

Argentina beat Peru 3-0 on Sunday, 11 October, in Maracaibo, Venezuela. The sets ended 25-12, 25-12 and 25-15.

Did Peru Qualify for the 2027 World Championship?

Yes, Peru secured its place by beating Brazil 3-2 in Saturday’s semifinal. Argentina also qualified, according to its national federation.

Who Was the Tournament’s Best Player?

Argentina’s Sofía Baldo was named most valuable player and scored 19 points in the final. Teammates Catalina Borrero Müller and Emma Oldani also made the all-star team.

Can the United States Face Peru at the World Championship?

Only if the US team also qualifies through NORCECA, its own regional confederation. The 2027 host and draw were not announced alongside the final.

Who Coaches Peru’s Under-19 Team?

Martín Escudero coaches the 14-player squad, according to the IPD. The state agency also funds the Peruvian Volleyball Federation.

Sources: Instituto Peruano del Deporte (IPD), release of 11 October; Federación del Voleibol Argentino, final report; Federación del Voleibol Argentino, semifinal report; Infobae Perú (all accessed 12 October 2026).

World.title: Peru Detains 12 Over Lima Bus Extortion
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PERU · CRIME

Key Facts — What happened Prosecutors detained 12 suspected gang members in Lima on Monday.

— Where Rímac and San Juan de Lurigancho districts in northern Lima.

— Alleged targets Informal minibus drivers, builders and businesses in Rímac.

— The numbers Weekly fee about US$35; builders asked for up to US$14,580.

— Seized Cash, firearms, dynamite, blasting fuses and QR payment codes.

— Still open Total sums collected and any court ruling are not yet known.

Prosecutors in Peru say a Lima gang charged minibus drivers weekly fees and demanded up to US$14,580 from builders. Twelve suspects were detained in dawn raids on Monday.

Peru’s organised-crime prosecutors detained 12 people on Monday, 12 October, in dawn raids on a Lima extortion gang. The group allegedly squeezed minibus drivers and builders in the capital, where the US State Department warns that crime is common.

The Public Ministry, Peru’s independent prosecution service, said the network called itself Los Injertos del Rímac Nueva Generación. Raids took place in the Rímac and San Juan de Lurigancho districts of northern Lima.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

How the Lima Extortion Gang Allegedly Worked

The operation was led by provincial prosecutor César Augusto Changa Echevarría of a specialised unit against organised crime. Police officers took part in the raids, which began before dawn, the prosecutors said.

Prosecutors say the gang targeted informal colectivo drivers, who run shared minibus routes across the district. Each vehicle allegedly paid a registration fee of S/150 to S/250 (about US$44 to US$73).

Drivers then owed S/120 (about US$35) a week, payable in person or through digital wallets. On top of that came S/1 to S/2 (about US$0.29 to US$0.58) for every trip.

That adds up to more than US$150 a month per vehicle before trip charges. Conversions use 3.43 soles per US dollar, the market rate of 12 October.

A second line of business allegedly targeted property owners, construction sites and companies across Rímac. Victims were told to pay S/20,000 to S/50,000 (about US$5,830 to US$14,580) under threats against their lives, workers or families.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Peru Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Dynamite and QR Codes Seized in Rímac Raids

Searches turned up cash, firearms, dynamite and blasting fuses, according to the prosecutors. Officers also seized notebooks, phone lines, QR payment codes and electronic devices, and immobilised vehicles allegedly used in the crimes.

The detainees include the alleged leader, known by the alias Tanque and identified by prosecutors as Joel Ruiz. His alleged second-in-command and other senior members were also held, the statement said.

Prosecutors accuse the network of extortion, robbery and homicide in the area. They did not give the number of victims, the total sum collected or details of any killings.

A Name Linked to an Earlier Rímac Case

The name echoes Los Injertos del Rímac, a gang that prosecutors targeted in September 2025. Diario Correo reported then that 12 suspects were detained for extorting colectivo drivers in Rímac, central Lima and Miraflores.

Caretas, a Lima news magazine, reported that prosecutors estimated that group’s take at up to S/2.85 million (about US$830,000). Monday’s statement does not say whether the new network grew out of the old one.

Peru Steps Up Its Fight Against Extortion

Peru’s government has made crime a priority, with President Keiko Fujimori announcing a Unified Command to fight it. Interior Minister César Astudillo has also asked the Senate for new legal and technological tools against extortion.

Astudillo proposed tighter limits on civilian firearms registered for hunting, sport and collecting. He said he wants to stop some purchase and import routes from supplying criminal organisations.

What It Means for You

For US travellers, the raid does not change the State Department’s Level 2 advice to exercise increased caution in Peru. The advisory, last reissued on 16 May 2025, warns that the risk of crime increases at night.

For US firms with building projects or suppliers in Lima, the case shows how extortion can reach construction sites. Prosecutors say the alleged demands on builders reached up to about US$14,580 per victim.

Payments through digital wallets and QR codes also leave a money trail for investigators to follow. Prosecutors have not said which payment apps the gang allegedly used.

What Is Not Known

Prosecutors have not said how many drivers or businesses paid, or how much money the gang allegedly collected. They also gave no details on the homicides they attribute to the network.

It is not known whether a judge has yet ruled on custody for the 12 suspects. No defence statement was available on Monday, and prosecutors did not say whether other members remain at large.

This account rests on the Public Ministry’s statement alone. By Monday evening, no Peruvian news outlet or police release had independently reported the raids.

What Comes Next

The next step is a court hearing, where prosecutors can ask a judge for pre-trial detention while the investigation continues. A detention is not a conviction, and all 12 suspects are presumed innocent.

Investigators will also analyse the seized phones, notebooks and payment codes to trace victims and money. Any new charges or arrests would depend on that evidence.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Lima’s Rímac district?

Prosecutors and police detained 12 suspected members of an alleged extortion gang on Monday, 12 October. The raids took place in Rímac and San Juan de Lurigancho.

Who did the gang allegedly target?

Prosecutors say it targeted informal minibus drivers, property owners, construction sites and businesses. Drivers allegedly paid weekly fees, while builders faced demands of up to about US$14,580.

What was seized in the raids?

Officers found cash, firearms, dynamite, blasting fuses, notebooks, phone lines, QR payment codes and electronic devices. Vehicles allegedly used in the crimes were immobilised.

Is Lima safe for US visitors?

The US State Department rates Peru at Level 2, which means exercise increased caution. It says crime is common in Peru and that the risk increases at night.

Sources: Public Ministry of Peru, statement of 12 October 2026; Ministry of the Interior, Astudillo proposals; Ministry of the Interior, Unified Command; US State Department, Peru travel advisory; Diario Correo, 19 September 2025; Caretas, 19 September 2025 (all accessed 12 October 2026).
