Two former MPs for New Social Contract have resigned in protest at the party’s decision to invite right-wing independent MP Mona Keijzer to a weekend conference.

Harm Holman, NSC’s former agriculture spokesman, and Ilse Saris, who covered social affairs, said they no longer felt at home in a party that was drifting towards right-wing populism.

Saturday’s general meeting in Breda ended in chaos when the party’s entire management board resigned following a mass walkout when Keijzer stepped up onto the stage. Acting chairman Ronald de Bruin said the situation had become “untenable” after around half the delegates left the room.

Keijzer had been invited to discuss her hardline conservative movement, Project 2029, which she launched after breaking from the farmers’ party BBB earlier this year.

Holman told TV late night news show Nieuwsuur: “NSC was a reasonable centre party in terms of its policies, but it has becoming a populist party that is moving further to the right. I don’t feel at home there.”

Saris said in a parting note: “In my eyes the party has completely departed from what NSC stood for.”

Een walk-out bij het NSC-congres het moment dat @MonaKeijzer het woord neemt. Vooraf was er al veel consternatie over Keijzer als gastspreker. Het was voor @DirkGotink reden om uit de partij te stappen. Nu loopt de helft de zaal uit https://t.co/4PD2YoYwfn — Nouschka van der Meijden (@NouschkavdM) October 10, 2026

The decision by NSC’s management board to invite Keijzer as a guest speaker prompted its last elected parliamentarian, MEP Dirk Gotink, to resign his membership.

Gotink, 45, said in a post on LinkedIn that seeking closer ties with Keijzer was “incomprehensible”, despite the NSC leadership insisting that there was no agreement to work with her.

Voters return to CDA

NSC won 20 seats in the November 2023 election, just three months after being founded by Omtzigt, who recruited many of his candidates from his old party, the Christian Democrats (CDA).

But the party’s support collapsed soon after Omtzigt joined the right-wing coalition with Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV, the right-wing liberal VVD and the BBB the following year.

Wilders blamed NSC for blocking his plans to introduce the “harshest immigration policy ever”, while Omtzigt resigned first as party leader and then as an MP, citing the toll on his health and family life.

Many of NSC’s voters reverted to the CDA at the election last October, while NSC itself was wiped out. Holman, 69, also said at the weekend that he had rejoined the Christian Democrats.

World.title: One-way traffic on IJssel river lifted but “drought is not over”
World.content:
The highways agency Rijkswaterstaat has lifted restrictions on the IJssel river that forced ships carrying freight from Arnhem to Zutphen to take a 300km detour.

A one-way system was imposed on September 24 after the river level dropped as a result of the summer drought both in the Netherlands and further upstream in Germany and Switzerland.

The agency said it was able to allow ships to travel in both directions now that the water level has risen to 1.45m above its baseline, but it warned that the drought period is “not over”.

Koninklijke Binnnenvaart Nederland, which represents inland waterway users, said the ending of the restriction was welcome, but shipping operators were still having to contend with limitations such as transporting lighter loads.

“The problems are not over. Low water is still having a big impact on inland shipping,” a spokesman said.

World.title: “Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke”
World.content:
Former junior Romanian swimming champion Vlad Pațurcă moved to the Netherlands alone at the age of 21. Since then he’s founded his own swimming school in Amsterdam-Noord, where he now coaches hundreds of people. He idolises former Dutch Olympic swimming champions and dreams of one day building a squad of competitive swimmers.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I was a competitive swimmer in Romania, a freestyle sprinter, and swam for the youth national team. In 2021 I visited the Netherlands for the first time. The first city I saw wasn’t Amsterdam but Assen, in the north, and I fell for the Dutch way of life straight away: the quiet, the order, the way everything seemed designed for people. After that I didn’t want to be anywhere else.

I moved here at 21, with little work experience and no idea how Dutch law or business worked, and started coaching at a large adult swim club. In my first months there I saw how many adults wanted lessons. In 2024 I opened my own swim school, Win and Swim, in Amsterdam-Noord.

I paid for the first pool lane out of my own pocket and started with five or six swimmers. Since then we’ve taught more than 300 adults.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

An international. The Netherlands is home now. Many of the people I teach are internationals too, often adults learning to swim from scratch.

How long do you plan to stay?

For good. I’ve built my business here and the plan is to grow it: more hours and new locations in Amsterdam first, then children’s lessons and other Dutch cities.

My dream is a performance squad, where I train competitive swimmers. Besides the swim school, I help companies with AI solutions.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

Not yet, and that’s a real challenge when you run a business. So far I’ve run Win and Swim almost entirely in English, and I’m learning Dutch now so I can take the business further.

In my first years here I did A1 through a free government course while I was living in Almere. After I moved to Amsterdam I wanted to continue with A2, but the free places go first to newcomers who need the lessons to integrate, for example to find work. I was already working and settled here, so I wasn’t in that group.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

My favourite thing is that things just work. When I opened my company, I entered my details online at the KVK chamber of commerce, went in the next day to sign and that was it: the company was open.

In Romania I’d have been running from one office to another, printing and signing papers. Here, sorting something out at the bank or the council is just as easy.

How Dutch have you become?

Dutch enough to appreciate the directness. People had told me the Dutch are cold. They’re not cold, just very direct, and at first that felt harsh. Now I value that nobody beats around the bush and nobody makes promises they don’t keep.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Pieter van den Hoogenband, Inge de Bruijn and Maarten van der Weijden. The first two are freestyle sprint legends, and sprint freestyle was my event. Van der Weijden came back from leukaemia to win Olympic open-water gold in 2008.

What’s your top tourist tip?

In summer, swim outdoors, but only at an official swimming spot (zwemlocatie), where the water quality is checked. Het Twiske, just north of Amsterdam-Noord, is a good one. And get on a bike. Here people of every age and every job cycle every day, and it’s the best way to see the country.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

Almost everyone here learned to swim as a child: around 94% of Dutch youngsters hold at least one swimming diploma. You’d expect a country of strong swimmers, but the reality is more nuanced. Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke, breaststroke with the head out of the water.

The system teaches survival rather than swimming as a sport, which makes sense in a country full of canals. As a result, many Dutch adults come back to lessons later to learn freestyle and the other strokes.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

Spend the day on my bike, out of the city, and end it with one last swim.

Vlad was speaking with Louis Gore-Langton

World.title: Jetten condemns planned US sanctions against ICC, urges dialogue
World.content:
Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten has condemned the United States’ decision to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court in The Hague and said the Netherlands would defend the institution “brick by brick”.

In a joint press conference with Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, Jetten said the announcement by Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday was “deeply regrettable”. He went on: “We’re very much disappointed by this escalation and condemn the announced sanctions.”

Jetten said the next six months would be a “crucial” time after the Trump administration delayed the onset of the measures to allow “time for states parties to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC.”

Rubio said the court was a threat to American servicemen who faced being prosecuted for their actions during overseas missions, even though the United States is not a member.

The US has also attacked the decision to serve arrest warrants on Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” he said.

Nobel Prize

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Jetten called for “open dialogue” with the US over the next six months “to prevent the sanctions being implemented in April”, but he added: “At the same time we are preparing for a more difficult situation.”

He would not say if the Netherlands, as the host of the ICC, would ask the European Union to activate its blocking statute, ordering EU-based businesses not to comply with the sanctions, but he said: “We will do everything to protect the ICC.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services. They are the first measures to be announced against the institution rather than individual staff members.

The Trump administration has so far sanctioned 13 judges and officials at the ICC, including the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and senior prosecutor Abdoulaye Saye, preventing them from travelling to the US or using banking services.

World.title: D66 wants children heard without parents’ consent in abuse cases
World.content:
Children who show serious signs of abuse would be interviewed quickly, and without their parents’ consent if necessary, under a draft bill published by coalition party D66 on Monday.

The proposal, by MPs Marijke Synhaeve and Hanneke van der Werf, has been put online so organisations can respond before it goes to parliament, broadcaster NOS reported. “What we want,” Synhaeve said, “is for children to be better heard, seen and helped.”

Currently, care workers can normally only contact a child if the parents or guardians agree. Exceptions are possible under strict conditions, but they are complicated and rarely used. Recent serious abuse cases have led leaders to consider altering policies.

Under what the MPs call the “child first act”, a specialist team would have to hear the child within 48 hours when there are signs of a criminal offence.

The team would include medical, youth care, safety and justice experts, and would draw up a plan covering protection, support and, if needed, prosecution.

The approach is based on the Barnahus model, Icelandic for “children’s house”, which is already used in many other countries.

Missed signals

D66 first announced the plan in June, citing two cases in which children’s calls for help went unanswered. The foster parents of a 10-year-old girl in Vlaardingen were jailed for 8 years last November for abuse that left her permanently disabled.

Government inspectors found that the girl had made several efforts to get help but was ignored.

In May, two women in the Groningen town of Stadskanaal were arrested on suspicion of severely abusing a 6-year-old girl and a 7-year-old boy. In both cases, signals from the children or people around them were not properly followed up, NOS said.

A majority of MPs backed similar ideas during a recent debate on domestic violence, news agency ANP reported in June. Far-right JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie also put forward the same idea in that debate.

Synhaeve said she does not expect the bill to create a lot of extra work or lead to more children being taken into care. She said it would instead improve cooperation between agencies.

World.title: Fire that damaged cables under railway bridge is suspected arson
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Police are investigating a fire under a railway bridge in Rotterdam that led to trains being cancelled over the weekend as a suspected act of sabotage.

The door to a technical area in Rotterdam-Delfshaven was forced open and a fire was started that damaged around 35 cables, 15 of which were destroyed, network operator ProRail said.

All trains between Rotterdam Centraal and Delft Campus were suspended until 9.15pm on Sunday as engineers worked to repair the damage.

The stretch of line is one of the busiest in the Netherlands, carrying long-distance trains from Amsterdam to Zeeland and Limburg via Holland Spoor station.

A police spokesman told Dutch News: “We have secured camera footage and we are examining it. Forensic investigators are also studying possible leads.”

Junior infrastructure minister Annet Bertram said she was shocked by the incident. “I find it appalling and worrying that this appears to be arson and a deliberate act,” she told NOS.

Schiphol disruption

In a separate incident, trains to Schiphol airport were disrupted for several hours by problems with an overhead power line, but ProRail has ruled out arson as a cause.

More than 20 sprinter trains between Amsterdam and Hoofddorp were cancelled between 1.30pm and 9pm as engineers worked to repair the fault at Riekerpolder. “It is an intersection, which means trains are not running in a large area,” a spokesman said on Sunday.

International services were also affected, with trains to Brussels starting and ending in Rotterdam.

World.title: Utrecht weighs tougher measures on landlords after lack of fines
World.content:
Utrecht fined only 1 landlord last year despite receiving almost 200 complaints for breaking rules designed to protect tenants. The city is now considering a tougher approach modelled on Rotterdam, which issued 25 penalties in the second half of the year alone.

The figures were reported by regional broadcaster RTV Utrecht. Rotterdam received 667 complaints in 2025, and its fines ranged from €1,000 to tens of thousands per offence.

The threat of a fine is often enough to resolve a dispute since many renters are too scared to even report illegal or abusive practice for fear of losing their homes amid the housing crisis, but the city showed that when tenants did make reports, rents fell an average of €350 for private tenants.

Under the “good landlord law”, which came into force in 2023, landlords cannot discriminate against or intimidate tenants. Deposits are capped at 2 months’ basic rent, and service charges may only cover actual costs.

Unlike Rotterdam, Utrecht gives landlords a warning before handing down a penalty. It says it wants to avoid having fines overturned in court for being too heavy.

Research published by the Federation of Private-Sector Tenants (FHCS) in December last year found that Utrecht lacked the resources to look for abuses itself and relied entirely on complaints from tenants. Only around half of those complaints were taken further, usually because of a lack of evidence.

Fines are also rare in other big cities. In The Hague, around 600 complaints in two and a half years led to dozens of penalty orders but only 3 fines, which are being contested, according to the FHCS.

Amsterdam’s public list of sanctions showed only 1 fine, for intimidating tenants, which could still be challenged. Last October, the city warned a landlord who would only rent to working Dutch women that he faced a fine of up to €10,000.

Utrecht has not yet decided whether to follow Rotterdam’s lead, but believes fines could deter landlords and prevent repeat offences. It aims to introduce a rental permit in 2028, so that rents can be checked before a home is let.

The city also plans to do more to inform tenants about their rights and its complaints hotline. Every council is required by law to run a hotline for complaints about landlords.

World.title: Four go on trial in Warsaw over arson attacks carried out on Russian orders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons. Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024. Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga. W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026 According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks. The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life. Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services. However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement. Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack. Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw. Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years. Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted. Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism. That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025 In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory. A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe. Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland. Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region. World.title: Israeli producer had access to data harvested by Poland using Pegasus spyware, say prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government. Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence. Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026 Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures. In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents. Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance. PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing. After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government. Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW). The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data. “Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office. Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola… Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026 The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”. “The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.” Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts. Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”. The former deputy head of Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau has been charged with unlawfully sharing material obtained through surveillance using Pegasus spyware, including communication involving PM @donaldtusk's daughter when Tusk was in opposition https://t.co/LyTuqbq0KQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2025 In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”. The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister. “They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.” Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government. The pair, who deny wrongdoing, could be jailed for up to three years if found guilty of unlawfully allowing use of the spyware https://t.co/TWjQR74IYT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026 Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings. In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information. The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF. 💬 Jest to dokument o tym, jak władza publiczna w Polsce sięgnęła po narzędzie ingerujące w prawa obywatelskie – powiedziała przewodnicząca komisji śledczej ds. inwigilacji systemem Pegasus @MagdalenaSroka, prezentując raport z prac komisji.https://t.co/MzA9gj4M0Y — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 12, 2026 Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings. Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family. Last year, a former deputy justice minister from the PiS government, Michał Woś, was indicted to stand trial over his role in the alleged illegal use of justice ministry funds to help the CBA purchase Pegasus. World.title: US wants Poland to join G20 “as soon as possible”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The United States wants Poland to join the G20 “as soon as possible” and intends to raise the issue with other members of the international forum at its forthcoming summit in December in Miami, the US State Department has told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Having previously endorsed Polish membership of the G20 in May, the US now says it intends to “continue discussions with G20 members this year on making Poland a full member as soon as possible”. “Poland’s long-term and steady economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant,” the State Department told PAP. Stany Zjednoczone oficjalnie zadeklarowały, że będą zabiegać o stałe członkostwo Polski w G20 https://t.co/lnZ583HIus — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) October 11, 2026 The G20, a major intergovernmental forum that brings together 19 major countries together with the European Union and the African Union, is set to meet at a golf resort owned by President Donald Trump in Miami on 14-15 December. Poland is also participating this year as a guest of the United States. PAP reports that the US has proposed that one of the points in the final declaration adopted by leaders at the conclusion of the summit refer to Poland’s permanent membership. However, this would require the assent of all current members, including Russia. The issue is likely to be discussed in a pre-summit online meeting of so-called “sherpas” negotiating the text of the declaration, reports PAP. After visiting Washington earlier this month, Marcin Przydacz, the head of President Karol Nawrocki’s international policy office, said that joining the G20 permanently is “Plan A”, but acknowledged that receiving a consensus from existing member states made this variant difficult. He added that Nawrocki would travel to London before the summit to discuss the possibility of continuing Poland’s guest status next year, when the UK will host the G20. At a meeting of G20 trade ministers last week, finance minister Andrzej Domański said that Poland has a good chance of being invited next year. Nawrocki also plans to visit G20 members Saudi Arabia and Argentina to canvass for support for Poland’s membership bid, Przydacz has confirmed. A third option would be for Poland to become a “permanent guest”, a status typically reserved for organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, but also held by Spain. The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026 Poland has long lobbied for membership in the group. In 2010, then-President Lech Kaczyński said “the place of my country is among the members of the G20”. In 2022, following the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Polish government argued that their country should replace Russia. Last December, the US invited Poland to join this year’s summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Poland was “assuming its rightful place” at the forum. Poland has argued that its membership is justified by its economy being on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world. Though G20 membership is not decided solely on that basis, the G20 does include most of the world’s 20 largest economies (only Switzerland and the Netherlands have larger economies than Poland but no G20 membership). Polish President @NawrockiKn “does not like” the fact that Donald Trump has invited Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami, says his chief foreign policy aide. However, Nawrocki still plans to attend the event, which Poland is invited to as a guest https://t.co/JojsFB4NX6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2026 In September, the United States provoked criticism from European leaders, including Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, when it announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be invited to the Miami summit. Subsequently, Przydacz confirmed that, although Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Trump, “does not like” the fact that Putin has been invited, the Polish president was still planning to attend the summit. Sikorski likewise said he would attend a G20 meeting of foreign ministers in Atlanta in October even if a Russian representative was there and agreed that Poland should not boycott the summit in December. World.title: Independent beats PM Tusk’s candidate in Kraków mayoral election
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Łukasz Gibała, an independent, has won the mayoral election in Kraków, Poland’s second-biggest city, beating Monika Piątkowska, the candidate backed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. With all votes counted by just after 1 a.m. on Monday morning, Gibała had 62.1% against 37.9% for Piątkowska, who had already conceded defeat shortly after 9 p.m. on Sunday night, when exit polls showed a large margin of victory for her opponent. “Today in Poland, more and more people realise that we don’t have to live in the reality that politicians in Warsaw project upon us,” declared Gibała as it became clear he had won. “More and more people realise that we, in our own towns and cities, know better what’s good for us than they do in Warsaw.” The victory marks a blow for Tusk – whose Civic Coalition (KO) party has its strongest support in large cities – just a year before he seeks to win another term at parliamentary elections. The prime minister had visited Kraków to campaign alongside Piątkowska. Dziś 11 października 2026 roku, po 24 latach, mieszkańcy odzyskali swoje miasto. Chciałbym podziękować wszystkim Krakowianom, którzy mi zaufali i zdecydowali się oddać ma mnie głos. To nasze wspólne zwycięstwo. Dziękuję mojej partnerce Adzie, sztabowi i współpracownikom ze… pic.twitter.com/0FsNYwjPkj — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) October 11, 2026 For Gibała, a wealthy businessman who has largely funded his own political career, this was victory at the fourth attempt, having stood in every mayoral contest since 2014, obtaining a growing share of the vote each time. He stood as an independent, promising to sort out the city’s finances, end cronyism in the appointment of municipal officials, improve public transport and reverse ticket-price increases, and hold a referendum on Kraków’s controversial clean transport zone for vehicles. He also pledged to favour residents over developers in planning decisions and to counteract the negative effects of tourism in what is Poland’s most-visited city, including by restricting short-term-rental properties. Gibała’s victory had been expected after he came top in the first round two weeks ago with 36.4% of the vote among the seven candidates who stood. Piątkowska trailed on 29.9%. The top two candidates then met in today’s run-off. Piątkowska was the joint candidate of Tusk’s centrist KO party and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which are both part of the national government. She has, since last year, been a member of the Senate in Warsaw. Previously, she worked in Kraków city hall during the mayoralty of Jacek Majchrowski, who held office from 2002 to 2024. Piątkowska received the personal backing of Tusk, who announced her candidacy in June alongside PSL leader and deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (though critics noted that they held the event in Warsaw rather than Kraków). Tusk also visited Kraków before the first round to support his candidate. Among her campaign promises were to seek to locate an AI “gigafactory” in Kraków, to boost the availability of housing for young people, and to implement a package of policies for women, including free mammograms, pram-friendly infrastructure, free menstrual hygiene products, and safer nighttime public transport. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Kraków’s election was held in unusual circumstances after the previous mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, also from KO, was removed from his position in May, just two years into his term. He had faced accusations of cronyism and poor financial management, as well as criticism over the introduction of the clean transport zone. A petition to hold a recall referendum received more than the 58,355 signatures required. In the subsequent referendum, 97.3% supported removing the mayor (Miszalski had appealed to his supporters not to vote in an unsuccessful effort to keep turnout below the 27% needed for the result to be binding). Before today’s election, both Miszalski and Majchowski had called on Cracovians to vote for Piątkowska. After his victory had become clear, Gibała declared that “11 October 2026 will be remembered as the day when, after 24 years, the inhabitants of Krakow regained their city”. The vote had been particularly closely watched as it came just a year before the parliamentary elections. Gibała’s victory has been celebrated by figures from the right-wing opposition, though the new mayor is not politically aligned with them (and indeed previously served as an MP in Tusk’s party). World.title: Polish security services report alleged assassination plot against PM Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. At the time of writing, no details have been released regarding where and how the alleged attacks were expected to take place, who might be behind them, or what the source of the information was. W związku z informacją, która wpłynęła do @PolskaPolicja i dotyczy możliwego zamachu na premiera @donaldtusk oraz wicepremiera, ministra obrony narodowej @KosiniakKamysz, minister koordynator służb specjalnych @TomaszSiemoniak oraz minister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji… — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 11, 2026 On Sunday morning, Jacek Dobrzyński, the spokesman for the security services, first announced that the police had received “information…regarding a possible assassination attempt” on Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz, who, as well as serving as defence minister, is also a deputy prime minister. Dobrzyński revealed that the Internal Security Agency (ABW), police and State Protection Service (SOP), which provides security for high-ranking officials, would meet to discuss the potential threat. Speaking after that meeting, interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka confirmed that the threat had first been identified by SOP, which passed the information on to the police. “We are taking this matter extremely seriously,” added Dobrzyński, speaking alongside her. He criticised “pseudo-experts” in the media who had expressed doubt about the announcement of a possible assassination attempt. “We’re talking about threats directed at the most important people in the country,” he added. “This information is so serious and credible that we’ve decided to share it with you now…We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out.” Dobrzyński did not divulge any details about the nature of the attack or where the warnings had come from, but said that he would be able to provide further information once the police and security services had carried out further investigation. "Sprawę traktujemy śmiertelnie poważnie. Mówimy o dużym prawdopodobieństwie spełnienia tych gróźb" Rzecznik prasowy ministra koordynatora służb specjalnych o możliwym zamachu na premiera i szefa MON. pic.twitter.com/2xoWrZJT2w — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 11, 2026 Government spokesman Adam Szłapka, speaking to broadcaster TVN, acknowledged that the authorities constantly receive a “cascade of indications” regarding potential threats. However, “this signal was more disturbing than previous” ones, he added. Szłapka also indicated that one element of the warning had come via email, but added that “it was not just an email” that had raised concern. Like Dobrzyński, he said that further information would be released in due course. Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reports that an unnamed “official close to the prime minister” had said that the threat came from “right-wing extremists” and that the perpetrators were Poles. Another source within the intelligence services told the newspaper that the threat was treated more seriously than others because it contained information about addresses linked to Tusk and Kosiniak-Kamysz. Poland has charged a 17-year-old with planning neo-Nazi terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. Two other Polish teenagers who were part of the same online community promoting neo-Nazism and violence have also been detained https://t.co/86AnIHWFe8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 22, 2026 Last month, police detained a 56-year-old man in the city of Przemyśl after he posted a video on social media threatening Tusk. Earlier in September, a 52-year-old man in the town of Oława was likewise arrested for making criminal threats against the prime minister online. Also in September, the security services detained three teenagers who were accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One of them was additionally charged with planning terrorist attacks on targets including a mosque and a school. This week has also seen Poland facing an unprecedented security challenge after three knife attacks took place on schools, leaving one person dead and many injured. In response, the police have since Friday carried out checks at over 64,000 locations, including many schools, and detained over 100 people, most of them teenagers found to have made threats or been in possession of weapons. World.title: Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar. They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time. 🔴Ubili kozę na zapleczu. Wkrótce decyzja sądu, zastanawia ruch prokuratury Sąd Rejonowy w Wałbrzychu w najbliższym czasie zdecyduje o losie trójki obcokrajowców, którzy pod koniec zeszłego roku niezgodnie z polskim prawem ubili kozę. Oskarżająca Hindusa i dwójkę Bengalczyków… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 7, 2026 The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar. After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time. The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”. However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.” Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska. The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat. The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed. Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat. Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers. Having fought off attempts by the ruling party to ban ritual slaughter, the industry is now hoping to expand further to cater to a growing market https://t.co/duOJTfHoLT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2022 However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too. Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients. Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves. World.title: Polish police detain more teens following school knife attacks amid fears of further incidents
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Following this week’s two knife attacks on schools in Poland, police have today carried out security checks on over 10,000 schools and detained at least 10 more people, many of them teenagers found to have made online threats or been in possession of weapons. Meanwhile, many parents decided not to send their children to school today, as rumours swirled online that this week’s attacks were somehow coordinated and that further incidents were planned on Friday. The issue has also sparked a political dispute, with the government criticising opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for previously vetoing laws intended to improve children’s safety. The opposition in turn accuses the government of failing to protect schools properly. 🚨 Ponad 10 tysięcy skontrolowanych placówek i 10 osób zatrzymanych w całym kraju. Bezpieczeństwo w szkołach priorytetem Policji ⬇️ Tragiczne zdarzenia, do których doszło w ciągu ostatnich dni na Mazowszu, wywołały w przestrzeni medialnej falę nieprawdziwych informacji,… pic.twitter.com/WVkYUdVO9C — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) October 9, 2026 On Thursday, a 39-year-old school caretaker was killed in an attack by a 15-year-old former pupil on a primary school. Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that the assailant had been wearing a head-mounted camera intended to broadcast the attack. That came a day after a 19-year-old student carried out a knife attack on another school, leaving eight people injured. Two other teens were also detained on suspicion of planning attacks in other locations. In response, Tusk announced on Thursday that police would carry out regular checks on schools. However, on Friday, many parents in the Masovia province around Warsaw, where both of this week’s attacks took place, decided to keep their children at home. Some districts closed schools entirely. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school by a 15-year-old former pupil. Yesterday, a knife attack by a 19-year-old at another school left eight people injured. The assailant also had a homemade explosive that failed to detonate https://t.co/xJAzhT6u3U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026 Concern was stoked by claims circulating on social media that this week’s school attacks were part of a coordinated action by a group of teenagers, who were planning further incidents on what they were calling “Bloody Friday”. Two schools in the town of Legionowo, just north of Warsaw, were closed on Friday after local authorities said they received “unconfirmed information that they were on a list” relating to the alleged group. Poland’s national police headquarters issued a statement on Friday morning saying that they were aware of the rumours but that “so far nothing indicates such an event is actually happening”. They urged people to remain calm, not share unverified information, and rely only on credible sources. At the same time, police and local authorities stepped up security in schools. At 9 a.m. on Friday, the national police headquarters announced that checks had been conducted at over 10,000 schools around the country and that ten people had been detained. Among those to be arrested was a 17-year-old in the town of Ełk, who had reportedly made online threats to attack other students, and a 13-year-old in Sochaczew who wrote in a chat that he would bring a machete to school. The boy later said it was a “silly joke”. In Bartoszyce, a school principal saw that an 11-year-old student had posted a photo of a knife alongside a statement indicating a threat. Police detained the boy and found an “imitation knife” in his backpack. In Ostrów Mazowiecka, police announced they had arrested a 15-year-old boy who had sent out images of himself in a Guy Fawkes-style mask, saying that he planned to take people’s lives. In Warsaw, police detained a 14-year-old who was found to be in possession of a concealed blade and 11 firecrackers. 🚨 Policjanci z Mokotowa niezwłocznie po otrzymaniu informacji o zagrożeniu bezpieczeństwa zatrzymali na terenie szkoły 14-latka, który posiadał nóż z ukrytym ostrzem. Nastolatek miał przy sobie także 11 petard hukowych. W sprawie prowadzone są dalsze czynności. Dokumenty… pic.twitter.com/lbQrqe2pgl — Policja Warszawa (@Policja_KSP) October 9, 2026 The situation has also taken on a political dimension. On Thursday, Tusk criticised Nawrocki for earlier this year vetoing a government bill intended to improve online safety by blocking harmful content. The president had argued that the measures were an “Orwellian” threat to free speech. In a hastily called vote in the lower-house Sejm on Thursday evening, Tusk’s ruling coalition passed a new version of the bill that will now be sent to the upper-house Senate. Once it receives final parliamentary approval, the legislation will return to Nawrocki for his signature or veto. Meanwhile, education minister Barbara Nowacka also noted that Nawrocki had vetoed a bill introducing new rights and responsibilities for school pupils, including greater powers to confiscate dangerous items. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Mieliśmy jedną z najmocniejszych propozycji zmiany prawa w Europie, która miała chronić w internecie przede wszystkim dzieci i młodzież. pic.twitter.com/dyxY6prGzB — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 8, 2026 In response, presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz criticised those who were “exploiting this issue for political purposes”, saying that “a political argument is the last thing we need right now”. Meanwhile, Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of focusing on “political warfare” instead of ensuring security in schools. “There is no coordination or top-down directives on what to do, where it is safe, and where there is risk or threat,” he wrote on social media, calling the situation “chaos”. World.title: Polish parliament approves ban on nighttime alcohol sales in shops
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours. The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved. #PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6 — tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026 The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package. The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently. Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales. In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements. The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400). Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage. The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks. Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops. The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show. The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005. They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026 In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed. Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. World.title: Sinatra Tribute Pairs Frank Sinatra Classics With 1930s Dining at Prague’s Mánes
World.content:
Prague’s Art Restaurant Mánes combines live performances of Frank Sinatra’s best-known songs with a three-course dinner inspired by traditional Czech cuisine of the 1930s.

The functionalist building offers views of the Vltava River and nearby Žofín Island, providing the setting for an evening dedicated to the music and style of Sinatra’s era.



The Sinatra’s Tribute musical programme features acclaimed soloists, including baritone Daniel Klánský and jazz singer Sophie Lamoš. They perform some of Sinatra’s best-known songs, including *My Way* and *Fly Me to the Moon*, accompanied by a group of musicians.

Rather than simply imitating the legendary American singer, the Sinatra Tribute offers its own interpretation of his musical legacy.

One of the programme’s highlights is a restored 1897 Steinway & Sons grand piano, an instrument once played by Czech composer and pianist Jaroslav Ježek.

The music is complemented by a three-course dinner served before the concert.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sinatra Tribute Koncert & Večeře / Sinatra Tribute Show & Dinner (@sinatratributeprague)

Created exclusively for the programme by Mánes Restaurant head chef Jaroslav Zahálka, the menu draws inspiration from Prague’s culinary traditions of the 1930s, reflecting the period associated with the evening’s musical theme.

Visitors can contact the venue for current dates, ticket prices and reservations.

World.title: From Lisbon to Hanoi, New Flight Options From Prague This Autumn
World.content:
The autumn school break is approaching, and travelers departing from Prague still have options for trips abroad.

However, those hoping to find cheap flights may struggle to secure a good deal, as fares tend to rise closer to departure and fewer seats remain available at lower prices.

Families face an additional challenge. When booking four tickets together, they may discover that the cheapest fare is available for only one or two passengers, forcing them to pay more for the remaining seats.



Airlines are also dealing with high fuel costs and strong competition, making it important to fill as many seats as possible.

A search conducted on Wednesday, October 7, found that Kraków and Gdańsk were among the cheapest destinations available for the autumn break week.

New flights from Prague and postponed routes

Prague Airport has announced several new connections for the autumn and winter seasons, although some airlines have postponed their planned launches until spring.

Smartwings, for example, has delayed the introduction of flights to Venice, Italy, and Bergen, Norway. Both routes were originally scheduled to begin before the autumn break but are now expected to launch in March.

Despite the changes, Prague Airport continues to list the destinations among its new routes, with their original launch dates still displayed. According to the current schedule, Smartwings’ next new connection is to Lisbon, with flights due to begin on October 23.

Travelers heading farther afield have another option. Vietjet Air launched its Prague–Hanoi service on Saturday, October 10. The route includes a stopover in Kazakhstan, rather than offering a nonstop connection to Vietnam.

Closer to home, easyJet’s new route from Prague to Hamburg provides another option for the break. Return fares were available for around CZK 4,000.

Marrakech joins the network as winter routes target skiers

EasyJet is also scheduled to launch flights from Prague to Marrakech, Morocco, on October 25. The new connection will increase competition on the route, although fares during the autumn break are relatively high.

A return ticket can cost as much as CZK 16,000, excluding baggage. Prices can be considerably lower outside the peak travel period.

Wizz Air is adding flights to Poprad, Slovakia, while Sky Alps is expected to begin services to Bolzano, Italy, in early December. Both destinations provide access to mountain regions popular with winter sports enthusiasts.

Another seasonal option is Eurowings’ planned route to Rovaniemi, Finland, which is scheduled to launch on December 20. Located on the Arctic Circle, the city is closely associated with Santa Claus and attracts visitors during the Christmas season.

World.title: RestaurantWeek Prague Returns With 75 Restaurants and Autumn Menus
World.content:
RestaurantWeek® returns to Prague from October 13 to November 18, offering diners the chance to try menus at around 75 restaurants across the capital at reduced prices.

The three-course menus available for CZK 490 or CZK 790, plus a reservation fee.



The autumn edition features a mix of established Prague restaurants and newcomers to the festival. Among the first-time participants are U Malířů 1543 in Malá Strana and Buddha-Bar Prague, both well-known names on the city’s dining scene.

Participating restaurants are incorporating seasonal ingredients into their menus, including pumpkin, game, poultry, forest fruits, plums and quince. Truffles and shrimp are also expected to feature prominently.

Pumpkin will appear in dishes ranging from soups to mousses, while restaurants focusing on seafood and creative interpretations of Czech ingredients will offer alternatives for diners looking to explore different flavours.

The festival aims to make restaurants more accessible while encouraging people to dine out and meet in person. This year’s edition includes a partnership with Singles Club, an initiative promoting face-to-face social connections as an alternative to app-based dating.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Singles Club (@singlesclubcz)

Connecting Prague restaurants with local producers

RestaurantWeek® is also collaborating with the Regional Food (Regionální potravina) project, which supports small Czech food producers. The partnership aims to connect restaurants with local suppliers and help regional products reach more customers.

For the first time, the festival will also recognise restaurants that work with regional ingredients, adding a new category to its traditional awards for popular and highly rated establishments.

Three-course menus cost CZK 490 or CZK 790, depending on the restaurant, with reservation fees of CZK 49 or CZK 79, respectively. Some venues offer a fourth course, an amuse-bouche, and are marked as premium on the festival website.

World.title: Prague’s SaSaZu Club to Host Central Europe’s Largest Halloween Party
World.content:
Bloody Sexy Halloween festival, described as Central Europe’s largest Halloween event, will return to Prague’s SaSaZu Club for its 2026 edition.

The two-night celebration will take place on Friday, October 30, and Saturday, October 31, promising an extensive lineup of shows, performances, and music acts.



Founded in 2009, the event has grown into one of the most attended Halloween parties in the region, regularly attracting more than 4,000 visitors each year. Organizers say this year’s edition will feature immersive decorations, live performances, and sets from both Czech and international DJs.

A traditional highlight of the weekend will be the Bloody Sexy Costume Contest, open to all attendees.

Participants can register at SaSaZu between 9 p.m. and midnight, with costumes judged on creativity, originality, and presentation. The winner, selected by audience applause at midnight, will receive a cash prize of CZK 40,000.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bloody Sexy Halloween (@bloodysexyhalloween)

The event will run across both nights with multiple performances and themed productions throughout the venue.

Tickets for Bloody Sexy Halloween 2025 are priced between CZK 510 and CZK 1,450, depending on the category (Regular, Badass Babes, or VIP).

They are available exclusively via the official website www.bloodysexy.cz

World.title: The Story Society Is Bringing an English-Language Book Community to Prague
World.content:
Meet Julia and Ioana, the founders behind The Story Society, a new English-language bookstore and community project in Prague.

Their idea combines a selection of books with a space for reading, book clubs, events and meeting other people.

The project is still in development, with the founders currently looking for a location and working towards opening the bookstore in early 2027.

Why a bookstore?

For Julia, the idea started from a personal need. “I wanted to create a place where introverted people like myself could spend time comfortably, discover books at their own pace and potentially meet others with similar interests,” she says.

But there was also a practical reason behind the idea. According to the founders, finding a wider selection of English-language books in Prague can be difficult, particularly when it comes to special editions. Ordering books from abroad can also mean higher shipping costs, taxes and waiting several weeks for delivery.

“I wanted to solve two problems. One is community, and the other one is buying books in English here,” Julia says.

The Story Society plans to source books from the UK and offer a selection that the founders feel is currently difficult to find locally.

What they hope The Story Society to be

The Story Society is intended to be more than a place to buy books, although the physical bookstore remains an important part of the idea. Julia and Ioana imagine a colorful, cozy space with areas for reading, book clubs and other events.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Story Society (@thestorysociety.prague)

They are also considering collaborations with authors and artists, pop-ups and other activities connected to books and the community around them. “We want to make a third place in Prague,” Ioana says.

The idea is that people could come not only to buy a book, but also to stay for a while, read, meet friends or take part in an event.

The expat/local divide

The Story Society was initially imagined largely with Prague’s expat community in mind. But “when the project took shape, we got a huge response from locals, and we learned that they are also interested in it,” Julia says. The attraction is the chance to have an English-language space where they can read books, meet people and be part of a bookish community.

That response has broadened the founders’ idea of who The Story Society is for. Rather than separating Prague’s expat and local communities, they hope the project can help mend the gap between them.

“If you like English, if you can speak English, and if you like books, we don’t care where you’re from,” Julia says. “Just be there and enjoy it with us.”

Where the project stands now

The Story Society doesn’t have a physical location yet. Julia and Ioana are currently exploring the market and looking for a suitable space in Prague’s city centre, while also working on the book supply and other practical foundations of the project.

In the meantime, they plan to take The Story Society to pop-ups and other events. These will give them an opportunity to introduce the project to more people, build a community around it and raise visibility for their crowdfunding campaign.

Everyone can help

For now, support can take different forms. Sharing the crowdfunding campaign, introducing the project to someone who might be interested or simply helping spread the word can help The Story Society reach more people as Julia and Ioana work towards opening their first space.

They also want people to feel that contributing does not necessarily mean making a financial donation. Ideas, feedback and suggestions can help shape the project as it develops. As the founders put it, “any thought counts.”

World.title: Which Stores Will Be Open in the Czech Republic on October 28
World.content:
Most large supermarkets and retail chains in the Czech Republic will close on Wednesday, October 28, as the country marks the Day of the Establishment of an Independent Czechoslovak State.

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area exceeding 200 square meters must close on the public holiday. The restriction covers most major supermarkets as well as large retailers selling clothing, electronics, furniture and other goods.



Major chains including Lidl, Kaufland, Albert, Billa, Penny Market and Tesco are expected to close their large stores for the day.

The restrictions apply nationwide and are based on Act No. 223/2016 Coll., which regulates retail opening hours on selected public holidays.

October 28 commemorates the establishment of an independent Czechoslovak state in 1918, following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire at the end of World War I.

Which shops can remain open

Not all retailers are subject to the closure requirement. The law provides several exceptions, allowing certain businesses to operate as usual.

These include:

Small grocery stores and convenience shops with a sales area of up to 200 square meters

Pharmacies

Shops at petrol stations

Retail outlets at airports

Shops located at railway and bus stations

Shops within medical facilities

Smaller shops are not required to open, however. Their owners can decide whether to operate on the holiday and may introduce shorter opening hours.

Customers are therefore advised to check the opening times of individual stores before setting out to shop.

What about shopping centres in Prague

Shopping centres may continue operating on October 28, even though their largest retail outlets must remain closed.

Smaller shops that fall below the 200-square-meter threshold may open, while restaurants, cafés, cinemas and other leisure businesses can continue serving customers.

Opening arrangements may differ between individual shopping centres, so visitors should check the holiday schedules published on their official websites before travelling.

World.title: Mayors and Independents Come First in Prague Elections as Pirates Fall Back
World.content:
The opposition Mayors and Independents (STAN) party came first in municipal elections in Prague, with 23 percent of the vote.

Led by Prague Deputy Mayor Petr Hlaváček, secured more than 23 percent of the vote, up sharply from 7.8 percent four years ago. The party recorded the largest increase among the main political groups contesting the capital’s city council.



The Spolu coalition, comprising the Civic Democratic Party (ODS) and TOP 09, finished second with approximately 22 percent. Its result was around three percentage points lower than in the previous election.

Praha Sobě, another group led by a serving deputy mayor, also improved its position. Under Adam Scheinherr’s leadership, it won nearly 18 percent of the vote.

The ANO movement, the strongest party in the Czech national parliament, finished fourth in Prague after losing support.

In 2022, ANO won 19.3 percent of the vote in the capital. This time, it failed to reach 15 percent.

The Pirate Party suffered an even steeper decline. After finishing third with 17.7 percent of the vote in 2022, it received just over 9 percent this time, narrowly securing representation on the Prague City Council.

The election results set the stage for negotiations over Prague’s next city government.

World.title: Police Car Ends Up in Vltava River, Three People Treated for Hypothermia
World.content:
A police car plunged into the Vltava River in Prague on Saturday morning after crashing through the guardrails of Hlávkův Bridge.

The vehicle’s two occupants and a man who jumped into the water to help them were treated by emergency crews for hypothermia.

The accident was reported to police at around 8 a.m. on October 10. A man and a woman, both approximately 30 years old, were inside the car when it went into the river.



A witness jumped into the water after the vehicle fell from the bridge and helped the occupants. Emergency services subsequently treated all three people at the scene.

Prague Emergency Medical Service dispatched three ambulances, a medical inspector and a rapid response vehicle to the incident.

All three were suffering from hypothermia but were not in life-threatening condition, according to emergency responders.

“We are very grateful to the rescuer for their help,” Prague Emergency Medical Service said in a statement, confirming that all three people were in its care.

Police are investigating the circumstances of the crash, including what caused the vehicle to break through the bridge’s guardrails and fall into the Vltava.

World.title: Ukraine signs minority education law: What it means for Hungarians in Transcarpathia
World.content:
The Ukrainian parliament’s adoption of the law on education in minority languages is an important step forward for the educational rights of Hungarians in Transcarpathia, Ukraine, the foreign minister said in a Facebook post on Monday.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán stressed in her post that the Ukrainian parliament’s decision was an important step forward, but the process had not yet been concluded.

“We await the Ukrainian president’s signature, the entry into force of the law and the actual implementation of the commitments,” she wrote.

Update: Since then, President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed the law.

She said she had consulted Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on current issues in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations on the margins of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg. “The adoption of the Ukrainian legislative amendment affecting the educational rights of national minorities gave our meeting particular significance,” she stressed.

“The decision is the result of many months of persistent Hungarian-Ukrainian negotiations. We worked with the involvement of representatives of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia to ensure that adequate legal guarantees protect the education of Hungarian children in their mother tongue and the operation of Hungarian schools,” Orbán added in her post.

The Ukrainian law is aimed at settling the educational rights of national minorities. The amendments concern school education, the issuing of education documents, the conduct of external assessments and the preservation of the special status of educational institutions.

The language of instruction will remain Ukrainian. At the same time, in schools where classes are taught in the language of an indigenous people of Ukraine or of a national minority speaking an official EU language, the use of that language alongside the state language is guaranteed in education, as well as in communication between students and other participants in the educational process inside the building and on the grounds of the institution.

The law makes it possible for schools where more than 50 percent of students study in a national minority language that counts as an official language of the EU to be granted the status of national minority educational institution.

The law’s adoption will facilitate the opening of the second and third clusters of the European Union’s accession negotiations with Ukraine, after Hungary signalled last week that it would not stand in the way of the launch of a new, for now technical stage of the negotiations if the Ukrainian parliament approved the law.
