World.title: Fake Hungarian government officials arrested after trying to get HUF billions from a man
World.content:
Two men have been remanded in custody in Hungary after allegedly posing as fake government officials from the newly assembled government asset protection and recovery office and attempting to extort HUF 2 billion (almost EUR 5.5 million) from a man in exchange for making criminal proceedings against him disappear.

The two men tried to make billions by posing as government officials

The suspects are accused of pretending to hold official government positions and claiming they could influence legal proceedings in the victim’s favour. According to the Budapest Regional Investigation Prosecutor’s Office, the scheme began in July 2026, when one of the men approached the victim at a petrol station and claimed to work for the national security services.

He allegedly told the man that he knew about criminal proceedings pending against him and offered to have the cases dropped in exchange for HUF 2 billion. The victim refused, but the fake government official reportedly contacted him repeatedly afterwards, attempting to put pressure on him. Among other claims, he allegedly told the man that he was under constant surveillance.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Alleged fake police operation

After the victim continued to reject the offer, two associates of the first suspect allegedly turned up at his home on 8 October. According to the prosecution, they posed as police officers and pretended to be carrying out an official procedure, claiming they were taking the man to the National Office for Asset Protection and Recovery.

The two fake government officials allegedly searched the victim, took his mobile phone and put him in a vehicle fitted with emergency warning lights before driving away with him. During the journey, they called their alleged accomplice. Acting on his instructions, they returned the victim to his home, handed back his phone and told him to contact the first suspect as soon as possible.

The three men were subsequently arrested in an operation involving the tactical unit of the National Police Headquarters’ Criminal Support Directorate, the National Protective Service and the Riot Police. Investigators suspect them of influence peddling by impersonating public officials, as well as unlawful deprivation of personal liberty committed by feigning an official procedure and causing significant harm.

Court orders two suspects held in custody

The Buda Central District Court ordered two of the suspects to be held in custody until 10 November, citing the risk that they might flee or go into hiding. The ruling is not final. According to the court, one suspect has close ties abroad through his family and employment, while the other allegedly attempted to evade police during his arrest. The court considered the seriousness of the suspected offences and the potential penalties when assessing whether the men would remain available throughout the proceedings.

The court also noted that the suspect who allegedly posed as a national security official had no previous criminal record and had made a full admission, providing a detailed account and co-operating with investigators. It therefore did not consider him to pose a risk of reoffending. Nevertheless, the court ruled that detention remained necessary at this stage because the suspects’ living arrangements, personal circumstances and financial situations had not yet been sufficiently established to justify a less restrictive measure.

The investigation concerns three alleged participants, although the latest custody order applies to the two men who faked being government officials. The suspects have been detained pending further proceedings. The allegations have not been established by a final court judgment.

World.title: Hungarian woman hides daughter from Italian father for 10 years, gets prison sentence
World.content:
A Hungarian woman has received a two-year suspended prison sentence for hiding her daughter from the girl’s Italian father for almost a decade, during which the child grew up without attending nursery or school.

Woman hid daughter from her father for a decade

The Mezőtúr District Court sentenced the 43-year-old woman for endangering a minor and suspended the prison term for four years. She has also been banned from working in any role involving the education, supervision, care or medical treatment of people under the age of 18 for two years. According to a statement from the Szolnok Court, the woman ignored a final court ruling that had terminated her parental custody rights and awarded custody of the child to her father.

From November 2014 until June 2025, she concealed the girl and refused to hand her over to the Italian man. The girl, now 15, was born in Italy to the Hungarian woman and her Italian partner. Their relationship subsequently broke down, and the mother took their three-month-old daughter to Hungary following an argument, cutting off contact with the father.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A whole childhood spent in hiding

According to the court’s findings, the girl grew up without attending either nursery or school. Her mother initially taught her, after which she educated herself using textbooks and the internet. The child lived largely within a small circle consisting of her mother and other family members. She reportedly feared that her father or the authorities would find them and separate her from her mother. The court said she knew her father mainly through what it described as frightening stories told by her mother.

Meanwhile, the Italian father made repeated efforts to locate his daughter. A businessman from Padua appeared on television programmes, searched for her on social media, hired a private investigator and offered a EUR 10,000 reward for information leading to her discovery. He also wrote to the Pope seeking help. In 2018, a joint Hungarian-Italian investigative team was established following an agreement between the countries’ interior ministers at the time, Hungary’s Sándor Pintér and Italy’s Matteo Salvini. The initiative did not lead to the girl being found.

Hungarian police later commissioned an expert illustration showing how the child might look and offered a reward of HUF 500,000 (EUR 1,370) for information. In 2023, the father also appealed to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni for assistance. He reportedly travelled to his former partner’s hometown of Mezőtúr several times in an attempt to see his daughter. The court proceedings eventually resulted in custody being awarded to the father, while an international warrant was issued for the mother.

Mother and daughter found in 2025

The long search ended in the summer of 2025, when Hungarian and Italian police carried out a joint operation in Mezőtúr and arrested the woman, who had been wanted by the authorities. Her daughter was with her at the time. Both were taken to the local police station. The Mezőtúr District Prosecutor’s Office brought charges on 21 July 2026. At a preparatory hearing on 6 October, the woman admitted the offence as charged and waived her right to a trial.

The prosecution, the defendant and her lawyer all accepted the court’s decision, meaning the judgment became final on the day it was delivered. The case highlights the consequences of the prolonged concealment of a child in defiance of a final custody ruling, as well as the years-long efforts made by the father and authorities to locate her.

World.title: Horror in Hungary: Man accused of attacking parents with a knife and setting fire to their home
World.content:
An 80-year-old woman died in a house fire in Szentendre, near Budapest, after her 51-year-old son allegedly attacked his parents. His father escaped, while firefighters later discovered the woman’s body in the badly damaged property.

A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder with particular cruelty after a fatal house fire in Szentendre on Sunday afternoon, 11 October. Police say the 51-year-old allegedly attacked his 82-year-old father with a knife before fleeing from officers. Firefighters subsequently discovered the body of a woman inside the burning family home.

According to Hungarian news outlet Blikk, the suspect, identified as András B., had a history of mental health problems. The authorities have not released further details about the circumstances of the woman’s death, citing the ongoing investigation.

Father escaped knife attack before son fled

Police were alerted on Sunday after an 82-year-old Szentendre resident reported that his 51-year-old son had attacked him with a knife. Officers arriving at the scene attempted to take the suspect into custody, but he fled. He was caught a short time later and taken into police custody.

The Pest County Police Headquarters confirmed that proceedings had been launched on suspicion of murder with particular cruelty. Investigators have declined to disclose further details while the case remains under investigation.

Blikk reported that the father, described as a respected professor, managed to escape the attack. He returned to the family property on Monday but was reportedly too distressed to speak to the newspaper.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fire destroyed much of the family home

The incident also involved a serious fire at the family’s house on Cseresznyés Road in Szentendre. According to Attila Csámpai, spokesperson for the Pest County Disaster Management Directorate, the flames broke out on the ground floor of the approximately 80-square-metre building before spreading rapidly to the upper floor and roof.

By the time firefighters arrived, much of the property was already ablaze. Emergency crews brought the fire under control by early evening and searched the building, where they discovered a woman’s body.

Police said the woman had suffered fatal burns. Her exact cause of death is being examined with the involvement of experts.

Although much of the house was destroyed, firefighters managed to prevent the flames from spreading to neighbouring properties.

Szentendre’s official Facebook page reported the incident on Sunday, describing it as a suspected deliberate arson attack. The local authority confirmed that one person had died and that police had detained the suspected perpetrator.

Neighbours describe a night of fear

The tragedy shocked residents of the otherwise quiet street. One neighbour told Blikk that they knew the family well and were deeply saddened by what had happened. They also described fearing that the fire might spread to their own home.

The neighbour said the wind was blowing in the opposite direction and firefighters worked quickly, helping to prevent the blaze from reaching nearby buildings. The family living next door reportedly spent the night without sleep because of the incident.

Blikk also reported that the suspect had previously displayed disturbing behaviour and that neighbours had complained about him. According to the newspaper, he had allegedly threatened another local resident with a knife on an earlier occasion.

Another local resident told Blikk that, after his arrest, the man appeared confused and shouted about Satan while waiting in a police car. These accounts have not been independently confirmed by the authorities.

World.title: German far-right politician resigns after posting ‘Greater Germany’ map which includes areas even from Hungary
World.content:
A politician from Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has resigned from a leadership position in its youth organisation after posting a controversial map depicting parts of several European countries, including Hungary, as territory of a unified Germany.

A ‘Greater Germany’ map with territories from Hungary included

Luca Mauritz Strauss, who reportedly used the online alias ‘Helmut’, shared the map on X on 3 October, accompanying it with the statement that German unity meant bringing the entire German people together in a single state. The map depicted Austria and much of Switzerland as part of Germany, alongside areas of France, Italy, Belgium, Poland and Hungary.

In Hungary, the most striking detail was the inclusion of Sopron and its surrounding area in western Hungary. The map also appeared to show smaller German enclaves in parts of Transdanubia associated with the region’s ethnic German communities. The post triggered widespread criticism and was subsequently deleted. Screenshots continued to circulate online, however, and the controversy attracted attention beyond Germany, particularly in France.

🇩🇪 “Back to the Reich?” Germany erupts in controversy over a “Greater Germany” map claiming territories of neighboring countries Luca Moritz Strauß, a senior figure in the youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, posted a map on X depicting a Germany that had absorbed Austria, Luxembourg, most of Switzerland, and parts of France, Poland, Italy, and other European countries. “German unity means a Germany that unites the entire German people in one state,” the politician wrote. The post sparked outrage in neighboring countries, particularly France, as the map depicted Alsace and Lorraine as German territory. Following the backlash, Strauß deleted the post and made his X account private. The AfD youth organization, Generation Germany, later announced that he had voluntarily stepped down from his leadership position. — NEXTA (@nexta_tv) October 11, 2026

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

AfD leadership distances itself from the post

According to German media reports, Strauss cited personal reasons for stepping down from his position on the federal committee of Generation Deutschland, the AfD’s youth organisation. The reports also indicated that the party leadership had exerted pressure on him to resign.

Strauss reportedly told German newspaper taz that his intention had been to draw attention to the shared history and common destiny of Germany and Austria. However, the map went considerably further, depicting territory belonging to multiple neighbouring countries as part of a larger German state. The youth organisation’s spokesperson distanced the group from the post, saying that patriotism did not require ‘historical map fantasies’.

AfD politician Torben Braga also offered a blunt assessment when asked why party leaders had not defended Strauss. According to Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), Braga said they had not done so because the post was ‘incredibly stupid’. Following the controversy, Strauss’ X account was reportedly made private or became inaccessible.

More on the EU: Ukraine approves key law on Hungarian minority rights, opening door to EU accession progress

Why the map caused concern in Hungary

The inclusion of Sopron is particularly sensitive in Hungary because of the region’s complicated history and its connection to the country’s post-First World War borders. Sopron and the surrounding area were at the centre of a 1921 plebiscite following the Treaty of Trianon, with the city ultimately remaining part of Hungary.

The map’s depiction of Hungarian territory as part of a unified Germany has therefore drawn attention well beyond an online dispute about historical borders. It also raises questions about the use of historical and ethnic arguments in contemporary nationalist politics.

The controversy has invited comparisons with the rhetoric of Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose government has used claims about historical ties and ethnic populations to justify territorial ambitions. However, the available reports do not establish that Strauss’ post represented an official AfD territorial policy.

The episode comes amid continued scrutiny of the AfD, one of Germany’s most prominent political forces, over its nationalist rhetoric and the positions expressed by members of its youth movement. Strauss’ resignation marks a clear distancing by the party from this particular post, although the precise circumstances surrounding his departure have not been fully established in the reports cited.

World.title: Uzbekistan explains legal protections for foreign investors in new video
World.content:
Foreign investors in Uzbekistan can learn more about their legal rights and the mechanisms available to protect their business interests through a new English-language video released by the country’s Business Ombudsman.

The video, prepared by the Business Ombudsman under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, aims to raise awareness of the legal safeguards available to international investors operating or considering doing business in the Central Asian country.

How foreign investors in Uzbekistan can protect their rights

The video explains the legal framework designed to protect foreign investors in Uzbekistan, with particular attention to interactions with government authorities and legal proceedings.

It also outlines how investors can submit complaints and appeals to the Business Ombudsman, an institution responsible for protecting the rights and legitimate interests of businesses.

According to the Business Ombudsman’s official website, the institution examines complaints concerning decisions or actions by government bodies and officials that may violate businesses’ rights.

The English-language video provides an overview of the available procedures and protection mechanisms, offering practical information for foreign companies and entrepreneurs interested in the Uzbek market.

World.title: Ukraine approves key law on Hungarian minority rights, opening door to EU accession progress
World.content:
Ukraine’s parliament has approved legislation protecting the education rights of national minorities, including Hungarian-language education. The decision removes a major obstacle to further progress in Kyiv’s EU accession talks, although Hungary says it will closely monitor how the new rules are implemented.

Ukraine’s parliament has approved a bill on the education rights of national minorities, paving the way for further progress in the country’s European Union accession negotiations.

The legislation guarantees Hungarian-language education and provides legal certainty for minority schools, addressing a key demand of the Hungarian government concerning the ethnic Hungarian community in Transcarpathia, western Ukraine.

The Ukrainian media reported the decision on Monday, 12 October. The bill will now be sent to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for signature.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán had said earlier on Monday that Budapest expected the Ukrainian parliament to approve the legislation, adding that the government was “waiting for news from Kyiv”.

Following the vote, attention will turn to the law’s implementation and the next steps in Ukraine’s EU accession process.

Hungary will monitor implementation of the law

Orbán welcomed the progress made in negotiations but stressed that passing the legislation would not be enough.

“The implementation is what will be very important after this; we will monitor it,” the foreign minister said ahead of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg.

The Hungarian government has already initiated the convening of an education subgroup under a bilateral intergovernmental committee. Representatives of Hungarian minority organisations in Transcarpathia are expected to participate in monitoring whether the promised guarantees are respected in practice.

Orbán also emphasised that Hungary has both bilateral and international tools to ensure compliance with the agreed conditions.

The legislation is part of a broader agreement reached between the Hungarian and Ukrainian governments in June 2026 on protecting the rights of ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine. The issue has played a central role in the dispute over Kyiv’s EU accession negotiations.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Could Ukraine unlock two more EU negotiating clusters?

The law’s approval opens the way for Hungary to allow the next procedural steps towards opening two additional groups of EU accession negotiating chapters.

Orbán said Budapest had approved the letters necessary to pave the way for an intergovernmental conference between Ukraine and EU member states.

However, sending these letters does not itself open the negotiating clusters. Further decisions are required, and key steps in the accession process depend on the unanimous support of all EU member states.

Ukraine’s accession talks have faced repeated obstacles in recent years. The previous Hungarian administration initially supported starting negotiations after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and Ukraine received candidate status in 2023. The EU formally opened accession negotiations in 2024.

Hungary subsequently blocked the opening of the first negotiating cluster, despite the European Commission assessing Ukraine as ready to proceed.

That cluster was finally opened in June 2026, following the agreement between the new Hungarian government, led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, and Kyiv on minority rights. A milestone linked to implementing the agreement was also incorporated into the accession process.

Negotiations on the second cluster began in July, but Hungary blocked further progress in September amid concerns surrounding the implementation of the minority rights agreement.

Last week, the Financial Times reported that Budapest could allow the procedural step of sending letters concerning two additional clusters. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha subsequently thanked Hungary for giving the process a preliminary green light.

What happens next?

The next step could be an intergovernmental conference at which EU member states and Ukraine formally advance the accession negotiations. The meeting could take place as early as Tuesday, according to a report by HVG’s EUrologus, following the approval of the education legislation.

The opening of further negotiating clusters would represent progress for Ukraine’s EU ambitions, but it would not mean that membership is imminent. Candidate countries must align their legislation with EU law across numerous policy areas, and each major stage of the process requires agreement from all member states.

World.title: Budapest mayor announces long-awaited bridge renovation starts today
World.content:
After more than a decade of delays, renovation work has begun on Budapest’s K Bridge, which provides access to Óbuda Island and the popular Sziget Festival. The overhaul will continue in several phases until the end of 2027, with motor vehicles barred from crossing during the first stage.

Mayor Karácsony announces well-known bridge’s renovation

Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony announced the start of the project, saying the first phase would run until June 2027. During this period, workers will renovate the roadway and the southern pedestrian pavement. Pedestrians will still be able to cross using the northern pavement, while cyclists must dismount and push their bicycles for safety reasons.

The restrictions will be temporarily lifted for two major events on Hajógyári Island. Work will pause during the Generali Gyerek Sziget children’s festival in June 2027 and the main Sziget Festival in August, allowing visitors and motorists to use the bridge without the construction-related restrictions. The final phase is scheduled to take place between September and December 2027. This stage will focus on renovating the northern pavement and protecting the bridge structure against corrosion.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A long-delayed Budapest project

The renovation has been on the city’s agenda for years. Construction plans were first completed in 2014 and reviewed in 2020, but the project was repeatedly postponed, primarily because of a lack of funding. The original construction permit also expired, requiring the plans to be updated as the bridge’s condition made repairs increasingly urgent.

The project eventually received the green light as part of a political agreement linked to the approval of Budapest’s 2026 budget. The Podmaniczky Movement made the reconstruction of K Bridge one of the transport investments it wanted included in the agreement in return for supporting the budget. The city subsequently allocated funding, completed the public procurement process and signed a construction contract with Strabag.

More on the Hungarian capital: Budapest’s City Park wins prestigious European award – What makes it stand out?

Only a smaller part of Budapest’s investments

Karácsony described the bridge works as the beginning of a wider wave of investment across the capital. He said an agreement with the national government and the use of European Union funding would help launch further developments in Budapest in the coming period. The mayor also asked residents to be patient as construction projects get under way across the city in the coming years.

For Sziget Festival, one of Hungary’s best-known summer music events, the planned pauses mean the bridge will remain accessible during the main festival period in August 2027. However, outside the designated breaks, pedestrians and cyclists will need to follow the temporary arrangements while the first phase is under way.

World.title: NATO’s Top Commander Unveils Plan for Victory Against Russia
World.content:
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), presented his so-called “Theory of Victory” at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday afternoon, bringing into public view a concept previously discussed only within the alliance’s senior military leadership. He warned that NATO would destroy “anything and everything” involved in a potential attack against an allied state.

The announcement comes amid heightened tensions between NATO and Moscow, following Russian airspace violations, cyberattacks and acts of sabotage. Western intelligence officials have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO’s resolve with a limited, deliberately ambiguous attack on its eastern flank in the coming months.

“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those may be,” the US general and former US Air Force pilot said. “We will, in short, ensure an attack against any ally proves utterly futile.”

The strategy takes its cues from Ukraine, where relatively inexpensive drones have upended conventional assumptions about military power. Under it, NATO would first seek to repel a Russian incursion using ground troops backed by low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-assisted targeting.

Once the Russian advance was repelled, the alliance would then seek to cripple Russia’s military command structure and bring the conflict to a swift conclusion. The concept also addresses hybrid warfare, including sabotage and cyberattacks, while emphasising the need to avoid unnecessary escalation.

“My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” Grynkewich explained.

The choice of Warsaw for the announcement is significant. Poland, one of NATO’s biggest defence spenders, borders Ukraine, Belarus and Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave, placing it on the alliance’s frontline in any confrontation with Moscow.

Yet NATO leaders have played down the prospect of a direct Russian attack. “I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn’t,” Grynkevicz said. “But deterring conflict also requires warfighting readiness. And readiness requires planning against what is possible, not just what is probable.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte too said on September 30 there was “no imminent threat” to allied territory, stressing that the alliance would detect any Russian military buildup.

When asked why go public with the plan now, Grynkevich said it was due to the heightened scale of Russian activity, and added that it is meant to send a message both to allies and their adversaries: “We’ve got this.”

“We are prepared now,” he said. “Could we be better prepared? Absolutely. But I’m very comfortable with what we have today.”

On the elephant in the room, however – the question of whether American troops would join the fight if Russia attacked NATO’s eastern flank – Grynkewich was less forthcoming. “Ultimately, it will be a political decision,” he said.

The presentation was a centrepiece of the two-day security conference in the Polish capital, attended by more than 2,500 politicians, military officials, diplomats and experts from 90 countries. Among the participants are Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and senior NATO representatives, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky addressed the gathering remotely.

World.title: Greece Unveils New Rules Banning Social Media Use Among Minors
World.content:
Greece’s government, in an attempt to address digital addiction, presented its new regulatory framework on Monday to curb social media use among minors under 15 years old.

“We believe in technology and its potential. That is why we must regulate it with a human-centric approach, particularly when it concerns the health and development of children,” said Akis Skertsos, Minister for the Coordination of Government Policies.

The legislation will take effect on January 1, 2027 and will initially apply to platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, LinkedIn and Instagram, while other social media will be added gradually. The measure concerns only social networks, not the overall use of the internet or other technology.

Implementation of the regulation will be based on the EU framework for digital services, the Digital Services Act, DSA, while violations will trigger the oversight and sanction mechanisms provided for by EU legislation.

The bill is being submitted to a parliamentary committee on October 13, and the government aims to bring it before a vote on October 22. The government announced its decision to ban social media among youngsters in April.

Greece already banned the use of mobile phones in schools in 2024 and launched the website parco.gov.gr, where parents can find instructions on how to use the parental control features available on various devices.

It has also developed the Kids Wallet App, which allows parents to store their child’s identity in digital form, while also enabling them to restrict or block access to applications and online services when the mobile device is being used by the minor.

World.title: EU’s Rule of Law Report Risks Becoming Toothless, Says Liberties
World.content:
The European Commission’s annual Rule of Law Report aims to identify emerging threats and prompt governments to address them before they escalate. But the failure to implement its recommendations raises questions about its ability to bring about meaningful change, according to the latest analysis by the Civil Liberties Union for Europe.

Liberties’ 2026 Rule of Law Gap Analysis, published on Monday, examines where the European Commission’s report falls short, assessing the implementation of country-specific recommendations while exploring its potential to prevent democratic decline and support the restoration of the rule of law.

According to the NGO’s analysis, at least 96 per cent of the European Commission’s recommendations have not been fully implemented, and 54 per cent show no or only limited progress, meaning the implementation gap “remains persistent and significant”. The lack of implementation means that 96 per cent of the recommendations issued in 2026 were repeated from previous years, with 65 per cent dating back to 2022.

“Now in its seventh year, the European Commission’s annual Rule of Law Report is an important assessment of the state of the rule of law across the Union,” notes Liberties. “This year’s Gap Analysis again points to a significant implementation gap and a failure to surface and address critical issues, whether at the national level or cross-cutting issues that impact the rule of law across the [European] Union.”

Liberties also addresses what it calls the European Commission’s “overly optimistic assessment” in this year’s report, where it claimed that “nearly 1 in 2 (47%) of the recommendations made in 2025 have since been addressed by Member States – either fully or partially”. In reality, the NGO says, this disguises a wide range of partial implementation and fails to unpack why some problems remain so entrenched.

Liberties criticises what it calls the EU’s “fragmented toolbox” for fighting democratic backsliding. The EU has various rule-of-law instruments at its disposal – infringement proceedings, Article 7, etc. – but what is missing is “an overarching framework that ties these instruments together”.

“The Rule of Law Report has the potential to provide that comprehensive overview, but risks instead becoming a ‘leftover tool’ – one that only picks up issues if unaddressed by the EU’s other mechanisms. As things stand, it fails to offer a comprehensive picture of the problems at hand nor a clear pathway to recovery, as illustrated by [our] case study on Hungary,” it says.

That case study looks at how Hungary’s political transition presents an opportunity to rethink how the Rule of Law Report can guide reforms and assess whether institutional safeguards work in practice.

Liberties also cites the decision to remove recommendations related to the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), because most of its provisions became legally binding for member states in August 2025, requiring all countries to effectively implement its provisions. “Consequently, the share of recommendations on ‘Media freedom and pluralism’ declined significantly, now accounting for only 6% of all recommendations, compared with 16-22% in previous years,” it notes.

“However, it is unclear at this stage,” it says, “whether removing these recommendations best serves the defence of media freedom and pluralism.”

For example, Liberties’ partners in Bulgaria, Croatia and Spain report continued political interference in the public service media, while they highlight in Croatia, Italy, Malta and Romania continued opaque media ownership structures, often with no legislative steps planned to address the issues.

“In Slovakia, actions by the government appear to be deepening existing EMFA violations rather than constructively addressing them,” it says.

World.title: Turkey Urged to End Escalating Internet Censorship
World.content:
Twenty-one international and Turkish human rights and press freedom organisations including the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network have issued a joint statement condemning the escalation of internet censorship in Turkey and urging social media companies to stop complying with disproportionate blocking orders.

“We call on the Turkish government immediately to cease the use of blocking orders and other restrictive measures that violate the right to freedom of expression, and to ensure that any restrictions on online content fully comply with Turkey’s obligations under international human rights law,” the organisations said.

The letter also had a message for social media companies which obey Turkish courts and government decisions.

“We urge social media platforms to take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to the suppression of independent media and violations of the right to freedom of expression,” the organisations said.

The statement, signed by ARTICLE 19, Human Rights Watch, the Freedom of Expression Association, IFOD, BIRN and other organisations, highlighted the scale of restrictions imposed in September.

According to IFOD data, in recent weeks, Turkish authorities ordered access blocked to at least 1,270 X accounts with a combined following of 35 million. X complied with at least 90 per cent of the orders by restricting access within Turkey.

The targeted accounts included journalists, academics, LGBTQ+ organisations, women’s rights groups and independent media outlets.

The organisations highlighted the blocking of independent news website T24, whose X account had 1.9 million followers.

A court cited 118 articles allegedly undermining the Turkish family structure and negatively affecting young people’s development concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.

The signatories said the order failed to explain why blocking the entire website was necessary or proportionate.

Most restrictions were imposed under Article 8/A of Turkey’s Internet Law, which allows authorities to block online content on grounds including national security and public order.

The organisations warned that recent legislative changes transferring blocking powers to the Presidency-linked Cybersecurity Directorate could further centralise censorship.

They criticised X and Meta for failing to explain their responses to blocking orders. “Neither X nor Meta have provided public explanations about their responses to the September-October censorship waves,” the statement said.

The statement comes amid growing pressure on journalists covering Turkey’s investment-fund scandal that involves senior government figures.

On October 10, journalists Mustafa Balci and Saban Sevinc were arrested over allegations of spreading misleading information about the investigation.

Two other journalists, Ismail Saymaz and Murat Agirel, were initially released under judicial control measures but subsequently placed under house arrest following a prosecution appeal.

World.title: Bosnia’s New Grand Mufti Looks Forward After Election by Muslim Community
World.content:
Nedzad Grabus. Photo: MINA.

After being elected the 14th Reis-ul-ulema, or Grand Mufti, of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Saturday, Nedzad Grabus said that the community must keep developing and answer the challenges of the time.

“Dear citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all our fellow citizens, rest assured that the Islamic Community will always stand up for what is good and oppose anything that is harmful to us and to society as a whole,” the newly elected Reis-ul-ulema said.

Grabus has been serving as the Mufti of Bosnia’s capital Sarajevo since 2021, and as argued for an autonomous, institutionally strong and effective Islamic Community. His campaign also featured proposals for a formal agreement between the Community and the state, modernised religious classes, steadier funding for returnee congregations and a bigger role for women.

The secret ballot for the role of Grand Mufti took place at the Gazi Husrev-bey Library in Sarajevo. Grabus received 230 votes. The 398-member electoral body needed an absolute majority of 200 votes, with a run-off for the top two if no one reached it. The electors are Assembly members, chief imams, heads of local councils and directors of institutions, and the term lasts seven years until 2033.

The Grand Mufti heads the highest religious authority of the Islamic Community, which covers Muslims in Bosnia, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia, as well as Bosniaks in the diaspora. Grabus succeeds Husein Kavazovic, in office since 2012, and takes up his duties on November 15.

Grabus thanked Kavazovic for his dignified and courageous leadership. Kavazovic congratulated his successor and said “new times will demand new steps” within the community.

The Bosniak member of Bosnia’s tripartite presidency, Denis Becirovic, said he believed Grabus would contribute to “interreligious dialogue, mutual trust, social justice and a culture of peace”.

Born in 1968 near Travnik, Grabus holds a doctorate from Sarajevo’s Faculty of Islamic Sciences. He was Mufti of Ljubljana and head of Slovenia’s Islamic Community from 2006 to 2021, where he oversaw the Muslim Cultural Centre in Ljubljana, before becoming Mufti of Sarajevo.

World.title: Czech Local Elections Deliver Warning to Babis’s Governing Coalition
World.content:
With all the votes counted by Sunday midday and on a relatively strong 48 per cent turnout, Czechia’s municipal elections of October 9-10 did not bring any major upheavals of the political scene, yet indicate some changes in voting preferences, less than a year after the coalition government of Prime Minister Andrej Babis took office.

Contrary to national elections, identifying a clear winner is difficult, especially so early after voting day: once again, the largest share of votes went to a network of local associations and independent candidates, who secured over 50,000 seats this year out of 62,000, and post-election coalition talks across Czech towns and cities can take weeks, if not months.

Czech voters also cast their ballot for a third of the Senate’s seats over the weekend, with 22 out of 27 mandates needing a second round on October 16-17.

With close to 1,500 council seats, Prime Minister Babis said the municipal elections confirmed that his ANO party “is the strongest political force at all levels”, except for the Senate. ANO emerged first in six out of 13 regional capitals, compared with eight in 2022, including in Karlovy Vary, Pilsen, Ostrava and Olomouc.

Despite the boast, most analysts point out that ANO underperformed compared to four years ago in terms of both municipal seats and the popular vote. It also recorded its worst-ever result in Prague and suffered a surprising setback in the northern city of Usti nad Labem, a long-time stronghold.

Meanwhile, ANO’s two junior partners in government also failed to mobilise their voters or reach their campaign goals. This includes the conservative Motorists for Themselves who, although focusing their campaign on larger cities, managed to break through only in Ostrava while suffering poor results in the country’s two largest cities of Prague and Brno. “I’m not happy about it, I’m not pleased,” admitted party leader and Foreign Minister Petr Macinka.

On top of that, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party of House Speaker Tomio Okamura came out of the elections with less than 170 municipal council seats. “We have to think about what we will have to change and how we will behave until the next elections,” SPD vice-chairman Radim Fiala said as the party prepares to hold a national conference to reflect on its poor results.

Released on Sunday, a national poll put this weekend’s local ballot into national perspective. ANO remains the strongest party by a large margin but slightly weakened from six months ago, winning over 31 per cent of the vote if a general election was held today. STAN would come second in any general election with close to 17 per cent of the vote, well ahead of ODS (11 per cent), the far-right SPD (7.5 per cent) and the liberal Pirates (7 per cent). Both the Motorists and KDU-CSL would not pass the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter the lower house.

STAN in the opposition lead

Among the opposition ranks, both the centre-right STAN movement and the Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) have been described as the main winners.

Far less prominent at the national level but known for its strong local networks at the municipal level, KDU-CSL once again secured the highest number of council seats out of all the parliamentary parties, close to 2,000. The first-round victory in the Senate of their chairman Jan Grolich can also be seen as a key achievement in strengthening the party’s clout and legitimacy.

But in line with the opinion polls from the past few months, it’s the STAN movement that stands out in this weekend’s ballot with the strongest momentum.

The party racked up the second highest number of municipal council seats and secured two senatorial mandates in the first round, with all its other candidates advancing to the second. Crucially, STAN also conquered Prague – edging out the current-ruling ODS by 1 percentage point – and their mayoral candidate Petr Hlavacek is widely expected to hold the keys to the capital following post-election talks.

Additionally, the coalition between STAN and KDU-CSL also emerged as the clear winner of the elections in Brno, the country’s second largest city. “We are the strongest opposition party, the results say so,” celebrated STAN chairman and former Interior Minister Vit Rakusan.

ODS, the largest opposition party in the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of parliament, is coming out of the weekend significantly weakened, underperforming in most regional capitals compared to 2022 on top of losing Prague and suffering a few unexpected first round senatorial defeats as well.

World.title: Greek Singer’s Death Throws Spotlight on Private Doctors’ ‘Wellness’ Claims
World.content:
When popular Greek singer Giorgos Mazonakis passed away suddenly at a private clinic in the upscale central Athens neighbourhood of Kolonaki last month, his fans were shocked.

Just 54 years old, Mazonakis was undergoing plasmapheresis, a medical procedure that removes plasma from the blood and replaces it with new plasma fluid. He suffered a heart attack and was pronounced dead on September 9.

Known officially as Therapeutic Plasma Exchange, or TPE, plasmapheresis can be used to treat a range of conditions, including myeloma, multiple sclerosis, and some leukaemias, by removing plasma from the patient’s blood and replacing it with fresh donor plasma or bottled human albumin solution.

The procedure, however, has also gained popularity as supposedly promoting ‘longevity’, ‘anti-ageing’, ‘mental clarity’ and ‘resilience’.

World.title: Spartan Takes Over Hvar with 3,600 Competitors from 63 Countries
World.content:
October 12, 2026 – The third edition of Spartan 100m & Sprint World Championship took place this weekend, cementing an important relationship between the world-renowned obstacle race and Croatia’s premier island.

One of the pleasures of covering life and tourism on Hvar for more than 15 years now (and with almost 10,000 articles on the island written) is that I have been able to watch the island evolve and to see how longer-term strategies play out. Fames for its sun, nightlife, beaches, lavender and UNESCO culture, Hvar does not have to work too hard to attract tourists, but there has been plenty of effort to diversity and prolong the tourist season over the years.

https://www.facebook.com/reel/2526211701200292

One area which the island has encountered particular success in over the last decade has been in the area of adventure tourism, with a successful partnership between the town authorities, tourist board, and Suncani Hvar hotels.

Various eye-catching events and arrivals over the years highlighted Hvar’s shoulder-season credentials as an excellent adventure tourism destination. These included hosting one of the world’s leading cycling teams, Bahrain Merida for three years as the headquarters for their winter training, as well as the world-famous Othillo Swimrun for several years.

A very welcome addition to the Hvar calendar for the last three Octobers has been Spartan, the world-famous obstacle course race, attracting athletes from all over the world. The timing of the event, just as the shoulder season is starting to die down, injects new life into the town, as well as bringing some much-appreciated late-season revenue for the hospitality providers. There is a wonderful and very youthful energy around the town over those four days, and you don’t have to be competing to join in the fun.

This year’s event was no exception, and it was a pleasure to see how this chameleon of a destination which offers everything transforms its focus to summer and the beach into showcasing its beauty and terrain for hardened athletes. And it will change again later this week, as the inaugural HVARMONY gathering – focused on the original attraction of Hvar tourism back in 1868, wellbeing.

A full report on the event was covered below by Slobodna Dalmacija, all photos by Samir Kurtagic/Spartan Hvar:

More than 3,500 athletes from 63 countries participated in the third edition of the Spartan event on Hvar, held from October 8 to 11, 2026. The four-day program featured world championships in the 100m and Sprint 5K disciplines, the Beast 21K and Super 10K races, and the Spartan Kids event. A total prize purse of $100,000 was provided for the two world championships, while the Hvar Beast also served as the second stop of the regional National Adriatic Series.

The competition took place along the Hvar waterfront and on courses connecting the coast, city streets, and the ascent to the Fortica fortress. The short course, featuring head-to-head finishes, captivated the audience during the 100m championship, while the longer races took competitors beyond the city center onto terrain that demanded not only obstacle-clearing skills but also endurance on the climbs.

Alongside athletes arriving from all over the world, a large number of locals also competed on the courses. Šime Ravlić, the Mayor of Hvar, highlighted both the participation and the organizational challenges posed by the adverse weather conditions:

“This year’s Spartan weekend presented a unique challenge for both competitors and organizers, and we are delighted that it exceeded all expectations. Adverse weather was an additional hurdle that the organizers successfully overcame; we sincerely congratulate everyone on the ground who saw this demanding project through to the end. In just three years of the Spartan event in Hvar, the number of participating countries has grown from 35 to 63—a clear indicator of the rising interest in this sport and in Hvar as a host destination. There is no need to elaborate on the global promotion generated by enthusiastic competitors alongside the organizers’ official channels. We are particularly pleased with the response from the islanders: 59 locals participated in the 5km, 10km, and 21km races—with some successfully completing all three—while 246 of the 530 competitors in the children’s race were from the island. The message conveyed to young people and islanders through the energy, perseverance, and spirit of these exceptional athletes—whom we hosted for nearly a week—is unmistakable. The Spartan event in Hvar is a success story; we therefore extend our thanks once again to the organization’s founder and leader, Joe De Sena, for his trust; to the local organizer for excellent cooperation; to the Ministry of Tourism and Sport of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian National Tourist Board for their support; and to all local…” …participants and collaborators. Together, we made this edition of Spartan spectacular.”

100M World Championship: a world title decided in mere seconds

Oliver Addy from England won the 100-meter world championship title. In the final, he clocked a time of 32.574 seconds, defeating Caleb Riley, who finished the course in 36.477 seconds. Third place went to Tommy Matthews, who recorded a time of 31.746 seconds in the bronze-medal race.

For Addy, who has been competing in OCR for four years, the victory in Hvar capped off a successful season, and he is already thinking about returning.

“I can’t believe this sport has brought me here. I’ve had a great season and can’t wait to see what’s next. I definitely want to come back next year and defend my title. I’m ready—I can’t wait!” said Addy.

In the women’s final, Poland’s Kasia Jonaczyk triumphed with a time of 40.882 seconds. May Yahalom from Israel took the silver with a time of 1:05.297, while the bronze went to American Jaleesa Himka, who clocked 32.740 seconds in the race for third place. Jonaczyk described what the title means to her immediately after the final:

“I can’t stop smiling; I still can’t believe it. Spartan was the most important race of the year for me. This title was the one thing I was missing. Honestly, for half the year I didn’t believe I could win it, and now here I am, talking to you. I feel like I’m in heaven,” said Jonaczyk.

In the final rounds of the 100m championship, placement is determined by head-to-head duels, meaning the times recorded by the finalists and bronze medalists were achieved in separate races.

The awards were presented by Josip Pavić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport; Rob Stull, President of the International Modern Pentathlon Union (UIPM); and Šime Ravlić, Mayor of Hvar.

The prize fund for this discipline totaled $70,000, split equally between the men’s and women’s competitions. The winners received $18,000 each, the runners-up $10,000, the third-place finishers $5,500, and the fourth-place finishers $1,500.

Sprint 5K World Championship: a fast start isn’t enough for gold

At the Sprint 5K World Championship—which featured a five-kilometer course and 20 obstacles—the fastest of the 56 competitors in the men’s field was the Dutchman Frank Oosterom. He won gold with a time of 39:54, ahead of Frenchman Gregory Basilic, who finished in 40:26, and Czech Richard Hynek, with a time of 40:39.

In the women’s competition, Zuzana Kocumova won the world champion title with a time of 47:35. The silver medal went to Sabrina Daolio, who finished the race in 48:00, while Henriette Bardrum took the bronze with a result of 48:43.

A prize fund of $30,000 was secured for the Sprint Championship, also split equally between the two categories. First place earned $7,000; second, $4,000; third, $2,000; fourth, $1,500; and fifth, $500.

The Beast race held on October 10 held additional significance for competitors in the Adriatic Series. Following the initial Super race in Sveta Nedelja, athletes gathered points on Hvar—over a 21-kilometer course featuring 30 obstacles—ahead of the series finale at Krvavec on October 17.

Italian athlete Claudia Bongiovanni won the women’s race on Hvar with a time of 2:41:37, while Norwegian Espen Berget triumphed in the men’s category with a time of 2:13:53.

The Adriatic Series combines three races into a single ranking for the Elite and Age Group categories. Points are awarded based on placement, with a victory earning 300 points. The final tally counts the two best results, meaning that even competitors for whom Hvar was their first race in the series can contend for the overall ranking by participating in the final Beast race at Krvavec. A Great Race and Over 500 Children on the Course

The Super 10K—featuring a 10-kilometer course and 25 obstacles—brought together competitors of varying experience levels, ranging from those for whom Hvar was their first Spartan race to seasoned participants with numerous races under their belts. At the starting line, the pre-race atmosphere was filled with dancing and laughter, as the group warm-up quickly turned into a social gathering before hitting the course.

The youngest participants had their own races, too; over 500 children took part in the Spartan Kids events. The shortest course, spanning one kilometer, was recommended for children aged four to six. The 1.5-kilometer race was open to children aged seven to 14, while the three-kilometer race was for those aged nine to 14.

Age-appropriate obstacles included climbing, crawling, and jumping, and every finisher was awarded a medal. Parents and friends cheered the children on from the sidelines, meaning the program for the youngest participants also brought together many families.

Over 300 Team Members and 143 Volunteers

More than 300 team members and 143 volunteers took part in executing the four-day program. Organization and production crews, race officials, and security teams managed the race operations, while volunteers assisted competitors and provided support on the ground. The arrival of athletes, along with their families and teams, generated additional demand for accommodation, hospitality services, and transport in October—well after the peak summer season. Josip Pavić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, highlighted the event’s contribution to extending the tourist season:

“The Spartan World Championship Hvar is an excellent example of how major international sports events can contribute to the development of year-round tourism and create added value for a destination outside the main tourist season. We are particularly pleased that, in mid-October, Hvar once again brought together thousands of participants and their supporters from over 60 countries, confirming the event’s strong international character and Croatia’s status as a sports-tourism destination. This year, the Government of the Republic of Croatia and the Ministry of Tourism and Sport recognized the project’s significance and provided €1,350,000 in co-financing. We are proud of this year’s results, as well as the growth the Spartan World Championship Hvar has achieved over the past three years.”

Hvar and Spartan to Continue Partnership in 2027

Spartan returns to Hvar from October 7 to 10, 2027. The fourth edition will offer an opportunity to experience the island from a new perspective. Organizers invite past participants to return and aim for a new personal best, and encourage those who watched the races from the sidelines this year to step up to the starting line themselves next autumn.

World.title: Hvar Tourism Returns to Its Wellbeing Roots with HVARMONY Gathering
World.content:
October 12, 2026 – Croatia’s premier island of Hvar prepares to mark 158 years of organised tourism in Europe by returning to its roots – meet HVARMONY.

Long before “wellbeing” had a name, Hvar was already living it.

Carl Honoré, Kristina Kuzmič, and Ivana Paradžiković are among the headliners of HVARMONY, a four-day gathering focused on how to live better, longer, and happier lives, taking place in Hvar from October 15 to 18.

From October 15 to 18, Hvar becomes a venue for discussing a seemingly simple yet increasingly important question: how can we live better, longer, and happier lives?

HVARMONY – The Art of Living is a new four-day event that bridges modern insights into health, longevity, movement, nutrition, mental resilience, and quality of life with the Mediterranean’s generations-old wisdom on the good life.

The idea behind HVARMONY is not to offer yet another list of rules for becoming a “better version of yourself.” Quite the opposite. In an era where wellbeing and longevity have evolved into global trends and massive industries, HVARMONY shifts the focus back to a simpler question: what do we truly need to live well?

The answers won’t be sought solely on stage. Over the course of four days, lectures and discussions will alternate with movement, workshops, outdoor activities, the sea, food, sound, and experiences that transform Hvar from a mere backdrop into an active participant in the event.

Among the headliners of this inaugural edition is Carl Honoré—the internationally acclaimed author of the bestseller In Praise of Slowness and a leading figure of the Slow Movement—who will speak about the value of slowing down in a world that constantly pressures us to speed up. Kristina Kuzmič—an international speaker and author followed by millions for her open and direct approach to topics such as parenting, mental health, life challenges, and self-relationship—is also coming to Hvar.

Joining the program alongside her are Ivana Paradžiković and a host of domestic and international authors, experts, and facilitators specializing in nutrition, movement, mental resilience, longevity, and quality of life.

Among them are Maja Brekalo, Dalibor Petrinić, Andrea Solomun, Goran Sajko, Mirela Anić, Mia Šoškić, Miriam Mack, Sebastian Orlić, Petra Hisinger, Mirta Primorac Šejić, TLEX Institute experts Neringa Thariani and Aleksandra Jovanić-Sinko, Nina Kraljić, and other program participants.

Hvar returns to its original tourism roots—in October.

The choice of Hvar and the timing is no coincidence.

Hvar’s organized tourism story began back in 1868 with the founding of the Hygienic Society, at a time when the island’s greatest assets were highlighted as its mild Mediterranean climate, sunshine, clean air, sea, and opportunities for rest and recovery.

The Hygienic Society’s first hotel opened on October 15, 1868—the very same date that, 158 years later, marks the start of the inaugural edition of HVARMONY. “Hvar began its organized tourism journey during the very time of year we would today call the off-season. The Sanitary Society’s first hotel opened on October 15, 1868, and Hvar’s comparative advantage back then was precisely its Mediterranean climate—sun, sea, clean air, rest, and recovery. That is why, for us, HVARMONY is not merely a reminder of the beginnings of tourism nearly 160 years ago, but also a message that Hvar is just as beautiful—and perhaps, in a unique way, even more so—outside the peak summer months, when its natural rhythm comes to the fore once again.

We did not envision HVARMONY as just another conference on well-being or longevity, but rather as a reminder that the art of living often lies in simple things: time spent with loved ones, good food, physical activity, being in nature, quality sleep, and the ability to simply slow down from time to time. The island teaches you this almost naturally. And perhaps that is precisely the link between a quality life and quality tourism: neither should be a race to accumulate more, but rather a quest for better balance.

I am particularly delighted that this idea was recognized right from its inaugural edition and that we will be joined in Hvar by a host of fascinating local and international authors, speakers, and experts—including Carl Honoré, Kristina Kuzmič, and Ivana Paradžiković. Their diverse perspectives embody exactly what we want HVARMONY to be: a place for exchanging ideas and experiences, and for finding simpler answers to the question of how to live better.” Director of the Hvar Town Tourist Board

A program that does not require following a strict schedule

HVARMONY does not follow a traditional conference format. Visitors can attend a single lecture, participate in a workshop, start the day with movement by the sea, discover Hvar through the story of its origins in health tourism, join a discussion in the historic Hvar Theatre, or simply take a few hours for themselves.

The program takes place at various locations across the town, including the Arsenal and Hvar Theatre, Bonj, and open-air seaside spaces. Each visitor can experience HVARMONY in their own way—whether by attending a single lecture or practice session, or by participating throughout all four days.

The event is organized by the Hvar Town Tourist Board as an initiative open to the general public. Most of the program is free of charge, though registration is required, as is advance sign-up for specific workshops and sessions with limited capacity.

HVARMONY aims to open up a conversation about health and longevity—without adding the pressure to live a perfect life. Because perhaps the art of living isn’t about constantly doing more. Perhaps it means recognizing what is enough for us, what is worth holding onto, and the pace at which we want to live. HVARMONY – The Art of Living October 15–18, 2026

For more info, visit www.hvarmony.com

World.title: Ryanair Expands Dubrovnik Flight Network, Adding Warsaw Route in 2027
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – Ryanair is expanding its Dubrovnik flight network as of next year, with a brand new Warsaw route operating four times per week in 2027.

Ryanair has announced a brand new route between Dubrovnik and Warsaw Modlin as part of the first package of new routes for the summer 2027 flight schedule. As stated in its media release, it is one of a total of 29 new routes presented ahead of the next summer season, as reported by both Dubrovnik Insider and Croatian Aviation.

Traffic on the new route will begin on the very first day of the summer schedule, the 29th of March 2027, and flights will operate until the 2nd of October 2027. Ryanair plans four weekly flights, every Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday. Boeing 737-800 aircraft have been announced for the route; in Ryanair’s fleet these have a capacity of 189 passengers. With four flights a week announced throughout practically the entire summer schedule, Ryanair will offer almost 42,000 seats in both directions, assuming that all planned flights are operated and that aircraft of the stated capacity are used on them.

The new route will further and better connect Dubrovnik with the Polish market during the busy summer season. Warsaw Modlin will therefore join the increasing network of destinations available from Dubrovnik, with the additional possibility of travel between the extreme south of Dalmatia and Poland.

World.title: Croatian Government Proposes Abolition of Pension Tax
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – The Croatian Government has proposed the abolition of pension tax, with around 541,000 people affected by the decision.

The Croatian Government has sent to Parliament a proposal for amendments to the Income Tax Act that proposes the complete abolition of tax on pensions. Poslovni reports that according to the proposal, the current reduction of the tax liability on a pension would be increased from 50 to 100 percent for the part of the pension on which income tax is calculated at the lower rate. In practice this means that income tax on such pensions would amount to zero euros.

The Government cited the example of a pensioner who receives a pension of 800 euros. With a personal allowance of 600 euros, the tax base amounts to 200 euros. If a tax rate of 20 percent is applied to it, the tax liability amounts to 40 euros, but under the current system it is reduced by 50 percent so the pensioner pays 20 euros in tax. Under the new proposal that tax would amount to zero euros.

It is estimated that the abolition of tax on pensions will reduce the revenues of local self-government units by around 180 million euros. Finance Minister Tomislav Ćorić earlier stated that around 541,000 pensioners would be covered by this change. The Government plans for the amendments to enter into force at the beginning of 2027.

World.title: Young Croatian Men Ending Up in Court Over Military Service Obligations
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – Young Croatian men are ending up being taken to court over no responding to calls for medical examinations for military service.

Multiple young Croatian men, including secondary-school students, have faced court proceedings recently because they failed to respond to calls for an examination to determine fitness for military service. Index reports that while some were fined, others were acquitted because the summons had not been properly delivered.

fined for failing to appear

The Municipal Court in Čakovec last month issued a final fine of 250 euros to a secondary-school student from Međimurje. The young man, who is training to become a car painter, did not appear in mid-June for a medical examination and psychological testing at the Čakovec Health Centre. In court he admitted the misdemeanour. Since he had not previously been fined for a misdemeanour and is supported by his parents, the court imposed a penalty lower than the statutory minimum, which ranges from 500 to 5,000 euros.

Similar cases also occurred at the Municipal Misdemeanour Court in Zagreb, which handed down several non-final judgments. A 19-year-old was fined 120 euros plus 30 euros in court costs because he overslept the examination appointment. In a written defence he explained that the previous night he had returned from a trip with his mother and grandmother. He said he immediately contacted the competent office, but was told he could only come if he appeared within five minutes, which was impossible for him. The same court also fined a student born in 2007 with 120 euros plus 30 euros in costs. In his defence he admitted the misdemeanour and explained that he had remembered the wrong examination date and was therefore one day late.

not all cases ended in fines

Not all cases, however, ended with fines. Last month the Municipal Misdemeanour Court in Zagreb acquitted a young man of the charge that he had failed to appear for an examination at the beginning of May. In court the young man stated that he had never received or signed the summons. He explained that four families live in his house. The court checked the return receipt and established that the shipment had been placed in the letterbox without the recipient’s signature, so there was no proof that the summons had been properly served.

In mid-September the Municipal Court in Varaždin handed down a similar non-final judgment. A young man born in 2007 was acquitted after telling the court that he had not personally received the summons because he was working in Germany at the time. He stated that it was possible that a family member or neighbour had collected it and disputed that the signature on the delivery note was his mother’s, whom he described as illiterate. The court compared the signatures and concluded that it had not been proven that the young man had personally received the summons. At the beginning of September the Municipal Misdemeanour Court in Zagreb acquitted another young man. He had not appeared for the examination back in July and in his defence stated that he could not have received the summons because he was working seasonally in a shop on the island of Čiovo. In this case too, the court established that the signature on the delivery note differed from his. It was concluded that the summons had not been properly served and the young man was acquitted of the charge.

World.title: Rijeka Receives New Infrastructure to Strengthen its Gateway Position
World.content:
October the 12th, 2026 – Rijeka has received brand new infrastructure that should further strengthen its position as a gateway to the markets of eastern and southeastern Europe.

In 2025, the Croatian transport and logistics sector was deeply marked by major infrastructure projects, growth in road and maritime transport, and a strong investment cycle in transport infrastructure. Nevertheless, overall freight traffic did not grow: during the year 132 million tonnes of goods were transported in Croatia, 1.1 percent less than in 2024. Ana Roksandic reports for Poslovni that road transport remained dominant with 94.8 million tonnes, with growth of one percent, while the largest drop was recorded in rail transport, where the quantity of goods transported fell by 21.2 percent, according to the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS).

The most important event of last year was the start of commercial operations of the Rijeka Gateway container terminal in September. The terminal, worth around 380 million euros, in the first phase has a capacity of 650 thousand TEU per year, with planned expansion to more than one million TEU. With this, Rijeka has received infrastructure that should further strengthen its position as a gateway for the markets of Central and Southeast Europe. A key precondition for realising that potential is the development of railway infrastructure and quality connection of Rijeka with Central European markets.

“With the commercial start of operations in September, Rijeka Gateway operated for only four months in 2025, which is why it can primarily be viewed as a year of launching and stabilising operations, and not as a full business year. That year laid solid foundations for further growth and development of the business. The first phase of terminal construction exceeds a value of 200 million euros, and with the planned expansion the total value of the investment in Rijeka Gateway will exceed 380 million euros.

Together with the value of the transport infrastructure, from roads to the railway interface in and around the port, the total investment reaches 600 million euros. More than the business results, we are proud of the entire team that, through dedicated work, togetherness and readiness for cooperation, achieved what only a year ago seemed like a major challenge – the successful launch of the terminal and an excellent start of operational work,” said Peter Corfitsen, President of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Will Croatian Pantheon Project be Completed Within the Deadline?
World.content:
October the 11th, 2026 – The massive and controversial Croatian Pantheon project has been a hot topic for a multitude of reasons, but will it actually be completed within the prescribed deadline?

The controversial Croatian Pantheon project is a data centre with a capacity of one gigawatt which would enable the employment of several thousand people during construction and later on. Poslovni reports that the Pantheon project is proceeding according to the planned schedule and should be completed within the set deadline, entrepreneur Jako Andabak revealed on Friday. Together with American partners, he stands behind the realisation of the Pantheon data centre in Topusko, worth a staggering 50 billion euros.

A solid and high-quality network

Andabak made the statement as part of the third edition of the Master Business Forum (MBF), a platform that brings together leaders of the business community, experts and institutional representatives from the region and beyond, which was held in Rovinj and gathered more than 80 speakers from the public, private and academic sectors. It is a data centre with a capacity of one gigawatt that would enable the employment of several thousand people during construction and later. In addition to the technological components, the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant is planned. With the project whose start is planned for 2027 and the start of the centre’s operation in 2029, Croatia will rank at the very top of the European and world technology industry because the latest solutions open up the possibility of development in wider application, Andabak said.

“We decided on putting it in Topusko because there we have land where it’s possible to realise a project that will not harm nature and the environment. By building a solid and high-quality network we will create the conditions for stable and safe power supply without impact on the environment, which has also been confirmed by a study,” Andabak emphasised. He added that the centre will exploit its own wells and use its own water sources and its own solution for cooling the system.

The potential of empty land

“There are solutions that I carry from childhood which say that when everyone does their part of the work, then everything is done simply,” Andabak said. He added that he has dealt with many things, and only a year ago he began to think about data centres. He also explained how the whole idea came about, and it started with livestock farming and sheep. “Back during the nineties, Croatia was home to a million sheep, and now that number is in the thousands. When you see data like that, you ask yourself how to utilise that empty land and potential,” Andabak said and added that solar first came to mind. As he stated, the area is very interesting in all segments, from cooling to energy supply.

Locals in Topusko have been vehemently against the giant Pantheon data centre, however, and concerns remain for the environment and for water usage regardless of reassurance that no harm will be done.
