World.title: Investigation reveals collection of ‘party fund’ during Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi’s tenure as School Education Minister, CCB tells Madras High Court
World.content:
The Central Crime Branch (CCB) of the Greater Chennai Police on Monday (October 12, 2026) told the Madras High Court that their investigation into an over ₹100 crore fraud case had revealed the collection of money termed as “party fund” from some of the private school managements in the State during the tenure of Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi as School Education Minister in the last DMK regime.

The submission was made in a counter affidavit filed before Justice V. Lakshminarayanan who was seized of a plea by Mr. Anbil Mahesh to quash the First Information Report (FIR) with respect to him alone. After taking the counter affidavit on file, the judge adjourned the hearing on the quash petition to October 29, 2026 at the request of the petitioner’s counsel Richardson Wilson.

In the counter, filed through State Public Prosecutor R. John Sathyan, the investigating officer said, the name of the former Minister was initially not included in the FIR and that only B.T. Arasakumar, president of an unregistered association of private schools and his co-accused Muthukumar had been named as accused for having reportedly collected crores of rupees from school managements.

Only after the investigation revealed the involvement of Mr. Anbil Mahesh too, the police had included him as the fifth accused and altered the FIR by including the charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

The court was also told that the previous approval required under Section 17A of the Act was obtained from the State government on September 7, 2026 and not on June 23, 2026 as claimed by the petitioner.

Refuting the petitioner’s contention that the approval ought to have been obtained only from the Governor and not from the government, the investigating officer said, the approval had been rightly obtained from the State government before commencing the investigation against the former Minister.

Plea to quash FIR

He urged the court to dismiss the plea for quashing the FIR on the basis of unsustainable and misconceived grounds.

“The Petitioner is deliberately seeking to agitate non-issues, confuse issues, and create unnecessary complications when none exists, solely with a view to drag on the proceedings and create unnecessary stumbling blocks into the investigation of the crime of such huge magnitude. The investigation has disclosed a series of circumstances concerning the petitioner’s conduct, interactions, official position and subsequent administrative action,” the counter affidavit read.

World.title: Petrol price down by Rs2.93 per litre, high-speed diesel rate up by Re0.61
World.content:
The government on Monday reduced the price of petrol by Rs2.93 per litre, but increased that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Re0.61 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs395.37 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs396.85 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 13 (Tuesday).

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: 4 men killed in landmine explosion near LoC in Azad Kashmir
World.content:
MUZAFFARABAD: Four men were killed on Monday when a landmine exploded near the Line of Control (LoC) in the Poonch district of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), according to the Directorate General of Public Relations (DGPR).

The DGPR said in a statement, citing initial reports, that the four men were at the site of the incident in Hajira tehsil to repair a pipeline carrying spring water, when the landmine floated into the area from the Indian side and exploded.

All four of them died on the spot, the statement said.

It added that due to unclear border demarcation in areas close to the LoC, floating unexploded landmines posed a persistent threat to civilians and livestock.

The DGPR statement had no further details of the incident.

Earlier, Poonch Divisional Commissioner Sardar Waheed Khan said while speaking to Dawn that Indian Army personnel had planted the landmine.

Former AJK prime minister Sardar Abdul Qayyum Niazi expressed grief over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families.

In a statement, he said India was killing Kashmiris — not only in the occupied territory but also along the LoC in Azad Kashmir — by planting improvised explosive devices and shooting people engaged in routine activities such as herding cattle, cutting fodder and collecting medicinal plants.

He blamed the continued loss of lives on the prolonged delay in resolving the Kashmir issue, which he attributed to India’s reluctance.

World.title: KP's policies will come from Islamabad now, not Kabul, says Kundi
World.content:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said on Monday that gone were the days when there would be no coordination between the Centre and the province, adding that “our policies will now come from Islamabad, not Kabul”.

“Gone are the days when there was no coordination between the Centre and the province. Gone are the days when we used to fight needlessly with another province … We will have coordination with the Centre; our policies will come from Islamabad … not Kabul, Jalalabad or Kahandar. It is clear,” Kundi said at a press conference in Peshawar a day after taking the helm in KP.

Kundi assumed executive control of the province after the Centre imposed governor’s rule in KP and emergency in 12 of its districts, citing security situation and alleged non-cooperation of the now non-functional provincial government.

In days preceding the Centre’s move, tensions between the federal government and the PTI-led KP government had remained high, initially just over the party’s planned march to Islamabad to demand the release of its founder, Imran Khan, and later over the Centre’s accusation that its provincial government was not cooperating on counterterrorism. Federal ministers also accused the PTI’s KP government of facilitating terrorists and not taking action against them — allegations seemingly behind Kundi’s Kabul reference as Pakistan continues to raise the issue of cross-border terrorism from Afghanistan.

The KP governor’s these remarks and those about about ending the lack of coordination between the province and the Centre came as he pledged enhanced support for the province’s law enforcers, who are on the frontline in the fight against terrorism.

He said the new setup in the province would “not compromise on police”, pledging enhanced support and a pay raise for its law enforcers.

The governor further stated that he called a meeting on security the previous day and that of the provincial apex committee earlier today. He said the Centre had “shown confidence in us” and to meet its expectations, “our first priority is the fight against terrorism”.

Kundi issued a message to the army, police, Frontier Constabulary (FC) and security institutions, saying: “Our committee, this government, is standing side by side with you and will support you fully.”

He said that all members of the newly-formed advisory council had today taken charge of departments assigned to them, and would share future plans.

He added that during Sunday’s high-level security meeting, it had been decided that development would be the second priority of the new setup while the first would be giving whatever resources were asked for to the police and the Crime Terrorism Department.

“I want to say on behalf of this government that we are by your side,” he said addressing law enforcers, adding, “Whatever weapons you want, whatever you need, we will get them to you.”

Kundi stressed, “We will not compromise on our police officers and personnel. We will equip them well.”

He added that yesterday, he spoke to the inspector general of police (IGP) and chief secretary, ordering that from now on, the KP police would no longer have the lowest salaries in the country.

“If they are not the highest, they will at least be equal [to those of the personnel in other areas].”

The governor also said that disbursements under the martyrs’ package would be increased, and the children of martyrs would be given free education.

Kundi also thanked the KP public for “rejecting the circus” that had been ongoing for a few days, referring to the PTI’s long march that began on Oct 4. “I thank KP’s public that they have rejected this 13-year nuisance,” he said, referring to the PTI’s rule in the province.

The governor also said that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had provided the provincial police 10 armoured personnel carriers (APCs) on behalf of the Centre. He noted that in his earlier meeting with the minister, Naqvi had assured him and the apex committee that police and security forces would be granted as much in funds as they required.

“Our priority, our focus, is peace plus development,” the governor stressed. “We will work 24/7, we will deliver hope to people, to our young people, to the business community … that this is not your fight now, it is ours.”

Kundi also called on young doctors who had been striking in the province, urging them to end their strike and assuring that their issues would be solved. He also addressed university staff that were protesting over salaries and employment.

Additionally, he called on the business community, saying that he would work with them to solve their issues.

“When there is peace here, people will come to do business and investment … and the youth will have employment,” he added.

Kundi also criticised the PTI and accused it of to “fight their case” to the Centre, adding, “We will fight our case with arguments, not with abusive language.”

Responding to a question, he said that work was being done on restoring internet services, and that the roads would also be opened up again in a day or two and life would return to normal.

Separately, the interior minister posted about the provision of APCs on X, saying that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had directed the immediate transfer of the vehicles in view of the prevailing security situation in the province.

“The fight against terrorism is our collective responsibility,” Naqvi said. “The federal government stands firmly with KP police and will extend every possible support to defeat terrorism and protect our people.”

Earlier in the day, Naqvi held a meeting of the newly established Area Development Secretariat in KP.

The ADS has established in KP districts placed under emergency to “restore law and order, safeguard the security of the citizens of Pakistan and ensure good governance and development”, according to an Oct 11 government order.

In his meeting, Naqvi said that consulting the tribal elders was the “most important” at this point in the fight against the terrorism in KP.

“We need to ask these (tribal) representatives about what their issues are so we can resolve them,” he said, reiterating the need to empower the KP police and law enforcement.

“If we are spending Re1 in other parts of KP, we need to spend Rs3 here,” Naqvi said.

Commenting on ADS, he emphasised that the federal government had established a separate secretariat to specifically deal with the problems of the 12 districts under emergency.

“KP is a single province,” he clarified, rejecting the impression that the establishment of ADS was an attempt to dissociate the merged districts from the province. “We will work collectively in these 12 regions,” Naqvi said, adding that the PM was also overseeing the developments.

Kundi, Naqvi chair apex committee meeting

Earlier in the day, Kundi and Naqvi co-chaired a meeting of the provincial apex committee, a day after the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province.

Addressing the meeting, Kundi — who is now in charge of running the province — asserted that under the new set-up, tackling terrorism would be the priority.

“We can sacrifice our development, but never security,” Kundi vowed as he noted a “lack of synergy” in counterterrorism efforts in the province.

“Now it will show that there is (synergy),” he said, adding that the administration will “fulfil the demands of the Counter-Terrorism Department and police”. He stressed that the administration will “work 24/7” as the federal government and the “people had put their faith in us”.

“We have to show the difference,” Kundi said, adding that there was no time for holidays or weekends. He stressed that the administration was moving towards “result-oriented” actions, rather than cosmetic measures.

Noting the scourge of terrorism in the province, the governor said that the “people have no freedom to live, travel and do other things” in districts such as Dera Ismail Khan, Tank and Waziristan.

He called for working towards restoring freedom of movement for people in terrorism-affected districts.

“People from our province also want peace, prosperity and development,” he said. Kundi expressed the hope that the new administration be remembered well.

“It should be written in history that these people came and restored peace in the province,” he said. The governor added that he will hold apex committee meetings regularly.

Co-chairing the meeting alongside Kundi, Naqvi remarked: “Today is the first time I can proudly say that the federal and the provincial governments are on the same page.

“In the past 2.5 years, we have seen many ups and downs,” Naqvi said. The minister stated that the most difficult work was that the war against terrorism was being fought with “no backend support”.

Criticising the PTI-led government, he said: “It was the [provincial] government’s job to lead the war against terrorism, but they did not do it. They kept bowing their heads only because they did not want to compromise.

“But any war, no matter how many resources you have, cannot be won until the government leads it,” he stressed.

“Not once, not twice; we requested them to work with us dozens of times,“ Naqvi emphasised.

“One thing I will ask you to note is that this is the same force, these are the same people, but the only difference you will see is that … the same people will show you results.”

He further said: “It’s not like things will change in a day; there will be difficult times. But all of us, including the governor, police, administration, and the federal government.

“We have to face and defeat them together. Our intentions are pure; God will help us produce results.“

According to an official handout, the forum directed relevant institutions to ensure “coordinated, effective and decisive” steps for eradicating terrorism and establishing sustainable peace.

“The forum made it clear that intelligence-based operations against terrorist activities would continue and all available resources would be utilised to improve the law and order situation,” it said, adding that the need to improve the operational capability of police and the CTD was also stressed.

The body decided to provide these departments with modern equipment, necessary vehicles, effective weapons, required personnel and all other necessary resources.

It was also agreed during the meeting that the resolution of problems being faced by the people, provision of basic facilities and service delivery at people’s doorstep would be ensured, the handout said.

For this purpose, suggestions from the public, their needs and priorities of the local population would be considered during policymaking, it added.

Kundi meets chief secretary, police chief

Earlier in the day, Kundi chaired a high-level security meeting with the new chief secretary, Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan, newly appointed Home Affairs Adviser Kifayatullah Khan, and Inspector General Zulfiqar Hameed.

In a post on X, Kundi said the meeting reviewed the security situation and counterterrorism efforts in KP.

“Our police officers stand on the front lines of this fight, making immense sacrifices to protect our people. Their welfare, fair compensation and the future of their families must remain a priority.”

He expressed his administration’s commitment to “strengthening the police and CTD and ensuring our personnel receive the support they deserve”.

“Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has sacrificed enough. Our priority is to protect our people and restore lasting peace,” the governor declared.

Kundi also met Minister for States and Frontier Regions Amir Muqam, who called on him at the Governor House, state-run APP reported.

The two leaders exchanged views on the prevailing situation in the province, with particular focus on maintaining peace, strengthening security and addressing issues affecting the lives of the people.

They emphasised the need for effective measures and close cooperation to improve the law and order situation and eliminate terrorism.

Kundi and Muqam contended that the people of KP had rejected the politics of chaos and confrontation, stressing that peace, stability and public welfare should remain the top priorities.

They reaffirmed their commitment to extending all possible cooperation and taking practical steps to counter security challenges and promote stability in the province.

A day earlier, Kundi addressed the first meeting of the KP Advisory Council — formed by the federal government after the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule — where he outlined similar directions.

“We have to fast-track things. There will be zero tolerance for corruption. Things should be done in a timely manner,” he said, adding that they would have to demonstrate a clear difference from the work done by their predecessors.

Sunday’s directives came after a meeting of the federal cabinet deliberated on the security situation in PTI-led KP. During the meeting, the cabinet noted the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

Subsequently, the federal government imposed emergency under Article 232 and governor’s rule under Article 234.

Soon after, it also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in the province. On the ground, shipping containers were placed around the city of Peshawar to block several roads, with heavy police deployment.

Meanwhile, federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, as the Centre sought to explain that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their October 3 talks .

The PTI has said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre has denied . It also calls for reviewing the counterterrorism policy and opposes military operations.

On the other hand, the Centre has been criticising the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objects to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

61 law officers removed; 27 new appointed

Following the proclamation of emergency in KP, the provincial law department de-notified 61 law officers of the advocate general’s office.

These included 26 additional advocates general (AGs), 31 assistant AGs and four advocates-on-record (AORs), according to a notification issued late on Sunday and seen by Dawn.

Another notification, dated Oct 11, was issued to appoint 27 new law officers, including 12 additional AGs, 13 assistant AGs and two AORs.

Out of these, six additional AGs, eight assistant AGs, and one AOR were stationed in Peshawar, along with an assistant AG in the Peshawar Service Tribunal.

One additional AG and one assistant AG were each stationed in DI Khan, Bannu, Swat and Abbottabad. Two additional AGs and an AOR were placed in Islamabad to represent KP.

The government had already de-notified then-AG Shah Faisal Uthmankhel and replaced him with a senior lawyer, Sanaullah, who was earlier serving as an additional AG representing the federal government.

Additional input by Waseem Ahmad Shah

World.title: Achakzai draws Balochistan parallel as he flays Centre over governor's rule in KP
World.content:
National Assembly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai on Monday drew a comparison between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, criticising the government’s move to impose emergency and governor’s rule in the former.

The federal government on Sunday imposed emergency in 12 districts of KP, and placed the province under governor’s rule, taking note of the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif chaired the federal cabinet meeting that approved the measure, and said regarding terrorism in KP and Balochistan that “the way common citizens are being martyred, the way police officials and security officials, children and mothers [..] there can be nothing more heart-wrenching”.

Speaking to media outside the Parliament House on Monday, Achakzai claimed that there was no writ of the state in half of Balochistan.

“But you don’t impose it there, because the chief minister there is your favourite,” he alleged.

Achakzai’s claim of a lack of the state writ in half of Balochistan was apparently in connection with the security situation in the province.

Both KP and Balochistan have been facing terrorism, and according to the data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), 199 terrorist attacks were recorded in August across Pakistan, out of which KP, excluding the merged districts, recorded 54 terrorist attacks, while Balochistan recorded 89.

Speaking alongside Achakzai, Senate Opposition Leader Raja Abbas Nasir also drew the Balochistan parallel. “If terrorism and peace were an issue … you should have imposed emergency in Balochistan first,” he said.

Voicing his criticism of the government’s Oct 11 move, he said: “They call themselves the torchbearers of the law and the Constitution. However, they first attacked the Constitution by coming into power through Form-47 and now by signing the orders of imposing emergency against a government that held a two-thirds majority.”

‘Assault on democracy’

In his remarks assailing the Centre’s move, Achakzai said, “This will not be tolerated. It is the responsibility of everyone who values Pakistan and democracy to unite against this.”

He said parties in the opposition would be asked to announce a “democratic struggle” against the move from tomorrow in areas where they had influence.

“We will not abuse anyone; we will not fire bullets — we don’t have any — and we will not throw even a stone on anyone.”

He said the move was an “assault on Pakistan’s Constitution and democracy”.

“It is the duty of every Pakistani, whether he is a judge, general, in government or not in government, to resist this.”

Centre’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP followed weeks of political tensions, with the PTI intending to march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. The march was led by suspended KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.

Achakzai said Afridi was just demanding access to and medical treatment for Imran.

He reiterated the demand for access to Imran and assured that the PTI leaders would not disclose the details of their conversation with Imran if meetings were allowed. They would only inform the public about his health condition, he said.

He added that the opposition was still willing to hold negotiations with the government, but would also “continue its struggle against this system”.

“They say that Mehmood doesn’t want to meet. Am I mad? Pakistan is not just the Prime Minister’s House or the speaker’s chamber; Pakistan is bigger than that,” added Achakzai, who has said that he would not hold any meetings with government representatives at the Prime Minister’s House or Office or at the chamber of the NA speaker.

He said he was ready to hold a meeting at anyone’s personal residence.

Achakzai then invited other political parties to attend a planned all-parties conference to discuss how the country should be run.

Gohar to approach PHC

PTI Chairperson Barrister Gohar Khan was also present on the occasion and announced that he would challenge the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP in the Peshawar High Court (PHC) tomorrow (Tuesday).

Moreover, a parliamentary party meeting the same day would decide on how to stage a protest in Parliament, he added.

“We will raise our voice at every forum. Our long march and protest are ongoing,” Barrister Gohar said, adding that the party would not accept emergency and governor’s rule in KP.

“Whatever happened on October 11 should not have happened. October 11 will be remembered as a black day in Pakistan’s democratic history,” he said.

In a statement, the PTI particularly lambasted the PML-N and its ally PPP, saying the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule would add another “black mark” to their democratic credentials.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram, in the statement, accused both parties of supporting undemocratic and unconstitutional measures while invoking the slogans of democracy.

Terming Oct 11 a “black day for democracy”, Akram asserted that neither PTI nor the people of KP would accept the “unconstitutional, undemocratic and unlawful imposition of governor rule and emergency in the province, or the removal of its elected government”.

He announced that the party would continue its peaceful democratic struggle through the courts, parliament, provincial assemblies and public mobilisation until justice was achieved.

Akram said that the PPP and PML-N should be judged against their political records rather than their repeated claims of championing democracy.

He recalled that PPP founder and former prime minister, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, dismissed the Balochistan government led by Sardar Attaullah Mengal in 1973, followed by governor’s rule and a prolonged confrontation with provincial leadership.

Akram also referred to governor’s rule in the then North-West Frontier Province during ex-PM Benazir Bhutto’s government in 1994, its imposition in Punjab under then-President Asif Ali Zardari in 2009, and the removal of the Balochistan government led by Nawab Aslam Raisani in 2013.

Criticising the PML-N, Akram cited the 1997 attack on the Supreme Court by party supporters, the nationwide emergency imposed during ex-PM Nawaz Sharif’s government in 1998, the “theft” of PTI’s electoral mandate in the February 2024 general elections, the subsequent usurpation of its reserved seats, and the passage of Constitutional amendments, adding that these actions further undermined democratic principles and the public’s electoral mandate.

The PTI information secretary urged political leaders to learn from the events of 1971, recalling that the Awami League had won a majority in the 1970 general elections but was unable to assume power through a democratic transfer.

He said that the failure to respect the electoral outcome and the political confrontation contributed to a national tragedy whose consequences remain deeply significant.

“Pakistan cannot afford to repeat the mistakes of denying political representation or marginalising smaller provinces, as national unity depends on constitutional rule, respect for the people’s vote and meaningful provincial autonomy,” Akram stressed.

He questioned the federal government’s justification for suspending the KP government, adding that terrorism required coordinated national action rather than political confrontation.

Referring to figures by the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), he said fatalities involving security personnel and civilians in KP had declined by 16 per cent during the first nine months of 2026, while nationwide fatalities had increased by 9 per cent, partly amid worsening violence in Balochistan.

The PTI leader called for a transparent assessment of these figures and the effectiveness of security policies.

Outlining the party’s next steps, he said that PTI would “challenge the decision before the courts, pursue all available constitutional remedies and raise the matter in parliament, provincial assemblies and other relevant forums”.

He said the party would continue peaceful public mobilisation until the elected government’s authority and the constitutional rights of the people of KP were restored.

The information secretary demanded the “immediate reversal of the emergency and governor’s rule, the restoration of the elected provincial government and meaningful dialogue to resolve the country’s political crisis”.

KP Bar Council announces strike

Separately, the KP Bar Council expressed its concern over the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule, and announced a strike of court proceedings tomorrow (Tuesday).

In a statement issued on Monday, the bar claimed the move was aimed at removing the provincial government over “political differences”.

It stressed that such an “extraordinary measure” must be subject to full compliance with the relevant constitutional requirements and prescribed procedures.

“The use of the federal structure for any political purpose raises serious concerns regarding parliamentary democracy and provincial autonomy,” it noted, terming the move a violation of KP’s autonomy.

The bar council expressed its determination that the legal community will play its role in the restoration of democracy and vowed not to remain “silent spectators”.

It further said the bar will hold an emergency meeting on Oct 17 to discuss its future course of action. The statement also demanded the immediate reopening of roads so routine life could be restored.

World.title: Educational institutions in Peshawar to remain open on Tuesday, BRT services to be restored
World.content:
All educational institutions in Peshawar will remain open on Tuesday, a statement by the city’s deputy commissioner (DC) has announced.

The statement, posted on Facebook, urged the public not to pay heed to any “fake notification or rumours” in this regard.

Educational institutions in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s provincial capital remained closed on Monday amid road blocks following the imposition of governor’s rule in the province.

Police personnel remained present on roads in the city on Monday, with heavier deployment where the Cantonment limit began.

Meanwhile, TransPeshawar, which manages the city’s BRT transport system, has announced that services would be restored from October 13 (Tuesday). “Service will be provided as usual on all routes,” it said in a notice.

The district administration has also imposed a ban on gatherings in Peshawar for seven days under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).

The order by the DC has also banned the display of weapons, and barred carrying spikes, ball bearings, laden batons, petrol bombs, or any instrument that could potentially be used for violence.

Educational institutions in DI Khan to remain closed

All public and private educational institutions in the district of Dera Ismail Khan, including schools, colleges and universities, will remain closed on Tuesday (Oct 13) under orders issued by the deputy commissioner.

A notification issued by the district administration said that all examinations and papers scheduled for Tuesday have also been cancelled.

The relevant departments and heads of educational institutions have been directed to ensure strict compliance with the orders.

DI Khan is one of the 12 districts were the Centre has also imposed emergency.

The Centre imposed governor’s rule in KP and emergency in 12 of its districts on Sunday, citing security situation and alleged non-cooperation of the now non-functional provincial government.

In days preceding the Centre’s move, tensions between the federal government and the PTI-led KP government had remained high, initially just over the party’s planned march to Islamabad to demand the release of its founder, Imran Khan, and later also over the Centre’s accusation that the provincial government was not cooperating on counterterrorism.

Additional reporting by Irfan Mughal

World.title: Omani FM to visit Pakistan from Oct 13-14, will attend Joint Ministerial Commission session
World.content:
Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi will undertake an official two-day visit to Pakistan on Tuesday, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Monday.

According to a statement issued by the FO, Albusaidi’s visit, taking place at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, will last from Oct 13-14.

The statement added that during the visit, the Eighth Session of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC) would be held in Islamabad, co-chaired by the foreign ministers of the two countries.

“The meeting would serve as an important platform to review the entire spectrum of Pakistan-Oman bilateral relations and to further strengthen cooperation in diverse fields,” the FO said.

Additionally, Albusaidi is expected to make a courtesy call on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during his visit.

According to the FO, the visit “reflects the longstanding fraternal relations between Pakistan and Oman and is expected to further deepen mutually beneficial cooperation across multiple sectors”.

On Saturday, DPM Dar chaired an inter-ministerial meeting in Islamabad today to review preparations for the upcoming JMC session, according to state-run Radio Pakistan.

The meeting reviewed the agenda, bilateral agreements, and arrangements for the co-chairing of the JMC session, it said.

According to Radio Pakistan, the session will focus on “deepening cooperation in trade, investment, industry, agriculture, finance, oil and gas, labour, consular affairs, security, defence, climate change, civil aviation, education, media, and culture”.

Dar highlighted the importance of the commission in strengthening bilateral relations. He directed stakeholders to ensure thorough preparations and effective follow-up to “secure tangible outcomes”, the outlet added.

World.title: High-level Brazil delegation meets CDF Munir; both sides agree to bolster military collaboration
World.content:
Pakistan and Brazil on Monday agreed to bolster their military-to-military cooperation as a high-level delegation from the Latin American country called on Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir.

According to a statement from Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the delegation led by Brazil’s Admiral Renato Rodrigues De Aguiar Freire, chief of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces, met the CDF at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi.

During the meeting, both military leaders discussed matters of mutual interest, the regional security landscape and avenues to bolster bilateral defence and security cooperation.

“They expressed satisfaction with the longstanding cordial relations between Pakistan and Brazil and agreed to further strengthen military-to-military collaboration,” ISPR added.

CDF Munir “emphasised Pakistan’s commitment to strengthening defence ties with Brazil”.

Admiral Friere appreciated the military’s professionalism and operational preparedness and acknowledged their contributions to regional peace and stability, according to ISPR.

“The visit reflects the shared resolve of Pakistan and Brazil to deepen defence cooperation and strengthen bilateral military ties,” the statement concluded.

The visiting admiral was presented with a guard of honour by a smartly turned-out tri-services contingent upon his arrival at the GHQ.

Brasilia has made efforts to boost ties with Islamabad as far back as 2018, when then-Brazilian ambassador Claudio Raja Gabaglia Lins visited the Sarhad Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Peshawar.

The two sides had agreed on steps to increase bilateral trade and establish a joint chamber of commerce and industry to facilitate businesspeople and investors.

World.title: Pakistan eye clean sweep as Sri Lanka seek consolation in final T20I
World.content:
Pakistan will look to complete a commanding series whitewash when they face Sri Lanka in the third and final Twenty20 International at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday, with captain Sahibzada Farhan keen to see his side continue its aggressive approach after two emphatic victories.

Having sealed the series 2-0, Pakistan head into the final encounter with their batting unit in impressive form, while Sri Lanka face the task of salvaging pride after being outplayed in both matches. The hosts’ 215-3 in the second T20I on Sunday was their highest-ever total in a home T20I, reflecting the intent they have sought to bring to the shortest format.

With the trophy already secured, Pakistan could consider resting key players and testing their bench strength. However, the management may be reluctant to disturb a combination that has begun to click, particularly with the top order delivering consistently and the bowling unit providing timely breakthroughs.

Farhan has led that transformation with scores of 89 and 73 in the first two matches, while Maaz Sadaqat has emerged as another major force. The youngster followed his 50 off 29 balls in the opening game with a blistering 96 off 51 deliveries on Sunday, underlining his ability to attack both pace and spin.

Farhan said Pakistan intended to maintain the same attacking mindset regardless of the opposition or the occasion.

“If I play my 50th or 100th T20 match, the demand of T20 cricket will remain the same. I will play the same way and attack in the same manner,” Farhan said in a video released by the Pakistan Cricket Board on Monday.

He explained that the team had specifically targeted improved returns during the powerplay, aiming to push its scoring beyond the 40-45-run mark and regularly cross 50 or even 60 in the first six overs.

The captain also expressed confidence in the batting depth available to Pakistan, pointing to Maaz, Saim Ayub and Hasan Nawaz as players capable of sustaining the momentum.

“Looking at the way we are batting, I believe we can comfortably score 200-plus,” he said, crediting the batters for delivering on that ambition.

Maaz’s latest innings was particularly encouraging, although he fell four runs short of what would have been his maiden T20I century. Farhan was equally impressed by the youngster’s fearless approach, saying: “He is playing brilliantly. It would have been great if he had scored a hundred, because a first T20 hundred is every batter’s dream.”

Maaz, meanwhile, said performances in franchise cricket had helped strengthen his confidence at international level.

“When you perform anywhere, it gives you a boost from within and builds your confidence. But when you perform for Pakistan, for your country, and help win matches, that is the most confidence-boosting feeling,” he said after Sunday’s match.

Pakistan’s bowling has also played a significant role in their dominance. Salman Mirza has been effective with the new ball, while Imran Randhawa produced a match-winning spell of three wickets for just 11 runs in four overs in the second T20I.

Imran, playing his first T20I series, said the team’s collective performance mattered more than individual achievements.

“For me, the most important thing was winning the series for Pakistan. That is enough for me,” he said, adding that the plans communicated to him had worked as intended.

The all-rounder also credited the team’s combination for their success, highlighting the contributions of Farhan and Fakhar Zaman at the top and the support provided by the bowling unit.

Pakistan could nevertheless consider bringing in left-arm wrist-spinner Sufyan Moqim, with leg-spinner Abrar Ahmed having enjoyed relatively modest returns in the series.

Sri Lanka, by contrast, have struggled to find answers despite changes in leadership, coaching and batting combinations.

New captain Kusal Mendis and head coach Gary Kirsten remain in search of a winning formula, with the visitors needing significant improvement in both their batting and fielding to challenge Pakistan.

Their bowlers were unable to contain the hosts on Sunday, with Maheesh Theekshana coming under pressure on a surface that offered little assistance. Missed opportunities in the field compounded their problems, allowing Pakistan to build a formidable total.

Fast bowler Nuwan Thushara acknowledged that Sri Lanka had let the hosts off the hook through their fielding lapses.

“If we had taken those catches, we could have reduced their total by another 20 to 30 runs,” he said, while stressing that his team would return with a better plan for the final match.

Sri Lanka could make changes to their bowling attack, with Viyaskanth Vijayakanth a possible option and Dushmantha Chameera potentially returning if fit. Their batting also needs to recover, particularly after Lahiru Udara’s impressive 91 in the opening match was followed by a quieter outing in the second.

Udara will be eager to make another strong impression, while Kusal Mendis and the rest of the top order must find a way to withstand Pakistan’s attack and provide a competitive platform.

Rawalpindi’s batting-friendly surface is again expected to favour stroke-makers, with pleasant evening conditions forecast for Tuesday. Another high-scoring contest could be on the cards, placing a premium on Sri Lanka’s ability to execute their plans and Pakistan’s determination to sustain their momentum.

For the hosts, a clean sweep would reinforce the aggressive philosophy Farhan has outlined and provide further confidence in a developing combination. Sri Lanka, meanwhile, must find a response to avoid ending the series without a consolation victory.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
