World.title: Over Two-Thirds of Myanmar’s Population Poor or at Risk of Poverty: UN
World.content:
More than 37 million people—over two-thirds of Myanmar’s population of more than 54 million—are experiencing or at risk of “multidimensional poverty,” according to the latest report from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released on Thursday.

Drawing data from a nationwide household survey of nearly 7,500 people in 2025, the UNDP’s latest analysis examines what it calls multidimensional poverty, which looks beyond income and also covers non-financial deprivation, including access to education and healthcare, and other basic needs, amid economic and political crisis and natural hazards.

It said nearly 18 million people (32.6 percent) in Myanmar are multidimensionally poor, while more than 19 million (35.5 percent) others are vulnerable. That brings the total figure to more than 37 million people (68 percent) who either face poverty or are at risk of falling into it.

“Myanmar may no longer dominate international headlines, but the hardships facing millions of people continue to deepen,” said Kanni Wignaraja, UN assistant secretary-general and UNDP regional director for Asia and the Pacific. “We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded.”

The survey found that people in rural areas are poorer than those in urban areas.

In terms of both severity and scale, the UNDP report highlights Rakhine State as the worst-affected area, with approximately 1.66 million residents enduring the most intense multidimensional poverty. Sagaing Region followed with a larger total of approximately 2.38 million people experiencing less severe poverty. Ayeyarwady Region ranked third.

The UNDP’s analysis indicated that poverty is driven by a combination of long-standing household vulnerabilities, including low education levels, insecure jobs and limited income, and wider pressures such as rising prices, natural hazards and armed conflict.

In war-torn Rakhine and Karenni (Kayah) states, poverty has been compounded by conflict, displacement and restrictions on movement.

To address poverty effectively, the report concluded that aid must provide intensive support to hard-hit conflict zones while reaching larger numbers of poor residents elsewhere, with assistance tailored to local needs.

World.title: Regime Shuts Down Myanmar’s Surging Online Gold Market
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has moved to ban online sales of gold and jewelry, citing the risk of flawed products and market destabilization.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Ministry announced it has suspended issuance of licenses for selling gold, raw gold, jewelry, art objects, and household items via online platforms. It threatened unlicensed traders with prosecution under the 2013 Essential Commodities and Services Law, which carries six months to three years in prison and fines up to 500,000 kyats (roughly US$ 240).

Under existing rules, online sellers must obtain a Commerce Ministry license, while those dealing in gold and gemstones must also secure a permit from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Conservation.

Industry insiders told The Irrawaddy that more than 700 businesses have applied for licenses to sell gold and jewelry online in recent years. However, the ministry has now refused to extend expired permits, with inspections and enforcement expected to begin at the end of this month.

Online gold and jewelry shopping has become popular in Myanmar over the past few years, with internet outlets hiring actors and celebrities to promote their livestream sales.

Traders say the clampdown follows growing complaints from buyers that jewelry purchased via livestream “flash sales” was later rejected by pawnshops or gold shops.

“Online customers have no way of verifying the weight, quality, or reference price of their purchases. That leads to disputes and losses,” one Yangon jeweler explained.

Last month, Mandalay police announced the arrest of 11 foreign nationals and 17 Myanmar citizens accused of running online gemstone scams. Authorities said the suspects were using fake jade to defraud buyers in livestream sales.

Online gemstone sales remain permitted provided merchants hold a license from the Myanma Gems Enterprise and refrain from selling gold.

While the Yangon Region Gold Entrepreneurs Association has set the domestic reference price for 24K gold at 7.1 million kyats per tical, the market price exceeds 10 million kyats — a gap of 3 million kyats. Before the 2021 coup, a tical sold for under 1.4 million kyats.

Business owners warn that banning online sales will hurt digital commerce and marketing, which had surged during the pandemic. “Shops that relied on livestream promotions will struggle. Now we can only depend on walk-in customers,” one trader said.

World.title: Tokayev, King Philippe Pledge to Deepen Kazakhstan-Belgium Ties in Joint Statement
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations, focusing on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and cooperation on international topics, according to a joint statement adopted by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe of the Belgians on Oct. 12.

The statement followed talks during the Belgian royal couple’s state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 11-14, which both officials described as an important milestone in bilateral relations.

Middle Corridor and digital technologies

The two countries underscored the growing role of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, as a reliable and sustainable transport link between Asia and Europe.

They also reaffirmed the importance of developing transport and logistics cooperation and enhancing connectivity between the two regions.

Digitalization, artificial intelligence and innovation were identified as increasingly important for sustainable economic development and competitiveness. The two leaders expressed interest in developing cooperation in artificial intelligence, big data, cloud technologies, supercomputing infrastructure and data centers.

During the press briefing, Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s interest in expanding cooperation across emerging industries, including digitalization and space technologies.

King Philippe, in turn, underlined Kazakhstan’s technological development, noting that the country was “at the forefront of digitalization” and had developed unique solutions, notably in artificial intelligence.

“We are keen to visit the Alem.AI center and discuss synergies between our countries,” he said.

Critical minerals and economic cooperation

The joint statement reaffirmed the importance of cooperation in critical minerals, petrochemicals, industry and mechanical engineering, and renewable energy.

The leaders welcomed the holding of a roundtable on critical minerals during the state visit, underscoring the strategic importance of cooperation in this field.

They also highlighted the potential to expand agricultural trade, develop the food industry and introduce modern agricultural technologies.

Tokayev noted that Belgium had invested more than $15 billion in Kazakhstan’s economy since 2005, describing economic cooperation as a cornerstone of bilateral relations.

The leaders welcomed the Kazakhstan-Belgium Business Council’s activities and the fourth meeting during the visit as an important mechanism for strengthening ties between the two countries’ business communities.

The statement also reaffirmed their commitment to the Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement between Kazakhstan and the European Union and its member states, signed on Dec. 21, 2015.

Education, healthcare and cultural ties

The two officials welcomed the Kazakhstan-Belgium Rectors’ Forum and expressed support for joint educational programs, academic mobility, scientific research and partnerships between universities and research centers.

They also reaffirmed the importance of strengthening healthcare cooperation, including enhancing the role of primary healthcare within the World Health Organization Global Coalition for Primary Health Care.

The leaders referred to the principles of the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration on Primary Health Care and the 2018 Astana Declaration, as well as initiatives to be discussed following the conference Towards the 50th Anniversary of the Alma-Ata Declaration: Building Strong Primary Health Care for Future Generations, scheduled for Oct. 14 in Almaty.

The discussions also featured cultural cooperation. Tokayev welcomed the presentation of works by Belgian artist James Ensor at Kazakhstan’s National Museum and cooperation between the Almaty Museum of Arts and KANAL-Center Pompidou.

Tokayev and King Philippe further welcomed the entry into force of the protocol amending the agreement between Kazakhstan and the Benelux countries on visa exemption for holders of service passports.

They also expressed their intention to conclude negotiations and sign a bilateral agreement on remunerated employment for family members of diplomatic missions as a deliverable marking 35 years of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and Belgium in 2027.

Commitment to international law and dialogue

On international and regional matters, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to multilateralism, international law and the United Nations’ central role in maintaining international peace and security, promoting sustainable development and addressing global challenges.

They agreed to intensify bilateral political dialogue on international affairs and economic development within the United Nations, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), and multilateral platforms in the Kazakhstan-EU and Central Asia-EU formats.

The statement also highlighted the importance of strengthening the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production and Stockpiling of Bacteriological (Biological) and Toxin Weapons and on Their Destruction, adopted on April 10, 1972.

The leaders expressed satisfaction with the outcomes of their talks and reaffirmed their determination to give new impetus to the Kazakhstan-Belgium partnership.

Both officials expressed confidence that King Philippe’s first state visit to Kazakhstan would lay the foundation for the further qualitative development of bilateral relations.

World.title: Kazakh President Terminates Maslikhats’ Powers, Orders Snap Elections
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree on Oct. 12 terminating the powers of maslikhats, local representative bodies at all levels, before the end of their term.

The decision followed consultations with Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Kurultai Chair Aibek Dadebay, in accordance with Article 88, Paragraph 5 of Kazakhstan’s Constitution, Akorda reported.

The Central Election Commission has been instructed to take all necessary measures to appoint, prepare and conduct snap elections to maslikhats at all levels.

World.title: Eagle Trains Hunter Too: Inside Shygys Salburyny
World.content:
ASTANA — In falconry, even the master has lessons to learn from the bird he trains. That understanding of an ancient hunting tradition emerged at this year’s Shygys Salburyny festival in the East Kazakhstan Region, where 176 falconers from 10 countries competed in the first Open Asian Cup in traditional falconry.

The annual festival drew nearly 15,000 visitors and more than 50 breeders and trainers of Kazakhstan’s native tazy hunting dogs to the Burkit Tobe ethnocultural complex in Bozanbai village on Oct. 8-10. Participants came from China, Georgia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Mongolia, Russia, Spain, Türkiye and Uzbekistan.

The gathering coincided with Kazakhstan’s efforts to secure further international recognition for its traditional hunting heritage. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) first recognized falconry as intangible cultural heritage in 2010, with Kazakhstan joining the multinational inscription in 2016.

A separate Kazakh nomination, “Salburyn, equestrian Festival with Tazy dogs and Burkyt birds,” covering traditional hunting practices involving golden eagles, tazy dogs and horsemanship, is under consideration for UNESCO inscription in 2026. Representatives of Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry and National Commission for UNESCO also visited Bozanbai during the festival.

For Turkish falconer and researcher Dr. Nedim Mutlu Kızılbuga, who first visited Kazakhstan in 2022 to study the country’s eagle-hunting traditions for his doctoral dissertation, the relationship between a hunter and a bird of prey has become a subject of both academic research and personal experience.

“People generally think that humans train eagles and use them for hunting. That is partly true, but during my field research, I realized something else: Eagles also train humans. When a falconer trains an eagle, without even realizing it, they learn to become more disciplined, hardworking, generous and patient,” Kızılbuga told The Astana Times.

“One of the most interesting findings of my dissertation was that it is not only the human who trains the eagle, but the eagle who trains the human,” he said.

Now on his fourth visit to Kazakhstan, Kızılbuga returns regularly to meet the local falconers he first encountered during his research.

Where precision decides the winner

The Open Asian Cup introduced a new competitive dimension to Shygys Salburyny, which began in Bozanbai in 2021 as Qansonar, a Kazakh term referring to ideal hunting conditions when animal tracks are visible on fresh snow, before becoming an international festival in 2022.

Golden eagles, hawks and falcons competed in exercises testing their responsiveness, flight control and hunting abilities. These included recalling birds from distances of up to 700 meters, shyrga, in which handlers swung a lure from side to side to test the birds’ ability to follow its movements, and live-prey hunting involving foxes, hares and pigeons.

Yeltai Muptekeyev, a competition judge, explained how the scoring system determined which participants advanced.

“Each category has its own rules. The participants are assessed based on their performance and timing. We have a scoring system, and those who earn the highest points advance. Even a difference of one point can determine the winner,” Muptekeyev told The Astana Times.

Young falconers learn together with their eagles

Among the participants was Aisulu Bekniyazova from Almaty, who discovered falconry through an Instagram casting announcement about a year ago. She began training under Ayazhan Daniyarkyzy, a falconer with five years of experience, and made her competitive debut in Bozanbai alongside her young golden eagle, Mangaz.

“I think one of the most special aspects of this sport is the bond between the eagle and its handler. The eagle I am holding is still young, just like me, and it does not have much experience yet. We are participating in a competition together for the first time,” said Bekniyazova.

Daniyarkyzy added that birds often come to reflect the character and temperament of their handlers.

“Aisulu is a little shy and sometimes nervous, but when she speaks, she expresses herself very clearly. She is the kind of person who prefers to prove everything through actions rather than words. (…) Mangaz has turned out to be a very quick learner, but Aisulu herself really surprised us,” Daniyarkyzy told The Astana Times.

Under the guidance of her own mentor, experienced falconer Sultanserik Beketuly, Daniyarkyzy also trains girls as young as 14, beginning with exercises that help handlers and birds become accustomed to one another.

“We begin with simpler exercises, such as calling the eagle to land on their hands. It is important for both the person and the eagle to get used to one another. You can gradually see when they begin to understand each other and establish a connection. Only after that does the actual training begin,” she said.

One practice, different traditions

For international participants, the competition offered a closer look at how hunting techniques and equipment differ across countries.

Spanish falconer Julen Bara Lanas, who has practiced falconry for 16 years and now directs a zoo in Spain, was visiting Kazakhstan for the first time. He observed differences in how birds are handled, particularly the use of horses and traditional equipment.

“In Spain, we use the left hand because we don’t ride on horseback. We are walking with the birds, and that is one of the differences I see between Spain and Kazakhstan. Also, in Spain, if you want to buy a glove, it is manufactured rather than made by an artisan. Here, I love that people have all these things handmade by themselves,” Lanas told The Astana Times.

Hungarian falconer Bence Fábos, who also hunts with golden eagles, noticed a similar distinction between hunting on foot and horseback.

“We hunt in Hungary only on foot. Here, you do it on horseback. This is the motherland of falconry, and I’m very happy to be here now. You have very good horses and birds,” said Fábos.

He also viewed falconry as a way for younger generations to maintain direct contact with nature amid growing reliance on technology.

“Falconry is part of nature. People who practice it become part of nature and live in it. This is very important because, as technology develops, we forget nature, animals and our culture,” he said.

The tazy’s place in Kazakh hunting culture

Birds of prey were not the only hunters tested in Bozanbai. The festival also included races for tazy, the Kazakh hunting sighthound traditionally used to pursue game across open terrain.

Erzhan Zhaiyk, from Asubulak village in Ulan district, won the tazy competition with his two-year-old dog.

“I have been training tazy dogs for about two years. The most important thing is training. I take my tazy out into nature every day, covering around 20 to 30 kilometers. If you maintain a proper diet and nutrition alongside regular training, the dog will get into very good physical condition,” said Zhaiyk.

Birds of prey were not the only hunters tested in Bozanbai. The festival also included races for tazy, the Kazakh hunting sighthound traditionally used to pursue game across open terrain.

“The tazy is a national treasure of the Kazakh people. Our ancestors have kept and raised tazy dogs since ancient times. As people used to say, one tazy could provide food for an entire village. Traditionally, we do not even call a tazy a dog. It is considered a sacred animal. Our ancestors valued tazy dogs very highly,” he said.

Birds of prey were not the only hunters tested in Bozanbai. The festival also included races for tazy, the Kazakh hunting sighthound traditionally used to pursue game across open terrain.

Beyond the falconry and tazy competitions, the festival featured traditional horseback events, including horse taming, mounted archery and tenge ilu, in which riders retrieve coins from the ground at a gallop. Visitors also watched tug-of-war and the traditional Tolagai strength contest, attended concerts featuring Kazakh performers and explored 50 yurts showcasing local crafts, cultural traditions and the history of East Kazakhstan’s districts, alongside an artisans’ fair.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Seek to Expand Partnership Across Key Sectors
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium are set to deepen cooperation in transport and logistics, critical minerals, energy, agriculture, digitalization and other priority sectors as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Belgium’s King Philippe in Astana on Oct. 12.

The talks marked the start of King Philippe and Queen Mathilde’s first state visit to Kazakhstan, which brings a high-level delegation of government officials, business leaders and academics to the country to strengthen bilateral ties and explore new partnership opportunities.

Tokayev described Belgium as a reliable and time-tested partner for Kazakhstan in Europe, highlighting the close ties the two countries have built over more than three decades.

“This landmark occasion opens a golden chapter in the history of our nations. It truly honors the friendship between our peoples. Belgium is a brilliant and time-tested partner of Kazakhstan in Europe. We deeply admire your beautiful country, its distinguished history and its enduring traditions,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted Belgium’s rich cultural heritage, scientific achievements and contribution to international dialogue.

“Over the past three decades, our countries have forged close ties founded on genuine friendship, mutual respect and trust. Next year marks the 35th anniversary of our diplomatic relations, an important milestone in our enduring partnership,” he said.

According to Tokayev, Belgium is among Kazakhstan’s leading investment partners, with more than $15 billion invested in the Kazakh economy since 2005. Bilateral trade increased by nearly 30% last year. More than 100 Belgian companies and joint ventures currently operate in Kazakhstan.

“Our government will continue to create favorable conditions for Belgian investors to expand their presence and pursue new opportunities. Their full and timely implementation will be under my personal monitoring and control,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev welcomed progress on facilitating travel between the two countries through amendments to the visa exemption agreement for holders of service passports.

The two leaders also exchanged views on international and regional issues.

“Kazakhstan and Belgium share firm commitments to international law, multilateralism and the peaceful settlement of conflicts. At a time of growing global uncertainty, dialogue, mutual trust and responsible diplomacy are more essential than ever,” Tokayev said.

He also reaffirmed the importance of Kazakhstan’s strategic partnership with the European Union, including agreements signed during his recent visit to Brussels.

Belgium sees new opportunities

King Philippe thanked Tokayev and said the visit aimed to strengthen relations between the two countries and explore new areas of cooperation.

“We know that over the past 35 years, our countries have formed unbreakable ties. They are based on what, in our own region, makes us special: diversity and connectivity. The three coming days will allow us to explore the potential and opportunities our countries offer each other,” he said.

He praised Kazakhstan’s development and its growing role in regional and international affairs.

“The continuing transformation of Kazakhstan into a world player is impressive. Only recently, the Kazakh people cemented constitutional reforms that reflect new ambitions for the people. By all standards, Kazakhstan is today a modern society built on ancient foundations and traditions. With a well-educated population, a large middle class and state-of-the-art infrastructure, Kazakhstan is ready to tackle challenges for the future,” King Philippe said.

The king highlighted Kazakhstan’s progress in digitalization and artificial intelligence. He also praised Kazakhstan’s role in promoting dialogue and understanding, noting the country’s multicultural society and its position at the heart of the Middle Corridor.

“Kazakhstan is now at the core of the Middle Corridor, literally in the heart of the region. As a bridge builder, Kazakhstan is more than ever the promoter of dialogue, the rules-based international order and the firm belief in multilateralism as a way to solve disputes. This is what fundamentally binds Kazakhstan with Belgium and the European Union,” Philippe said.

The two leaders also expressed expectations for the upcoming fourth Kazakh-Belgian Business Council and other meetings, which they said would provide platforms for turning shared ambitions into tangible results.

World.title: Brazilian Expert Says Kazakhstan’s Foreign Policy Offers Lessons for Brazil
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s balanced foreign policy, advances in artificial intelligence and institutional reforms offer valuable lessons for Brazil, while cooperation in critical minerals, energy and logistics could strengthen ties between the two countries, said Márcio Coimbra, director of Casa Política and president of the Monitor da Democracia Institute, in an interview with The Astana Times.

Coimbra is visiting Central Asia for the first time, with plans to travel to the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan before continuing to the Caucasus. He said the region’s rapid development and growing geopolitical importance deserve greater attention in Latin America.

“But it’s a part of the world that Latin America doesn’t look at with the right attention. And it calls my attention because it’s becoming very developed very fast here,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s balanced diplomacy offers lessons for Brazil

Coimbra identified Kazakhstan’s ability to maintain constructive relations with major global powers as one of the country’s most valuable experiences for Brazil.

Coimbra said Brazil could learn from Kazakhstan’s foreign policy approach, notably its emphasis on national sovereignty and economic interests.

“I’ve always defended that Brazil needs to be defending Brazil’s sovereignty. And I think that you do it in a very smart way here,” he said.

He described Kazakhstan’s approach as balancing Beijing, Brussels and Washington while prioritizing national economic interests.

“Because then you put your economic interests first and Kazakhstan first,” he said.

Coimbra said Brazil could apply similar principles to its own foreign policy. He also emphasized the need to strengthen ties between Brazil and Kazakhstan, which share challenges and opportunities as middle powers.

Cooperation in critical minerals, AI and energy

Coimbra highlighted critical minerals, artificial intelligence, renewable energy and agriculture as promising areas for bilateral cooperation.

Both countries possess substantial natural resources, including critical minerals, but face challenges in developing domestic processing capacity. He noted that China remains a major processor of rare earth elements, creating opportunities for countries to diversify supply chains and develop their own industrial capabilities.

He also pointed to Kazakhstan’s progress in artificial intelligence, including the development of data centers and a large language model based on its national language.

Brazil’s extensive hydropower resources could support cooperation in digital infrastructure. Coimbra said Kazakhstan and Brazil could explore partnerships connecting Kazakhstan’s data center ambitions with Brazil’s clean electricity supply.

He also identified opportunities in oil and gas expertise, agricultural production and logistics, including connections between Kazakhstan’s Middle Corridor and Latin American trade flows.

“Things that are missing to you are in Brazil. And things that are missing in Brazil you have here,” he said.

Reforms should reflect national values

Coimbra welcomed Kazakhstan’s institutional reforms, including the transition to a unicameral parliament and the introduction of the Kurultai, describing them as steps toward a political system rooted in the country’s history and culture.

He said countries should develop institutions suited to their own circumstances rather than simply importing foreign models.

“Every country has the right to find its own system that adapts to its own culture,” he said.

Turning potential into practical partnerships

Despite shared economic interests, Coimbra said geographic distance, limited direct air connections and a lack of information have constrained relations between Central Asia and Latin America.

He noted that reaching Kazakhstan from Brazil involves multiple flight connections, making travel more difficult and expensive. He said stronger transport links would help bring the regions closer together.

Coimbra called for stronger business links, targeted investment projects, technology transfer and more structured cooperation between the two countries’ private sectors.

He also proposed leveraging multilateral platforms, including the United Nations, the G20 and BRICS, to align positions on sustainable development and global governance.

“The single largest opportunity lies in creating a strategic commodity and infrastructural bridge,” he said, emphasizing the need to move beyond broad agreements toward practical, co-financed projects.

For Coimbra, stronger Kazakhstan-Brazil relations would bring together complementary resources, energy capabilities and technological ambitions while giving both countries greater room to pursue their economic interests independently.

World.title: Yandex Services Resume in Kazakhstan: Outage Reveals Challenges of Urban Mobility in Digital Age
World.content:
ALMATY – A disruption to Yandex’s taxi and delivery services on Oct. 11 left users across Kazakhstan struggling to book rides, highlighting the role digital platforms play in everyday mobility in the country’s largest cities. As passengers in Almaty and Astana sought alternative ways to reach their destinations, ride-hailing service inDrive reported a sharp increase in demand, creating an imbalance between passengers and available drivers.

The disruption affected the company’s taxi-booking and delivery platform, while users also reported problems with other Yandex products, including Yandex Music, Yandex Pay and Yandex Cloud. Technical problems appeared after a drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in the Russian Vladimir Region on Oct. 11, forcing the facility to shut down. The incident was followed by service interruptions in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia.

Yandex services have since resumed operation in Kazakhstan, although the company is continuing work to stabilize their performance. Technical teams are working to restore consistent service, but the company has not provided a definitive timeline for completing all recovery work.

In large cities, where people depend on a combination of buses, taxis and other transport options, these services perform interconnected roles. Public transport follows fixed routes and schedules, while ride-hailing offers door-to-door trips and can help cover journeys that are less convenient by bus. When a major platform becomes unavailable, finding a suitable alternative can be difficult, particularly when demand rises suddenly.

inDrive faces a surge in demand

The outage prompted passengers to turn to alternative ride-hailing services. Arsen Tomsky, founder and chief executive of inDrive, said the company had experienced a sharp increase in passengers and orders in Kazakhstan.

“Since this morning, inDrive in Kazakhstan has seen a sharp influx of passengers and orders. This creates an imbalance between supply and demand,” Tomsky wrote on Threads on Oct. 11.

He said the company had reduced its commissions to attract more drivers, bringing them down to the minimum required to cover mandatory taxes.

“Today, we will most likely further limit the bargaining range to curb excessive price increases,” Tomsky added.

Why an outage in Russia affected Kazakhstan

Yandex Go Kazakhstan said it operated in accordance with Kazakhstan’s legislation and that personal data belonging to Kazakh users was stored on servers in Kazakhstan and in jurisdictions providing appropriate data protection. However, the company explained that its digital products rely on distributed computing infrastructure, with individual components located in different countries.

“A failure in one of the infrastructure components in one country can affect the availability of certain functions in another,” Yandex Go representatives said.

The company said technical teams were working to restore affected services and redistribute workloads across its infrastructure. It did not provide an exact timeline for the full restoration of all functions.

Data localization does not guarantee uninterrupted services

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development said servers used to store Kazakh users’ personal data were operating normally inside the country. The ministry stressed, however, that keeping personal data within Kazakhstan does not mean that every component of a digital platform operates independently of infrastructure abroad.

“Ensuring uninterrupted service is of primary importance to users. Therefore, storing data within Kazakhstan and ensuring the resilient operation of digital platforms are separate tasks that require a comprehensive solution,” reads the statement.

The ministry said it was working with Yandex and Kazakh infrastructure organizations to provide the necessary support for restoring services. It was also coordinating with other taxi and delivery platforms to help ensure their resilience under increased demand.

Urban mobility depends on more than one service

Public transport remains an important alternative for many journeys, but buses and taxis do not always serve the same needs. Fixed routes may work for regular commutes, while ride-hailing can be particularly useful for trips outside convenient public transport connections, late-night travel or journeys requiring a direct route.

The outage did not mean that public transport itself had failed. Rather, it illustrated how a problem affecting one part of the urban mobility system can create additional pressure elsewhere, especially when passengers turn to the same alternatives at once.

For drivers and couriers, the disruption also affected access to the platforms through which they receive orders and earn income. For passengers, it raised immediate questions about availability, waiting times and the cost of reaching their destinations.

With services back online in Kazakhstan, the focus has shifted from restoring access to ensuring stable operation. The disruption nevertheless exposed a broader challenge for digital services that have become part of everyday city life: keeping them reliable when technical problems in one location can affect users far beyond it.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Startup Ecosystem Enters New Phase as Funding and AI Adoption Surge
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s startup ecosystem is moving from a period of rapid expansion toward a more demanding stage focused on revenue, international customers and global growth, according to the first national study of the country’s startup landscape.

The Kazakhstan Startup Landscape 2026 report was presented Oct. 3 at the AI & Digital Bridge 2026 forum. The study maps more than 1,500 startups and technology companies and examines how businesses develop from their first sales to international expansion. It was prepared by RISE Research & Advisory with Astana Hub and Sapa Group with the support of the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development.

The findings show an ecosystem that has grown considerably in just a few years. The number of startups in the study’s database increased from around 300 in 2020 to more than 1,500 in 2026. Nearly 60% of active startups were founded between 2023 and 2026, highlighting how young the ecosystem remains.

From $20 million to more than $460 million

One of the clearest signs of the ecosystem’s development is the growth of venture financing.

According to the study, venture funding increased more than 23-fold from 2020, when it stood at around $20 million. RISE forecasts that venture investment in Kazakhstan could exceed $460 million in 2026. More than 200 companies in the database have attracted venture funding, while 45 have raised more than $1 million.

The growth reflects a broader transformation of Kazakhstan’s technology sector. In 2022, startups connected with Astana Hub attracted $130 million in investment, while digitally delivered services exported through the ecosystem reached $165 million.

By 2025, IT service exports through Astana Hub had reached 328 billion tenge (US$681 million), with 537 companies exporting IT services to 111 countries.

The country’s startup ambitions also received a major boost with the emergence of its first unicorn. Higgsfield AI, a generative AI video company, surpassed a $1 billion valuation in September 2025, becoming Kazakhstan’s first startup to reach unicorn status.

The achievement marked a significant shift from earlier ambitions. In 2025, Kazakhstan was still working toward creating its first unicorn by 2027.

AI is becoming part of the startup model

Artificial intelligence has quickly moved from being a specialized technology to becoming a core part of Kazakhstan’s startup landscape.

The new study found that 82% of surveyed companies use or position AI as part of their product.

This trend is consistent with the broader development of Kazakhstan’s AI sector. A RISE report published earlier in 2026 found that the country had more than 100 AI startups, while venture investment in AI increased from approximately $14 million in 2023 to $73 million in 2025. AI accounted for more than half of all venture investment in Kazakhstan last year.

The growing number of AI companies is also reflected in accelerator programs. In 2025, the Astana Hub Battle featured startups working on AI platforms, rehabilitation technologies, marketing and business automation.

The next challenge is making money

While the number of startups and investment deals is growing, the research suggests that the ecosystem’s next challenge is not simply creating more companies but helping them build sustainable businesses.

For startups that generate revenue, the path to the first sale can be relatively short: 76% reported reaching their first revenue within a year. However, international expansion remains more difficult.

Among scaling companies, 40% already have paying customers abroad, compared with 16% of early-stage companies. In other words, startups become significantly more likely to convert international ambitions into actual sales as they mature.

The research indicates that almost half of surveyed startups see foreign markets as a key direction, but interest does not automatically translate into international revenue. This is where Kazakhstan’s growing network of accelerators and international programs becomes particularly important.

Programs such as Silkway Accelerator have helped local companies establish connections outside Kazakhstan. By 2023, 49 startups that had participated in the program had entered international markets, collectively reaching a valuation of $250 million and raising $8.1 million during the fourth accelerator stream.

More recently, Kazakh startups have expanded into markets such as the United States. For example, smart parking company Parqour expanded to 25 countries and secured long-term contracts with parking operators in San Francisco.

Efforts to facilitate this expansion are continuing. In April 2026, Astana Hub and IT Park Uzbekistan announced plans to establish an international technology hub in Malaysia, intended to help Central Asian startups enter Southeast Asian markets including Malaysia and Singapore.

Who is building Kazakhstan’s startups?

The study also provides a picture of the people behind the companies. Around 42% of founders are between 31 and 40 years old, while 82% have higher education. More than half, or 56%, had previously launched a business.

Women account for 21% of founders, above the 15% global benchmark cited in the study.

These figures suggest that Kazakhstan’s startup community is not made up exclusively of young first-time entrepreneurs. A significant share of founders combines formal education with previous business experience, potentially giving them an advantage when navigating investment, hiring and international expansion.

At the same time, the relatively young age of the ecosystem means that many companies are still moving through the earliest stages of development.

Building an ecosystem beyond the capital

The growth of startups is also accompanied by efforts to expand access to technology infrastructure and entrepreneurial support beyond Astana and Almaty.

Regional IT hubs have been established across Kazakhstan to provide entrepreneurs with access to education, mentorship and startup support. In 2024, the opening of the Ulytau Hub brought the number of regional innovation centers to 17.

The broader Central Asian environment is also becoming more favorable for technology companies. The 2026 Global Startup Ecosystem Index ranked Central Asia as the fastest-growing startup subregion in the world, with Kazakhstan among the countries contributing to the region’s momentum. Kazakhstan ranked 71st globally, with its startup ecosystem growing 26.5% annually.

From growth to global competitiveness

The study ultimately points to a change in the central question facing the country’s startup ecosystem. A few years ago, the priority was building the infrastructure necessary for startups to emerge. Today, Kazakhstan has more than 1,500 startups in the research database, hundreds of companies that have attracted venture investment and its first unicorn.

The next stage will depend on whether these companies can consistently generate revenue, attract international customers and scale beyond the domestic market.

The country’s growing venture market, expanding AI sector and international accelerator programs provide a foundation for that transition. But the study suggests that the measure of the ecosystem’s maturity will increasingly be determined not by how many startups Kazakhstan has, but by how many can become sustainable global businesses.

World.title: Air Astana to Launch Two New Routes to Oman in October
World.content:
ASTANA — Air Astana will launch weekly flights from Almaty and Astana to Salalah, Oman, starting Oct. 23 and 24, respectively, expanding air connectivity between Kazakhstan and the Middle East.

The Almaty-Salalah service will begin on Oct. 23, operating once a week on Fridays, while the Astana-Salalah route will launch on Oct. 24, with weekly flights on Saturdays. Both routes will be operated by Airbus A320 aircraft, reported Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee under the Transport Ministry on Oct. 9.

Currently, SalamAir operates flights between Almaty and Muscat, Oman’s capital.

The new routes are expected to strengthen trade, business and tourism ties between Kazakhstan and the Sultanate of Oman.

World.title: From Uzbekistan to EU: Where Armenian goods are exported after Russia imposes restrictions
World.content:
Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

On 10 October, a preferential trade regime for Armenian goods exported to the European Union came into force. Under the EU decision to apply autonomous trade measures, the bloc will liberalise around 80% of imports from Armenia by removing import duties. The measures will cover a wide range of goods, including agricultural products.

The European Union has decided to support Armenia in response to restrictions that Russia has imposed on Armenian goods. Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian agencies responsible for enforcing the restrictions cited alleged failures to meet quality standards. However, it later became clear that Armenia’s closer integration with Europe had prompted the measures.

Exports of Armenian-origin goods to EU countries have grown for several months. In effect, this trend began before the preferential trade regime came into force. From January to June 2026, Armenia exported more than $516m worth of goods to the EU. This marked an increase of more than 80% compared with the same period last year.

Exports to EU countries are now expected to grow further. At the same time, Armenia is seeking other markets.

The local outlet Factor TV analysed the results of these efforts. Drawing on data from the Ministry of Economy and the Food Safety Inspection Body, it compiled a list of countries that received significant volumes of Armenian goods. The findings show that products traditionally exported to Russia now go to Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, Ukraine and Iraq.

More than 94% of exports went to three countries

According to data from the Food Safety Inspection Body, Uzbekistan, Georgia and Ukraine accounted for more than 94% of Armenia’s fruit exports in June 2026:

48% of fruit exports went to Uzbekistan,

around 34% went to Georgia,

approximately 12% went to Ukraine.

Georgia took the lead in July, accounting for around 35.3% of exports. Uzbekistan followed with 21%, Kazakhstan with 13%, Ukraine with 10.5% and Iraq with around 8.2%.

By comparison, in June 2025, Russia alone accounted for 86.7% of Armenian fruit exports. The figure rose to 87.2% in July.

State budget compensation for exporters

In response to the restrictions Russia imposed, the Armenian government launched support programmes for local exporters. These include subsidies and cash compensation, including payments to cover export duties in other markets.

In June and July, the government paid around 3.96bn drams ($10.3m) in compensation to exporters of strawberries, apricots, sweet cherries, plums, nectarines and peaches.

Over these two months, the state covered costs associated with around 90% of the export volume:

“The total volume of strawberry, apricot, sweet cherry, plum, nectarine and peach exports reached around 16,752 tonnes. The state budget provided compensation for 15,083 tonnes.”

Support programmes also continued in August. The government allocated around 4.52bn drams ($11.8m) that month to support exports and purchases of agricultural produce. This sum also covered costs for exporters of vegetables and flowers.

How the compensation was distributed

The figures for June and July show that apricots and sweet cherries accounted for 81% of the 3.9bn drams ($10.3m) allocated to fruit exports:

The government allocated around 1.86bn drams ($4.8m) for apricots.

Sweet cherries received around 1.33bn drams ($3.5m).

The government also paid compensation for strawberry, peach, nectarine and plum exports, but the amounts were smaller.

Exporters do not receive compensation automatically for every kilogram of produce they ship abroad. They must apply to the Ministry of Economy and submit customs or transit declarations, along with invoices confirming the exports. The ministry reviews each application and pays the compensation if it finds no discrepancies in the documents.

Under the government’s decision, compensation rates per kilogram stood at 770 drams ($2) for strawberries, 200 drams ($0.5) for apricots, 250 drams ($0.6) for nectarines and 400 drams ($1) for sweet cherries. For some fruits, the compensation came close to the average market price. In June, for example, strawberries sold for an average of 933 drams ($2.4) per kilogram.

Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

World.title: Non-medical support during childbirth in Armenia: who are doulas and what do they do?
World.content:
Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

The first certified doulas appeared in Armenia six years ago. Yet few women know that they can turn to doulas for support during pregnancy, childbirth and even after giving birth.

Doulas are not medical professionals. They help women manage labour pain through massage and breathing techniques, while also providing emotional support. Women now have a choice about who accompanies them during these hours. Some still prefer to have their husbands, mothers or sisters by their side. Others choose to give birth with a doula.

A doula with a woman in labour in the antenatal ward. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Most doulas enter the profession after a negative personal experience

Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova says women decide to become doulas after giving birth themselves. Sometimes they want to share a positive experience. More often, however, they turn to the profession because of a negative experience.

“I took a long journey to get to this point. I gave birth twice. My second birth was therapeutic and healing. I realised that a woman’s preparation, knowledge and expectations largely determine how childbirth unfolds. The problem is that women often have expectations that do not match reality. This can lead to traumatic consequences,” she says.

Иветта с мужем и сыновьями

Yvetta says her husband stayed by her side during both births. The first was a terrifying experience for both of them. The second went differently because they had both prepared for it. This time, they could talk to each other, joke and even dance during labour. She remembers the birth as “a wonderful process”.

She recalls that seven days before her second child was born, she listened to a lecture by an American doula. She remembers everything that might prove important during childbirth:

“Before that lecture, I was determined not to let anything that happened during my first birth happen again. For eight months, I told my doctor that I refused to give birth naturally. I insisted on a caesarean section. But that one-hour lecture changed everything for me. I realised I could understand my hormones and my surroundings, and that I could control many things. Ultimately, I could simply give it a try.

“My second birth went smoothly, without anxiety, and so quickly that after I was discharged, I kept telling my husband I wanted to offer to help pregnant women during labour and reassure them. Of course, those plans never came to fruition because they were unrealistic expectations.”

Yet the idea stayed with Yvetta for the next ten years. Eventually, she began working with pregnant women and women in labour, but as a photographer. Her family was living abroad at the time, where maternity photography was very popular. When she moved to Armenia, she expected to find plenty of clients for similar photo shoots. However, she says, almost all women in labour there turned down her offers.

“Either they invited me into the maternity ward not to take photographs that would capture this important moment in their lives, but simply because they did not want to be alone. But a photographer cannot intervene; they are like a shadow. Their presence should be as discreet as possible. I realised that, ultimately, I could not help women.”

Immediately after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Yvetta’s dream of becoming a doula came true during the coronavirus pandemic, when many training centres moved their courses online. Yvetta completed a course, passed her exams and received an international doula certification. She became the first doula in Armenia.

Who are doulas?

Doulas are trained professionals who support pregnant women, women in labour and those who need help during the postnatal period. They prepare women for childbirth and stay by their side throughout labour in the delivery room. Doulas provide informational, emotional and physical support.

During labour, doulas help women through massage, pressure techniques and touch. Sometimes they simply offer encouragement; at other times, they explain what is happening in a woman’s body at that moment. They suggest different positions and help women feel comfortable and safe throughout the process. This can increase the likelihood of a positive birth outcome.

Yvetta helps a woman in labour manage the pain.

According to Yvetta, in countries where many women use doula services, they start looking for a doula in the early stages of pregnancy, sometimes even when planning to conceive:

“Since doulas can take on only a small number of pregnant women each month, women book their services well in advance. They try to avoid complications this way, as there may be no available doulas when they go into labour. The situation in Armenia is different. Women who have given birth before usually contact us earlier in their pregnancy. First-time mothers tend to get in touch later, around weeks 28–30, when they start preparing for childbirth.”

Yvetta believes women should not leave the search for a doula until the final weeks of pregnancy. Sometimes doulas have to turn women away because the medical facility where they plan to give birth does not allow them into the maternity ward.

Armenia’s Ministry of Health has yet to recognise how much the work of a trained doula differs from the support a husband, mother, friend or anyone else can provide. Armenian law also contains no regulations governing their work.

There are only five or six doulas in Armenia

Most trained and received certification through Doula Link, a platform run by Russia’s Institute for Perinatal Support. They thereby became members of the European Doula Network. This allows them to provide doula services in Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Serbia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Italy, Israel and Panama.

In Armenia, people regard doulas as unqualified assistants.

A 2020 order issued by the health minister gives all women in labour the right to have a companion present during childbirth. However, some medical facilities still refuse to let doulas into the delivery room.

Moreover, some maternity hospitals charge a fee for allowing a companion to attend the birth. The Ministry of Health does not regulate this practice.

Why do women turn to doulas?

Yvetta says women in Armenia mainly choose to give birth with a doula because they want someone they trust by their side. They need someone who understands what is happening and what to do, can keep track of the situation and looks after them. They also hope to avoid traumatic experiences, including obstetric violence.

“Of course, having a support person present cannot guarantee that a woman will never experience abuse. But a doula is someone who will listen to her and understand her. I am convinced that in 99% of cases involving abuse, doctors do not intend to cause harm.

“They often intervene to reduce certain risks. Yet they do not answer the woman’s questions or explain why they have decided to intervene, even when the intervention involves surgery. A doula will at least ask why the intervention is necessary and why it needs to happen at that particular moment. Women feel safer when a doula is by their side,” Yvetta says.

A mother with her baby after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

In 2024–2025, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted a study of women’s experiences during pregnancy and childbirth in 16 countries across Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Armenia.

The study found that 67% of the women surveyed had experienced at least one form of obstetric violence.

In Armenia, around 55% of respondents said medical staff had performed obstetric interventions without their consent or any explanation. Meanwhile, 32% reported mistreatment by medical staff, highlighting a lack of information or pressure to make them agree to certain interventions.

Another 27% reported poor-quality care, such as inadequate staff qualifications. Around 15% of women experienced verbal aggression, while 5% reported physical violence. Eleven per cent of respondents reported various forms of sexual violence, including excessive or inappropriate touching.

Why don’t women turn to doulas?

Yvetta admits that 80% of the pregnant women who contact her are foreigners who, for various reasons, give birth in Armenia. Local women tend to be more cautious. The main problem, in the doula’s view, is a lack of information. Stereotypical attitudes also play an important role. Many people see childbirth as something women must go through on their own, without any need for additional support.

Waiting for childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

“But this is the wrong approach, because every woman in labour is vulnerable. It is very important that, by the end, she feels like a winner because she has brought a new person into the world, rather than feeling broken and miserable after enduring unbearable suffering. Unfortunately, most women still prefer to overcome their fears of childbirth and pain not with a doula’s help, but by paying for a caesarean section. They believe this will solve the problem,” she says.

Sometimes women do not turn to doulas because they assume their services will be expensive. Yvetta does not specify how much she charges. However, she says she sometimes helps pregnant women entirely free of charge because she sees this work as her mission.

“Being a doula is a calling. This work is first and foremost about your inner world and your heart, and only then about your skills.”

She recalls that when she first started working as a doula, she sometimes returned home exhausted and upset. She even considered giving it up. Poor working conditions and hostility from doctors and hospital administrators were the main sources of stress. She also felt distressed when her presence created additional difficulties for the woman in labour.

Now she knows which maternity hospitals allow her to do her job most effectively. Some doctors there see doulas not as competitors but as professionals who support their work. Every birth has therefore become a wonderful experience for her.

“Now I come home happy because I no longer suffer alongside a woman during labour; instead, I help her avoid suffering. I can see that my work makes a difference. I see a woman who was screaming in pain and fear stop screaming, get up and start dancing,” Yvetta says.

Yvetta with the parents of a baby born with her support

Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

World.title: ‘Take off your hijab and come into class’: what is happening in Azerbaijan’s schools?
World.content:
The hijab ban in Azerbaijan’s schools

In Azerbaijan’s schools, a ban on wearing the hijab has led to female students being barred from classes, demands for female teachers to remove their headscarves and protests. On 12 October, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of 37 people in connection with incidents over compliance with school uniform rules. As a result, parents demanding that schools allow their children to attend lessons now face criminal proceedings.

The authorities justify the restrictions by citing the need for a uniform school dress code and secular education. However, the consequences for students barred from classes are tangible: they must give up religious clothing to attend lessons.

At the heart of the dispute is the question of how the state exercises its authority to set school dress code requirements and how these restrictions undermine children’s right to education.

Schoolchildren show solidarity with classmates who wear hijabs

Videos shared today from several settlements in Baku show schoolchildren gathering at school entrances. Some of the girls are wearing hijabs. Students at School No. 322 are protesting the ban on wearing hijabs and demanding that the girls be allowed to attend classes.

A video published on 9 October and filmed outside School No. 69 in Baku shows schoolchildren refusing to go to lessons in solidarity with their classmates who wear hijabs.



Protest outside School No. 69 in Baku’s Balakhany settlement: “The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education.”

Schoolchildren have also staged protests at a school in the village of Mollaoba, in the Masally district.

A video shared from School No. 9 in the Jalilabad district shows girls being barred from entering the building because they wear hijabs. In another video, published in the Baku settlement of Khokhmeli, parents warn that they will stop sending their sons to school as well.

Protesters are expressing their discontent in various ways: gathering outside schools, refusing to attend classes and calling for boycotts. But they all have the same demand: girls who wear hijabs must not be denied access to education.

The solidarity shown by classmates demonstrates that the conflict affects not only girls who wear hijabs and their families. The restrictions also affect relationships between students and the learning process.

The consequences of missing classes go beyond the material a child fails to learn in a single day. When every visit to school brings arguments over clothing, the ability to continue studying comes into question. While families face demands to change their religious practices, children bear the brunt of this confrontation.

From school uniform requirements to a ban

Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 309, adopted on 21 September, prohibits additional items of clothing that violate uniform school dress code requirements and contradict the principle of secular education. Although the document does not explicitly mention the hijab, complaints from schools indicate that, in practice, the provision applies specifically to headscarves.

It is important to distinguish between the wording of the resolution and the consequences of its implementation. Barring female students who wear hijabs from classes effectively amounts to a ban on wearing this head covering. When authorities present such measures solely as a way to enforce school uniform rules, the issue of restricting children’s access to education takes a back seat. The amendments introduced by the resolution do not, however, explicitly provide for suspension from classes as a separate measure. This raises the question of what legal grounds school administrations rely on when adopting this practice.

On 9 October, the Baku City Education Department announced inspections to check whether students and teachers comply with clothing requirements. This suggests that the problem extends beyond decisions made by individual school administrations. The resolution, the mechanisms for enforcing it and the way schools apply it must be considered together. Yet in a system that places particular emphasis on parental responsibility, the question of who must ensure that children have access to education remains unanswered.

Criminal proceedings launched against protesters

In a statement issued on 12 October, Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry directly linked the detention of 37 people to events surrounding the introduction of uniform school dress code requirements. Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 233 of the Criminal Code, which provides for liability for organising actions that disrupt public order or actively participating in them.

The ministry accuses the detainees of provoking confrontations with education workers in Baku, damaging educational institutions and attempting to obstruct school operations and traffic. However, the statement does not specify which schools sustained damage or what specific actions the detainees allegedly committed. It also does not disclose their names or ages.

The lack of this information raises serious questions, particularly against the backdrop of protests involving schoolchildren. Are any of the detainees minors? On what grounds do law enforcement agencies distinguish between peaceful protest and the specific actions they accuse the detainees of committing?

The ministry says the measures are necessary to ensure the safety of students and teachers. However, opening a criminal case amid protests over the right to education could deter other families from taking part in similar demonstrations. Parents demanding that schools allow their children to attend classes must now also consider the risks associated with participating in protests.

Aliyev’s remarks and the Iranian factor

On 2 October, speaking at the 8th congress of the New Azerbaijan Party, Ilham Aliyev placed particular emphasis on the role of education in safeguarding ideological security:

“Therefore, we must protect ourselves from ideological provocations. How? First and foremost, of course, through education.”

The president also criticised Azerbaijani-language media outlets operating in neighbouring countries. Although he did not explicitly mention Iran or the hijab in this part of his speech, some political commentators interpret his remarks as a signal directed against Iran’s religious influence in Azerbaijan.

Asif Narimanli, a political commentator close to the authorities, links the events surrounding the hijab ban to attempts by Iran at “political and ideological interference”. In this context, he refers to a religious gathering in Qom and a protest in Istanbul. Aygun Muradkhanli, a journalist at a pro-government media outlet, has also argued that religious groups opposing the ban have links to centres abroad.

This interpretation risks pushing demands to allow female students who wear hijabs to attend classes into the background, as debate over foreign influence takes centre stage. Families defending the right to religious choice find themselves in a situation where they are effectively expected not only to explain their position but also to prove their political loyalty. However, general claims about Iranian influence do not, in themselves, justify treating an individual schoolgirl’s decision to wear a hijab as a security threat. Allegations of foreign interference require evidence of specific links and actions.

Parents’ rights and the state’s obligations

Article 18 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights enshrines parents’ right to ensure the religious and moral education of their children in accordance with their own beliefs. Articles 5 and 14 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child also recognise the role of parents in raising their children and guiding their development.

These rights must be protected with due regard for the child’s evolving capacities, freedom of conscience and best interests. The secular nature of education does not negate a family’s right to provide religious education for its children. Ensuring that the educational process remains secular and barring schoolchildren from classes because of their religious clothing are fundamentally different measures.

Authorities enforcing these restrictions must explain what specific obstacles headscarves create for the learning process and why they consider excluding a child from classes necessary. When access to education becomes a means of pressuring a family to abandon its religious choices, invoking secularism to justify such restrictions loses its meaning.

Teachers risk losing their jobs

Following the approval on 6 October of separate dress code requirements for teachers, reports emerged of pressure on teachers who wear hijabs. Teachers told Toplum TV that some schools in Sumgayit were demanding that they remove their hijabs or submit letters of resignation. Journalist Arzu Abdulla reported a similar situation at School No. 90 in the Ramana settlement.

For teachers, the issue concerns not only their religious beliefs but also their livelihood. Requiring them to submit letters of resignation can create the impression that they are ending their employment voluntarily. However, when teachers must choose between giving up religious clothing and losing their jobs, the voluntary nature of that decision becomes questionable. Restrictions on teachers’ clothing, when authorities have not justified them on the grounds of professional requirements, also call into question the value of the experience they have accumulated over years of work.

Public reaction: protests and support for the ban

Public opinion on the ban is divided. Press Council chairman Rashad Majid defends the restrictions as necessary to protect the secular nature of the state and says he sees foreign influence behind the protests. Jailed journalist Polad Aslanov, by contrast, announced a hunger strike to protest restrictions imposed on female students and teachers who wear hijabs.

Comments on a HamamTimes post about protests at a school in the Buzovna settlement also include claims that the protesters have links to Iran. Other discussions express a different view: some participants oppose children wearing hijabs but nevertheless believe that barring schoolchildren from classes for this reason is unacceptable.

Turkey’s reaction and previous crackdowns

On 3 October, protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan’s consulate in Istanbul in a demonstration. They demanded that the restrictions be lifted and called on the Turkish authorities to intervene. However, on 7 October, Omer Celik, spokesperson for Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), said that groups opposing Azerbaijan had no ties to either the party or the government.

Protests against the hijab ban in Azerbaijan have previously led to arrests and criminal proceedings. On 6 May 2011, police intervened during a demonstration outside the Education Ministry, followed by arrests and the opening of a criminal case. Abgul Suleymanov, known for taking part in protests against the hijab ban, was arrested that year and later sentenced to 11 years in prison on charges he denied. In September this year, authorities placed him under administrative arrest for another 30 days. His family links the arrest to his posts about the hijab.

The current events are unfolding against a backdrop of previous crackdowns. The successive decisions on dress code requirements for schoolchildren and teachers, inspections to enforce them, and the arrest of 37 people have now become part of a single process. However, assessing the consequences of this policy requires more than the authorities’ statements about secular education. It is necessary to establish how many children have missed classes, how many teachers have faced the threat of losing their jobs, and on what grounds the authorities arrested the protesters.

The hijab ban in Azerbaijan’s schools

World.title: Russian passport in Abkhazia: ticket to better life or risky luxury?
World.content:
A reform of the consular department at the Russian Embassy in Abkhazia has cut the time needed to process citizenship applications by a factor of 3.5. This seemingly dry statistic illustrates one of the most important and contentious aspects of life in Abkhazia.

For some Abkhaz people, a Russian passport offers the only way to see the world. For others, it provides a chance to build a career or enjoy a decent retirement. For still others, it raises doubts and fears.

Most countries around the world do not recognise Abkhazia as an independent state, leaving its passport with virtually no value beyond the republic’s borders. In practice, this means that Abkhaz passport holders cannot travel anywhere except Russia. Many residents of Abkhazia therefore acquire a second citizenship, Russian citizenship. But freedom of movement is not the only issue.

Processing applications 3.5 times faster

Until recently, residents of Abkhazia frequently complained about the slow-moving queue for Russian citizenship. The consulate could accept applications from only 120 people a month, despite a waiting list of 3,000. As a result, applicants faced a wait of more than three years.

To address the problem, Russia’s new ambassador to Abkhazia, Vyacheslav Gladkov, sought assistance from the Russian presidential administration. Experts from the Senezh Management Workshop joined the effort. They specialise in modern workplace organisation based on the methodology of the state-owned Rosatom corporation. Their main task was to eliminate unnecessary steps in the document submission process, simplify logistics and spare applicants a lengthy wait.

Abkhazia State University also supported the project. Student volunteers from its law faculty took on the initial consultations and helped applicants complete their citizenship paperwork correctly.

By the end of September 2026, the consulate had increased its application processing rate 3.5-fold. The embassy expects to reduce the backlog significantly by the end of the year.

But who are the people queuing for Russian citizenship, and why do they need it? Are there also people in no hurry to obtain it, even under the simplified procedure?

To find out, we spoke to residents of Sukhumi and collected their stories.

A passport as a way out of isolation

For 38-year-old Diana Chelidze, obtaining a Russian passport means an end to the isolation she has experienced for almost her entire adult life.

Diana lived in Russia as a child and attended school there, but her parents never managed to obtain Russian citizenship for her. She later tried to resolve the matter herself but ran into insurmountable bureaucratic obstacles. She finally obtained the long-awaited document after Russia resumed issuing passports to Abkhaz residents under a simplified procedure in 2025.

“I waited for this opportunity for many years. I spent my entire youth within the borders of Abkhazia and Russia. The first place I travelled to after getting my passport was Istanbul. It’s an indescribable feeling to simply buy a ticket and fly somewhere. I’m now actively saving for a trip to the Maldives. I’m 38, and only now have I gained the opportunity to see the world. I’m incredibly happy to have this freedom,” Diana says enthusiastically.

Starting a career and securing a pension

While a Russian passport has given Diana the freedom to travel, many of her compatriots see it not as a luxury but as a basic necessity for social and professional stability.

Liana Georgievna Avidzba, 71, worked throughout her life but now receives a meagre Abkhaz pension of 6,000 roubles [around $70].

“It’s practically impossible to live on that amount today. I obtained a Russian passport solely so I could use my Soviet-era employment record to qualify for a Russian pension. Now that I have the document, I’ll start the pension application process straight away,” Liana says.

Young people who see their future in Russia have different reasons for seeking citizenship. Milana Kvitsinia, a student at a Russian university, is currently applying for citizenship.

“Without a Russian passport, it’s extremely difficult to find a decent, formal job in Russia today. Employers are reluctant to hire foreign nationals. I’m studying in Russia and plan to stay there for work, so a passport is a necessity for me,” Milana explains.

A second citizenship? No, thank you!

But not all residents of Abkhazia are eager to become Russian citizens.

Albina, a mother of three boys aged 10, 12 and 17, is deliberately putting off applying for Russian passports for her sons. Her main fear is that the authorities will register them for military service and conscript them into the Russian army.

“People tell me that dual citizenship will allow the boys to choose where they do their military service. But I don’t believe that. I see how the authorities immediately register the sons of my friends who are studying in Russia for military service. Their parents live in constant fear that the boys will be sent to the front.

I’m sure they will never stop issuing [Russian] citizenship here. When my sons grow up, they can apply themselves if they want to. But as their mother, I’m not going to take that risk for now,” Albina says.

Leonid Topchyan, 24, is ethnically Armenian and believes he has no need for a Russian passport at all. He and his parents run a family business in Abkhazia, growing mandarins, persimmons and feijoa. They use the fruit to make homemade compotes, fruit pastilles and dried fruit for sale.

“I work on my own land and make my living from agriculture. I’m happy with how things are. I simply don’t need a Russian passport.

If I ever apply for a second citizenship, it will only be Armenian. I can’t travel to Armenia at the moment, although many of my friends and relatives go there even with Abkhaz passports. The local Armenian community helps them a lot,” Leonid says.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.
