Georgia marks 1,700 years of Christianity: Patriarch and officials reflect on faith, identity and the future
World.content:
1,700 years of Christianity in Georgia

An international academic symposium titled “God, Homeland, Human” took place at the Radisson hotel in Tbilisi to mark 1,700 years since Georgia declared Christianity its state religion.

The event was attended by Georgian Patriarch Shio III, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and President Mikheil Kavelashvili.

The main political message of their speeches was that Christianity, national identity and traditional values should form the foundation of the Georgian state and society. They presented the preservation of these values as a response to the challenges of the modern world.

Key points from the speeches

● Cooperation between the state and the Church: Irakli Kobakhidze said that the government would continue to protect Georgia’s Christian heritage and national values in close cooperation with the Church.

“The state pays particular attention to these enduring values. In close cooperation with the Church, we will firmly defend the heritage on which our national unity and development rest.”

● National identity and statehood: According to Shalva Papuashvili said, a state may temporarily lose its independence, but preserving its national identity leaves open the possibility of restoring it.

“The world has once again entered an era of great change. Technology, economic relations and the international order are changing rapidly. However, as history has taught us time and again, societies that preserve their identity stand firmest during periods of change,” Papuashvili said.

● Seven eternal values: Mikheil Kavelashvili identified God, the Homeland, the Individual, the Native Land, Language, Faith and Family as the foundations of thinking rooted in Georgian statehood. In his view, these values help preserve national identity in the age of globalisation and artificial intelligence.

“Today, as the modern world faces a crisis of values and geopolitical upheaval, we have a duty to ask a fundamental question: what should form the foundations of the Georgian state, society and individual?

These seven symbols form the basis of our identity. Even today, as the age of globalisation and artificial intelligence seeks to devalue human identity, these eternal values serve as our main existential shield,” Kavelashvili said.

“God, Homeland, Human” — an international symposium marking 1,700 years since Georgia declared Christianity its state religion. Tbilisi, 11 October 2026.

● Technology and spirituality: Patriarch Shio said that technological progress should serve humanity and that the growth of knowledge should not distance society from faith and spiritual values.

“Technology should serve humanity, not humanity technology. Knowledge should not distance us from faith, and progress should not make us forget spirituality,” Shio III said.

● Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region: The Patriarch addressed the residents of these regions and expressed hope that peace, unity and brotherly relations between Georgia’s historic regions would be restored.

“We must continue to live peacefully alongside our homeland,” the Patriarch said, expressing hope that “brotherly unity and love will be restored between us”.

● Ties with emigrants: Shio III addressed Georgians living abroad, saying that the Church prays for them and awaits their return to their homeland.

1,700 years of Christianity in Georgia

World.title: Saturday march in Tbilisi highlights systemic problems in prisons. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 682 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office launches investigation into National Bank Council member
World.content:
Georgia national bank member in corruption probe

Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office has launched an investigation into the possible unlawful involvement of Nana Keinishvili, a member of the National Bank of Georgia’s Council, in business activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, its investigative department launched a probe under Article 337 of the Criminal Code, which criminalises the unlawful involvement of a public official or an equivalent person in business activities. The investigation follows complaints by the management of Bitexchange LLC, which were forwarded by the National Bank.

According to an investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, the National Bank fined cryptocurrency company Bitexchange, in which Keinishvili had unsuccessfully sought a stake, in what could be seen as an act of retaliation.

The National Bank said that, in order to protect the institution’s reputation, its Council would consider at its next meeting temporarily suspending Keinishvili’s participation in Council meetings while the investigation is under way, until the circumstances of the case are fully clarified.

Nana Keinishvili was elected to the National Bank’s Council in September 2023. From 2012 to 2016, she served as a member of parliament representing the ruling Georgian Dream party and as deputy chair of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said former president Salome Zourabichvili should be asked how she selected Nana Keinishvili as a candidate for the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

“This once again shows how important it is for parliament to also familiarise itself with these matters and, in this case, examine in detail the issues surrounding the election of Council members. Salome Zourabichvili herself should answer the remaining questions. What matters is that the state is responding to this issue,” Papuashvili said.

He added, however, that he could not go into the details of the investigation.

It has emerged, however, that the parliament speaker, like current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, voted in parliament in favour of appointing Nana Keinishvili to the National Bank of Georgia’s Council.

Details of the case

According to the National Bank, it reviewed submissions from the management of Bitexchange LLC and conducted a preliminary internal investigation within the scope of its authority.

The materials were forwarded to the relevant authorities for legal assessment, as the matter falls outside the mandate established for the National Bank by law. The bank expressed hope that the facts of the case would be established objectively as soon as possible.

The bank also explained that Bitexchange, a virtual asset service provider, had been fined following a routine inspection for violating anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing regulations.

Nana Keinishvili

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the management of Bitexchange claims that Keinishvili is involved in business activities and directly controls a network of companies subject to regulation by the National Bank.

They allege that shares in these companies are registered in the names of her family members and affiliated individuals. The company’s management also claims that Keinishvili attempted to acquire a stake in their business.

The Prosecutor’s Office notes that Georgia’s Law on the Fight Against Corruption prohibits public officials from engaging in business activities. Furthermore, under the Organic Law on the National Bank of Georgia, members of the National Bank’s Council and their family members are prohibited from being partners in a Georgian financial sector entity or a legal entity affiliated with one.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the investigation will examine the circumstances surrounding Nana Keinishvili’s possible unlawful involvement in business activities. The public will be informed of the results of the investigation in due course.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty investigation

The National Bank has not disclosed the amount of the fine. However, according to the investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Nana Keinishvili demanded a stake in a cryptocurrency company regulated by the National Bank. The company’s owner refused to give up a share, after which the National Bank fined the company 572 million lari (approximately $211.85 million).

The investigation also found that Keinishvili and her family members own and manage profitable businesses regulated by the National Bank.

Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty obtained documents indicating that the National Bank and the State Security Service had been aware of information about Keinishvili’s alleged violations for at least several months. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty sent inquiries to both agencies on 6 October.

World.title: Azerbaijan media council urges vigilance over social media manipulation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 12. The Media and Broadcasting Council of Azerbaijan has urged citizens not to fall for manipulations on social media.

This was reflected in a statement by the Media and Broadcasting Council of Azerbaijan.

According to the statement, the approval of unified dress codes for students and educators in Azerbaijan serves to uphold the principle of secular education and ensure a consistent approach within the educational environment; however, certain circles are attempting to deliberately politicize the issue, shift it into a religious context, and turn it into a source of artificial public tension.

Coordinated activities, particularly on social media platforms, are further exacerbating these concerns. Notable trends include the mass dissemination of identical or similar content, including negative comments and reactions, across various accounts within short timeframes, as well as calls inciting people to violate public order.

The coordinated nature of this process, evidenced by the sustained intervention of a limited number of accounts across numerous posts and the intensification of activity during specific time intervals, indicates a troll attack and information manipulation orchestrated from a single center abroad.

The primary objectives of such interventions are to distort genuine public opinion, create an illusion of mass discontent through the artificial activity of specific accounts, divert attention from the core issue, and turn the topic into a tool for certain political agendas.

The Media and Broadcasting Council urged citizens, media entities, and social media users to remain vigilant against such incidents, to be mindful of the coordinated activities of suspicious accounts, to refrain from disseminating manipulative content without verification, and to avoid being swayed by artificially generated waves of information.

World.title: Renewed mineral sands mine bid 'a turd in glitter', resident says
World.content:
The Victorian government is "manipulating" its own planning system to fast track approval for a mining project it already rejected, a leading planning expert claims.

The Fingerboards Mineral Sands Project proposed for eastern Victoria was knocked back by the government in 2021, because it would "pose a significant risk to the environment and valuable horticulture industry".

But the government is now considering what it calls a "new and modified" bid to get the project off the ground, a description that RMIT emeritus professor of planning and environment Michael Buxton said was a "blatant deception".

"The project is not a different project and it's not substantially altered," he said.

Michael Buxton worked at the Victorian planning department for more than a decade. (ABC News: Sean Warren)

Nearby residents who have spent years fighting the mine have a different description of the latest proposal.

"All they've really done is rolled a turd in glitter to make it look shiny," organic vegetable grower Kane Busch said.

The company behind the project, Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM), rejected these claims and said its new bid for approval included significant changes.

GCM said the site was a rich source of a range of minerals, which had been deemed critical by the Australian government.

Global race for critical minerals

Miners have been exploring the Lindenow Valley, 270 kilometres east of Melbourne, for mineral sands since the 1970s.

Irrigated areas of the Lindenow flats. (ABC Rural: Emma Field)

Between 2015 and 2023, global demand doubled for mineral sands, which contain concentrated amounts of heavy minerals such as rare-earth elements.

Organisations from mining giants such as Rio Tinto to junior mining companies have had a stake in the region, but no project has ever been considered commercially or environmentally viable.

After almost a decade of review, in November 2021 the Victorian government rejected a mining project proposed by Kalbar Resources, later Kalbar Operations.

In 2023, Kalbar was renamed to Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM) and submitted a "rescoped" proposal.

Gippsland Critical Minerals has dug a test pit on its Fingerboards mineral sands site. (ABC Rural: Fiona Broom)

Dr Buxton, who has been involved in planning for 50 years, including at the Environment Protection Authority and state planning department, said the government failed to follow proper process by accepting the Fingerboards project for a second review.

"The minister could have just refused to consider this application — and in my view, should have," he said.

Australia's strategic focus on critical minerals for economic and national security reasons was behind the renewed push for the East Gippsland mineral sands mine, he said.

"Since it was rejected a few years ago, the whole issue of critical minerals has now become an international issue," Dr Buxton said.

"This has provided companies with the opportunity to argue that it's a critical resource."

Under the state government's critical minerals road map launched in December 2024, which outlines efforts to build a globally competitive critical minerals sector, eight mines are at various stages of approval.

University of Sydney professor of global governance Susan Park said she was "not surprised at all" that rejected minerals projects were getting a second look.

Dr Park said trade and security agreements between Australia and allies such as the United States were driving state and federal support for mining projects.

"It might not have been viable five years ago, but obviously the demand is continuing to grow and this means that mines that weren't considered possible back then may now be viable," she said.

The proposed Fingerboards mine site, 25 kilometres west of Bairnsdale. (Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals)

In February, the Australian government gave the Fingerboards proposal Major Project Status, which gives "strategically significant projects" extra support to navigate regulatory approvals.

GCM bills the project as a major source of "ex-China production" of the rare-earth oxides dysprosium and terbium, elements on Australia's critical minerals list.

China controls almost all of the world's production and rare-earth refining.

Terbium and dysprosium oxides, used in renewable energy and military technologies, are almost completely supplied by China.

Site 'still unsuitable' for mine

The Lindenow Valley is a highly fertile region known for its leafy salad vegetables, brassicas and sweet corn.

Up to 2,000 workers harvest about 200,000 tonnes of food every year.

The Mitchell River and countless creeks run through the landscape to the Gippsland Lakes, which are protected under the international Ramsar Convention on Wetlands.

In 2021 an inquiry and advisory committee found the environmental effects of the Fingerboards project could not be managed.

In rejecting the application, then-planning minister Richard Wynne cited "unacceptable" impacts on biodiversity, air quality, agriculture and water.

Mr Busch said he could see the location of the proposed mine from his family's 100-year-old farm in the "pristine" Lindenow Valley.

"If we look at the reasons why the mine wasn't allowed to go ahead in the first place, it's the dust contamination risk, he said.

" We're amazed that it even got another shot. "

Dr Buxton said the site remained unsuitable for a mining project, and demand for resources should not influence planning decisions.

He said the government would use planning processes to rubber stamp the project.

"The critical factor should be the impacts on the environment and the social impacts … not the cost of the development or whether or not the Western world needs critical minerals."

Mine footprint cut, company says

The Victorian government declined an interview but said the project was still being considered.

"As this project is currently being assessed it would be inappropriate to comment further — no decision has been made," a spokesperson said.

GCM chief executive Michelle Wood said it was "misleading and false" to claim the project proposal had not been rescoped.

"We've done substantial redesign work over a number of years," she said.

"We have made those changes and adjusted according to what the community have told us."

Michelle Wood says the proposal has undergone "substantial redesign work". (Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals)

She said the company reduced the proposed footprint of the mine by 27 per cent and cut the rate of mining by 40 per cent.

Mining would be excluded from a 1.5-kilometre buffer to the Lindenow Valley horticulture area, up from 600 metres, and from three gullies located between the pits and the Mitchell River.

Ms Wood said the project was not being fast-tracked through the environmental assessment process and the community would be given the opportunity to have its say.

World.title: Quick hits: Cummins blasts and Maharaj juggles as Smith pulls up lame
World.content:
Pat Cummins's explosive knock pushes Australia clear, Keshav Maharaj produces some magic in his follow-through and Steve Smith doesn't join his teammates in the field.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Maddinson's manic start

Maddinson picked up where he left off. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Nic Maddinson hooked the first ball of the innings for four, so it was no surprise that he got a move on when day four began with Australia needing quick runs to set up a victory.

He hit two boundaries in his first three balls faced, but both were off the edge. Then, after watching opening partner Travis Head chip a tame shot to mid-on, Maddinson decided to force the issue.

Through cover, down to third man, back over the bowler … the controversially selected 34-year-old made a real statement as he raced to within one shot of a maiden half-century.

But it came to an end on 48 off 38 balls when Anrich Nortje uprooted his middle and leg stumps with a searing yorker.

A famous Test inning? Perhaps not, but a career high likely to earn him another chance to prolong his strange Test career.

2. Maharaj's bizarre juggling take

Maharaj surprised himself with his bizarre juggling effort. (Fox Cricket)

With Matt Rensaw having pushed into the 80s and looking destined for a second century for the match, it felt like the South Africans were in need of something extraordinary to dismiss the Queenslander.

And although not quite a work of art, Keshav Maharaj's diving return catch was certainly out of the ordinary.

With Renshaw having chipped one back towards the bowler, the finger spinner did well to get down in his follow-through, before juggling the ball once, twice, taking his eye of the cherry, and ultimately securing it in his palm while lying on the turf.

He looked as surprised as anyone to have taken the catch, which was confirmed after a lengthy review by the TV umpire.

3. Cummins's late cameo

Pat Cummins made a quickfire cameo. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Australia was surprisingly circumspect during the middle session, with Matt Renshaw and Beau Webster doing little more than keeping the scoreboard ticking over.

Pat Cummins clearly had no plans to declare on Renshaw when he had a second ton for the match in the offing, but when Renshaw was caught out, the captain took it on himself to up the tempo.

He wasted little time attacking the spin of Simon Harmer, smacking his fourth ball for six over long-on and adding three more in his next four deliveries from the off-spinner before declaring on 6-314 having clattered 32 off 12 to take his team to a 420-run lead.

4. Smith sidelined

Steve Smith injured his finger as he took a catch on day three and copped a blow to the helmet on day four. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Steve Smith's slips catching changed the game on day three but soon after Cummins's declaration it became clear he would not have the same impact on day four.

Smith stayed in the pavilion when the Australian team took to the field for South Africa's run chase on account of a sharp blow he copped to the helmet from an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting.

He carried on to 27 before holing out, but the after-effects of that head knock appeared to keep him sidelined.

He also hurt his finger taking the catch that ended South Africa's first innings, which could have caused issues in the slips.

5. Renshaw's dream Test continues

Comfortably the top scorer in the match, Matt Renshaw added his maiden Test wicket late on day four. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Matt Renshaw couldn't have dreamt it better.

With shadows lengthening in Durban, and with South Africa's innings threatening to steady, Australia's freshly minted golden boy was thrown the ball.

South Africa captain Temba Bavuma had faced 18 balls for his one run and was set on seeing his team to stumps, but he was unable to contend with the drift and turn of Renshaw's part-time off spin, the Queenslander drawing the batter forward and having him caught at short leg by a diving Maddinson.

Renshaw was mobbed by his teammates as he celebrated his maiden Test wicket and Australia marched on to be six wickets from victory at stumps on day four.

That came after the southpaw had once again led Australia's efforts with the bat, peeling off 82 to add to the 190 he made in the first innings.

Remarkably, Renshaw remains the only player to pass 50 in the match.

World.title: 'Nearly nothing left' of Canberra massage parlour after crash, then robbery
World.content:
The owners of a Canberra massage parlour are picking up what remains of the pieces of the business after a car ploughed into it on Friday, injuring five people.

Three employees were initially pinned under the car, which remained deep inside the building for some time after being driven into Harmony Tree Therapeutic Massage and Day Spa in Weston.

The massage parlour was then targeted by thieves on the night of the crash, with a staff member's phone, car keys, house keys, and ATM card stolen.

Three spa employees were pinned under the vehicle when it crashed through the shopfront. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

Harmoney Tree employee Hannah Maloney, who was not present during the crash, told ABC Radio Canberra one of the three employees taken to hospital remained there with a broken hip.

"They had to have two operations … but their condition is stable now," Ms Maloney said.

She said the other two employees who were taken to hospital after being trapped under the vehicle had now returned home.

'A second later the building was smashed'

The vehicle remained deep inside the massage parlour for some time after three workers were freed from underneath it. (ABC News: Robert Baird)

Ms Maloney said staff who were there during the incident had told her "it happened so fast they did not even know what happened".

"A second later they realised the building was smashed," she said.

" She did not even notice the car was inside. They were just totally shocked. "

Ms Maloney said it had been a particularly difficult time for one of the store's owners, Sukanya Loasoe, who had given birth just five days before the crash.

Harmony Tree employee Hannah Maloney says the business has been "smashed to pieces" by the car. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

"She's crying, actually. She's worried," Ms Maloney said.

"She was still in recovering time, that kind of busy time, and then this unexpectedly happens.

" The car just smashed everything to pieces, [there's] nearly nothing left. "

Ms Maloney said despite it being a challenging time for the business, she and the other staff were grateful to the community for the offerings of love and support they had received.

"We are really grateful … [for our] family and friends, and even wonderful customers that have tried to give us support," she said.

"We hope that we can reopen our door soon."

World.title: Tasmania's EDs taking the hit for health system failure, report finds
World.content:
The Australasian College of Emergency Medicine (ACEM) has warned that Australia's health system is not equipped for the growing number of older patients presenting in emergency departments.

The national State of Emergency report, released this morning, said the health system, from primary care, residential aged care, home support, to hospital services, was ailing from insufficient planning.

It claimed successive federal, state and territory governments had not done enough to prepare for the volume or complexity of care as Australia's population aged.

A Tasmanian health professional has called the lack of capacity "a crisis". (Unsplash: Frederic Köberl)

The report said emergency departments (EDs) were often being left to fill gaps, leading to ambulance ramping, overcrowding, corridor care and access issues.

Older people represented close to a quarter of the nation's nearly nine-million presentations. The rate was highest in regional, rural and remote areas.

Patients left on trolleys or chairs

ACEM Tasmania branch chair Juan Ascencio-Lane said he did not have to predict what would happen in the state without intervention.

"We don't need to look forward — we are in this crisis right now," he said.

" When you boil it down, what's at stake is people's lives. "

Juan Carlos Ascencio-Lane says a fix to the health crisis is needed now. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough )

Tasmania has Australia's highest proportion of people aged 65 and over.

Older people are significantly more likely to be classified in higher urgency categories, arrive by ambulance and be admitted to hospital.

The report found that between 2018-19 and 2023-24, the number of older attendees at Tasmanian EDs increased by 19 per cent, compared with 2 per cent in younger people, and 17 per cent nationally.

ACEM recommends that 90 per cent of patients requiring hospital admission access a bed within eight hours, but that occurred only 40 per cent of the time in older patients locally and 54 per cent nationally.

The report found that older people are significantly more likely to be classified in higher urgency categories, arrive by ambulance and be admitted to hospital. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The report said extended wait times meant the elderly were often left "frail and in pain", without adequate rest, nutrition and dignity, and vulnerable to deterioration.

"These patients are often left on a trolley or on a chair in a bright, noisy emergency department where staff are really pushed to the limits to care not just for them, but for the acute new patients," Dr Ascencio-Lane said.

He said the toll on staff was "enormous".

"We want to provide high-level care, particularly for these older people," he said.

"This is causing a huge amount of stress and burnout, with nurses and doctors in particular, who are looking for alternatives within their employment."

Tasmania has the highest proportion of people aged 65 and over in the nation. (Supplied: Pexels)

Urgent action needed

The report projected a 411-per-cent increase in ED arrivals of people aged 85 and over by 2050.

ACEM has made a series of recommendations and implored governments to take urgent action.

They include strengthening alternative acute care pathways via programs integrating hospitals, aged care, community services, and Aboriginal health organisations, as well as more telehealth support for residential aged care.

It also recommended more funding hospitals to deliver more services in the community.

The pressure on hospital emergency departments is expected to increase. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The not-for-profit group, which trains emergency physicians, also recommended improving patient flow by increasing inpatient beds, and ongoing training for rural EDs to treat patients locally.

It is also calling for at least 10,000 additional aged care beds by 2028, 24/7 access to a registered nurse, and incentives to take on residents with complex conditions, dementia or behavioural symptoms.

Federal, state blame game

The federal government is responsible for primary and aged care, with states and territories in charge of hospitals.

State Health Minister Bridget Archer said Tasmanians should not have to rely on hospitals for care, but often had nowhere else to go.

"These Tasmanians are not statistics," she said in a statement.

" They are Tasmanians who deserve dignity, compassion, and a proper place to recover, and this growing national crisis demands an immediate response from the Federal Labor Government. "

Federal Minister for Health and Ageing Mark Butler said the government had eased hospital pressure through increased funding, more aged care beds, expanded bulk billing and Urgent Care Clinics.

Mark Butler says the federal government has eased hospital pressure through a raft of measures. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"There are real pressures facing the aged care system right now, and we continue to work with states and territories in good faith," he said.

"It is time for state governments to deliver on their promises to give Australians access to health services, when and where they need them."

World.title: Council sued over alleged historical abuse at daycare services
World.content:
Seven people are suing a New South Wales council over alleged child sexual abuse at a daycare service in the 1990s.

From July 1994 to November 1999, David Neil Tuck was licensed as a carer and operator by Eurobodalla Shire Council.

Laura-Jane Phoenix-Singh alleges that from the age of seven, she was groomed and repeatedly sexually assaulted by Mr Tuck while attending the service.

She is one of the claimants alleging in the Supreme Court that Eurobodalla Shire Council failed to protect them from Mr Tuck's abuse.

Laura-Jane Phoenix-Singh says she was seven when the alleged abuse began. (Supplied)

"There were policies and protocols and legislation that needed to be followed," Ms Phoenix-SIngh said.

"The question that can be asked is were they followed?"

Mr Tuck took his own life in 2001 while on bail for child sexual assault charges.

A spokesperson for Eurobodalla Shire Council said in a statement that Mr Tuck was registered with the council 30 years ago, while also running a private childcare business.

"We acknowledge that this has been a distressing situation for everyone impacted by the conduct and actions of Mr Tuck and we empathise with those individuals and their families," the statement said.

'Absolutely calculated'

Mr Tuck operated three home-based daycare services on the Far South Coast in the 1990s: Karoola Cottage and Bluemoor Childrens Services in Surfside and High Street in Batemans Bay.

Hailey, who asked that her surname not be used, began attending Mr Tuck's care service as a five-year-old. She went before and after school, overnight and on weekends.

Hailey was five years old when she began attending Bluemoor Childrens Services. (Supplied)

"That persona that he put forward as being happy to help out and watch people's children … these are the children he was abusing," she said.

Hailey alleges that between 1996 and 1999 she was groomed and repeatedly sexually abused by Mr Tuck.

The statement of claim filed in the Supreme Court alleges the council received multiple reports about Mr Tuck's daycare operations.

The allegations ranged from exceeding the maximum number of children allowed to be in his care to a member of the public making a complaint to the police about Mr Tuck "having a bus full of kids in the bush".

Do you know more? Contact Toby Hemmings via hemmings.toby@abc.net.au

via If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

"He was repeatedly breaking rules and not following the requirements of the day care scheme," Hailey said.

"Had [the council] acted on that, he should have been shut down almost immediately."

It has also been alleged that two notifications were made to the NSW Department of Community Services about "sexually inappropriate conduct" and Mr Tuck "lying in bed and cuddling a child in his care".

"The first warning issued to him was within three months of opening, but in the end he was deregistered for fraud," Hailey said.

In 1999 Mr Tuck was accused and convicted of forging parents' signatures on time-sheets, which led to his deregistration.

Laura-Jane Phoenix-Singh is one of seven plaintiffs suing Eurobodalla Shire Council. (Supplied)

Ms Phoenix-Singh said she believed up to 45 children may have been abused by Mr Tuck.

"He was absolutely calculated, it was well thought out," she said.

"We must put blame where it belongs and that is absolutely always on the perpetrator.

"But when we're thinking about institutional child sexual abuse, institutions and the structures and systems that are responsible for them need to be accountable."

Duty of care

The statement of claim alleges that Eurobodalla Shire Council had "ultimate operational control" and "supervisory responsibility" for Mr Tuck's actions while he was licensed to operate the services.

It is argued that the council breached its duty of care by failing to adequately investigate or respond to complaints about Mr Tuck, and could have deregistered him or limited his services.

A spokesperson for Eurobodalla Shire Council declined to comment on the ongoing cases but said in a statement that it now provided a "completely different and modern service".

"We operate under rigorous standards and requirements, and we are regularly audited and undertake accreditation processes, where child safety is at the centre of service delivery," the spokesperson said.

In a directions hearing on Monday all seven matters were adjourned until February 2027.

World.title: Doctor banned for prescribing drugs to patient, then buying them back
World.content:
A doctor who prescribed a vulnerable patient addictive pain medication and bought it back off them for his own use has been banned from practising for a year, a tribunal has ruled.

South Australian GP Richard Taverner, 43, also prescribed drugs in the names of his relatives for his own personal use over several months in 2018 and 2019 and failed to accurately record his consultations with the patient.

The Medical Board of Australia referred a complaint about the doctor to the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal, which found Dr Taverner's conduct "fell significantly below" what was expected of a GP.

"The conduct was egregious because it entailed the exploitation of a patient over a lengthy period of time," the tribunal said in its decision.

"At all times, the [doctor] knew that what he was doing was wrong."

According to a tribunal decision published online, Dr Taverner took on a difficult to manage patient who was dependent on prescription medication in mid-2018, and disclosed to the patient that he personally had "abused various drugs of addiction".

"During a consultation, the [doctor] disclosed to the patient that the respondent also had a history of drug abuse," the decision said.

The GP prescribed medication to patient, then bought it back off them, the tribunal found. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The tribunal noted that in about mid-2019 Dr Taverner entered an arrangement with the patient where he would prescribe oxycodone — an addictive and tightly controlled opioid medication — which the patient would have dispensed at a pharmacy.

"The patient would then give the oxycodone to the [doctor]," the tribunal decision said.

"The [doctor] would provide the patient with cash to pay for the prescription, and the patient would retain any change for his own use."

The tribunal found that "arrangement" amounted to "professional misconduct".

"It was dangerous to the patient, and to himself. It endured over a lengthy period of time," the tribunal said.

GP 'failed to maintain accurate or adequate clinical records'

The tribunal said that "contrary to recommendations" Drug and Alcohol Services South Australia made in letters to Dr Taverner, he continued to prescribe sedative and anxiety medications to the patient "at a frequency that was greater than clinically appropriate" while knowing the patient had a history of opioid dependence.

It also found Dr Taverner misappropriated oxycodone for personal use from a medication store at the practice where he then worked, and had "failed to maintain accurate or adequate clinical records" by deleting prescriptions from the patient's clinical records.

The tribunal banned the doctor from practising for a year. (ABC News: Eugene Boisvert)

On other occasions, he "falsified a presentation of a severe migraine requiring the prescription" and inaccurately recorded consultations with the patient, including failing to record his assessment of the patient's mental health.

"These failures occurred due to the respondent intending to prevent anyone from discovering his arrangement with the patient, and because he knew prescribing oxycodone to the patient was wrong," the tribunal said.

GP 'took full responsibility'

The tribunal noted the board had placed restrictions on Dr Taverner upon learning of the allegations in June 2022, and he had not returned a single positive result while he had been subject of an "intense regime of drug testing".

It also noted he "took full responsibility for his failures", had insight into his vulnerability and had told the tribunal he was "ashamed" he had not provided the patient with proper care.

"The tribunal finds that [Dr Taverner] does not now pose a risk to the public because of the supports he has in place to reduce the risk of relapse," the tribunal said.

The tribunal reprimanded Dr Taverner, cancelled his registration last month and disqualified him from applying to re-register for a year.

It said a longer ban would have been imposed had the doctor "not so successfully rehabilitated from his addiction". It also noted he had successfully worked part-time as a general practitioner for almost four years since the conduct occurred.

World.title: Man arrested over weekend death of Melbourne woman
World.content:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

A 31-year-old man has been arrested over the death of 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner at a Melbourne apartment block over the weekend.

Ms Bonner was found dead in the apartment block in Carlton just before 2am on Saturday.

The 31-year-old Carlton man handed himself in at a police station and is expected to be interviewed by detectives.

Investigators believed the parties were known to one another.

A 60-year-old man was arrested on Saturday but was released pending further enquiries.

Jayda Allen Bonner, 21, was described by her aunt as a "gentle soul with a heart of gold". (Supplied)

Victoria Police said the investigation into Ms Bonner's death remained ongoing.

Ms Bonner was a Yagera woman with family in Queensland.

She was described by her aunt, Kellie Carter-Bell, as a "gentle soul" with a "heart of gold."

Ms Carter-Bell said the family had been so concerned about Ms Bonner's welfare that they had recently sought help from police.

"We begged for their help, and because we were ringing them and not Jayda, their attitude was, 'Well, what do you want us to do?'"

Victoria Police did not respond to the family's claim, with a spokesperson telling the ABC it could not comment while an investigation was underway.

World.title: AI inquiry urges independent safety watchdogs inside companies
World.content:
Australia should require AI companies to submit to independent safety checks, reserve computing power for local use and give security agencies early access to new models, a parliamentary committee has recommended.

The bipartisan inquiry examining artificial intelligence has presented "early advice" to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the wake of the OpenAI breach, in which autonomous agents gained unauthorised access to Medicare statistics.

The committee has endorsed investment in data centres, backed by national standards covering resource use, additional electricity generation and community consultation.

It has also urged a review of Australia's copyright settings, which would be at odds with creative groups seeking stronger enforcement of existing protections rather than changes to accommodate the AI industry.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will make the decision about whether to implement many of the recommendations. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The recommendations were outlined in a letter sent to Mr Albanese on Monday night, signed by the committee's Labor chair Jo Briskey and Liberal deputy chair Jonno Duniam, with a final report due at the end of November.

The federal government has signalled it hopes to introduce legislation outlining national standards for data centres and frontier AI models by the end of this year and pass the laws through parliament in early 2027.

Push for independent experts inside AI companies

The committee has recommended the government put independent experts inside leading AI companies that would have access to their systems and a duty to report safety findings and incidents to government.

Security agencies like the Australian Signals Directorate should receive early access to new models as a condition of arrangements allowing frontier AI labs to train them in Australia.

The government has been urged to immediately review protections used across its data repositories, particularly those holding sensitive and national security information.

It has also been advised to monitor the risk of AI helping to develop biological weapons.

Alongside those safeguards, the committee has questioned whether existing copyright rules were delivering for Australian creators or supporting local AI development.

Copyright rules under scrutiny

The committee noted current copyright arrangements were "not facilitating" licensing deals for Australian culture and content.

"The status quo sees the work of Australian artists, musicians and media outlets used overseas without adequate control or payment," the letter said.

They also acknowledged frontier AI labs had indicated existing copyright settings were a "barrier" to undertaking training in Australia.

The committee recommended the government "examine" current copyright settings and prioritise ensuring that Australian creators "retain control over how their works are used, that they are paid, and that AI systems reflect Australian values and culture".

But Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) chief executive Annabelle Herd told the inquiry last week that existing licensing systems could support AI training without rewriting copyright protections to suit foreign companies.

"They should come to the negotiating table, not to the prime minister's office," she said.

OpenAI breach drives calls for oversight

Last month it was revealed OpenAI's experimental models accessed government websites without authorisation during training, including a Services Australia portal hosting Medicare statistics.

OpenAI has apologised for both the incident and its handling of the response, which included a months-long delay in detecting the issue and notifying the government about it.

All eyes on OpenAI at inquiry It had been pencilled in for a centrestage performance, tapping into a bit of Silicon Valley star power, but it's a bruised OpenAI that's set to limp into the Australian political spotlight today.

The letter from the committee said the OpenAI breach demonstrated the need for "appropriate and robust safeguards" to protect Australian data and those who own and use it.

It was recommended the safeguards apply to frontier AI developers deploying models and agents in Australia, ensuring there was "proper and transparent accountability and oversight mechanisms" along with "well-established practices to deal with incidents that may occur in the future".

Frontier labs should also be required to monitor and report incidents to the government in a "timely manner".

"This should include an obligation or duty to monitor risks and clear reporting deadlines," the letter said.

OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon last week said the company would "support a framework on mandatory disclosures".

Australia cannot simply be 'consumer' of foreign AI

It was recommended the government establish an ongoing parliamentary joint standing committee to monitor AI, which could conduct "rapid reviews" of new regulation when required.

This committee would also be reported to at "regular intervals" on serious events and incidents, including cyber incidents involving AI, unintended actions of agents and models as well as "misuse" of the technology.

The letter recommended reserving a share of computing capacity for national security and university research, with health and social services also among the potential beneficiaries.

"The overarching objective should be to ensure that Australia is not merely a consumer of AI technologies developed elsewhere, but a trusted, competitive and strategically capable participant in the global AI industry," the letter said.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Several Labor MPs want government to retain ATO credit card payments; Russia continues striking energy facilities despite ceasefire, says Zelensky
World.content:
Russia has kept up its attacks on energy assets despite US President Donald Trump claiming there were pledges from both sides to support an “energy ceasefire” in the war, Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said after another day of strikes.

“Last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there would be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia,” the Ukrainian president told Fox News in the US. “We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities.”

There were attacks on six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday, Zelensky said, that left 33 people injured.

“I think it was Putin’s answer to President Trump. And the message from Russia was very clear – they don’t know anything about the energy ceasefire. It’s a pity, because they always find reasons not to stop this war. Which is why I think we need more pressure on Russia.”

Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv twice on Monday, according to statements from Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported by The Kyiv Independent and others. Reuters reported that a ​Russian strike on a high-rise ‌residential building killed two ​people and injured at ​least seven. A separate strike hit a factory in the city of Vinnytsia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected a 60-day ceasefire proposed by Zelensky, Reuters reported from Moscow. Instead, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia would be willing to halt attacks on the day Ukraine holds a presidential election. Zelensky said Ukraine was “ready to respect an energy ceasefire” if Russia did the same.

World.title: Burnham triggers talk of a Brexit reversal after accusing Russia of meddling in vote
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeBrexit Burnham triggers talk of a Brexit reversal after accusing Russia of meddling in vote David Crowe October 13, 2026 — 6:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A new claim about the Brexit referendum has set off an almighty row in Britain over Russian interference – and fuelled arguments about whether the country might one day rejoin the European Union. The victors of the 2016 vote are crying foul after Prime Minister Andy Burnham named Russian state agencies as key culprits in trying to influence the referendum. UK Labour’s Newest MP, Sagal Abdi-Wali, takes a selfie with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other colleagues at Westminster Hall on Monday. Getty Images Meanwhile, the “Remainers” who opposed the split from Europe are praising Burnham for finally admitting what some observers said at the time was a clear case of foreign interference. The timing is especially sensitive. Burnham believes Brexit has damaged Britain over the past decade, so he wants to tighten ties with the EU in talks next month in the hope of lifting growth.



But his stance is heresy for the “Leave” campaigners who suspect Burnham will one day call a new vote to reverse Brexit. Burnham’s new quotes about old votes triggered headlines on Monday, when he went public about advice he received when he became prime minister and asked about foreign interference in the referendum. A pro-European campaigner wears a “Stop Brexit” in London in June. Bloomberg “I don’t think we knew back then the extent to which there was state-sponsored interference in the British democratic process,” Burnham said. “But I asked the question coming into Downing Street: Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”



The referendum result was reasonably close: 51.9 per cent voted to leave and 48.1 per cent voted to remain. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Can Burnham save Britain? Finally, he reveals his plans – with one glaring omission Burnham made his remarks on a podcast, the Rest is Politics, with hosts Alastair Campbell, a former Labour press secretary, and Rory Stewart, a former Conservative cabinet minister. Both are “Remainers” and wanted to canvass this issue with Burnham. The prime minister, in turn, wanted the security advice in the public domain. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he said. “I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”



It is hardly new to talk about Russian interference in the 2016 referendum. Parliamentary committees looked into the problem and journalists investigated the “bot farms” run by allies of Russian President Vladimir Putin. It is new, however, for the prime minister to name the Russian state as the source of foreign interference in the fraught 2016 vote. Russian President Vladimir Putin. Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP This is an elemental issue in British political circles, where every participant is known and labelled as either a member of the Leave or Remain camps. Merely having a discussion about whether Brexit was a good idea or not can send some observers into conniptions. “Brexit has done more harm than good,” Burnham told voters in a speech last month. That drew a total rejection from the Conservative Party, which does not want a new referendum. Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, made his name as a key advocate for Brexit and insists it was the right thing to do, but he blames the Conservatives for doing it badly.



Several economic reports say Brexit failed to deliver the growth boost the Conservative government claimed. The Remain camp dismiss the findings. The polarised debate also shapes the argument about migration, because the split with Europe has made it more challenging to send asylum seekers back across the English Channel. Boris Johnson, who argued for Brexit and became prime minister three years after the vote, reacted within hours of Burnham’s new comments. “This is just not true,” he said on Monday. Johnson said security officials told him there was no evidence of successful interference in the referendum when he asked upon becoming foreign secretary soon after the vote. Former UK prime minister Boris Johnson at a literary festival in Ukraine last month. Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Other members of the Leave campaign fulminated online about Burnham’s remarks. Farage called the prime minister a liar and denied there was any Russian interference. Labour ministers chose to tread carefully. They had to be careful not to blame voters for being duped by Moscow, so they said that they did not believe the Russian influence had been successful. This line was repeated by Burnham’s office, and then by the prime minister himself in parliament.



When Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister had implied the referendum result was illegitimate, Burnham denied this outright. A spokesperson for No. 10 Downing Street made sure the media got this message, saying: “We believe the referendum result was legitimate.” This is a tricky dance around the facts. How can anyone measure the impact of a foreign interference campaign? Brexit was decided by a margin of 3.8 per cent of the votes cast. Turnout was 72.2 per cent. There is no reliable way to prove whether the foreign influence was effective or not. Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch. Getty Images Reform UK leader Nigel Farage speaks at a press conference on Monday. Getty Images What comes next? Burnham will meet EU leaders next month for another negotiation on the Brexit terms. He promises a deal to lift growth and help manage migration, without needing another referendum.



“I am not reopening the referendum. I respect the referendum result,” he told parliament. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Bregrets? They’ve got a few. Most Brits now think leaving EU was a mistake While Burnham may be able to negotiate a successful deal, the idea of a new referendum is unlikely to evaporate as the nation changes. Polling firm YouGov issued findings last Thursday that said 52 per cent would vote to rejoin the EU – a reversal of the result a decade ago. YouGov also found that 22 per cent of those who voted to leave a decade ago would now vote to rejoin. Some voters are clearly suffering some “regrexit” over the nation’s fortunes. In naming Russia as a culprit, Burnham may be able to slyly discredit the referendum outcome and build more support for his stance on Europe. But he will not be doing this alone.



Putin will be helping with every new instance of Russian interference, sabotage or hybrid warfare in Europe. Every threat will prove the case for greater unity among European democracies. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Why Brisbane should embrace pink and restore an appetite for colour
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArchitecture Opinion Why Brisbane should embrace pink and restore an appetite for colour Izzie White Contributor October 13, 2026 — 6:00am

October 13, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Brisbane is at the beginning of its cosmopolitan journey. It’s a remarkable thing – cities breed art, culture, diversity, vibrancy and economic resilience the world over. This changing social landscape will mean our buildings change too. How do we hold on to what makes Brisbane, Brisbane? If we look overseas at cities much older than ours – New York, London, Copenhagen, Paris – their unique identities developed long before globalisation in a time when building materials were bound by geographic proximity. Each city’s architecture is distinct, a representation of available building materials, and a response to climate and local culture. Miss Midgley’s boutique heritage guest house in New Farm. Hannah Puechmarin The challenge for Brisbane, indeed any modern city facing rapid development, is the impeded ability of designers to safeguard a coherent city identity. It’s not an easy job. Each new development competes with its predecessor, and the idea of hiring an architect to produce something that looks like the neighbour isn’t exactly a priority for a paying client.



On top of this, global trade networks have resulted in a universal sameness, as glass towers continue to emerge in our cities regardless of climate, culture or context. Brisbane does have a lot to be proud of – the success of Howard Smith Wharves, South Bank and the Riverloop. These are urban interventions worthy of a global city. But I also notice a blight, slowly spreading across the hallmark hills of our suburban city. We’ve lost our appetite for colour.



In response to this chromatic drought and in search of a cohesive city identity, I propose a new solution, however unconventional. We should paint the town pink. Literally. Queensland architecture has been defined by its colourful character homes for more than a century. Standing atop Paddington or Highgate Hill, stilted timber cottages climb the rolling hillscapes painted every colour imaginable, from buttercup yellows to sage greens with frosted trims or deep olive accents. Why have we been such a colourful city for so long? A typical assortment of colour in heritage Brisbane buildings. Izzie White Creative It’s not just aesthetics, it’s a climate response. Light colours have always been integral to the Queensland climate to reflect heat, but intense whites introduce unbearable levels of glare. I know I’m not the only pedestrian to be unsuspectingly blinded when rounding a corner on a new development. It sounds light-hearted, but cities are nothing if not defined by the experience of walking through them. What’s a better alternative to keep our city cool but stop us disappearing under a sea of blinding anonymity?



Our heritage buildings have been kind enough to leave us a clue. Brisbane is built on top of a volcanic rock called Brisbane Tuff, deposited by cataclysmic events a long time ago – meaning it’s finite and specific to our city. The pink clue hiding in plain site. Izzie White Creative It was a miracle material for the European colonists who quickly put the convicts to work quarrying the stone out of Kangaroo Point and other quarries around the city. Perhaps the best standing example of tuff architecture is the All Saints’ Anglican Church on Wickham Terrace, Spring Hill.



Now, the stone is largely rationed for heritage restoration projects, famed for its colourful composition ranging from purples, teal and rust browns. But its most endearing colour is blush pink. This blush pink is representative of a geology and history that only Brisbane has. Splashes of pink on Miss Midgley’s guesthouse. Hannah Puechmarin It extends beyond our European history, acknowledges a landscape swallowed by the slow and gradual development of our city. As a paint colour, it shifts glare but reflects heat, but blush pink goes further. It mirrors our native bottlebrush, grevillea and blossoming gums – an alternative to the foreign but persistent Jacaranda purples and Poinciana reds.



Lucky for me, I’m not the first person to reintroduce our city to this charming colour. Local architecture firm Richards and Spence with artist Bruce Reynolds, alongside Hassell and REX architecture, recently delivered an office building that shows exactly how colour can be used to transform modern city making. Located at 205 North Quay, the building could be mistaken for a typical office tower with delicate and lacey bronze shading system, if it wasn’t for the pink concrete landscape it hovers over. The North Quay precinct in central Brisbane has embraced pink. Izzie White Creative This pink outdoor plaza weaves around landscape and towers above you in a way that feels remarkably like being in a quarry cut from pink stone. I wonder where they got that idea from. With so much heritage, colour, climatic reasoning and personality to choose from, it is peculiar indeed to see so many new projects decide to plant olive trees instead of banksias, and choose all white instead of pink.



Understanding who we are as a city requires an intimate examination of our relationship with our land, landscape, First Peoples and climate – it is the basis of who we are as a city, and it will be what makes Brisbane, Brisbane. Heritage homes were commonly pink before becoming blindingly white. Izzie White Creative Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: US health giant scraps weight-oriented Juniper to launch women’s health clinic
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyHealthcare US health giant scraps weight-oriented Juniper to launch women’s health clinic David Swan October 13, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US telehealth giant Hims & Hers Health is bringing its women’s health brand, Hers, to Australia, retiring Juniper, the weight-loss service Sydney start-up Eucalyptus launched in 2021. The switch completes the company’s $1.6 billion takeover of Eucalyptus earlier this year. Eucalyptus’ men’s health brand, Pilot, moved to Hims in August. Eucalyptus co-founder Tim Doyle. Oscar Colman Eucalyptus co-founder and former chief executive Tim Doyle, now senior vice-president of international at Hims & Hers, said Hers would turn Juniper into a full women’s health clinic, adding hair loss and menopause programs. “Juniper’s been historically very weight-oriented, with a sprinkle of menopause,” Doyle said.



He expected some customers to be put off by the switch to an American brand, but said the change would be a net positive within one to two years. Related Article Apps Would you pay $1500 a month for a health app? “It would be dumb to say there’s going to not be any friction on day one,” he said. Doyle said Pilot had become “a relic of a bit of a different time”, adding that the local brands lacked “the same ring” as Hims & Hers. Hims & Hers vice-president of product, international, Rebecca Holdt said existing Juniper patients would keep their Australian practitioners and care team, and their treatment plans, pricing and medications would carry over.



Gus Wood will run the Australian business as general manager, with Matt Vickers, a GP who has worked at Eucalyptus since 2019, as chief medical officer of Hims & Hers Australia. Eucalyptus employs about 250 people in Australia, Doyle said, and the team had grown at the same rate since the takeover as it did before. He said the acquisition was “about capabilities and growth”. Part of that is artificial intelligence. Doyle said Hims & Hers had hired much of the applied AI and engineering team from Cruise, the driverless car start-up, to build tools for health coaching and care management, and the Australian business was already using some of them. Jessica Shepherd, Hers’ chief medical officer. “The biggest change happening at the moment is people can get reasonably good quality health advice for free in a matter of seconds from the LLMs [large language models],” Doyle said.



In August, Hims & Hers rebuilt its US Hers app so weight-loss patients deal with an AI, their care team and their doctor in a single conversation, with the AI passing questions that need clinical judgment to a provider. The company’s fine print says the AI’s responses “can make mistakes” and are not a medical diagnosis. Juniper’s AI chatbot. Australian customers will get a new Hers app from today. Holdt did not say whether Australian patients’ health data would stay in Australia. She said the Hers team would work with Juniper staff “to make sure data remains safely stored in accordance with all applicable laws”. Hers will prescribe TGA-approved weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro when clinically appropriate, with programs starting at $349 a month. The menopause program costs $99 for an initial consultation, with treatment from $17 a month, and the hair loss program has a $24.99 initial consultation fee.



In the US, Hims & Hers built much of its weight-loss business on compounded GLP-1s – cheaper copies of Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro – made by pharmacies. Australia banned such compounded versions from October 2024, and Doyle said the US business is now predominantly selling on-label medications. The company did not say how many Australian women are on a weight-loss program through Juniper. Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum holding his son at the IPO on June 14, 2022. Photo: Supplied. Hims & Hers is known in the US for heavy consumer marketing, including Super Bowl advertising. Australia bans advertising prescription medicines directly to the public, and Holdt said Hers would focus on educating women about their symptoms rather than promoting medicines. The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners said subscription telehealth services focused on prescribing risked putting financial return ahead of patient safety.



“Subscription type telehealth services are not a substitute for the comprehensive care that you get from a specialist GP that knows a patient and their history,” RACGP president Michael Wright said. Wright said medicines such as GLP-1s and menopausal hormone therapy needed careful assessment and regular monitoring. He said fragmented care had previously led to patients being prescribed weight-loss drugs when their medical history showed clear reasons not to. He did not refer to Juniper or Hers. Related Article Weight loss ‘Talk to your doctor’: Pharma giants’ weight loss ads skirt Australian law Hers practitioners assess patients in a phone consultation before prescribing. Jessica Shepherd, Hers’ chief medical officer and a US-registered obstetrician-gynaecologist, said the company could share consultation notes and treatment plans with a patient’s GP if she consented. Doyle also welcomed calls for telehealth-specific regulation as a grey market had emerged, and expected national telehealth standards within 12 months.



“It is so easy to start a digital health business at the moment, and so better regulatory frameworks for how and who can start those is probably going to be a really good thing,” he said. Hims & Hers is now looking at several markets in Europe and South America, Doyle said. “I think we’ll have more to say there in the coming weeks and months.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump Michael Koziol October 13, 2026 — 5:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: Federal agents searched the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar in a dramatic escalation of the Trump administration’s pursuit of the Somali-born representative who is up for re-election in three weeks. Authorities have been conducting a criminal investigation into Omar over allegations of immigration fraud. The 44-year-old and her family received asylum in the US in the 1990s, and she has served as an elected member of Congress from Minnesota since 2019. Homeland Security officers leave the Washington residence of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite President Donald Trump has called Omar “garbage”, and frequently targets her with abuse, along with the large Somalian community in Minnesota. “She comes from Somalia,” he told a rally in Tennessee on Saturday. “They don’t have a government, they don’t have police, all they have is crime and squalor.



“These people from Somalia, what they’ve done to Minnesota should never be allowed. Let’s see what happens – JD Vance and our people are looking at it very strongly.” Homeland Security Investigations agents were seen searching Omar’s Washington home on Monday (US time). Trump’s border tsar Tom Homan confirmed on Fox News that agents executed a judicially approved warrant as part of an ongoing investigation. The raid on Omar’s home in Washington took place just three weeks before the midterm election, where she is on the ballot. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite Omar told her followers on X that she was OK. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponise federal law enforcement,” she wrote. “For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”



Democratic leaders in the House of Representatives called the raid “deeply disturbing” and said it raised serious questions about the weaponisation of the federal government against Trump’s adversaries. Trump and far-right extremists had subjected Omar to vile personal attacks and baseless accusations for years, they said. Omar represents the city of Minneapolis in Congress. Bloomberg “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” The Department of Justice has historically avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.



Trump has repeatedly claimed Omar married her brother as part of an immigration scam, which she denies. At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said it was a fact. Related Article Trump's America Minneapolis politician attacked as White House changes tune on shooting “We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States,” he told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson in an interview. “There may be more to this … Something’s going to happen. This is an ongoing investigation.” Separately, Vance told Johnson on a podcast the administration believed Omar had definitely committed immigration fraud, and that he and White House deputy chief-of-staff Stephen Miller were working out how to build the case against her. Minnesota, under Democratic Governor Tim Walz, has been an epicentre for opposition to Trump, particularly on immigration. Federal immigration agents shot and killed two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in that state early this year.



It is also home to the highest Somali population in the US – about 2 per cent. Last week, Trump urged the people of Minnesota to “fight back” because the state was being “taken over by Somali immigrants”. Related Article US midterm elections Trump caves in on taxpayer-funded ads, rages about coverage of rally crowds “You have been robbed, and abandoned by your State Government. Your Governor is an incompetent thief who doesn’t want to get involved,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” With AP

World.title: ASX set to edge up, Wall Street steady; Meta rises after unveiling AI model
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, Wall Street steady; Meta rises after unveiling AI model Damian Troise October 13, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US stocks kicked off a busy week with mixed trading on Wall Street that is keeping the market hovering around its all-time high. The S&P 500 rose 0.1 per cent and is trading around its record set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 228 points, or 0.4 per cent, in early afternoon trade. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.2 per cent. Wall Street made a steady start to its week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures pointing to a gain of 15 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.8 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.58¢. Energy stocks had some of the biggest gains as oil prices jumped. Chevron rose 1.4 per cent.



Technology stocks were the biggest weights on the market. Micron Technology fell 2.8 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices fell 2.4 per cent. They are among several companies in the sector with big stock values that tend to have a heavy influence on the market. They have also been the driving force behind the broader market’s record gains throughout the year. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The Putin ‘solution’: Donald Trump’s strange deal is destined to fail Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Those companies could face more scrutiny from investors during this round of corporate earnings as Wall Street tries to get a better sense of whether the stock gains made during the frenzy over artificial intelligence can translate into future growth. “AI continues to support growth, reinforcing the outlook for tech and critical suppliers across the supply chain,” wrote Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at Principal Asset Management, in a report. “Yet uncertainty about AI’s long-term impact persists, making future gains more reliant on earnings delivery rather than potential.” Meta bucked the trend after it released a long-awaited artificial intelligence model, a milestone that will test whether its multibillion-dollar push to rebuild its AI organisation has improved its technology enough to compete among leaders.



Known as Muse Wonder, the new model is the company’s most capable since Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg overhauled his AI operation through an aggressive hiring push that put new talent at the helm. The company claims the model, dubbed “Watermelon” internally, is a big leap over its own predecessors, with “frontier capabilities” that its leadership say put it on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude when it comes to coding, or working through financial or legal questions. Meta shares closed 3.3 per cent higher. Stocks are reaching for records often because of the tech sector, but remain very volatile on a daily basis, partly because of big shifts in oil prices and their impact on bond yields and inflation. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 2 per cent to $US106.77 per barrel. Prices have been swinging between $US96 and nearly $US110 over the last month over uncertainty about the US war with Iran and its continued impact on global energy supplies and inflation. Prices jumped despite President Donald Trump’s announcement on social media Friday that he struck a deal to buy Russian diesel with Russian President Vladimir Putin, aiming to tamp down a spike in fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections. The plan, though, runs counter to US efforts to cut the flow of money Russia gets from oil and gas sales that can be used to pay for its war against Ukraine. Higher oil prices have been driving gasoline prices higher. That’s a direct hit to many people’s wallets, as gasoline is usually a necessary expense. The rise in diesel is more indirect, raising the costs for just about any shipped product, which usually results in higher prices for everything from food to clothing.



The surge in energy prices and its impact on the broader economy will be a key focus this week as Wall Street reviews several important economic updates. They include fresh data on the housing market, inflation and retail sales. The big updates this week involve reports about inflation hitting consumers and businesses. On Wednesday, the government will release the closely-watched consumer price index, or CPI, which measures price changes for a wide range of products and services. Economists expect the index to show the rate of inflation worsened to 3.6 per cent in September from 3.4 per cent in August. A report on inflation called the producer price index will be released on Thursday and is also expected to show that inflation remains stubbornly high. It measures inflation faced by businesses before it hits consumers. Related Article Analysis

AI The tech world believes in second chances, but does Oliver Curtis deserve a third? An update on how consumers are reacting to high prices will be released on Thursday. Economists expect the report on retail sales for September to show that households pulled back on spending.



The rate of inflation by any measure remains well above the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent. That prompted the central bank to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects another rate hike before the year ends. Inflation and expectations for high interest rates have been driving Treasury yields higher in the bond market. The 10-year Treasury yield, which influences mortgage rates, recently touched its highest level since 2002. It has since eased a bit and stood at 5.24 per cent late Friday. US bond trading was closed Monday for the Columbus Day holiday. Higher mortgage rates have been weighing on the housing market and Wall Street will get an update on home sales on Tuesday. The latest round of corporate earnings updates ramps up this week with financial results from banks. Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo will report their results on Tuesday and Bank of America will report its results on Wednesday. They have been reporting record profits throughout the year and Wall Street expects more of the same for the latest quarter. Markets in Europe gained ground and markets in Asia were mostly lower. Markets in Tokyo were closed for a holiday.
