World.title: You’re probably washing your pants wrong. Here’s how to do it right
World.content:
LifestyleFashionStyle You’re probably washing your pants wrong. Here’s how to do it right Jolie Kerr October 13, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s a frustrating truism of laundry that there are no hard-and-fast rules about how often you should clean a pair of pants. That makes it tricky to know when, exactly, it’s time for our legwear to take a spin in the washing machine. But there are some clear signs that tell us it’s time to do so. “Invisible soils like sweat and body oils naturally build up, leading to dinginess and odours if they aren’t cleaned regularly,” says Kim Romine, a fabric care scientist at Procter and Gamble. “Signs that your garment needs washing include visible stains, noticeable odours and the fabric feeling oily or stiff from soil buildup.” That’s a helpful start, but there is more to know about how, and how often, to wash a pair of pants. No, your jeans don’t need to be washed after every wear. Getty Images You must wash pants that have been exposed to contaminants



Regular washing is crucial to keeping pants free of stains and odours and to maintain the integrity of the fabric. But there are also times you must wash pants: when they have been in contact with such contaminants as pesticides, occupational chemicals or biological soils (blood, urine, feces, vomit), wash them as soon as possible. Avoid placing contaminated clothing in a laundry bag or hamper with other items, and wash them in a load separate from other clothing and household linens. OK, but won’t overwashing ruin my pants? Related Article Pets Does your pet sleep on your bed? You probably need these cleaning tips Not as much as you might think, though washing pants does contribute to overall wear and tear. Actually, the real culprit is the dryer. If you want to preserve the look and longevity of your pants, whether they’re yoga pants, pyjama pants or expensive jeans, wash them regularly according to the expert guidelines below, but try to avoid using the dryer. Air-drying pants – on a line or rack or laying them flat – or using a no- or low-heat dryer setting, is the best way to balance the need to wash these garments with ensuring they look good and last a long time. Is it better to wash pants inside out or right side out?



“Washing pants inside out is generally recommended,” Romine says. It helps protect the fabric’s outer surface from fading, abrasion and the pilling that can occur in the wash. “Additionally, most soils accumulate on the inside, where the fabric contacts your skin,” she says. “Turning pants inside out exposes these areas to more agitation, improving soil removal.” But if the outside of the pants is heavily soiled or stained, Romine adds, “washing them right side out can help target that dirt more effectively.” A note on undergarments, or lack thereof If you’re a member of the commando set, you’ll need to wash your pants accordingly. “No question,” says Robert Cardiff, the co-founder of Laundry Sauce, “if you’re going commando, treat those pants more like underwear. That means washing leggings and yoga pants every single wear, and bumping up the frequency on anything else that sits close to your skin. Your pants, and everyone around you, will thank you.” Avoid washing activewear with bulky items like hoodies and jeans, which cause friction. Getty Images How, and how often, to wash different types of pants



The good or bad news, depending on your perspective, is that even the experts don’t agree on how often to wash pants, so treat these recommendations as rough guidelines. And before laundering pants, Romine says, “always check the care label for specific instructions, as some fabrics may have unique washing requirements”. Yoga pants, workout pants and leggings “These should be washed after every wear because they trap sweat and body oils, which can cause odours and skin irritation,” Romine says. To target these soils, turn leggings and workout and yoga pants inside out before washing. Cold water and a delicate cycle is best for preserving such garments. Avoid washing them in the same load as towels and fleece, which can transfer lint, as well as with heavy or bulky garments such as hoodies and jeans, which cause friction that leads to pilling and other damage. Don’t use fabric softener when washing leggings or workout and yoga pants, as it can leave a coating that traps odour-causing bacteria. Air-dry to prevent fading and shrinking and to preserve the garment’s longevity. Tracksuit pants Cardiff recommends washing tracksuit pants every three to five wears, “assuming you’re not sweating heavily in them. But once they start losing their shape or smelling less than fresh, it’s time.” Unless the exterior is visibly soiled, wash casual pants inside out to target body soils and bacteria. Use cold water and air-dry, or use a low-heat dryer cycle to maintain the fabric.



Pyjama pants Score one for the shower-at-night crowd: these can be worn two to three times before washing, Romine says, “especially if you shower at night before putting on your pyjamas. However, if you sweat heavily during the night or spill anything on them, it’s time to wash them.” Khakis and chinos Overwashing khakis and chinos “is actually one of the fastest ways to ruin them. It breaks down the fabric and fades the colour,” says Cardiff, who recommends washing them every two to three wears. “Spot-clean them when you can, air them out between wears, and save the full wash for when they’ve genuinely earned it.” Cords



“Corduroy is a thicker fabric that doesn’t absorb sweat as readily as lighter materials,” Cardiff says, “but the texture can trap dust and debris over time.” He recommends washing them infrequently – every four to five wears – and turning them inside out to retain their colour and texture. Air-drying, or using a low-heat dryer setting, also can help prevent fading and other signs of wear and tear. Linen pants “For casual use, wash linen pants every one to two wears,” Cardiff says. “If it’s been a hot summer day, after every wear.” The fabric is highly prone to shrinking, so it’s important to wash linen garments in cold water only and to air-dry them. Jeans Ideally, says Kiya Babzani, founder of the men’s denim store Self Edge, you should wash your jeans every five to seven wears – but he’s also OK with washing them every 30 to 45 wears. “I had to balance the advice because it’s so against what denim culture tells you,” he says. He recommends washing your jeans every month or every other month, “unless you’re in a really dirty environment or you’re getting something on them all the time.” To prevent premature fading, turn jeans inside out, wash them in cold water and let them air-dry.

Actor Selma Blair was taken into custody after a flight from Los Angeles to New York for being physically abusive and injuring two flight attendants, authorities said on Monday (New York time).

Blair, 54, was taken into custody late on Sunday night when the Delta Air Lines plane was parked at the gate at New York’s John F. Kennedy Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. There was no immediate response to a request for comment from the airline.

Actress Selma Blair has been arrested for an in-flight incident in which two flight attendants were injured. AP Photo/Chris Pizzello

Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said.

The FBI is investigating, the statement said. Messages seeking comment were left for the FBI and state and federal prosecutors’ offices in New York.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Several Labor MPs want government to retain ATO credit card payments; Russia continues striking energy facilities despite ceasefire, says Zelensky
World.content:
Russia has kept up its attacks on energy assets despite US President Donald Trump claiming there were pledges from both sides to support an “energy ceasefire” in the war, Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said after another day of strikes.

“Last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there would be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia,” the Ukrainian president told Fox News in the US. “We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities.”

There were attacks on six Ukrainian energy facilities on Monday, Zelensky said, that left 33 people injured.

“I think it was Putin’s answer to President Trump. And the message from Russia was very clear – they don’t know anything about the energy ceasefire. It’s a pity, because they always find reasons not to stop this war. Which is why I think we need more pressure on Russia.”

Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv twice on Monday, according to statements from Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported by The Kyiv Independent and others. Reuters reported that a ​Russian strike on a high-rise ‌residential building killed two ​people and injured at ​least seven. A separate strike hit a factory in the city of Vinnytsia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected a 60-day ceasefire proposed by Zelensky, Reuters reported from Moscow. Instead, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia would be willing to halt attacks on the day Ukraine holds a presidential election. Zelensky said Ukraine was “ready to respect an energy ceasefire” if Russia did the same.

World.title: Burnham triggers talk of a Brexit reversal after accusing Russia of meddling in vote
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeBrexit Burnham triggers talk of a Brexit reversal after accusing Russia of meddling in vote David Crowe October 13, 2026 — 6:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A new claim about the Brexit referendum has set off an almighty row in Britain over Russian interference – and fuelled arguments about whether the country might one day rejoin the European Union. The victors of the 2016 vote are crying foul after Prime Minister Andy Burnham named Russian state agencies as key culprits in trying to influence the referendum. UK Labour’s Newest MP, Sagal Abdi-Wali, takes a selfie with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other colleagues at Westminster Hall on Monday. Getty Images Meanwhile, the “Remainers” who opposed the split from Europe are praising Burnham for finally admitting what some observers said at the time was a clear case of foreign interference. The timing is especially sensitive. Burnham believes Brexit has damaged Britain over the past decade, so he wants to tighten ties with the EU in talks next month in the hope of lifting growth.



But his stance is heresy for the “Leave” campaigners who suspect Burnham will one day call a new vote to reverse Brexit. Burnham’s new quotes about old votes triggered headlines on Monday, when he went public about advice he received when he became prime minister and asked about foreign interference in the referendum. A pro-European campaigner wears a “Stop Brexit” in London in June. Bloomberg “I don’t think we knew back then the extent to which there was state-sponsored interference in the British democratic process,” Burnham said. “But I asked the question coming into Downing Street: Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”



The referendum result was reasonably close: 51.9 per cent voted to leave and 48.1 per cent voted to remain. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Can Burnham save Britain? Finally, he reveals his plans – with one glaring omission Burnham made his remarks on a podcast, the Rest is Politics, with hosts Alastair Campbell, a former Labour press secretary, and Rory Stewart, a former Conservative cabinet minister. Both are “Remainers” and wanted to canvass this issue with Burnham. The prime minister, in turn, wanted the security advice in the public domain. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he said. “I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”



It is hardly new to talk about Russian interference in the 2016 referendum. Parliamentary committees looked into the problem and journalists investigated the “bot farms” run by allies of Russian President Vladimir Putin. It is new, however, for the prime minister to name the Russian state as the source of foreign interference in the fraught 2016 vote. Russian President Vladimir Putin. Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP This is an elemental issue in British political circles, where every participant is known and labelled as either a member of the Leave or Remain camps. Merely having a discussion about whether Brexit was a good idea or not can send some observers into conniptions. “Brexit has done more harm than good,” Burnham told voters in a speech last month. That drew a total rejection from the Conservative Party, which does not want a new referendum. Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, made his name as a key advocate for Brexit and insists it was the right thing to do, but he blames the Conservatives for doing it badly.



Several economic reports say Brexit failed to deliver the growth boost the Conservative government claimed. The Remain camp dismiss the findings. The polarised debate also shapes the argument about migration, because the split with Europe has made it more challenging to send asylum seekers back across the English Channel. Boris Johnson, who argued for Brexit and became prime minister three years after the vote, reacted within hours of Burnham’s new comments. “This is just not true,” he said on Monday. Johnson said security officials told him there was no evidence of successful interference in the referendum when he asked upon becoming foreign secretary soon after the vote. Former UK prime minister Boris Johnson at a literary festival in Ukraine last month. Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Other members of the Leave campaign fulminated online about Burnham’s remarks. Farage called the prime minister a liar and denied there was any Russian interference. Labour ministers chose to tread carefully. They had to be careful not to blame voters for being duped by Moscow, so they said that they did not believe the Russian influence had been successful. This line was repeated by Burnham’s office, and then by the prime minister himself in parliament.



When Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister had implied the referendum result was illegitimate, Burnham denied this outright. A spokesperson for No. 10 Downing Street made sure the media got this message, saying: “We believe the referendum result was legitimate.” This is a tricky dance around the facts. How can anyone measure the impact of a foreign interference campaign? Brexit was decided by a margin of 3.8 per cent of the votes cast. Turnout was 72.2 per cent. There is no reliable way to prove whether the foreign influence was effective or not. Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch. Getty Images Reform UK leader Nigel Farage speaks at a press conference on Monday. Getty Images What comes next? Burnham will meet EU leaders next month for another negotiation on the Brexit terms. He promises a deal to lift growth and help manage migration, without needing another referendum.



“I am not reopening the referendum. I respect the referendum result,” he told parliament. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Bregrets? They’ve got a few. Most Brits now think leaving EU was a mistake While Burnham may be able to negotiate a successful deal, the idea of a new referendum is unlikely to evaporate as the nation changes. Polling firm YouGov issued findings last Thursday that said 52 per cent would vote to rejoin the EU – a reversal of the result a decade ago. YouGov also found that 22 per cent of those who voted to leave a decade ago would now vote to rejoin. Some voters are clearly suffering some “regrexit” over the nation’s fortunes. In naming Russia as a culprit, Burnham may be able to slyly discredit the referendum outcome and build more support for his stance on Europe. But he will not be doing this alone.



Putin will be helping with every new instance of Russian interference, sabotage or hybrid warfare in Europe. Every threat will prove the case for greater unity among European democracies. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Why Brisbane should embrace pink and restore an appetite for colour
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArchitecture Opinion Why Brisbane should embrace pink and restore an appetite for colour Izzie White Contributor October 13, 2026 — 6:00am

October 13, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Brisbane is at the beginning of its cosmopolitan journey. It’s a remarkable thing – cities breed art, culture, diversity, vibrancy and economic resilience the world over. This changing social landscape will mean our buildings change too. How do we hold on to what makes Brisbane, Brisbane? If we look overseas at cities much older than ours – New York, London, Copenhagen, Paris – their unique identities developed long before globalisation in a time when building materials were bound by geographic proximity. Each city’s architecture is distinct, a representation of available building materials, and a response to climate and local culture. Miss Midgley’s boutique heritage guest house in New Farm. Hannah Puechmarin The challenge for Brisbane, indeed any modern city facing rapid development, is the impeded ability of designers to safeguard a coherent city identity. It’s not an easy job. Each new development competes with its predecessor, and the idea of hiring an architect to produce something that looks like the neighbour isn’t exactly a priority for a paying client.



On top of this, global trade networks have resulted in a universal sameness, as glass towers continue to emerge in our cities regardless of climate, culture or context. Brisbane does have a lot to be proud of – the success of Howard Smith Wharves, South Bank and the Riverloop. These are urban interventions worthy of a global city. But I also notice a blight, slowly spreading across the hallmark hills of our suburban city. We’ve lost our appetite for colour.



In response to this chromatic drought and in search of a cohesive city identity, I propose a new solution, however unconventional. We should paint the town pink. Literally. Queensland architecture has been defined by its colourful character homes for more than a century. Standing atop Paddington or Highgate Hill, stilted timber cottages climb the rolling hillscapes painted every colour imaginable, from buttercup yellows to sage greens with frosted trims or deep olive accents. Why have we been such a colourful city for so long? A typical assortment of colour in heritage Brisbane buildings. Izzie White Creative It’s not just aesthetics, it’s a climate response. Light colours have always been integral to the Queensland climate to reflect heat, but intense whites introduce unbearable levels of glare. I know I’m not the only pedestrian to be unsuspectingly blinded when rounding a corner on a new development. It sounds light-hearted, but cities are nothing if not defined by the experience of walking through them. What’s a better alternative to keep our city cool but stop us disappearing under a sea of blinding anonymity?



Our heritage buildings have been kind enough to leave us a clue. Brisbane is built on top of a volcanic rock called Brisbane Tuff, deposited by cataclysmic events a long time ago – meaning it’s finite and specific to our city. The pink clue hiding in plain site. Izzie White Creative It was a miracle material for the European colonists who quickly put the convicts to work quarrying the stone out of Kangaroo Point and other quarries around the city. Perhaps the best standing example of tuff architecture is the All Saints’ Anglican Church on Wickham Terrace, Spring Hill.



Now, the stone is largely rationed for heritage restoration projects, famed for its colourful composition ranging from purples, teal and rust browns. But its most endearing colour is blush pink. This blush pink is representative of a geology and history that only Brisbane has. Splashes of pink on Miss Midgley’s guesthouse. Hannah Puechmarin It extends beyond our European history, acknowledges a landscape swallowed by the slow and gradual development of our city. As a paint colour, it shifts glare but reflects heat, but blush pink goes further. It mirrors our native bottlebrush, grevillea and blossoming gums – an alternative to the foreign but persistent Jacaranda purples and Poinciana reds.



Lucky for me, I’m not the first person to reintroduce our city to this charming colour. Local architecture firm Richards and Spence with artist Bruce Reynolds, alongside Hassell and REX architecture, recently delivered an office building that shows exactly how colour can be used to transform modern city making. Located at 205 North Quay, the building could be mistaken for a typical office tower with delicate and lacey bronze shading system, if it wasn’t for the pink concrete landscape it hovers over. The North Quay precinct in central Brisbane has embraced pink. Izzie White Creative This pink outdoor plaza weaves around landscape and towers above you in a way that feels remarkably like being in a quarry cut from pink stone. I wonder where they got that idea from. With so much heritage, colour, climatic reasoning and personality to choose from, it is peculiar indeed to see so many new projects decide to plant olive trees instead of banksias, and choose all white instead of pink.



Understanding who we are as a city requires an intimate examination of our relationship with our land, landscape, First Peoples and climate – it is the basis of who we are as a city, and it will be what makes Brisbane, Brisbane. Heritage homes were commonly pink before becoming blindingly white. Izzie White Creative Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: US health giant scraps weight-oriented Juniper to launch women’s health clinic
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyHealthcare US health giant scraps weight-oriented Juniper to launch women’s health clinic David Swan October 13, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US telehealth giant Hims & Hers Health is bringing its women’s health brand, Hers, to Australia, retiring Juniper, the weight-loss service Sydney start-up Eucalyptus launched in 2021. The switch completes the company’s $1.6 billion takeover of Eucalyptus earlier this year. Eucalyptus’ men’s health brand, Pilot, moved to Hims in August. Eucalyptus co-founder Tim Doyle. Oscar Colman Eucalyptus co-founder and former chief executive Tim Doyle, now senior vice-president of international at Hims & Hers, said Hers would turn Juniper into a full women’s health clinic, adding hair loss and menopause programs. “Juniper’s been historically very weight-oriented, with a sprinkle of menopause,” Doyle said.



He expected some customers to be put off by the switch to an American brand, but said the change would be a net positive within one to two years. Related Article Apps Would you pay $1500 a month for a health app? “It would be dumb to say there’s going to not be any friction on day one,” he said. Doyle said Pilot had become “a relic of a bit of a different time”, adding that the local brands lacked “the same ring” as Hims & Hers. Hims & Hers vice-president of product, international, Rebecca Holdt said existing Juniper patients would keep their Australian practitioners and care team, and their treatment plans, pricing and medications would carry over.



Gus Wood will run the Australian business as general manager, with Matt Vickers, a GP who has worked at Eucalyptus since 2019, as chief medical officer of Hims & Hers Australia. Eucalyptus employs about 250 people in Australia, Doyle said, and the team had grown at the same rate since the takeover as it did before. He said the acquisition was “about capabilities and growth”. Part of that is artificial intelligence. Doyle said Hims & Hers had hired much of the applied AI and engineering team from Cruise, the driverless car start-up, to build tools for health coaching and care management, and the Australian business was already using some of them. Jessica Shepherd, Hers’ chief medical officer. “The biggest change happening at the moment is people can get reasonably good quality health advice for free in a matter of seconds from the LLMs [large language models],” Doyle said.



In August, Hims & Hers rebuilt its US Hers app so weight-loss patients deal with an AI, their care team and their doctor in a single conversation, with the AI passing questions that need clinical judgment to a provider. The company’s fine print says the AI’s responses “can make mistakes” and are not a medical diagnosis. Juniper’s AI chatbot. Australian customers will get a new Hers app from today. Holdt did not say whether Australian patients’ health data would stay in Australia. She said the Hers team would work with Juniper staff “to make sure data remains safely stored in accordance with all applicable laws”. Hers will prescribe TGA-approved weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro when clinically appropriate, with programs starting at $349 a month. The menopause program costs $99 for an initial consultation, with treatment from $17 a month, and the hair loss program has a $24.99 initial consultation fee.



In the US, Hims & Hers built much of its weight-loss business on compounded GLP-1s – cheaper copies of Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro – made by pharmacies. Australia banned such compounded versions from October 2024, and Doyle said the US business is now predominantly selling on-label medications. The company did not say how many Australian women are on a weight-loss program through Juniper. Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum holding his son at the IPO on June 14, 2022. Photo: Supplied. Hims & Hers is known in the US for heavy consumer marketing, including Super Bowl advertising. Australia bans advertising prescription medicines directly to the public, and Holdt said Hers would focus on educating women about their symptoms rather than promoting medicines. The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners said subscription telehealth services focused on prescribing risked putting financial return ahead of patient safety.



“Subscription type telehealth services are not a substitute for the comprehensive care that you get from a specialist GP that knows a patient and their history,” RACGP president Michael Wright said. Wright said medicines such as GLP-1s and menopausal hormone therapy needed careful assessment and regular monitoring. He said fragmented care had previously led to patients being prescribed weight-loss drugs when their medical history showed clear reasons not to. He did not refer to Juniper or Hers. Related Article Weight loss ‘Talk to your doctor’: Pharma giants’ weight loss ads skirt Australian law Hers practitioners assess patients in a phone consultation before prescribing. Jessica Shepherd, Hers’ chief medical officer and a US-registered obstetrician-gynaecologist, said the company could share consultation notes and treatment plans with a patient’s GP if she consented. Doyle also welcomed calls for telehealth-specific regulation as a grey market had emerged, and expected national telehealth standards within 12 months.



“It is so easy to start a digital health business at the moment, and so better regulatory frameworks for how and who can start those is probably going to be a really good thing,” he said. Hims & Hers is now looking at several markets in Europe and South America, Doyle said. “I think we’ll have more to say there in the coming weeks and months.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump Michael Koziol October 13, 2026 — 5:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: Federal agents searched the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar in a dramatic escalation of the Trump administration’s pursuit of the Somali-born representative who is up for re-election in three weeks. Authorities have been conducting a criminal investigation into Omar over allegations of immigration fraud. The 44-year-old and her family received asylum in the US in the 1990s, and she has served as an elected member of Congress from Minnesota since 2019. Homeland Security officers leave the Washington residence of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite President Donald Trump has called Omar “garbage”, and frequently targets her with abuse, along with the large Somalian community in Minnesota. “She comes from Somalia,” he told a rally in Tennessee on Saturday. “They don’t have a government, they don’t have police, all they have is crime and squalor.



“These people from Somalia, what they’ve done to Minnesota should never be allowed. Let’s see what happens – JD Vance and our people are looking at it very strongly.” Homeland Security Investigations agents were seen searching Omar’s Washington home on Monday (US time). Trump’s border tsar Tom Homan confirmed on Fox News that agents executed a judicially approved warrant as part of an ongoing investigation. The raid on Omar’s home in Washington took place just three weeks before the midterm election, where she is on the ballot. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite Omar told her followers on X that she was OK. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponise federal law enforcement,” she wrote. “For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”



Democratic leaders in the House of Representatives called the raid “deeply disturbing” and said it raised serious questions about the weaponisation of the federal government against Trump’s adversaries. Trump and far-right extremists had subjected Omar to vile personal attacks and baseless accusations for years, they said. Omar represents the city of Minneapolis in Congress. Bloomberg “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.” The Department of Justice has historically avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.



Trump has repeatedly claimed Omar married her brother as part of an immigration scam, which she denies. At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said it was a fact. Related Article Trump's America Minneapolis politician attacked as White House changes tune on shooting “We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States,” he told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson in an interview. “There may be more to this … Something’s going to happen. This is an ongoing investigation.” Separately, Vance told Johnson on a podcast the administration believed Omar had definitely committed immigration fraud, and that he and White House deputy chief-of-staff Stephen Miller were working out how to build the case against her. Minnesota, under Democratic Governor Tim Walz, has been an epicentre for opposition to Trump, particularly on immigration. Federal immigration agents shot and killed two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in that state early this year.



It is also home to the highest Somali population in the US – about 2 per cent. Last week, Trump urged the people of Minnesota to “fight back” because the state was being “taken over by Somali immigrants”. Related Article US midterm elections Trump caves in on taxpayer-funded ads, rages about coverage of rally crowds “You have been robbed, and abandoned by your State Government. Your Governor is an incompetent thief who doesn’t want to get involved,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.” With AP

World.title: ASX set to edge up, Wall Street steady; Meta rises after unveiling AI model
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, Wall Street steady; Meta rises after unveiling AI model Damian Troise October 13, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US stocks kicked off a busy week with mixed trading on Wall Street that is keeping the market hovering around its all-time high. The S&P 500 rose 0.1 per cent and is trading around its record set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 228 points, or 0.4 per cent, in early afternoon trade. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.2 per cent. Wall Street made a steady start to its week. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures pointing to a gain of 15 points, or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.8 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.58¢. Energy stocks had some of the biggest gains as oil prices jumped. Chevron rose 1.4 per cent.



Technology stocks were the biggest weights on the market. Micron Technology fell 2.8 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices fell 2.4 per cent. They are among several companies in the sector with big stock values that tend to have a heavy influence on the market. They have also been the driving force behind the broader market’s record gains throughout the year. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The Putin ‘solution’: Donald Trump’s strange deal is destined to fail Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Those companies could face more scrutiny from investors during this round of corporate earnings as Wall Street tries to get a better sense of whether the stock gains made during the frenzy over artificial intelligence can translate into future growth. “AI continues to support growth, reinforcing the outlook for tech and critical suppliers across the supply chain,” wrote Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at Principal Asset Management, in a report. “Yet uncertainty about AI’s long-term impact persists, making future gains more reliant on earnings delivery rather than potential.” Meta bucked the trend after it released a long-awaited artificial intelligence model, a milestone that will test whether its multibillion-dollar push to rebuild its AI organisation has improved its technology enough to compete among leaders.



Known as Muse Wonder, the new model is the company’s most capable since Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg overhauled his AI operation through an aggressive hiring push that put new talent at the helm. The company claims the model, dubbed “Watermelon” internally, is a big leap over its own predecessors, with “frontier capabilities” that its leadership say put it on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude when it comes to coding, or working through financial or legal questions. Meta shares closed 3.3 per cent higher. Stocks are reaching for records often because of the tech sector, but remain very volatile on a daily basis, partly because of big shifts in oil prices and their impact on bond yields and inflation. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 2 per cent to $US106.77 per barrel. Prices have been swinging between $US96 and nearly $US110 over the last month over uncertainty about the US war with Iran and its continued impact on global energy supplies and inflation. Prices jumped despite President Donald Trump’s announcement on social media Friday that he struck a deal to buy Russian diesel with Russian President Vladimir Putin, aiming to tamp down a spike in fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections. The plan, though, runs counter to US efforts to cut the flow of money Russia gets from oil and gas sales that can be used to pay for its war against Ukraine. Higher oil prices have been driving gasoline prices higher. That’s a direct hit to many people’s wallets, as gasoline is usually a necessary expense. The rise in diesel is more indirect, raising the costs for just about any shipped product, which usually results in higher prices for everything from food to clothing.



The surge in energy prices and its impact on the broader economy will be a key focus this week as Wall Street reviews several important economic updates. They include fresh data on the housing market, inflation and retail sales. The big updates this week involve reports about inflation hitting consumers and businesses. On Wednesday, the government will release the closely-watched consumer price index, or CPI, which measures price changes for a wide range of products and services. Economists expect the index to show the rate of inflation worsened to 3.6 per cent in September from 3.4 per cent in August. A report on inflation called the producer price index will be released on Thursday and is also expected to show that inflation remains stubbornly high. It measures inflation faced by businesses before it hits consumers. Related Article Analysis

AI The tech world believes in second chances, but does Oliver Curtis deserve a third? An update on how consumers are reacting to high prices will be released on Thursday. Economists expect the report on retail sales for September to show that households pulled back on spending.



The rate of inflation by any measure remains well above the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent. That prompted the central bank to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects another rate hike before the year ends. Inflation and expectations for high interest rates have been driving Treasury yields higher in the bond market. The 10-year Treasury yield, which influences mortgage rates, recently touched its highest level since 2002. It has since eased a bit and stood at 5.24 per cent late Friday. US bond trading was closed Monday for the Columbus Day holiday. Higher mortgage rates have been weighing on the housing market and Wall Street will get an update on home sales on Tuesday. The latest round of corporate earnings updates ramps up this week with financial results from banks. Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo will report their results on Tuesday and Bank of America will report its results on Wednesday. They have been reporting record profits throughout the year and Wall Street expects more of the same for the latest quarter. Markets in Europe gained ground and markets in Asia were mostly lower. Markets in Tokyo were closed for a holiday.

World.title: You’re probably washing your pants wrong. Here’s how to do it right
World.content:
LifestyleFashionStyle You’re probably washing your pants wrong. Here’s how to do it right Jolie Kerr October 13, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s a frustrating truism of laundry that there are no hard-and-fast rules about how often you should clean a pair of pants. That makes it tricky to know when, exactly, it’s time for our legwear to take a spin in the washing machine. But there are some clear signs that tell us it’s time to do so. “Invisible soils like sweat and body oils naturally build up, leading to dinginess and odours if they aren’t cleaned regularly,” says Kim Romine, a fabric care scientist at Procter and Gamble. “Signs that your garment needs washing include visible stains, noticeable odours and the fabric feeling oily or stiff from soil buildup.” That’s a helpful start, but there is more to know about how, and how often, to wash a pair of pants. No, your jeans don’t need to be washed after every wear. Getty Images You must wash pants that have been exposed to contaminants



Regular washing is crucial to keeping pants free of stains and odours and to maintain the integrity of the fabric. But there are also times you must wash pants: when they have been in contact with such contaminants as pesticides, occupational chemicals or biological soils (blood, urine, feces, vomit), wash them as soon as possible. Avoid placing contaminated clothing in a laundry bag or hamper with other items, and wash them in a load separate from other clothing and household linens. OK, but won’t overwashing ruin my pants? Related Article Pets Does your pet sleep on your bed? You probably need these cleaning tips Not as much as you might think, though washing pants does contribute to overall wear and tear. Actually, the real culprit is the dryer. If you want to preserve the look and longevity of your pants, whether they’re yoga pants, pyjama pants or expensive jeans, wash them regularly according to the expert guidelines below, but try to avoid using the dryer. Air-drying pants – on a line or rack or laying them flat – or using a no- or low-heat dryer setting, is the best way to balance the need to wash these garments with ensuring they look good and last a long time. Is it better to wash pants inside out or right side out?



“Washing pants inside out is generally recommended,” Romine says. It helps protect the fabric’s outer surface from fading, abrasion and the pilling that can occur in the wash. “Additionally, most soils accumulate on the inside, where the fabric contacts your skin,” she says. “Turning pants inside out exposes these areas to more agitation, improving soil removal.” But if the outside of the pants is heavily soiled or stained, Romine adds, “washing them right side out can help target that dirt more effectively.” A note on undergarments, or lack thereof If you’re a member of the commando set, you’ll need to wash your pants accordingly. “No question,” says Robert Cardiff, the co-founder of Laundry Sauce, “if you’re going commando, treat those pants more like underwear. That means washing leggings and yoga pants every single wear, and bumping up the frequency on anything else that sits close to your skin. Your pants, and everyone around you, will thank you.” Avoid washing activewear with bulky items like hoodies and jeans, which cause friction. Getty Images How, and how often, to wash different types of pants



The good or bad news, depending on your perspective, is that even the experts don’t agree on how often to wash pants, so treat these recommendations as rough guidelines. And before laundering pants, Romine says, “always check the care label for specific instructions, as some fabrics may have unique washing requirements”. Yoga pants, workout pants and leggings “These should be washed after every wear because they trap sweat and body oils, which can cause odours and skin irritation,” Romine says. To target these soils, turn leggings and workout and yoga pants inside out before washing. Cold water and a delicate cycle is best for preserving such garments. Avoid washing them in the same load as towels and fleece, which can transfer lint, as well as with heavy or bulky garments such as hoodies and jeans, which cause friction that leads to pilling and other damage. Don’t use fabric softener when washing leggings or workout and yoga pants, as it can leave a coating that traps odour-causing bacteria. Air-dry to prevent fading and shrinking and to preserve the garment’s longevity. Tracksuit pants Cardiff recommends washing tracksuit pants every three to five wears, “assuming you’re not sweating heavily in them. But once they start losing their shape or smelling less than fresh, it’s time.” Unless the exterior is visibly soiled, wash casual pants inside out to target body soils and bacteria. Use cold water and air-dry, or use a low-heat dryer cycle to maintain the fabric.



Pyjama pants Score one for the shower-at-night crowd: these can be worn two to three times before washing, Romine says, “especially if you shower at night before putting on your pyjamas. However, if you sweat heavily during the night or spill anything on them, it’s time to wash them.” Khakis and chinos Overwashing khakis and chinos “is actually one of the fastest ways to ruin them. It breaks down the fabric and fades the colour,” says Cardiff, who recommends washing them every two to three wears. “Spot-clean them when you can, air them out between wears, and save the full wash for when they’ve genuinely earned it.” Cords



“Corduroy is a thicker fabric that doesn’t absorb sweat as readily as lighter materials,” Cardiff says, “but the texture can trap dust and debris over time.” He recommends washing them infrequently – every four to five wears – and turning them inside out to retain their colour and texture. Air-drying, or using a low-heat dryer setting, also can help prevent fading and other signs of wear and tear. Linen pants “For casual use, wash linen pants every one to two wears,” Cardiff says. “If it’s been a hot summer day, after every wear.” The fabric is highly prone to shrinking, so it’s important to wash linen garments in cold water only and to air-dry them. Jeans Ideally, says Kiya Babzani, founder of the men’s denim store Self Edge, you should wash your jeans every five to seven wears – but he’s also OK with washing them every 30 to 45 wears. “I had to balance the advice because it’s so against what denim culture tells you,” he says. He recommends washing your jeans every month or every other month, “unless you’re in a really dirty environment or you’re getting something on them all the time.” To prevent premature fading, turn jeans inside out, wash them in cold water and let them air-dry.

World.title: West Auckland butcher gets 1000 applications for meat packer job
World.content:
Audio player for " West Auckland butcher gets 1000 applications for two jobs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/business/1866377%2Fwest-auckland-butcher-gets-1000-applications-for-meat-packer-job

West Auckland butcher gets 1000 applications for two jobs Morning Report Download MP3 6m

A West Auckland butcher feels he could have built "something to go to Mars" with the calibre of applicants for a meat packer role.

New Lynn's Aussie Butcher managing director Reuben Sharples told Morning Report he was swamped with more than 1000 CVs after advertising for a full time staff member.

The country's unemployment rate is the highest its been in more than a decade - described as "crisis-level" among young people in particular.

Sharples said he couldn't believe the 120 emails he received from applicants for the role.

How have you found jobhunting or hiring? Share your stories with us: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

"I thought, 'Oh my God, that's so many.' But then our admin said, 'No, you've got another 870-odd on SEEK.

"They're still coming through now, so over 1000 ... for a meat packers role. So pretty overwhelming actually.

"It was like, 'Oh, how do I deal with this?'"

The interest was crazy he said, as was the expertise among the applicants.

"I think the biggest difference was I could have started up lots of businesses. I had someone that had 20 years of aviation security experience."

Those vying for the job included several rest home workers and a computer engineer.

"[Could] probably build something and go to Mars ... with all the people that actually applied."

It was daunting to see people looking for work whose skill sets were "10, 20 times" what was required, Sharples said.

After trawling through the applications he ended up hiring three people, including an apprentice.

His advice to young people looking for work was to avoid showing up with parents and also to tap into friends and family networks.

World.title: 'Postcode lottery': Nine paediatric respiratory doctors from two regions serve whole country
World.content:
Audio player for " Audit finds access to respiratory care depends on location " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/health/1865632%2Fpostcode-lottery-nine-paediatric-respiratory-doctors-from-two-regions-serve-whole-country

Audit finds access to respiratory care depends on location Morning Report Download MP3 6m

A child's access to life-saving specialist respiratory care in New Zealand may depend on where they live.

There are just nine public respiratory paediatricians serving the entire country, with 14 regions reporting no dedicated service, or no service available at all.

Those figures come from a new national audit done by Asthma NZ and the University of Auckland, which highlights significant gaps in respiratory care.

Asthma was the number one condition causing potentially avoidable hospital admissions for children under five in 2025.

Has where you live affected the healthcare you can get? Share your stories with us iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Data from 2023 showed respiratory diseases were the country's third-leading cause of death.

University of Auckland respiratory health expert Amy Chan, who carried out the audit, said the data provided a map of where respiratory services were and what they looked like

"What's most concerning is really a postcode lottery. Where you live depends on how easy you can access care. And for some New Zealanders, that's no care at all, unfortunately," Chan said.

"I found nine paediatric children respiratory doctors service all of New Zealand. That's just such a small number, servicing over 600,000 children."

The audit found the nine doctors were just in two regions, in Auckland and in Christchurch.

"Without these doctors flying out from Starship to get to different parts of New Zealand, then there would be no paediatric respiratory service or specialist service, even though we have very rare sick children. So I think the concern is there is if someone resigns or retires, that's just on the brink of collapse. There is just not enough specialists to service the need," she said.

Four districts - Tairāwhiti, Whanganui, Wairarapa and the West Coast - did not have a respiratory physician at all, Chan said.

"That's really concerning where there's nothing. And there's an international benchmark. So based on what is safe in terms of our respiratory need ... we are actually 35 adult specialists short across all of New Zealand," she said.

Chan said a national co-ordinated strategy was needed to address the issue.

"We've actually done some work pulling a multidisciplinary group together to drive a national strategy. We're just waiting for the new government to be confirmed so we can work in partnership with the government once we know who's in Parliament," she said.

Health New Zealand's Dr Richard Sullivan. RNZ / Calvin Samuel

Health New Zealand clinical executive national director Dr Richard Sullivan said the agency recognised the significant impact respiratory disease had on individuals, whānau and communities across New Zealand.

"Health NZ met with Asthma NZ and has only recently received copies of the BREATHE Strategy and audit report. We are taking the time to review the material and consider any implications for Health NZ," he said.

"Until that work is complete, Health NZ is not in a position to comment on the specific findings of the audit or the recommendations contained within the Strategy."

World.title: National adamant its superannuation stance has not changed
World.content:
Audio player for " National's approach to superannuation " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1865995%2Fnational-adamant-its-superannuation-stance-has-not-changed

National is adamant its stance on superannuation has not changed since its fiery criticisms of other parties' failure to tackle the problem earlier in the year.

An economist is urging action, while political friends and foes alike are lobbing in their own criticisms.

The party unveiled its fiscal plan on Monday, setting out how policies would be paid for.

In stark contrast to ACT's own fiscals unveiled the day before, there was no sign of a specific plans to raise the age of eligibility for superannuation.

Instead, a commitment to the stance Willis agreed on TVNZ's Q+A on Sunday, to discuss the path forward in a broader cross-party accord over the retirement system with bitter rival Labour, which has promised to keep the age at 65.

Audio player for " Assessing the fiscal plans with economist Shamubeel Eaqub " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1865995%2Fnational-adamant-its-superannuation-stance-has-not-changed

Assessing the fiscal plans with economist Shamubeel Eaqub Morning Report Download MP3 7m

National leader Christopher Luxon had promised in early May - ahead of the Budget - that "we will go to the election with another election policy around superannuation and lifting the retirement age for sure".

And when unveiling the Budget, Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis lambasted other parties on the matter, saying those "who say they won't do anything about it are prepared to rob everyone in this country under the age of 50 for their own political expediency".

"This is not a tomorrow problem, it's for today," she said at the time, "people often talk about the rising super bill as if it's something in the future. It's happening right now".

Both indicated on Monday they would have liked to make change but were clear their promised election policy was merely to hold those cross-party discussions, which Willis committed to hold within 100 days of a new government.

"It requires a political consensus, and we don't have that currently," Luxon said.

Willis said she stood by "every single one of my previous comments".

Labour's Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said it was a conversation that needed to happen - but National had balked at specifying a year to begin raising the age and seek a mandate for it at the election.

She said Labour would not increase the age from 65, "because it all comes down to affordable choices", and indicated the accord would focus on "the retirement system as a whole".

Labour Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds says a lower retirement age should be considered for Māori and Pasifika people. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"The one area where the government is not looking is around revenue to support the increasing age of the increasing age of our population, but there are key areas where we can agree.

"In KiwiSaver employer contributions, we both agree to the 6 percent - other parties don't. So we want to try and where we can find agreement, we should."

Edmonds said many Māori and Pasifika people died under age 65, and a lower age for those groups should be looked at.

Like National, she hesitated to commit to changes without strong public support.

"You need to have the strong mandate to do it. They wanted the mandate to do it, they could have put it in their policy ... that conversation still continues, even if they're in government, [or] we're in government."

Coalition partners

National's coalition partners this term had opposing views, with New Zealand First's Winston Peters saying the two parties had been lying about the need to fund super for four decades, and nothing had changed.

Peters said it was a lie that superannuation was unaffordable.

"We can afford it, but we can't afford it with them because they can't run a sound economy. We in New Zealand First can."

Asked about the calls for cross-party agreement, he said National and Labour had "more agreements together than anybody else lately ... loneliness can have that effect on some people!"

He said National's fiscal plan did not stack up.

"Have they got $32 billion going off to India in the next $15 years? Have they got up to $22b going off to Paris in the next wee while? If that's not there they have no fiscal plan, do they?

"They don't have a fiscal plan, nor does ACT, it's pretence now."

ACT's proposal was to lift the age every year, by three months, until it reached 67 in 2035. Party leader David Seymour questioned National's commitment to raising the age, saying that party always planned to raise the age "in the future".

"That is why the government balancing the books is also just somewhere off in the future."

He said New Zealand needed to be "honest with each other about our financial situation".

Asked if National had missed an opportunity to take a position on when to raise the age to the election and have the public vote on it, Seymour said New Zealand had missed an opportunity.

"The country needs leadership to balance the books and get on top of the debt, rather than sending the bill to future taxpayers too young to vote in this election.

"But the reason we need an ACT party is to take these hard positions when nobody else will."

Greens, Opportunity

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the fiscal plan was "business as usual for the National Party, and business as usual is cooked".

"It's the reason that we're in the mess that we are at the moment, with the highest unemployment in 11 years, 47,000 more children living in poverty today ... [National] have managed to downgrade every fiscal metric that they inherited."

She aligned with Peters' view, saying that although the working age population was declining compared to retirees, "we have, as the retirement commissioner has pointed out, one of the most affordable retirement regimes in the world, and the fact that we have universal superannuation means that we have amongst the lowest rates of elderly poverty in the OECD.

"We can afford to ensure that everybody retires with dignity, and that means that we have to fix the tax system."

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says New Zealand can afford to ensure that everyone retires with dignity. RNZ / Nick Monro

National's rhetoric at the Budget compared to its actions on the campaign trail "tells you everything that we already know about the National Party, which is where they will pander for votes, and where - when their polling is down - they'll punch down and get back into beneficiary bashing".

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said National's plan was lacking vision and "in our view, that is a low-emissions future, and we have not seen a credible climate plan from National".

She was pleased to see the commitment to a cross-party accord, but disappointed to see a lack of commitment on superannuation.

"This has happened so many times in elections where politicians talk about the need for change, but they're not willing to put those solutions out there on the table.

"If we weren't to implement our own tax policy, I think getting, particularly getting Labour and National to sit around the table together and figure out a way forward [is a good step] ... but I think New Zealanders don't trust that they will follow through, and I guess we've seen that today with the fiscal plan from the Nats."

"It is always politically difficult, but I think New Zealanders are ready for an honest conversation about superannuation."

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong says National's plan is lacking in vision. BLESSEN TOM / RNZ

Economist

Economist Michael Reddell told RNZ he would prefer to raise the age of Super to 70 "pretty quickly", saying a government could start straight away and do it over 10 years.

Reddell said the reality was the 65 age was set in 1898, when "most people didn't live to 65".

He said there was already 42 percent of people aged 65 to 69 working, and 30 percent of the population over 65 was between 65 and 69.

"So, if we make a significant dent in that pretty quickly, we bring the superannuation costs down a long way."

He suggested ACT's policy of raising the superannuation age by three months every year, reaching 67 by 2035, was a "bit tame".

"Sixty-seven is a start, but it's not really very much.

"Life expectancy had been increasing two years a decade for the last four or five decades."

He pointed to Denmark which was going to reach 69 by 2030, "we should be pushing further".

"It just doesn't make sense to be paying a universal pension at 65."

He said "we should see the ageing population as a good thing" and as people are "healthier at 65 than they ever were in the past, it's reasonable to expect that they should be working," though he acknowledged there would always be some people who were physically unable to.

He added it was good for people to have workplace community connections at that age.

World.title: More to child poverty than school uniform costs, advocates say
World.content:
Audio player for " School uniforms putting strain on families " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1865475%2Fmore-to-child-poverty-than-school-uniform-costs-advocates-say

School uniforms putting strain on families Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The founder of children's charity KidsCan says there needs to be a focus on reducing child poverty overall.

It comes as the Labour Party says it will cut back-to-school costs for families by making school uniforms cheaper and allowing for "affordable, generic" alternatives to be used as well.

The ACT Party earlier this year also said it would campaign on cutting uniform costs, calling them "absolutely ridiculous".

KidsCan founder and chief executive Dame Julie Chapman said it could be challenging for families who had limited choice.

"We know that it is challenging for families to afford school uniforms," she said.

"The more choice they have certainly can help to limit those costs as well."

Chapman said 169,000 children were living in material hardship.

"This is one mechanism for that, but I think we've also got to put the focus back on reducing child poverty overall, because that is still a massive issue for New Zealand."

Secondary Principals Council chair Steve McCracken. Supplied / Whangaparāoa College

Chair of the Secondary Principals Council Steve McCracken said he was surprised by the announcement.

"School uniforms in one sense offer a sense of pride and a sense of belonging for the connection to the school and the area that they're in, but there is that cost factor that is attributed to the need for that," he said.

McCraken said many schools already helped families pay off uniforms.

Expanding the school donations scheme or increasing funding for operations could be alternatives to support families, he said.

"[It] doesn't take away the impact on families particularly at the start of the year, but there could be ways of supplying things like refill and teaching resources that would offset some of the further costs for young people and their families as they start school."

McCracken said he could see the Labour Party's perspective.

But it wasn't just uniforms, Chapman said one of biggest challenges in the schools KidsCan supported was the need for food.

"That has increased year on year, and the last two terms have seen our biggest food distribution, the biggest amount of need we have seen since we've been going, and that's 22 years," she said.

World.title: Local leaders and election candidates clash over Queenstown fast-track housing
World.content:
Audio player for " Queenstown-Lakes residents oppose fast-track proposals " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1866014%2Flocal-leaders-and-election-candidates-clash-over-queenstown-fast-track-housing

"This is being done to us," Queenstown's mayor told a packed Arrowtown hall on Monday as local leaders and election candidates clashed over out-of-zone fast-track housing in the Whakatipu Basin.

The fiery public meeting on Monday night laid bare political differences over who should get the final word on the future of the district - local councils or fast-track panels.

A crowd of more than 400 locals heard that about 11,000 homes could be fast-tracked in Queenstown and Wānaka, including many beyond the district's agreed growth boundary.

Queenstown Lakes District mayor John Glover refuted claims from central government that his council was not delivering enough housing of its own.

"We are one percent of the country's population, and we just built five percent of the entire housing stock in the country last year," he said.

Out-of-zone developments risked putting local roads and services under severe strain without solving affordability, he said.

"For something that is such an emotive issue for our community, I would like to have seen more response from government than just say, 'look, you're just not doing enough'."

Queenstown Lakes District mayor John Glover. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The meeting was organised by Queenstown Smart Growth Initiative, which formed in opposition to the proposed Ridgeburn community near Arrowtown.

The group feared the project could congest roads and harm local tourism.

Group spokesperson Hanna Pettit said council planning had already made space for 23,600 extra homes in Queenstown - independently of any fast-tracked projects.

She said fast-track legislation appeared to be taking decision-making out of the community's hands, and it was communities that would foot the bill if something went wrong.

"Ridgeburn's 1250 homes and there's a number of others around the 1000-home mark that we're talking about. So when we're talking about a small community [like Arrowtown] that will have a significant impact on how the community functions," she said.

Queenstown Smart Growth Initiative spokesperson Hanna Pettit. RNZ / Katie Todd

Incumbent Southland MP Joseph Mooney defended the legislation, citing Ridgeburn's earlier withdrawn application as proof that fast-tracked developments had to meet strict criteria.

"I think that's indicative that the process actually working as it should. The developer will have to provide evidence that the development, if it were to go ahead, for example will satisfy that the impact on traffic is very appropriately raised. Because everyone in this room knows how congested our region is," he said.

"The fast-track panel will have to determine whether the regional or national benefits of the application outweigh the adverse effects."

Labour candidate Peter McDonald challenged Mooney to stand with his community.

Labour candidate Peter McDonald. Supplied / Labour Party

"With respect to Joseph the current incumbent … since I've been up in Queenstown and been part of these discussions, hearing Joseph doubling down, doubling down and basically telling everybody here that they're wrong and Joseph and Chris Bishop are right … that's been really hard," he said.

"Joseph, you still have an opportunity to cross the road and stand with your community on this. You didn't take it tonight, but there's still an opportunity to do that."

New Zealand First candidate Jason Herrick said he personally believed all new housing developments in the Queenstown area should be put on hold until infrastructure caught up.

"I've been coming to Queenstown for many, many years … it's horrible to come to Queenstown now, you end up spending a lot of time in traffic," he said.

"What we need to focus on is the big ideas. It's going to take big and bold to get Queenstown out of the rut it is in."

The Opportunity Party candidate Bianca Beebe said Queenstown was being treated as an economic cash cow while local infrastructure suffered.

She said she was among more than 3000 people who had signed a national petition challenging the use of fast-track legislation for major housing developments beyond district plan boundaries.

World.title: Wallabies admit they 'faced the music' after harrowing All Blacks loss
World.content:
It was brutal, but the Wallabies knew they had to confront the reality of Saturday night's defeat to the All Blacks sooner rather than later.

"The group came together Sunday morning, faced the music a little bit," Wallabies fullback Tom Wright said in Sydney on Monday.

By "music", Wright was referring to the 50-19 scoreline dished out by the All Blacks at Eden Park, which meant their hold of the Bledisloe Cup will stretch into a 24th consecutive year.

Having made a promising start to narrowly trail 17-14 at half-time, the Wallabies were blown away in the second term.

Wallabies thrashed by All Blacks The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

The All Blacks shifted gears after the break, scoring five tries to one as they added another chapter to the Wallabies' dismal history at Eden Park.

The Wallabies have not defeated the All Blacks at their spiritual home since 1986.

The result also brought the Wallabies' six-match unbeaten run to an end, after their recent form created hope they could snap their Auckland losing streak.

"No-one wants to be on the receiving end of 50 points and no-one wants to be on the receiving end of a loss," Wright said.

"But at 17-14, we were right in the contest.

"The game was there to be taken. We squandered a couple of chances."

The All Blacks have held the Bledisloe Cup since 2003. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Among those opportunities was a line-out throw deep inside All Blacks territory early in the second half.

The All Blacks chose not to contest the line-out as they prepared to counter a driving maul.

Instead, the Wallabies wasted an ideal attacking platform and the chance to claim the lead by giving away a penalty at the set-piece, allowing the All Blacks to exit their 22.

The home side proceeded to move play down field, resulting in Cam Roigard's 48th-minute try.

"It's a game of moments," Wright said.

"We earned opportunities to get close to their line really early in the second half.

"We weren't disciplined enough to execute a play and that was right down on their try line.

"We were pleased with how we started the second half and then there was a snowball effect of moments."

Wright noted the All Blacks "physically imposed themselves" during the match while also dominating one of the key battlegrounds: contestable kicks.

The All Blacks retained possession from eight of their 11 contestable kicks, with Roigard particularly effective from scrum half.

All six of the contestable kicks he launched were retrieved.

The All Blacks dominated the aerial battle against the Wallabies. (Getty images: Fiona Goodall)

The Wallabies could not compete with the All Blacks in this part of the game, despite having aerial threats such as wingers Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen.

They enjoyed the upper hand in contestable kicks when they defeated the world champion Springboks 42-38 in Perth late last month.

"We saw that the ABs were able to apply pressure the same way we've done previously," Wright said.

Back on Australian soil, the Wallabies have shifted their attention to Saturday's return Test against the All Blacks at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

The Bledisloe Cup may not be at stake, but the Wallabies' pride is on the line as they look to end a 12-Test losing run against their trans-Tasman rivals.

With the post-match review of the Eden Park defeat done and dusted, Wright maintained the Wallabies were moving forward.

"I certainly don't think there's any mental scars," Wright said.

World.title: Renshaw's dream Test continues with first wicket to put Aussies on top
World.content:
Matt Renshaw's dream Test has continued at Kingsmead, with the Queenslander picking up his maiden Test wicket after peeling off 82 earlier on day four.

Renshaw had South Africa captain Temba Bavuma (1) caught at short leg as shadows lengthened in Durban, before Pat Cummins nicked off Tristan Stubbs (1) to reduce the hosts to 4-102 at stumps.

South Africa will require another 319 runs for an unlikely triumph, with Cummins having earlier set the hosts a target of 421 by declaring at 6-314 on the stroke of tea.

However, Australia may be forced to push for victory without the fielding brilliance of vice-captain Steve Smith, who did not take to the field with his teammates after being struck on the helmet by an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting.

Steve Smith copped a blow on the helmet early in his innings. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Smith continued his dig before eventually being dismissed for 27, before Renshaw once again led the Australians with the bat, making his way to 82 before falling to a remarkable, improvised return catch from Keshav Maharaj.

The score added to the Queenslander's first-innings knock of 190, as he remained the only batter to pass 50 in the Test.

With Australia chasing quick runs late in its innings, Cummins was responsible for an explosive 12-ball 32 cameo that featured four sixes, while Beau Webster finished unbeaten on 39.

Josh Hazlewood made the first two of Australia's breakthroughs, nicking off Ryan Rickleton (2) in the fourth over of the innings and trapping David Bedingham LBW for 46 before Renshaw and Cummins did the late damage to set up an exciting final day's play.

Relive all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: Butters suggests changes to AFL player movement 'wouldn't be a bad thing'
World.content:
Zak Butters says he contemplated going public with his planned move home to Victoria while playing out his final season at Port Adelaide.

The Western Bulldogs unveiled their star recruit at Whitten Oval today following his blockbuster move as a free agent on a nine-year deal worth $2 million a season.

With a year left on his contract at the Power, Butters knew he was leaving Alberton following open conversations with the club at the end of last season.

He discussed going public with his plans with manager Peter Lenton.

"I definitely contemplated and thought about that," the midfielder said.

"But I think the AFL landscape isn't probably quite ready for it."

NRL players can sign deals with rival clubs once they enter the final year of their contract or earlier if given permission.

Butters unveiled by Bulldogs after 'megadeal' Zak Butters is finally unveiled as a Western Bulldogs player as Port Adelaide receives four first-round picks in a five-team mega trade ticked off by the league.

Deals are often announced during the season.

The AFL system is more restrictive, with listed players coming off contract only able to officially move in the off-season through trade, free agency, drafts and the supplemental selection period.

"The way I play football and the way I train, I feel like I'd be able to show up and front up and do it," Butters said.

"But definitely, I feel like in the future, I couldn't see why it wouldn't be a bad thing."

Butters, a three-time All Australian, was strongly courted by the Bulldogs, Geelong, Collingwood and Richmond throughout the year.

Geelong was viewed as the frontrunner for his signature, but Butters denied he or his management ever indicated to the Cats they were his first preference.

The ball magnet insisted he never completely made up his mind until returning home to his family property at Darley, west of Melbourne, after the Power's season had ended.

"I guess I probably took my time to do that," Butters said.

"It's a pretty long contract and it's probably the rest of my career so I wanted to make sure I get it right.

"I probably leaned towards different clubs at different stages but, ultimately, I got to where I wanted to get to."

Zak Butters (right) pictured with Bulldogs supporter Hunter Zerafa. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

The Bulldogs pulled heavily on Butters's heartstrings in their pitch, drawing on his boyhood fandom for the club.

A handwritten letter from 11-year-old Hunter Zerafa, accompanied by a 20-cent coin taped inside, begging Butters to pick the Bulldogs revived childhood memories.

"I thought back to when I was younger and loving Bulldogs players and looking up to them and coming down to open trainings," Butters said.

"I used to have birthday parties at Whitten Oval when I was a kid.

"I've still got the letter at home, and the 20 cents is still in there. I might have to invest it."

AAP

World.title: Izzi Batt-Doyle smashes Australian marathon record with run in Chicago
World.content:
Adelaide's Izzi Batt-Doyle is Australia's new marathon queen after breaking the national record with a stunning run at the year's penultimate major, the Chicago Marathon.

Batt-Doyle ran a time of 2:20:38 to take 46 seconds off the mark set by fellow South Australian Jess Stenson in Valencia in December.

It also lowered the 31-year-old's own personal best by two minutes and 21 seconds.

"I'm very, very happy. I feel a sense of relief, because it's something I really felt I could achieve and it's been on my mind the past couple of years," Batt-Doyle said.

"I'm really proud I could achieve it today and I'm so happy."

Assefa's Achilles rupture Tigst Assefa ran the final two kilometres of the Berlin Marathon with a badly damaged Achilles tendon, which required immediate surgery to repair. She still ran the third-fastest women's marathon in history.

Batt-Doyle was sixth overall in the women's race, which was won by defending champion Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia in 2:13:33.

"The field here is so great, but smaller on the professional side," Batt-Doyle said.

"You don't have masses of people in groups."

Batt-Doyle was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks.

"[We were] isolated the whole race," she said.
