Tech.title: Elon Musk Bragged About His Grok Lego Star Wars Haul. Then X Users Punked Him
Tech.content:
There's been a disturbance in the force. Only it's more like a farce.

It seems that Elon Musk, while crowing on X about how useful his Grok Bot AI agent was in ordering some Lego Star Wars kits on Sunday, managed to reveal via a screenshot to his more than 240 million followers not only the 10-digit Lego order number of his purchase, but also what he paid for the sets, the delivery and billing addresses, the last four digits of his credit card, and the email address his bot used to buy the bricks from Lego.

Faster than the Millennium Falcon making the jump to light speed, the inevitable happened. An X account holder named Enderman posted screenshots of interactions with Lego's customer service chatbot on its website, where the user seemingly managed—using the email and order number Musk kindly, but recklessly, provided—to get the system to cancel Musk's order.

It’s a Trap!

Within a couple of hours—possibly to see whether Enderman's scheme was actually successful—Musk replied and said his order had not been canceled after all.

But by this point, the folly of posting the purchase details on his account must have been evident. For example, another X user went back to Lego's AI assistant, called “Sophia,” and supposedly used the same details to reopen the delivery, this time increasing the order count to 400 and changing the delivery address, all while using Musk's original payment method. “Perfect! I'll get your Lego adventure back on track,” Sophia replied according to screenshots posted on X.

Upping the ante to 400 sets could be seen as conservative, as a glance at WIRED's Spend Elon Musk’s Money tracker reveals that if you wanted to blow $1 trillion of Musk's cash on plastic bricks, it might have been possible to buy one billion $1,000 Death Star sets, each with 9,023 pieces.

Lego declined to comment when WIRED contacted the company to confirm if such activity took place on Musk's personal Star Wars order. However, internal safeguards for Lego's AI assistant could have flagged unusual activity on the purchase, and so hopefully fleshy humans were tasked with checking the changes.

Attack of the Clones

On Saturday, Musk suggested that Grok could make purchases online with a simple prompt. In this post, Musk suggested that all brave users needed to do to let Grok buy stuff for them was upload a picture of their credit card so the bot could search the web for deals and then complete the purchase. AI companies like Meta and OpenAI have also highlighted the utility of using their respective agents for shopping tasks.

However, at the end of last year, Visa warned about fraud in agentic commerce, advising that bad actors were building legitimate-looking sites that could fool AI agents into purchasing fake items simply by offering gear at super-low prices.

“Once the AI agent completes the purchase … the malicious merchant can harvest payment data and instantly use it for unauthorized transactions,” according to Visa's blog. Visa added that it observed a 25 percent increase “in malicious bot-initiated transactions” in the latter half of 2025, but in the US, this figure jumped to 40 percent.

Tech.title: Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
Tech.content:
When Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development.

Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today.

The Muse Wonder models will be available though an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent.

Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky, with some researchers not sticking around for long.

Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups.

Tech.title: They War-Gamed Dimming the Sun. It Went Even Worse Than You Think
Tech.content:
When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.

“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”

The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.

The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.

Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”

The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It's not 15 years from now; it's in the next decade, easily.”

Tech.title: ‘The Sixty-Year Mission’ Brings the Legacy of ‘Star Trek’ to a New Generation
Tech.content:
William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.

When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”

Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.

“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.

As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.

Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”

Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”

Tech.title: Google Fitbit Edge: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Tech.content:
Google’s screenless Fitbit Air made a splash, but it’s been three years since the company updated its display-equipped Charge 6. That older tracker is showing its age, lacking newer automatic workout detection, deeper health metrics, and an IP68 rating. That's where the new Fitbit Edge comes in.

Announced on Monday, it is the successor fitness tracker fans with a screen preference have been waiting for. It sits in a sweet spot at $180—not as costly as a Google Pixel Watch but offering a similar experience in a slimmer, pill-shaped design. And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app. Preorders are available now, and it goes on sale on October 27.

The Fixable Fitbit

The Fitbit Edge in Obsidian with Active Band (left), Magnet Band (middle), and Performance Loop Band (right). Courtesy of Google

The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google’s efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability.

If you find the Pixel Watch’s round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6’s 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. The difference is noticeable, and that extra real estate could make a real impact when glancing at your metrics mid-workout.

The Edge borrows a few more attributes from the Pixel Watch, including an altimeter that uses atmospheric pressure to measure elevation changes. That means it can record elevation gain and loss during outdoor activities, track floors climbed, and add more context to your outdoor stats. It also has a far-field skin temperature sensor, replacing the standard device temperature sensor found in other Fitbits. By bringing some of the Pixel Watch’s more advanced hardware to a fitness-first wearable, Google is giving the Edge a compelling middle-ground position in its lineup at a Fitbit-friendly price.

Tech.title: How Apple Puts Indigenous Languages on the iPhone Keyboard
Tech.content:
Chuck Hoskin Jr. fondly recalls watching a room full of Cherokee immersion students crowd around a screen to watch How to Train Your Dragon. Except Hiccup and Astrid weren't speaking English—the protagonists were speaking Cherokee, dubbed by voices from the local community.

“They're hearing it in our mother tongue—that didn't happen a generation ago,” Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, tells WIRED. “We're a long way, thankfully, from rote classroom instruction and memorization to a world where kids can see the sort of creativity that sparks imagination and helps every kid become more articulate and literate.”

The Cherokee Nation has around 1,500 active speakers left, and most are over 70. Hoskin Jr. says the community is rapidly losing that generation, which is why it has spent time training up second-language learners. It even has a baby immersion program, hoping their first words are Cherokee.

“The foes we’ve had historically are the so-called Age of Discovery, colonization, the displacement of our people economically and geographically, boarding schools,” he says. “But it's nothing compared to the mathematics we’re up against now. Which is why we’re filled with this urgency every day to do all we can to find partners that can help us accelerate what we want to do.”

One of those accelerants is Apple. The Cherokee Nation has long collaborated with the iPhone maker, and Cherokee was the first Native American language included in iOS in 2010. Today, Apple says its iOS keyboard supports more than 200 languages and language variants, with a handful added last year in iOS 26, like Haitian Creole and Nez Perce. In iOS 27, it expanded support for Indigenous languages to include other Native American languages like Blackfoot, Comanche, and Northern East Cree.

Tech.title: Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
Tech.content:
US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.

The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.

Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”

Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.

The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.

Tech.title: AlterMe Review: Fitness Built Around My DNA
Tech.content:
On the days I had poor sleep the night before, the app recommended a lighter workout or recovery session—the 15-minute breathwork session has become a particular favorite. On the days I’d slept well, I was tasked with a more strenuous session depending on my current level, from beginner to level 6.

While the workouts are easy to access and follow, I found them short—20 minutes was the average workout time, with 40 minutes being the longest session I tried. But it is possible to stack the workouts if you want to push yourself further. There’s also a way to track activities such as a run or group workout outside the guided library of workouts.

I trust that the app was recommending workouts to suit my health stats and genetic traits, and I mostly felt good when following them. But there were some days when I was feeling terrible due to poor sleep, and the app was telling me that my readiness score was high, which left me feeling a little confused. But I dutifully obliged with the suggested workout—even if I did opt for a shorter 20-minute session. On the days I had forgotten to wear my ring to bed the night before, the app would ask me to self-score from 1 to 10 on how I was feeling before a workout was suggested.

AI Nutrition Coach and Body Scanning

Exercise is just one piece of the fitness puzzle, and one of the pros of the AlterMe app is that it has a nutrition tracker. Rather than having it provide a single diet plan, I like the way the app can generate meal and snack ideas by referencing my DNA to keep me hitting my macro targets. You can generate a recipe and then log it if you decide to make it. Simply by clicking “generate recipe” I could get breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack ideas in under 20 seconds. The recipes are pretty enticing too—Zesty Lemon Herb Grilled Chicken Qith Roasted Green Beans and Quinoa was one I tried. But I found the snack ideas most helpful, as I’m always thinking about snacks—Roasted Edamame With Smoked Paprika and Sea Salt is a particular favorite.

In the Nutrition tab of the app, I could access personalized calorie and nutrition guidance based on my DNA results, weight, BMI, activity level, and weight-loss goals. My DNA report suggested I have an average response to protein and a low response to carbs and fats. I like how easy it is to log food in the Nutrition tab in the app and instantly see whether I’d hit my protein, fat, and carb macro goals. I often forgot to track everything I ate, but on the days I remembered to do so, I found it easy to track my calorie intake and meals.

Tech.title: GTA 6 Blamed for PlayStation Pro 5 Shortages
Tech.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the most-anticipated game of 2026, and it’s already being blamed for gaming console shortages, especially the PlayStation 5 Pro. The high-end Sony console is currently out of stock on Sony.com and is selling on auction sites for $1,100 and over.

Part of the reason for high console demand is that GTA 6 will be exclusive to PlayStation 5/Pro and Xbox Series X/S when it comes out on Nov. 19, and no other platforms have been announced yet.

In September, Sony reportedly advised distributors that the PlayStation 5 Pro would be in short supply until 2027, citing “temporary market supply constraints and high demand.” The most severe bottleneck limiting PlayStation distribution is a global crisis in memory and storage components driven by the AI infrastructure squeeze, or RAMageddon.

More from CNET

The PS 5 Pro promises better frame rates for a number of games as well as enhanced 4K processing, while the Rockstar Studios game is also designed to work on the “vanilla” PS5.

Yet, GTA 6 isn’t the only recent high-profile PlayStation release: The PS5-exclusive Wolverine — by the makers of Spider-Man and Spider-Man 2 — has reportedly sold 2.16 million copies since September.

The PlayStation 5 Pro debuted in November 2024 for $700, but its retail price has since increased to $900.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the long-awaited sequel to Grand Theft Auto 5, which first appeared in 2013. The crime-based game reportedly offers a playable area twice the size of the previous game’s. It’s available for preorder for $80.

Representatives for Sony did not respond immediately to CNET’s request for more information.

Tech.title: Apple Home Event Rumor Roundup: Everything We Expect to See Tomorrow
Tech.content:
Coming only a few short weeks after Apple’s big fall event where the company announced its first foldable iPhone Duo, Apple is holding another event tomorrow called “Welcome Home.” Instead of focusing on iPhones and Macs, this event will be announcing Apple’s home tech, including what we expect to be all-new devices and new ways to use Siri AI.

CNET will be at the event to give you live updates and get hands-on with Apple’s plans for your home, but for now here’s what the rumors tell us. If reports are right, Apple may be releasing a new kind of smart display, an update to the HomePod line, an Apple TV and more. Let’s take a look.

A Siri smart display, possibly the “HomeView”

An Apple smart display could allow Siri to get much more creative. Bloomberg/Getty Images

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be readying a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home. Now we have specific reports from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg that say Apple’s event will focus on the display, which is possibly called the HomeView and will ship sometime in November. This device is ruored to have an A18 chip and come in two designs, one for tables and one for wall mounting.

More from CNET

Smart displays can add a lot of functionality to smart speakers, if you don’t mind using voice assistants. Smart touchscreens are great for getting visual information, watching videos or viewing to-do lists, so a display like this is likely to have a bit of Apple TV and Safari in it, too. While the Apple TV 4K, iPad and current HomePod models can already act as HomeKit hubs, I expect Apple to offer a real UI and UX experience designed for smart displays, making it a stronger argument for having in your home alongside other devices.

However, a Siri smart display faces steep competition against established brands like Amazon’s Echo Shows and Google’s Nest Hubs, so Apple will need to carefully differentiate this “HomeView.”

Is it likely? I think it’s very likely, based on how many insider reports have mentioned this smart display, but I don’t think we have a good idea exactly how it will look and operate yet. Watch for more news on this tomorrow.

Updates to the HomePod line

Is a new HomePod Mini on the way? Chris Monroe/CNET

Along with a smart display, rumors are flying that Apple will give its HomePod smart speaker line the first major update in years. It’s the ideal time to update the HomePod line, too, although it’s possible some of these reports have confused plans for a smart display with a new smart speaker, both of which could fall under the HomePod label.

If a new HomePod speaker is on the horizon, reports indicate that it would be a new type of HomePod Mini. That’s not surprising — the original HomePod has often been critiqued for being over $300, which is why Apple focused on the less expensive Mini model afterward. One welcome leak I’ve seen is that there will be new colors for the HomePod Mini 2, including green and pink, and a faster S-series chip.

Is it likely? Yes, I’d say this is about as likely as a Siri smart display, if Apple wants to continue developing the HomePod line. Hopefully we’ll be able to hear how it sounds in person if Apple is ready to unleash a new smart speaker.

A new Apple TV

Apple TV is due for an upgrade, too. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The same reports that say a smart display and new HomePod are on the way also mention Apple is planning to release a new Apple TV model. This model is rumored to have upgraded specs, with a faster N1 processor, 8GB RAM, Wi-Fi 7 and an upgraded Siri remote, possibly with more AI features.

It’s a product line that’s sort of connected to the smart home, especially if Apple is launching a smart display. The company hasn’t released a new set-top box since 2022, so it’s about time for another. This could also give the Apple TV new hardware for extra Siri AI tricks. There’s also been some speculation that this will be compatible with the new HomePods, allowing you to set up multiple units in a surround sound-style home cinema.

Is it likely? I think it’s strange that Apple would combine smart home products with a TV announcement, as they’re not especially related. But the reports we have about a new Apple TV are very specific, so it looks like there’s a strong chance Apple will update the line, although we don’t know if we’ll be able to get hands-on with new models.

Little Apple security cams — with no recording

Recent rumors says Apple is ready to enter the home security world with its own products. Although we don’t know much, reports from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman say these will be tiny cameras that, interestingly, won’t record any video. No recording means Apple won’t have to worry about cloud storage and may be able to avoid charging extra subscriptions for them.

The cameras are rumored to have some kind of presence-sensing or human-recognizing technology as well as AI video descriptions, suggesting Apple Home will be running analysis on the video even if it won’t record permanently. The phrase “facial recognition” was also mentioned, but this doesn’t seem nearly as likely to me. This may be related to a rumor about Apple’s Ring-like doorbell camera, which may come with Face ID for unlocking a door, but this would likely be separate from the non-recording indoor security cameras.

Is it likely? I’m betting on some kind of home security announcement, and I expect Apple would like to have its own camera line, but I don’t know if this exact product will be released. However, the extra details do lend this rumor legitimacy.

An LG collab for a new thermostat

Apple may be partnering with LG for some smart home devices, and there are even reportedly leaked product concept photos circulating on the internet. One of the biggest potential releases is an Apple-friendly thermostat. The photos show a round, Nest-like thermostat dial, and rumors say it will include far-sight presence sensing, a humidity sensor and several temperature calibration options.

2. LG Smart Thermostat



• Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.

• Calibrated Temperature/Temperature Offset options. pic.twitter.com/Q8AAaxy4ey — pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026

Alongside the thermostat, the Apple/LG combo is expected to release a sensor that can measure the temperature at specific locations and feed that information back to the thermostat hub. That would be no surprise, because models from Nest, Ecobee and others have similar satellite sensors, although Apple’s may have adhesive strips to attach its version to the wall.

Apple partnered with LG years ago to support Apple-friendly security cameras, but those lines were rarely updated and quickly became obsolete. Maybe Apple is ready to try again with a different approach.

Is it likely? If Apple really is partnering with LG for a new wave of home devices, I think a thermostat is likely. But this is starting to be a lot of products to announce at a single October event that won’t be publicly streamed.

Further LG collabs for smart lock and maybe more

The other big rumor centering around an LG collaboration is an Apple smart lock. While many smart locks work with Apple and Apple Home Keys, the tech giant hasn’t been involved in the development of a smart lock before.

It could have automatic unlocking, tapping your phone to unlock and a variety of keypad management options. That’s not surprising, but the rumored product images show a round, twist-to-unlock, light-up outdoor keypad, and I haven’t seen anything like that before.

If Apple does release a smart lock, Ring will have beaten it to the punch with its own announcement of its first-ever lock, which will include Alexa compatibility and a unique thumbturn that can generate a charge when the battery dies.

EXCLUSIVE 👀



First look at LG’s upcoming smart home lineup:



LG Video Doorbell Wired

LG Floodlight Cam

LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In

LG Indoor Cam Plug-In pic.twitter.com/vblGECQLM1 — そすのふか (@ringo_tech) October 7, 2026

Other rumors and purported product images suggest the LG partnership could also yield a video doorbell, floodlight camera, outdoor camera and indoor camera. These seem to be LG-branded devices, however, and I can’t imagine Apple releasing products that look like this.

Is it likely? Now this is a lot of new gadgets to announce at once. I think a smart lock is about as likely as a smart thermostat; those are both strong fields for Apple to enter. For the rest of the cameras, I’m doubtful. The indoor camera could be connected to the rumors of Apple’s no-video model. If the LG partnership line is this large, I wouldn’t be surprised if Apple is saving it for a separate announcement later on.

What role will Apple Intelligence play in all this?

Apple Intelligence will fuel many Siri AI capabilities in the Apple Home app. That’s especially true of AI video descriptions, which Apple is bringing to supported security cameras (there are very few right now, but some of Aqara’s camera hubs are compatible). I’m testing these uses of Apple Intelligence now, but if Apple releases any of its own security cameras, you can bet they’ll use AI features in the same way.

Will there be any iPad news at this event?

There are rumors that Apple will announce an iPad Mini sometime this month, but it probably doesn’t have much to do with this event. This is a strictly smart home-focused release.

Tech.title: Our Moon Is Becoming ‘Earth’s Junk Drawer,’ Former NASA Attorney Warns
Tech.content:
If you have a spare $12,995 laying around, you can use it to send your pet’s ashes to live forever on the moon.

Celestis calls itself “the most compelling pet memorial service on or off the planet,” allowing customers to send a “symbolic portion” of their pet’s ashes to live forever on the lunar surface. (Prices are the same for human remains, Celestis says.) It’s part of a growing wave of companies looking to capitalize on the regulatory gray area that the moon inhabits.

A Japanese beverage company sent up a payload that looked like one of its Pocari Sweat energy drinks in 2014. Artist Jeff Koons sent up 125 mini-sculptures in 2024; each one corresponded to an NFT that collectors could purchase back on Earth. One man has even raised $227,000 to put a giant cross on the moon. All told, humans have left nearly 500,000 pounds of stuff on the moon’s surface to date, most of which consists of government-sent lunar landers, surveyors and other dead spacecraft.

More from CNET

This explosion of commercial lunar activity is technically legal, says Steve Mirmina, a professor of space law at Georgetown University and former NASA attorney.

“I searched and searched the law, and unfortunately, there’s no law against launching race cars,” he said, referring to Elon Musk’s launching of a Tesla Roadster in 2018. “We don’t have a government agency with the legal authority to regulate what happens on the moon.”

Existing US law doesn’t sufficiently regulate what we actually send to the lunar surface, Mirmina argues in Lawful but Awful: U.S. Regulation of Commercial Activities on the Lunar Surface, published Sept. 19 in Air and Space Law. Without a more sustainable legal framework, we risk turning the moon into “Earth’s junk drawer.”

Who regulates the moon?

To date, 118 countries are parties to the Outer Space Treaty, which was originally enacted in 1967 during the height of the Cold War. It stipulates that space is free for use by all countries, and that they have a duty to avoid harmful contamination in space.

The 2020 Artemis Accords further enshrined norms of space sustainability into international law. While not legally binding, it constitutes “soft law” norms that shape best practices in space.

Countries are left to enforce compliance on the private space companies within their borders. In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration governs rocket launches, and NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services program partners with American companies to deliver payloads to the moon. But Congress hasn’t given any one agency the authority to regulate what private companies are actually putting on those payloads.

“It’s not very useful that they can regulate launch if they can’t regulate what happens after the rocket’s in space,” said Mirmina. “Basically, NASA, the FAA, even the State Department – they’re all kind of pointing at each other, hoping somebody did something. And then nobody had the legal authority to do anything.”

Real-world costs of unchecked commercialization

No one wants to gaze up at the night sky and see an energy drink . None of this activity has affected our view of the moon so far, and most of it falls into the “annoying” category more than the “truly reprehensible.” But Mirmina worries that there’s no legal safeguard in place to halt some truly awful conduct.

What’s happening on the moon right now has already stirred outrage from a number of different groups. Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren wrote a letter to NASA in 2023 asking the agency to stop sending human remains to the moon.

“It is crucial to emphasize that the Moon holds a sacred position in many Indigenous cultures, including ours,” Nygren wrote. “The act of depositing human remains and other materials, which could be perceived as discards in any other location, on the moon is tantamount to desecration of this sacred space.”

There’s also the question of how to be good caretakers for future generations. Moon landings produce something called “plume–surface interactions,” in which exhaust from descending spacecraft kicks up rocks and dust at speeds faster than a bullet. When new payloads land with increasing frequency, yesterday’s pet ashes or energy drink s could become tomorrow’s projectiles. Unlike on Earth, the moon has a very thin atmosphere with little erosion, so every item placed on the surface stays “forever,” as Celestis promises customers.

“They become shrapnel for future lunar missions,” Mirmina says. “It’s just a lot easier to prevent it than it’s going to ever be to try to clean it up.”

Stewardship before it’s too late

Everything is hard in space, especially agreeing on the right way to behave in a domain that seems so distant and invulnerable. But it’s also one corner of the government with rare bipartisan approval: Roughly three-quarters of Americans have a favorable opinion of NASA, and seven in 10 say it is essential that the US continue to be a world leader in space, according to the Pew Research Center. Most also support NASA’s goal of sending astronauts back to the moon in 2028.

“Before we’ve really even explored the moon, we’re already tossing up junk to live on there forever,” Mirmina says. “If you care about space or stewardship or the environment, we should preserve it for future explorers and not ruin it before they get there.”

Tech.title: When Are the iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2 and iPhone 18E Coming Out?
Tech.content:
Now that the latest high-end iPhones, the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo have been announced, many people are waiting to see when they’ll be able to get their hands on the standard iPhone 18. Apple decided to split the launch of this iPhone family, and rumors point that the standard model may not arrive until next year, potentially alongside the iPhone 18E.

We’re still not sure if Apple will ever make a sequel to the iPhone Air, but if it does, there’s a good chance it’ll be in the spring lineup next year as well.

While we still won’t know anything until Apple announces the devices, here’s what the rumors say about the remaining iPhones from this generation.

More from CNET

When are the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro available to buy?

According to Apple’s website, you can “get ready” to preorder the Duo on Oct. 12, with the official preorder window opening on Oct. 16. If you want to be able to walk into a store and grab one for yourself, the iPhone Duo will be available on Oct. 23. Apple’s new foray into the foldable world has certainly got a lot of attention, and from our hands-on with the device, it seems to have been worth the wait.

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max were officially released on Sept. 18, though you might run into some backorder issues due to the popularity of the new phones. According to Apple’s online store, you can pick up models in-store or wait approximately three weeks to have it delivered (both of those depending on location and configuration).

iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2

As for the standard iPhone 18 and the iPhone Air 2, rumors have pointed to a delayed release, as they were nowhere in sight during the announcement event last month. The shift may be a strategic one to a biannual cadence for Apple, with fall and spring launch dates. This isn’t unlike how Samsung launches its flagship Galaxy lineup at the beginning of the year, with its foldable lineup debuting in the middle of the year.

“The base iPhone 18 model announcements are expected to be pushed into spring 2027. This staggered launch marks a notable change in Apple’s release cadence, with a strong emphasis on premiumization,” said David Naranjo, associate director of Counterpoint Research.

Whether this potential delayed release is related to manufacturing restrictions, RAM shortages or just prioritizing its best hardware first remains to be seen, but if the rumors are true, those looking for an entry-level iPhone may need to wait until next year.

This is also a smart move on Apple’s part, as those who might have been looking for a non-pro iPhone may just end up buying the higher-end models instead of waiting. The timing would all coincide with Apple’s E series launch.

Where’s the iPhone 18E?

The iPhone E series has typically been released the following spring after the more powerful models, so there don’t seem to be any surprises here. The budget-focused (for Apple) device will likely be a pared-down version of the regular iPhone called the iPhone 18E, providing essential features from the current generation without many of the bells and whistles.

The iPhone 17E, which launched at a $599 price, hits a sweet spot for functionality and affordability, even though it’s now priced at $699. However, it remains to be seen whether the iPhone 18E, too, will see the price jump that we’ve seen with this current generation of iPhones.

The 17E was announced in March 2025 and was available in stores the following week. If history repeats itself, we may see the iPhone 18E land in early to mid-March of 2027 — hopefully alongside the debut of the standard iPhone 18.

Tech.title: The Best Things to See in the October Night Sky Right Now
Tech.content:
The Orionid meteor shower peaks Oct. 21–22 and remains active through early November, producing up to 20 meteors per hour at its peak when viewed from a dark-sky location.

October has given skygazers plenty to work with. Saturn reached opposition on Oct. 4 and remains the planet of the month, shining at its brightest of the year and remaining visible throughout the night after rising around sunset.

The Draconids peaked October 8–9 under a nearly moonless sky. Now the Orionids are building toward their peak on Oct. 21–22, when they can produce up to 20 meteors per hour from a dark location. And all eight planets are visible somewhere in October’s sky for observers willing to be out at different times of night.

More from CNET

Here’s the breakdown of what’s still ahead and what you’ll need to see each one.

You can see all eight planets this month

Mercury is visible just before sunset for several days in October. Stellarium

Every planet in the solar system is easily seen at some point this month, with Mercury being the most difficult. That’s not unusual, thanks to its proximity to the sun. Here’s a quick rundown on the best times to view each planet in October.

Mercury: Mercury is in elongation (the farthest it can get from the sun) on Monday, making that day and the two or so days before and after the best possible time to view Mercury.

Venus: Venus will spend most of the month right next to the sun, making it virtually impossible to see. However, by the end of the month, it will begin to separate from the sun, making it visible just after sunset. The best view will be on Oct. 31, but the view will get better going into November.

Mars: Mars will be visible in the night sky every night in October. It rises from the eastern horizon right around 2 a.m. ET and stays there until the sun comes up.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are going to be pretty close together all month, so most of the same rules apply, except that Jupiter rises about two hours later than Mars on most nights in October.

Saturn: Saturn is living its best life in October. It’s visible almost right at sunset ET and stays visible in the night sky until sunrise.

Neptune: Neptune is also visible every day in October and follows a very similar path to Saturn. It rises in the east, streaks across the sky and sets in the west right around sunrise. They’re actually pretty close together in the night sky every night during the month, so if you can find Saturn, Neptune isn’t far off, but you’ll definitely need magnification to see it.

Uranus: Uranus is visible the entire month and follows a very similar path through the sky as Saturn and Neptune, but its trek happens later at night. It rises on the eastern horizon about two hours after Saturn and follows it across the sky, but never really catches up, ending up in the high western sky when sunrise comes.

Through Oct. 10: Draconids Meteor Shower (Ended)

The Draconids meteor shower is in the Draco constellation near Vega. Stellarium

The Draconids meteor shower is a minor meteor shower that occurs every year around the first week of October. It officially started on Oct. 6 and ran until Oct. 10, making it one of the shortest meteor showers of the season. It was fed by the 21P/Giacobini-Zinner comet, which is part of the Jupiter family of comets.

Draconids meteors appear to originate from the Draco constellation. It sits high in the western sky in the northern hemisphere this time of year, with a slight lean to the north. If you’re using a sky map app, all you need to do is find Vega, and you’re already in the right neighborhood to catch Draconids.

The peak is a little tame, at around 10 meteors per hour most years, but it has a history of surprising astronomers. In 1933 and 1946, Draconids spat out thousands of meteors an hour in what were two of the most intense meteor showers of the 20th century.

Oct. 10: The last good chance to see the Milky Way (Ended)

The Milky Way captured with the Tiny1 camera. TinyMOS

The very best time to view the Milky Way is at a new moon in the warm months of the year, from May to August. This is when the Milky Way iwas high in the sky all night, giving night owls great views and plenty of time to photograph it.

September and October are great for this because the Milky Way was at its highest point between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. local time, giving the early birds a chance to snap some sweet photographs of the Milky Way. After October, the Milky Way is too low on the horizon to allow really good pictures of it until the following May.

Oct. 21: Orionids meteor shower

The Orionids meteor shower will be low to the horizon in the east when its peak occurs.

Orionids is the better-known of the two October meteor showers. This one officially started on Friday and runs until Nov. 7. It’s possible to spot a meteor from Orionids any night during the month, but the shower reaches its peak on the evening of Oct. 21. Meteors for this shower come from the 1P/Halley comet, which also feeds the Eta Aquariids meteor shower that happens every year in May.

This is a slightly more active meteor shower than the Draconids, and you can expect about 10 to 20 meteors per hour. The moon is set to be about 76% full that night, so you can probably expect to see fewer meteors thanks to lunar light pollution. The Orion constellation, where the meteor shower will appear to originate, doesn’t pop up over the eastern horizon until after midnight, so make sure to pack some coffee if you’re staying up late for this one. If you can find the stars Betelgeuse, Capella and Rigel, then you should be able to find Orion easily. They’re in the same general area.

The Orionids meteor shower is best known for its bright, fast-moving meteors, which leave long trails that can last for over a minute and sometimes result in fireballs. Their brightness will be a boon, with the three-quarters-full moon in the sky hindering viewing.

Oct. 26: The Hunter’s moon

A full moon rises behind the Washington Monument. NASA/Bill Ingalls

October’s full moon falls close to Halloween this year, perfect for spooky views. According to The Old Farmer’s Almanac, October’s full moon reaches its peak on Oct. 26 at 12:12 a.m. ET. It’ll also be over 90% full for a couple of days before and after, giving you a solid five days to check it out.

October’s full moon isn’t quite a supermoon. A full moon is only classified as a supermoon when the moon is in perigee and full at roughly the same time, and October’s full moon misses the mark by a couple of days. October’s full moon is the last normal full moon of the year. November and December close out 2026 with supermoons before January opens with the final supermoon of this cycle.

Oct. 27: The moon eclipses the Pleiades

The moon will eclipse the Pleiades before either rises in the sky, but most people will still get to see part of it. Stellarium

Pleiades is one of the best star clusters to view in the night sky. They’re known as the Seven Sisters, and in terms of clusters of stars, it’s one of the easiest to see. The exception is on Oct. 27, when the moon will cross in front of them, blocking them almost entirely from view. When this happens depends on where you’re located.

The moon begins passing in front of them before sunset in Eastern time, and moves out of the way around midnight. Those on the East Coast will start the night in the middle of this little eclipse, while those on the West Coast will glimpse it at the very end. Finding it should be simple enough since the moon is the easiest thing to see in the night sky.

All month: Constellations and asterisms

The sky is continuing its rearrangement from summer into autumn, and there are tons of constellations to gaze at over the course of the month. Many of September’s constellations appear again, including both Dippers, Aquarius, Pegasus, Pisces and many others. October plays host to a few new ones in the night sky cycle, including Taurus, Cetus, Auriga and Orion, which will appear low on the horizon as they begin their months-long ascent into the sky for the winter.

There are some smaller asterisms to observe as well, including the Coffin of Delphinus, the Circlet of Pisces and the Northern Cross. We recommend using a sky map to find them all, as there are quite a lot. That’s good news, because even if you don’t go out during one of the big events in October, you’ll still have plenty of objects to look for in the night sky.

Tech.title: I Tested the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s Batteries and Was Awestruck by One Change
Tech.content:
Battery life might be the iPhone 18 Pro’s sleeper feature.

When Apple announced the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the phones were instantly overshadowed by their new sibling, the iPhone Duo, which has a passport-size design with a tiny iPad-like folding screen. That doesn’t mean that Apple’s latest pro phones don’t have their own appeal.

On paper, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s marquee features are the new variable aperture and the addition of manual controls in the Camera app, aimed at the niche audience of professional photographers and creative types. But my testing found that the phone’s battery upgrades should appeal to everyone. That’s in part because the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have larger batteries than their 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max counterparts, as revealed in a teardown by the tech repair site iFixIt.

Beyond the increased battery capacity, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have the power-efficient A20 Pro chip and run on iOS 27, which has several behind-the-scenes improvements to reduce power consumption. At a time when companies, including Apple, are raising phone prices – the 18 Pro starts at $1,199 and 18 Pro Max at $1,299 – it’s reassuring to see that the new Pro models are more than just a yearly iteration and improve on the 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max’s fast charging and long battery life.



How do they compare to the iPhone 17, iPhone Air and older iPhone models?



CNET tested the Apple phones’ four ways to find out: a battery stress test, a video streaming battery test, a wired charging test and a wireless charging test. These results, along with our lab data from previous years, show that the iPhone 18 Pro Max has the longest-lasting battery life of any phone Apple has ever made. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro is the fastest-charging iPhone. The performance of both phones in my testing and review is why each has earned a CNET Editors’ Choice Award.

Key takeaways

Lab testing across video streaming and battery stress tests shows that the 18 Pro Max delivers the longest overall battery life of any iPhone to date, driven by a larger battery capacity and the power-efficient A20 Pro chip and iOS 27.

The 18 Pro is Apple’s fastest-charging phone, reaching 53% battery in 15 minutes and 82% in 30 minutes.

Despite being a prior-generation model, the iPhone 16 Plus still holds the best score in the 45-minute multitasking battery stress test, edging out both the 17 Pro Max and 18 Pro Max by 1 percentage point.

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have an incredible battery life

As part of my 45-minute endurance test, I played the game Arknights: Endfield to stress the phone’s battery.

CNET has two battery benchmark tests (video streaming and stress tests) to rate battery performance. We averaged the scores from both tests for each phone to determine the final ranking. If you’re looking for a phone with the longest battery life between charges, get an iPhone 18 Pro Max, which came out on top.

Because we’ve used these tests for years, we can compare new iPhones against older models. If you have an iPhone 15 or 16, upgrading to an iPhone 17 will get you a noticeably longer battery life out of the box. Keep in mind that display brightness, the strength of your carrier’s signal and how you use your phone all have a tremendous impact on the battery life you get from any phone. If you’re someone who is obsessively online, a phone with an incredible battery life might not be enough for you. Obviously, battery life isn’t the only consideration when shopping for a new phone, and normally, I’d recommend holding onto your phone for 3 to 4 years if possible.

In CNET’s 3-hour video battery test, where we streamed a video over Wi-Fi with the screen at full brightness, the iPhone 18 Pro had the highest remaining charge. What’s notable is how it did compared with the iPhone 17 Pro, which lost 8% more in the same test. That’s quite the improvement in just a single year. The $929 iPhone 17, $270 less than the 18 Pro, might be the most surprising result, placing fourth in the test. It proves you don’t need to buy a $1,300 phone to get great battery life.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max landed second in the 3-hour streaming video test.

In CNET’s 45-minute battery stress test, during which I played games, streamed videos, scrolled social media and took a video call with the screen at half brightness, 2024’s iPhone 16 Plus still holds the best result. The 18 Pro Max and 17 Pro Max placed second, just a single percent behind the 16 Plus. The iPhone 17 lands in the third spot, again an impressive result that shows that the standard model will be more than enough for most people, even a year after it came out. The iPhone 18 Pro placed last in this test, but keep in mind that its result was better than many Android phones, such as the Pixel 11 Pro and Galaxy S26.

Looking at our results, the iPhone 17 Pro Max and 18 Pro Max are nearly identical in battery life, even though the new phone scored a percentage point higher in one test. So if you’re able to get a deal on the 17 Pro Max, Apple stopped selling it, save money, go for it.

The iPhone 18 Pro is the fastest charging iPhone

We run two 30-minute charging tests, one of which is for wired charging.

At some point, you’re going to need to recharge your iPhone’s battery and one discovery I had from testing was just how much Apple improved wired charging on both the new Pro models. We have two charging tests (wired and wireless) to rate recharging performance. As with our battery tests, we averaged the scores from the two tests to determine the final ranking. If you want the fastest-charging Apple phone, then buy an iPhone 18 Pro.

In our 30-minute wired charging test, starting with the battery at 0% and charging with the included cable, the iPhone 18 Pro added 82%, reaching 53% after 15 minutes. Compare that with the iPhone 17 Pro, which saw a 74% increase in the same test. That’s an 8% gain between model years and a wild improvement!



So why the big difference here? The iPhone 17 Pro supports 40-watt fast charging, whereas the iPhone 18 Pro supports 60-watt fast charging. Both require using or purchasing a wall plug that supports those speeds.



The 18 Pro Max added 77% in the same 30-minute test and hit 48% at the 15-minute mark. This is another 8% improvement from last year – the 17 Pro Max gained 69%.

Again, the notable performance came from the iPhone 17, which recharged its battery from empty to 69%, matching the 17 Pro Max.

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max support 25-watt Qi2.2 wireless charging via MagSafe, like the 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. In our 30-minute wireless charging test, the 17 Pro beat the new 18 Pro by just a single percent. The 18 Pro Max placed just after the iPhone Air in the same test. Keep in mind that the 18 Pro Max has the largest battery capacity of any iPhone we tested. Though the 17 Pro Max has a large battery, too, it came in third for this test.

The iPhone Duo and final thoughts

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s most innovative and expensive phone. Patrick Holland/CNET

Apple will release the iPhone Duo on Oct. 23. We are excited to test its battery and charging capabilities, but at this time, we’ve only had brief hands-on time with the foldable phone at Apple’s event last month.

While battery life and charging speeds are not the primary reasons to choose one iPhone over another, they are among the most important considerations. Out of Apple’s current lineup, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max will give you the most battery life. But I think most people will be fine with the standard iPhone 17. Think of it as getting the most battery life for your dollar.

The iPhone Air is Apple’s slimmest phone (until the Duo goes on sale), but still has a good battery life despite its petite proportions. And while the iPhone 17E is Apple’s most affordable phone, it has a battery life that beats out most of the older iPhone models that we tested.

Lastly, if the poor battery health on your current iPhone is making you want to upgrade, it’s worth considering a battery replacement. It’ll cost you $50 to $130, depending on which model you have; even less if you replace it yourself. Doing so will add a couple more years to your phone’s longevity and save you hundreds of dollars.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI Is Building a Dossier on You. Here’s What’s Actually in It
Tech.content:
Meta’s Muse AI agent launched in late September with a mascot designed to be irresistible — and a security architecture that proved to be anything but reassuring.

Within weeks, a security researcher demonstrated a working zero-day vulnerability capable of hijacking the assistant — one that Meta’s own documentation acknowledged was straightforward to exploit. A journalist separately reported that Muse had accessed his private Apple Messages without permission. Meta disputed the claim, but it was serious enough to prompt Apple to update macOS privacy settings in response.

Muse requests extensive access to personal data, including passwords, full disk access, email messages, calendar, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp. By default, Meta also appears to use your interactions with Muse to train its AI models, so you have to manually opt out in the settings.

More from CNET

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

AI agents are marketed as providing convenience by acting on your behalf. But the trade-off is privacy and control. You’re handing over your personal information to a black box with little visibility into how it’s used. Multiple incidents are fueling a conversation about the dangers of agentic AI and whether they require higher security standards before being granted access to user data.

And given Meta’s track record of privacy fines, data sharing and security issues, it’s worth proceeding with caution. Earlier this month, a lifestyle blogger reported that the social media platform’s AI asked intrusive questions about her kids and pieced together private information about her life from her posts. Meta’s controversial smart glasses have received pushback on multiple fronts — from its facial recognition software to the way it captures and stores data.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Muse uploads iOS or Mac data even when you tell it not to

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Muse could hand over data to human callers

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

Muse has the most robust data collection

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the privacy concerns mentioned in this story.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.

Tech.title: Fitbit Edge May Be the Sweet Spot for Smartwatch Noncommittals
Tech.content:
If you’re lukewarm on smartwatches but not minimalist enough to go completely screenless, Google may have found your Goldilocks option.

The new $179 Fitbit Edge, unveiled Monday, sits between the $100 Fitbit Air and $400 Pixel Watch 5 in price, features and form factor. It gives you a color screen, built-in GPS and many of the health sensors you’d expect from a smartwatch, but in a slimmer, lighter package with up to a week of battery life.

The concept isn’t new for Fitbit. Previous trackers like the Inspire and Charge paired a simple screen with Fitbit’s health and fitness tracking while working with both iOS and Android; if anything, the screen-less Fitbit Air was the departure. But it’s been three years since the Charge 6, and Google now has a lot more to pull from across its wearable lineup. The Edge combines some of what I like about the minimalist Air with features that have trickled down from the Pixel Watch 5.

More from CNET

Whether that combination hits the sweet spot remains to be seen.

The Fitbit Edge is available for preorder on Monday and goes on sale Oct. 27.

The mini screen

I’m a big fan of the minimalist Fitbit Air, which hides almost every trace of tech behind sleek bands. Aesthetically, it’s my ideal; practically, not so much. I inevitably glance down expecting to see the time, only to get annoyed at this thing seemingly freeloading on my wrist because all the payoff is in the phone app.

Apparently, I want my cake and to eat it too. That’s where the Edge comes in.

Its 1.34-inch color AMOLED display is 46% larger than the one on the Charge 6 and has an always-on option. There’s also a physical side button for pausing workouts and accessing menus.

The Edge keeps with the same style choices that make the Air and Pixel Watch 5 stand out, and as a lover of all things color, I’m here for it. It comes in Obsidian, Fog, Olive and Canyon combinations, with interchangeable options including a performance loop, magnetic band and metal links. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition that costs an additional $50.

Google

Google also redesigned the interface with tiles that resemble the Pixel Watch UI, including watch faces with complications and quick access to workouts and health metrics. It still runs Fitbit’s own operating system rather than Wear OS, so this isn’t a miniature Pixel Watch as it lacks access to the Play Store and Gemini. But it does mean you can use the Fitbit Edge with the iPhone as well as Android phones.

You can get weather, alarms, timers, media controls and turn-by-turn directions. The Edge can also mirror notifications and incoming calls from your phone and send canned replies to messages on Android.

But there’s no microphone or speaker, so you can’t take calls from your wrist as you would on a smartwatch. There’s also no NFC for Google Wallet or tap-to-pay, an odd omission considering the older Charge 6 had it.

More smartwatch-like health and fitness tracking

The Edge also borrows plenty from the smartwatch side when it comes to health and fitness.

Unlike the Fitbit Air, which relies on your phone for GPS, the Edge has built-in GPS and an altimeter. It also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen and skin temperature and supports ECG readings.

Google says heart-rate tracking is 40% more accurate than on the Charge 6, a claim I’m especially interested in testing against a chest strap once I get the Edge on my wrist.

It tracks more than 50 exercise types and can automatically recognize more than 40. Google says it has also improved automatic detection since launching the Air, including the ability to recognize racquet sports.

During workouts, you can see metrics like pace and heart rate zones on your wrist, which I missed on the Air. The Edge can also broadcast live heart rate data to compatible exercise equipment, so you can see your heart rate on a treadmill or other supported machine.

The Edge comes with three months of Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 per year after that. Premium unlocks the AI-powered Google Health Coach and Health Guardian, which measure monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Health Guardian is also coming to the Fitbit Air, but Google hasn’t said when.

Seven-day battery comes with an asterisk

Battery life is one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over a smartwatch.

Google rates it for up to seven days per charge, but there’s a massive caveat. That’s the estimate with the raise to wake setting. If you prefer an always-on display (which I do) then the estimate dwindles down to two days, according to Google.

Google

For me, the deciding factor may be how quickly raise to wake responds. The entire reason I missed having a screen on the Air was the ability to glance down and instantly see the time. If I’m waiting for a black screen to wake up, I might as well have the Air on and just pull out my phone.

Charging is a mixed bag, too. Five minutes on the charger gets you about a day’s worth of battery, but a full charge takes about 90 minutes. Knowing my charging habits — where I don’t have a lot of downtime to recharge my wearable devices for an hour plus — I don’t need hands-on time to predict that I’ll probably never see this thing at 100%.

The Edge uses the same charger as the Air, and Google says you can move between Fitbit devices and the Pixel Watch without interrupting your health data. I can already envision a scenario where I’d use an Edge most days and swap in the Air when I forgot to charge, or want something less distracting. Whether I’d actually buy two devices to accomplish that is another question.

Fitbit’s first tracker with a user-replaceable battery

The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, making it Fitbit’s first tracker designed with this level of repairability. Google has already moved in this direction with the Pixel Watch 4, which was redesigned without adhesives to make repairs easier. My colleague Katie Collins even replaced its screen herself despite describing herself as an “ambitious amateur.”

The battery on the Fitbit Edge is replaceable.

Bringing that approach to a smaller, less expensive tracker could help extend its life, especially since batteries inevitably degrade over time. Google says repair options vary by region and recommends self-repair only for people with the technical expertise to do it safely.

Fitbit Edge: Bottom line

At $179, the Edge costs nearly twice as much as the Fitbit Air and more than Fitbit’s other entry-level trackers. But compared with the Pixel Watch or Samsung’s Galaxy Watch, the price could feel like a deal if you’re prioritizing fitness features and don’t need other smartwatch features like contactless payments. For people who want GPS, a screen and notifications, and found the Air came up short, that extra money buys a lot. Few trackers this capable sell at this price: The next step up would be something like the $249 Apple Watch SE 3 or the $300 Samsung Galaxy Watch 7.

On paper, that makes the Edge a strong pick for people like me who aren’t ready to choose a smartwatch that’s only able to work with an iPhone or an Android phone. Now I need to find out whether it’s my Goldilocks wearable, or whether I’ll end up back with the smartwatch-and-band combo I once thought was my happy medium
